result.text: The paper tackles dataset distillation—compressing large training sets into a few synthetic examples that yield similar model performance—by improving how meta-gradients are computed for the bi-level optimization that defines the problem. The key insight is that reparameterizing the network and convexifying the inner optimization via a frozen finite-width neural tangent kernel (NTK) makes implicit-gradient calculations more accurate and tractable, and that analytically solving for final-layer parameters given the body parameters reduces bias in those implicit gradients. Methodologically, they derive and implement a reparameterized convexified implicit-gradient (RCIG) algorithm that uses implicit differentiation on the bi-level objective, approximates the inner problem with a convex NTK-based surrogate, and parameterizes the model to enable closed-form final-layer updates; this yields large empirical improvements over prior distillation methods across ImageNet, Tiny-ImageNet, and CIFAR-100.

The paper addresses how to design policies for Markov decision processes when both the objective and constraints are expressed as dynamic coherent risk measures, which complicates standard constrained MDP solution techniques. The key insight is that if the risk objectives and constraints admit a Markov risk transition mapping, the constrained risk-averse control problem can be cast in a Lagrangian form whose policy-synthesis subproblems admit a difference-of-convex structure. The authors propose an optimization-based method that constructs Markovian policies by solving these DCPs using the disciplined convex-concave programming (DCCP) framework, thereby generalizing the linear-program approach for expected-cost constrained MDPs. They validate the approach numerically on a rover navigation task using CVaR and EVaR measures, demonstrating tractable policy synthesis and effective risk control.

The paper tackles the limited scale of training data for open-vocabulary object detection by enabling web-scale weak supervision; while vision–language pretraining has improved recognition, detectors still lack the vast box-level annotations needed to generalize to many classes. The key insight is that self-training—using a competent detector to generate pseudo-box labels on large collections of image–text pairs—can effectively expand detection datasets if one carefully designs the label space, filters pseudo-annotations, and makes training efficient. The authors introduce OWLv2 (a strong baseline detector) and OWL-ST (a scalable self-training recipe) that produce high-quality pseudo-boxes and scale from ~10M to over 1B examples, yielding large gains on rare LVIS classes (e.g., boosting AP from 31.2% to 44.6% for classes with no human boxes) and demonstrating that web-scale training can unlock open-world localization akin to advances in classification and language models.

The paper studies the computational complexity of finding envy-free (and sometimes proportional) allocations of indivisible resources when agents observe only neighbors in a given social network, focusing on parameterized complexity with respect to structural parameters of the network and similarities among agents/items. The key insight is that restricting the network structure (e.g., bounded treewidth or bounded clique-width) or exploiting bounded similarity measures can render otherwise hard allocation problems tractable, while these tractability gains are essentially tight. Methodologically, the authors develop fixed-parameter algorithms that leverage dynamic programming over decompositions (treewidth, clique-width) and parameter-aware reductions to solve broad fragments of the envy-free allocation problem, and they match these positive results with lower-bound reductions showing no substantially faster algorithms exist under standard complexity assumptions.

The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently approximating the Pareto set for NP-hard multiobjective combinatorial optimization (MOCO) problems without expensive per-instance search. Its key insight is that a single, preference-conditioned neural model can directly generate high-quality approximate Pareto solutions for any trade-off preference, thereby learning a continuous mapping from preferences to solutions instead of producing a finite set of discrete solutions. Methodologically, the authors train this model with a tailored multiobjective reinforcement learning algorithm inspired by decomposition-based MOEA/D, conditioning the policy on preference vectors and optimizing it to cover the Pareto front; experiments on multiobjective TSP, VRP, and knapsack problems show superior solution quality, inference speed, and model efficiency compared to baselines.

The paper addresses how to learn effective state representations for reinforcement learning, particularly for robotic object-manipulation tasks, by leveraging 3D scene understanding; existing learned or hand-engineered low-dimensional states can be insufficient for complex visual observations. The key insight is that supervising an encoder with a latent-conditioned Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) forces the latent space to capture object geometry and appearance across multiple views, producing a representation better aligned with downstream control needs. The method trains an encoder to map multiple camera images into a latent code while a NeRF decoder reconstructs images from that code, using the NeRF reconstruction loss as supervision, and then uses the learned latent as the RL agent’s state input (NeRF-RL), showing improved performance on tasks like hanging mugs, pushing, and opening doors.

The paper addresses how to best use learned preference-based reward models to align language models, asking which monotone transformations of rewards are preferable and how to combine multiple reward models for multi-objective alignment. The key insight is that interpreting alignment probabilistically for Bradley–Terry style reward learning yields a natural transformation—the log-sigmoid of centered rewards (LSC)—which both downweights already-high-scoring outputs and makes transformed rewards interpretable as probabilities so they can be combined by summation to reflect logical conjunction. The method applies the LSC transformation to reward model outputs before using them in RLHF, emphasizing improvement on poor outputs to reduce underfitting and reward hacking and enabling principled aggregation of multiple properties; experiments on making models both helpful and harmless show substantial gains over using raw rewards.

The paper addresses how differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DPSGD), while protecting privacy, can amplify disparate impact across groups in trained models. The key insight is that inequitable gradient clipping in DPSGD causes gradient misalignment between groups—small or underrepresented groups have their gradients disproportionately clipped, steering optimization toward objectives that favor majority groups and thus increasing unfairness. To mitigate this, the authors propose a method that prevents gradient misalignment by adjusting the clipping/aggregation process (e.g., group-aware or adaptive clipping strategies) so that per-group gradient contributions are preserved more faithfully before noise addition, thereby reducing the disparate impact introduced by standard DPSGD.

SegVol addresses the lack of a 3D foundation segmentation model that can universally and interactively segment a wide range of anatomical structures in volumetric medical images. The key insight is that large-scale pretraining on massive unlabeled CT data combined with a substantial labeled set, plus a design that supports both semantic and spatial prompts, yields a generalizable model capable of segmenting hundreds of anatomical categories. The method scales training to 90K unlabeled and 6K labeled CT volumes to learn rich 3D representations, implements a zoom-out–zoom-in inference mechanism for efficient and precise processing of volumetric scans, and incorporates interactive prompting to guide segmentation; experiments across 22 tasks show SegVol outperforms competitors on 19 tasks, with gains up to 37.24%, and ablations validate the contribution of its key design choices.

The paper tackles hyperspectral image reconstruction from coded aperture snapshot spectral compressive imaging (CASSI), addressing shortcomings of existing deep unfolding methods that neither estimate scene-specific degradation nor capture long-range dependencies. The key insight is to make unfolding degradation-aware by estimating degradation parameters (from the compressed measurement and physical mask) to guide each iterative step, and to replace CNN modules with a transformer tailored for mixed local and non-local modeling. Methodologically, they propose a Degradation-Aware Unfolding Framework (DAUF) that injects estimated degradation and ill-posedness degree into the iterative solver and design a novel Half-Shuffle Transformer (HST) that efficiently fuses local content and global context; plugging HST into DAUF yields DAUHST, a transformer-based deep-unfolding HSI reconstructor that outperforms prior art with lower computational and memory cost.

The paper addresses how decentralized stochastic gradient descent (D-SGD) generalizes in non-convex, non-smooth settings and how network topology affects its stability and test performance. The key insight is that the consensus model learned by vanilla D-SGD enjoys topology-aware algorithmic stability that scales as O(N^{-1}+m^{-1}+\lambda^2) in expectation (with N samples, m workers, and 1+λ the spectral gap), leading to an in-average generalization bound O(N^{-(1+α)/2}+m^{-(1+α)/2}+λ^{1+α}+φ_S) that remains non-vacuous even when connectivity is poor (λ close to 1), so better spectral gaps (stronger connectivity) improve generalization and early consensus control helps. Methodologically, the authors derive stability bounds for D-SGD under non-convex non-smooth assumptions by analyzing the effect of topology via the spectral gap, translate these stability results into generalization bounds, and validate the theory empirically with VGG-11 and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny-ImageNet.

The paper tackles the challenge of producing accurate, compatible, and scalable post-training quantization for large language models, addressing limitations of existing loss-error-based PTQ methods that rely on non-adaptive min–max affine quantization grids and often require specialized kernels or heavy compute. The key insight is that min–max affine grids are disrupted by outliers in inverse-Hessian diagonals, so instead of fixing a static grid one should learn loss-error-aware quantization grids that adapt to the model’s sensitivity. The proposed LeanQuant method integrates learned loss-error-aware grids into the iterative loss-error-based quantization framework, supporting affine and non-uniform quantizers and avoiding custom data formats or exotic kernels, which yields models with higher fidelity and broader framework compatibility. Empirically, LeanQuant matches or outperforms competitive baselines on recent LLMs and scales to very large models (e.g., Llama-3.1 405B) with modest hardware and time requirements.

The paper tackles the computational and modeling limitations of post-hoc Shapley feature attributions—namely their exponential cost and inability to be used for training-time regularization—by making Shapley values intrinsic latent representations within neural networks. The key insight is to define a Shapley transform that maps inputs into Shapley representations for a given function and to implement that transform as a differentiable neural module so that explanations become first-class, layer-wise quantities that can be computed efficiently and regularized during training. Methodologically, the authors construct ShapNets by composing Shapley modules into shallow and deep architectures, prove that Shallow ShapNets recover exact Shapley values while Deep ShapNets preserve Shapley properties like missingness and accuracy, and empirically show that these models enable fast, layer-wise explanations and explanation-aware training with competitive predictive performance.

The paper tackles the problem of reducing computation, storage, and communication during gradient-based training by updating only a sparse subset of a neural network’s parameters across iterations. The key insight is that a fixed mask selecting the parameters with the largest Fisher information provides a simple, effective proxy for which weights matter most for the task, so those parameters can be the only ones updated repeatedly. The method builds a sparse mask by computing Fisher scores for parameters, selecting the top-k, and then training while keeping all other weights frozen; experiments on transfer learning and distributed training show this fixed-Fisher-mask approach matches or outperforms existing sparse-update methods while lowering memory and communication overhead.

The paper tackles efficient computation of the Projection Robust Wasserstein (PRW) distance, a max–min formulation over the Stiefel manifold designed to mitigate the curse of dimensionality in high-dimensional optimal transport. Its key insight is a novel reformulation of the entropy-regularized max–min PRW problem that enables a Riemannian block coordinate descent (RBCD) strategy with much lower per-iteration cost than prior Riemannian gradient-ascent-plus-Sinkhorn schemes. The proposed RBCD alternately updates blocks on the Stiefel manifold using closed-form or cheaply computed steps while solving simpler transport subproblems, and the authors prove an arithmetic complexity of O(ε−3) to reach an ε-stationary point—vastly improving on the O(ε−12) bound for RGAS. Empirical results on synthetic and real datasets confirm the method’s scalability and superior efficiency, particularly when the sample size is very large.

The paper tackles the problem of achieving optimal tradeoffs between privacy, utility, and computation for differentially private training in both federated and centralized settings, where existing matrix factorization (MF) mechanisms either cannot be applied or are outperformed at low privacy budgets. The key insight is that constraining MF mechanisms to banded lower-triangular matrices—having at most b̂ nonzero diagonals—retains strong privacy amplification properties while enabling more practical participation patterns and improved utility. Methodologically, the authors construct and analyze banded MF mechanisms, prove they admit the same privacy amplification as DP-SGD, and demonstrate how to use them to support relaxed multi-participation in cross-device federated learning (with a production deployment) and to strictly improve or match DP-SGD performance in centralized training across all privacy budgets.

The paper tackles the barrier that domain expertise and heavy preprocessing create for applying machine learning to blockchain transaction graphs by providing a standardized, ML-ready dataset collection. Its key insight is that broad progress requires uniform, labeled graph representations for both UTXO (e.g., Bitcoin) and account-based (e.g., Ethereum) blockchains so researchers can focus on modeling rather than data wrangling. To realize this, the authors build Chartalist, an open platform that ingests raw blockchain data, converts it into labeled graph datasets with standardized schemas and features, and publishes these ready-to-use datasets and tooling to lower the entry cost and foster reproducible ML research across diverse blockchains.

The paper tackles the problem of reducing computation for short, trimmed video classification by selecting a small subset of informative frames that both speeds up models and can improve accuracy. Its key insight is that frames should be selected jointly rather than independently so the chosen set covers complementary, “storytelling” moments and avoids redundant or hard-to-classify frames. The proposed SMART method formulates frame selection as a joint optimization (implemented as a lightweight selection module that works with different backbones) to pick a distributed, informative subset of frames per video. Evaluated across multiple benchmarks, SMART yields 4–10× computational savings while consistently improving or matching accuracy and even boosting state-of-the-art recognition on several datasets.

DecodingTrust addresses the insufficient and fragmented evaluation of GPT model trustworthiness by proposing a broad, systematic benchmark targeting real-world risks such as toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial and out-of-distribution robustness, privacy leakage, ethics, and fairness. The key insight is that a comprehensive, multi-perspective assessment reveals previously undocumented vulnerabilities and trade-offs—e.g., GPT-4 often scores better on standard safety benchmarks but can be more susceptible than GPT-3.5 to jailbreaks and instruction-based attacks because its stronger instruction-following amplifies susceptibility to malicious prompts. The authors construct a unified evaluation suite—datasets and challenge scenarios spanning toxicity induction, bias probes, adversarial demonstrations, privacy extraction tests, and ethical dilemmas—and run extensive experiments on GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 to quantify failure modes and compare behaviors, releasing the benchmark and data for community use.

The paper tackles the problem of deforming and animating neural radiance fields (NeRFs) for arbitrary objects without relying on category-specific priors like SMPL, which limits generality. Its key insight is to use a category-agnostic cage-based deformation prior—an enclosing polygonal mesh with sparse vertices—so each 3D point in the radiance field is relocated by barycentric interpolation of deformed cage vertices, turning the cage into a generalized constraint that preserves fine geometry. Methodologically, they integrate this cage-driven warping into the NeRF pipeline by projecting sample points into new positions via the cage mapping during rendering and training, enabling geometry editing, object animation, and deformation transfer on diverse shapes while retaining detailed appearance.

The paper addresses the challenge of training multi-instrument automatic music transcription (AMT) models from real-world recordings, where paired, time-aligned score annotations are rare and expensive to produce. The key insight is that a transcriber and an alignment module can be trained jointly using unaligned symbolic scores as supervision, augmented by pseudo-labeling and pitch-shift augmentation, so that explicit manual alignment is unnecessary. The proposed method, NoteEM, iteratively learns to align digitized scores to performances while training a transcription network on the resulting soft alignments and pseudo-labels, leveraging only synthetic data plus unaligned score–audio pairs to achieve strong generalization; this yields state-of-the-art note-level accuracy on MAPS, large cross-dataset gains, and robust performance even when trained on small self-collected datasets.

The paper tackles regret minimization in stochastic shortest path (SSP) problems when costs are chosen adversarially and transition dynamics are unknown, including the challenging bandit-feedback case. The key insight is to combine optimism-based exploration for unknown transitions with adversarial-cost-aware learning mechanisms to control cumulative cost regret relative to the optimal hitting-time policy, leveraging problem-dependent quantities like state/action counts, diameter D, and optimal expected hitting time T_★. Methodologically, the authors design algorithms that attain Õ(√(S^2 A D T_★ K)) regret in the full-information setting and Õ(√(S^3 A^2 D T_★ K)) in the bandit setting by carefully integrating confidence sets for transitions, episodic planning under optimistic models, and adversarial-cost-adaptive updates, and they further provide near-optimal algorithms for the special case of a stochastically oblivious adversary to close the gap to known lower bounds.

The paper addresses the opaque mechanisms by which attention-based encoder–decoder networks produce alignment matrices across different sequence-to-sequence tasks and architectures. The key insight is that hidden states can be decomposed into a temporal component (position-dependent, input-independent) and an input-driven component (content-dependent, position-independent), and that the relative reliance on these components explains how attention patterns are formed. Methodologically, the authors propose and apply this decomposition to analyze attention behavior in both recurrent and feed-forward encoders/decoders, showing consistently that tasks requiring positional cues use the temporal component more while content-sensitive tasks leverage the input-driven component, illuminating a unified view of attention formation despite architectural differences.

The paper addresses the security risk that Large Language Models (LLMs) can be covertly manipulated via Trojan-style prompt attacks in realistic black-box settings. Its key insight is that universal, stealthy trigger tokens and poisoned discrete prompts can be discovered and optimized solely through API queries and few-shot examples, enabling reliable, transferable manipulation without white-box access. The proposed TrojLLM framework combines a trigger-discovery algorithm that searches for universal input-level triggers via black-box queries and a progressive Trojan poisoning algorithm that iteratively crafts poisoned prompts to maximize attack efficacy and transferability across models. Experiments show TrojLLM can successfully implant Trojans in real-world LLM APIs such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 while preserving performance on clean inputs, highlighting practical risks and suggesting avenues for defense.

The paper tackles the problem of automated feature engineering for tabular prediction, where existing methods rely on predefined search spaces and validation-only selection, failing to leverage insights from prior experiments. The key insight is to harness LLMs’ reasoning to propose feature-generation rules and to feed them structured feedback about past experiments via decision trees expressed in natural language, enabling iterative refinement without manual search-space specification. The method, OCTree, generates candidate feature rules through an LLM, evaluates them with tree-based models, encodes the performance and feature-impact diagnostics as decision-tree-based natural-language reasoning, and returns that reasoning to the LLM to iteratively improve rule proposals. Experiments show OCTree consistently improves downstream model performance across benchmarks, outperforming existing automated feature engineering baselines.

The paper addresses the problem of crafting adversarial point clouds for 3D deep learning models in a way that preserves surface continuity and realism, rather than applying non-manifold pointwise perturbations. The key insight is that deforming the underlying 2D parameterization of a surface (the parameter plane) via a learned stretching field can produce smooth, realistic adversarial examples with minimal geometric distortion while effectively fooling classifiers. Their method learns a generative mapping from a 2D parameter plane to the 3D surface, then optimizes a stretch field in the parameter domain to maximize classifier loss subject to regularization that preserves surface smoothness; the resulting adversarial point clouds are sampled from the deformed manifold. Experiments demonstrate these manifold-based attacks yield more transferable, less detectable, and higher-success adversarial examples than prior non-manifold perturbation techniques.

The paper tackles data-free quantization of deep neural networks, aiming to reduce bit-widths for weights and activations without access to training data or specialized hardware while preserving accuracy. Its key insight is that restricting quantizers to uniform maps limits performance, but non-uniform quantization must preserve the network’s algebraic operations, so viable transforms are continuous automorphisms of (R+*, ×), i.e., power functions x ↦ x^a. The method, PowerQuant, therefore searches a single exponent per layer by minimizing layer-wise reconstruction error—an optimization the authors show is locally convex with a unique solution—and implements the learned power-law quantization by simple, low-overhead modifications to activation functions at inference, yielding substantial accuracy gains over prior data-free schemes.

result.text: The paper addresses the bottleneck in core-guided MaxSAT-style optimization where repeated strengthening of solution bounds via cardinality constraints is expensive because SAT encodings and solvers handle such constraints poorly. The key insight is to perform core-guided search directly within pseudo-Boolean (PB) solvers so that cardinality constraints are handled natively and cutting planes reasoning can derive stronger, more effective constraints for bounding. The method integrates core extraction and iterative lower/upper bound refinement into a PB optimization framework, using cutting planes to strengthen and reformulate objectives efficiently and alternating bounding searches more often; experiments on diverse benchmarks show this core-guided PB approach significantly outperforms previous pseudo-Boolean optimizers.

The paper addresses how to design and initialize diagonal state space models (SSMs) as efficient, easy-to-implement alternatives to the S4 layer for sequence modeling, focusing on why a diagonal restriction can match S4’s strong long-range performance. The key insight is that although almost every SSM has an equivalent diagonal form in theory, initialization is critical: a particular diagonal approximation of S4’s HiPPO-derived matrix recovers S4’s convolutional kernel in the infinite-state limit, explaining why the DSS-style initialization preserves performance. Building on this, the authors systematically analyze parameterization and computation choices for diagonal SSMs, derive simple, stable initialization schemes, and present S4D—a minimal two-line kernel computation implementation—that empirically matches or exceeds S4 across image, audio, medical time-series tasks and the Long Range Arena.

The paper addresses the high memory cost of adapting large pre-trained models to downstream tasks: existing parameter-efficient transfer learning (PETL) methods reduce the number of trainable parameters but still require backpropagation through the full backbone, limiting memory savings. The key insight is to avoid backpropagating through the backbone by training a separate, small “ladder” side network that receives intermediate activations from the frozen backbone via lightweight shortcut connections and makes task predictions, so only the side network and the ladder connections need gradients. The method, Ladder Side-Tuning (LST), inserts these ladder shortcuts at multiple layers, trains the compact side network on those intermediate features while keeping the backbone fixed, and thus achieves substantially larger memory reductions (≈69% vs ≈26% for comparable parameter budgets) and competitive or better accuracy than Adapter and LoRA across NLP and vision-and-language benchmarks, including improved scaling on larger T5 models.

The paper addresses tabular scenario-based question answering (TSQA), where systems must answer questions grounded in mixed-format scenarios that include both text and structured tables—a common and challenging setting for tasks like high-school exam questions that require synthesizing multiple table cells and integrating domain knowledge. The key insight is that converting useful parts of tables into natural-language sentences and selectively feeding those sentences into strong machine reading comprehension (MRC) models can make TSQA more tractable. To this end the authors introduce GeoTSQA, a 1k-question geography dataset with tabular scenarios, and propose TTGen, a table-to-text generator that synthesizes candidate sentences from tables and uses a ranking model conditioned on the scenario, question, and domain knowledge to select the most informative sentences for a downstream MRC solver. Their TTGen-augmented MRC approach significantly outperforms several strong baselines on GeoTSQA.

The paper addresses the problem of "narrow vision" in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, where the gating mechanism routes inputs so strictly that individual experts see limited data and underfit their sub-tasks, constraining overall generalization. The key insight is that moderate mutual distillation among experts can broaden each expert's effective training signal by sharing useful features and predictions learned by other experts, improving individual expert competence on their assigned inputs without collapsing specialization. The proposed method, MoDE, implements mutual distillation regularization across experts during training—encouraging them to mimic useful aspects of each other’s outputs while preserving gating-driven specialization—and is validated across tabular, NLP, and CV benchmarks, with an "expert probing" analysis that empirically shows distilled knowledge improves per-expert and overall MoE performance.

The paper addresses the problem of inferring the objective (cost) functions that underlie human sensorimotor behavior when motor noise is signal-dependent, rather than assuming a cost a priori and merely comparing predicted to observed actions. Its key insight is to frame this as an inverse optimal control problem within a partially observable Markov decision process that separates the agent’s and experimenter’s inference problems and explicitly models the probabilistic evolution of states and beliefs under signal-dependent noise. Methodologically, the authors derive a probabilistic formulation and an approximate belief-propagation equation for the linear–quadratic Gaussian setting with signal-dependent noise, extend the framework to cases where the experimenter has partial observability of state variables, and validate the approach on synthetic and real experimental data. This enables recovering the implicit costs and benefits guiding sequential sensorimotor behavior, unifying normative optimal-control explanations with descriptive data-driven inference.

The paper examines channel pruning for CNNs and identifies two overlooked problems in existing pruning criteria: many widely-used criteria produce nearly identical filter importance rankings (Similarity), and some criteria yield scores so close they cannot reliably distinguish redundant filters (Applicability). The key insight is that these issues stem from underlying statistical properties of trained convolutional weights—specifically that filter weights per layer approximately follow a Gaussian-like distribution (Convolutional Weight Distribution Assumption)—which explains why different metrics correlate and fail to separate importance. Methodologically, the authors validate this assumption with extensive statistical tests and then empirically analyze and compare layer-wise and global pruning behaviors across diverse criteria, showing how similarity and score indistinguishability lead to similar pruned structures and limited discrimination of redundancy.

The paper addresses the tradeoff between expressivity and scalability in permutation-equivariant graph learning: standard message-passing GNNs are insufficiently expressive to represent all permutation-equivariant functions, while higher-order architectures that are universal require tensorial or subgraph enumerations that scale exponentially and ignore graph sparsity. The key insight is that by using sparsity-aware heuristics inspired by graph isomorphism techniques, one can design permutation-equivariant networks whose computational cost adapts to the number of edges and local structure, yielding a continuum of models that interpolate between efficient message-passing and fully expressive higher-order schemes. Concretely, the authors introduce SpeqNets, a class of architectures that build higher-order representations only over selected node tuples determined by sparsity-sensitive selection rules and then apply permutation-equivariant aggregation and transformation, achieving universality while drastically reducing memory and time compared to full k-order methods. Empirically, SpeqNets retain much of the predictive power of expressive higher-order networks and outperform standard GNNs and graph kernels on node- and graph-level supervised tasks while scaling to larger, sparse graphs.

The paper addresses improving certified robustness of deep classifiers by directly increasing input-space margins while avoiding overly conservative regularization from loose Lipschitz estimates. Its key insight is that maximizing margins in the output (logit) space together with accurate, differentiable upper bounds on the model’s Lipschitz constant—computed specifically along vulnerable directions—more directly enlarges input-space margins than prior methods. The method implements a scalable algorithm that leverages activation monotonicity and layerwise Lipschitz continuity to produce tight, differentiable Lipschitz bounds and uses these bounds in a training objective that dynamically maximizes logit margins while regularizing the Lipschitz constant; the approach also yields layer designs with controllable Lipschitz properties and empirically improves robustness on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny-ImageNet.

The paper tackles hard-exploration reinforcement learning where learning directly on target tasks is infeasible and no explicit learning-progress signal exists to build curricula. The key insight is to train a task generator that adaptively samples parameters of a procedural generator to produce a curriculum by trading off task difficulty (agent expected return) and behavioral similarity to the target, with similarity estimated adversarially from agent trajectories. The method implements this by coupling a black-box procedural task generator with a task discriminator that judges behavioral closeness to the target and using adversarial training to update the generator so it produces a sequence of varied tasks that gradually guide the agent toward the (possibly unknown-parameterized) target task distribution, with experiments showing improved exploration and learning.

The paper tackles extreme compression of large language models to 1–2 bits per parameter, where post-training quantization hits diminishing returns and existing fine-tuning of compressed weights relies heavily on straight-through estimators (STE) whose limitations are poorly understood. The key insight is that STE can be suboptimal for quantization-aware fine-tuning of LLMs and that a more principled, representation-agnostic optimization framework can both unify prior heuristics and yield better convergence and accuracy. The authors introduce PV-Tuning, which generalizes and improves existing fine-tuning strategies by treating quantized representations explicitly during optimization and providing convergence guarantees in restricted settings; empirically, PV-Tuning yields superior 1–2 bit vector quantization results on models like Llama and Mistral and achieves Pareto-optimal 2-bit quantization for the Llama 2 family.

The paper tackles multi-modal multi-label emotion recognition, where existing fusion approaches create a single shared representation that ignores modality-specific and label-specific discriminative features and fails to model label–modality dependencies. Its key insight is that learning modal-separated, label-specific features via contrastive reconstruction and then aggregating them with a shuffle-based strategy can better capture fine-grained modality-to-label dependencies and label co-occurrence patterns. The proposed CARAT method first performs reconstruction-based fusion to contrastively learn per-modality, per-label representations, and then applies a shuffle-based aggregation to enrich complementary interactions among labels before final prediction. Experiments on CMU-MOSEI and M3ED show CARAT outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods.

The paper tackles improving generalization and multi-task performance in visual robot manipulation by leveraging large-scale video generative pre-training. The key insight is that a unified GPT-style transformer trained to predict both future images and robot actions from paired language instructions, image observation sequences, and robot states can learn transferable spatiotemporal representations that greatly improve downstream manipulation performance. They realize this with GR-1, a straightforward end-to-end model that is pretrained on large video corpora and then finetuned on robot datasets, and demonstrate via experiments on the CALVIN benchmark and real robots that pretraining boosts success rates substantially (e.g., overall from 88.9% to 94.9% and zero-shot unseen-scene generalization from 53.3% to 85.4%).

The paper addresses the challenge of robust RGBT (RGB and thermal) visual tracking, where existing methods struggle to perform cross-modal feature interactions across all network layers because full-layer fusion incurs prohibitive computational cost. The key insight is that (1) modality-specific cues reside at different layers and their complementary information can be captured via their differences, and (2) the computational burden of all-layer interactions can be mitigated by dynamically ordering fusion to reduce token processing. To realize this, the authors propose AINet which incorporates a Difference-based Fusion Mamba (DFM) that fuses RGB and thermal features with linear complexity by leveraging their feature discrepancies, and an Order-dynamic Fusion Mamba (OFM) that adaptively changes the scan order of layer tokens to efficiently perform interactions across all layers; combined in a progressive fusion framework, this approach yields state-of-the-art performance on four public RGBT tracking benchmarks.

The paper addresses fairness and proportionality in approval-based committee elections, noting that existing strong axioms like priceability and the core still permit committees that can be seen as unfair. The key insight is that market-based explanations—modeled after Lindahl-like personalized prices and contributions—can be strengthened to guarantee more robust fairness by ensuring stability and balance of these price assignments. The authors introduce two solution concepts, stable priceability and balanced stable priceability, which require that voters’ payments and candidate prices form a stable market outcome (akin to a Lindahl equilibrium) so that no group can profitably deviate, and they provide constructive methods to test and produce such committees, arguing these select arguably fairer outcomes with intuitive economic justifications.

The paper addresses how to empirically verify whether observed sequential decision-making data satisfy the Markov assumption, which underlies reinforcement learning methods. The key insight is that by comparing predictive performance moving forward (using past and present information) versus backward (conditioning additionally on future information), one can nonparametrically detect violations of the Markov property without assuming a specific form for the data-generating distribution. The authors develop a Forward-Backward Learning test that constructs and compares conditional models to assess whether the present state suffices for future prediction, and they demonstrate its effectiveness on synthetic examples and a mobile health dataset to show when higher-order or partially observable models are needed to identify optimal policies.

The paper addresses blind omnidirectional image quality assessment (BOIQA), where existing methods fail to model how human observers browse 360° images, leading to poor perceptual fidelity predictions. The key insight is to mimic the multi-assessor viewing process by generating multiple plausible viewport sequences and modeling both spatial distortion/semantic features and their temporal transitions, thereby capturing how local degradations and viewing order jointly affect perceived quality. The proposed Assessor360 framework creates pseudo-viewport sequences using a generalized Recursive Probability Sampling (RPS) that combines content and detail cues, processes each viewport with a Multi-scale Feature Aggregation (MFA) module containing Distortion-aware Blocks (DAB) to fuse distorted and semantic features, and feeds sequences into a Temporal Modeling Module (TMM) to learn viewport transitions, yielding state-of-the-art performance across multiple OIQA datasets.

The paper addresses the problem of sampling from a target distribution known up to normalization by designing a particle-based deterministic flow that minimizes a discrepancy to the target. Its key insight is to follow the Wasserstein gradient flow of the Kernel Stein Discrepancy (KSD), yielding a tractable, differentiable loss functional whose gradients can be evaluated without knowing the normalization constant and which admits efficient, parameter-free optimization like L-BFGS. The resulting method, KSD Descent, updates a set of particles by directly minimizing empirical KSD via gradient-based quasi-Newton steps (or other deterministic optimizers), and the authors analyze its convergence properties and empirically demonstrate competitive performance while also identifying situations where the nonconvex loss produces spurious local minima that trap the algorithm.

The paper addresses whether and how one can unsupervisedly factorize (disentangle) the latent symmetry factors of a data manifold—i.e., recover a Lie-group-induced decomposition—solely from observations of its orbit. The key insight is that if the manifold’s true metric is known and each factor has nontrivial holonomy, then invariant subspaces under diffusion reveal the manifold’s de Rham decomposition, so disentangling reduces to metric learning. The proposed method, GEOMANCER, is a nonparametric algorithm that estimates subspaces preserved by random-walk diffusion on the manifold to approximate the de Rham decomposition and thereby separate factors; experiments on synthetic manifolds demonstrate its ability to recover complex factor structure and show that unsupervised disentangling is possible given metric information.

The paper addresses the problem of social bias present in pretrained sentence encoders (like BERT) and the lack of effective sentence-level debiasing methods that preserve downstream utility. The key insight is that a lightweight, post-hoc neural "fair filter" can transform encoder outputs into debiased representations by explicitly reducing correlation with bias indicators while retaining semantic information. The method trains this FairFil network with a contrastive learning objective that pushes filtered embeddings away from bias-word-associated directions and pulls them toward semantically matching sentence representations, enabling reduced bias on real-world datasets without retraining the original encoder and maintaining strong task performance.

The paper addresses the weakness of open-source LLMs in using real-world APIs by creating a complete tool-use pipeline to teach models to plan and execute multi-step API calls. The key insight is that large-scale, realistic instruction tuning with explicit solution-path annotations and expanded reasoning search can close the gap with closed-source models, so they build ToolBench (16,464 real RESTful APIs across 49 categories) and use ChatGPT to generate diverse instructions plus chain-of-call solution paths. Methodologically, they introduce a depth-first search decision-tree algorithm to broaden and evaluate multiple reasoning traces, fine-tune LLaMA on the ToolBench dataset to produce ToolLLaMA, add a neural API retriever to recommend APIs, and validate performance with an automatic evaluator ToolEval, showing strong execution, generalization to unseen APIs, and competitive performance with ChatGPT.

The paper addresses community discovery and link prediction on graphs by proposing a probabilistic latent-variable model that yields interpretable, sparse node embeddings. The key insight is to combine a ladder variational autoencoder hierarchy with gamma-distributed latent variables so that multi-layer stochastic representations are non-negative and sparse—making each dimension naturally interpretable as membership strength in a community or topic—while a novel recognition model enables fast inference. Concretely, the method models each node with a deep hierarchy of gamma latent variables, decodes link probabilities from the bottom-layer embeddings via a nonlinear function, and trains the model end-to-end (optionally incorporating node features/labels) using the gamma ladder VAE framework with a modular GNN-based encoder for scalability and empirical gains on benchmarks.

The paper addresses the problem of removing bias from already-trained machine learning models—including large-scale deep neural networks—via a practical post-processing procedure that provably preserves accuracy. Its key insight is that a carefully designed post-processing transformation can be shown to have provably small excess Bayes risk (i.e., be near-optimal), meaning one can correct fairness violations after training without much sacrifice in classification performance. The authors propose a scalable algorithm that applies this theoretically justified adjustment to model outputs, prove bounds on its excess Bayes risk, and empirically demonstrate on standard benchmarks that it outperforms prior post-processing methods and matches in-processing approaches, especially for models trained at scale.

The paper tackles low-quality output in large-language-model-based explainable recommendation (LLM-based ER), specifically addressing lack of personalization, inconsistency, and noisy or questionable explanation data; its key insight is that a specialized backbone LLM fine-tuned with reward signals explicitly measuring explainable-quality can teach the model to produce personalized, informative, and consistent explanations even when trained on imperfect datasets. Methodologically, the authors introduce LLM2ER as an LLM-based ER backbone and design two explainable quality reward (EQR) models that quantify desirable explanation traits, then apply reinforcement learning fine-tuning (RLHF-style optimization) with these rewards to obtain LLM2ER-EQR. The resulting system uses the EQR-guided policy updates to prioritize personalization, informativeness, and coherence in generated explanations, and experiments on three real-world datasets show improved fluency, diversity, informativeness, and personalization compared to baselines.

The paper addresses improving zero- and few-shot generalization of vision-language models by exploiting unlabeled test-time data via transduction. The key insight is that constraining transductive label assignments with the text-encoder’s knowledge—implemented as a KL divergence regularizer—guides learning toward semantically consistent predictions and outperforms vision-only transductive approaches. The method, TransCLIP, is a plug-and-play module that formulates a regularized maximum-likelihood objective combining model logits and a KL penalty toward text-encoder priors, and optimizes it with an iterative Block Majorize-Minimize (BMM) algorithm that decouples and efficiently updates sample assignments with convergence guarantees.

The paper tackles regret minimization in stochastic shortest path (SSP) problems when costs are chosen adversarially and transition dynamics are unknown, including the challenging bandit-feedback case. The key insight is to combine optimism-based exploration for unknown transitions with adversarial-cost-aware learning mechanisms to control cumulative cost regret relative to the optimal hitting-time policy, leveraging problem-dependent quantities like state/action counts, diameter D, and optimal expected hitting time T_★. Methodologically, the authors design algorithms that attain Õ(√(S^2 A D T_★ K)) regret in the full-information setting and Õ(√(S^3 A^2 D T_★ K)) in the bandit setting by carefully integrating confidence sets for transitions, episodic planning under optimistic models, and adversarial-cost-adaptive updates, and they further provide near-optimal algorithms for the special case of a stochastically oblivious adversary to close the gap to known lower bounds.

The paper tackles the mismatch between standard transformer architectures and the iterative nature of many learning algorithms, asking how transformers can more efficiently emulate iterative computation when doing in-context learning on data-fitting tasks. Its key insight is that introducing an explicit recurrent "loop"—re-running a smaller transformer multiple times with shared weights and preserved hidden state—injects iterative structure that lets the model perform multi-step computation without a large parameter budget. The method trains a looped transformer that shares parameters across iterations and feeds back latent states between passes, and evaluates it on a suite of synthetic and real data-fitting problems to compare accuracy and efficiency. Experiments show the looped transformer matches or approaches the performance of a much larger standard transformer while using under 10% of the parameters, indicating iterative recurrence is an effective way to learn learning algorithms.

The paper addresses the limitation of existing graph contrastive learning (GCL) methods that rely on GNN encoders and the homophily assumption, which can fail when node attribute similarity matters more than network homophily. The key insight is to jointly preserve both attribute-level similarity and structural information by constructing and contrasting multiple complementary views of the graph rather than depending solely on local GNN message passing. The proposed method, ASP, builds three views—original, attribute, and global-structure—and performs multi-view contrastive learning across them to capture attribute relationships and global topology concurrently. Empirical results on real-world networks with varying homophily levels show that ASP consistently outperforms representative baselines.

The paper studies the vulnerability of counterfactual explanations—used to give recourse to individuals affected by algorithmic decisions—by showing they can be manipulated via small perturbations, so ostensibly similar inputs yield drastically different recommended changes. The key insight is that lack of robustness in counterfactuals enables an attacker or model designer to create classifiers that appear fair under standard audits yet, under slight perturbations, produce much lower-cost recourse for targeted subgroups. Methodologically, the authors formalize a vulnerability framework, introduce an objective to train models that exploit this instability to reduce recourse cost for chosen groups, and empirically demonstrate on loan and violent-crime prediction datasets that certain subgroups can receive up to 20× lower-cost recourse under perturbation. These findings highlight a new failure mode for counterfactual explanations and motivate research into robust, manipulation-resistant recourse methods.

The paper addresses the problem of efficient, generalizable trajectory similarity computation, noting that existing deep-learning methods require heavy preprocessing and produce immature trajectory embeddings with limited generality. The key insight is that embedding map grids with a knowledge-graph–inspired GRot method and then using a prompt-based trajectory embedding trained with unsupervised contrastive learning can better capture grid neighborhood relations, trajectory structure, and point order while avoiding costly supervised preprocessing. The method first learns robust grid representations via GRot, feeds those into a prompt trajectory embedding network that aligns grid and trajectory spaces through a customized prompt paradigm, and trains the whole model with contrastive learning using novel positive-sample generation strategies to provide generality. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets show KGTS outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

The paper addresses domain adaptation under subpopulation shift, where source and target distributions differ in the input or representation space and one seeks provable methods to transfer labels reliably. Its key insight is that label propagation from a teacher classifier can both transfer and improve labels on the target domain under a realistic expansion assumption (from Wei et al.), enabling error reduction beyond the teacher while admitting finite-sample guarantees. Methodologically, the authors analyze a label-propagation framework that iteratively spreads labels through a graph built on unlabeled target (and optionally a third unlabeled) data, leverage existing generalization bounds to derive end-to-end guarantees, and instantiate the theory by adapting consistency-based semi-supervised algorithms to practical domain-adaptation tasks, showing empirical gains.

The paper tackles non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM), i.e., decomposing an aggregate household power signal into per-appliance consumption, with a focus on accurately modeling appliances that operate in multiple discrete states and transition between them. The key insight is that explicitly separating state estimation from per-state power regression—and enforcing temporal consistency of state sequences—improves disaggregation accuracy and generalization to unseen appliances. To realize this, the authors propose MSDC, a dual-CNN architecture where one convolutional branch predicts a distribution over discrete appliance states and the other predicts the power level associated with each state, and they couple these outputs with a conditional random field (CRF) that models state transitions; evaluated on REDD and UK-DALE, MSDC yields substantial MAE and SAE improvements over prior methods.

The paper tackles the often-overlooked bottleneck of parallel environment execution in reinforcement learning systems, which limits overall training throughput despite advances in other system components. The key insight is that a carefully designed, highly parallel execution engine—separating environment simulation from Python and exploiting efficient multithreading and batching—can dramatically increase environment step throughput across hardware tiers. The authors implement EnvPool, an open-source C++/multi-threaded environment pool with language bindings and compatibility layers for existing RL libraries, demonstrating orders-of-magnitude speedups (e.g., up to 1M frames/s on Atari and 3M frames/s on MuJoCo on a DGX-A100, and 2.8× faster than Python subprocesses on a laptop). By providing a plug-and-play, high-throughput environment backend, EnvPool enables much faster iteration and scaling for RL research and training pipelines.

The paper investigates why Adam, which blends adaptive learning rates and momentum, often converges faster but generalizes worse than SGD by disentangling the separate effects of adaptive learning rate and momentum in a diffusion-theoretic framework. The key insight is that adaptive learning rates help escape saddle points effectively but do not bias optimization toward flat minima, whereas momentum induces a drift that aids saddle escape while leaving flat-minimum selection largely unchanged—explaining SGD’s superior generalization when combined with momentum. Based on this analysis the authors propose Adaptive Inertia, a novel optimizer that applies parameter-wise adaptive inertia (momentum) to retain fast saddle escape while incorporating a bias toward flat minima similar to SGD, and they provide theoretical support plus empirical results showing improved generalization over both SGD and conventional adaptive methods.

The paper tackles the problem of generative commonsense reasoning, where pre-trained text generation models often produce implausible sentences because they do not explicitly use structured commonsense relations. The key insight is that integrating a knowledge graph of concept relations into a pre-trained sequence-to-sequence model can provide relational constraints and richer concept semantics, improving plausibility and generalization to unseen concept sets. The authors introduce KG-BART, which augments BART with graph-attention modules that encode concept nodes and their relations from a knowledge graph and fuse these graph representations into the encoder–decoder generation process. Experiments on the CommonGen benchmark show substantial gains over BART (e.g., +5.80 BLEU-3, +4.60 BLEU-4) and demonstrate that KG-BART’s outputs can also serve as useful contextual background for downstream commonsense QA tasks.

The paper addresses the limitation of current self-supervised learning (SSL) methods which tend to only disentangle simple augmentation features (e.g., rotation, color) and fail to modularize more abstract generative semantics; it frames the desideratum for representations using a group-theoretic definition of disentanglement. The key insight is that disentangling complex semantic factors can be achieved by iteratively inducing and enforcing invariance to group elements: by partitioning data into subsets corresponding to entangled group actions and training for subset-invariant features, one can progressively recover independent generative factors. The method, Iterative Partition-based Invariant Risk Minimization (IP-IRM), alternates between partitioning training samples into two subsets tied to a latent group element and minimizing a contrastive loss that enforces invariance across each subset, and the authors prove convergence to a fully disentangled representation and validate the approach on multiple benchmarks.

The paper tackles the challenge of improving compact models in self-supervised learning by transferring knowledge from larger self-supervised teachers to smaller students, addressing that small networks lag behind larger ones in SSL performance. The key insight is that preserving the teacher’s relative similarities among data points in embedding space—rather than matching absolute embeddings or designing new pretext tasks—provides an effective supervisory signal for the student. Methodologically, they train the student to mimic the teacher’s pairwise similarity structure (compressing the representation) and show this compression objective yields strong practical gains: e.g., a compressed AlexNet surpasses prior methods and even the fully supervised AlexNet on ImageNet linear and nearest-neighbor evaluations.

The paper addresses the gap between deep learning’s empirical success on high-dimensional data and statistical theories whose sample complexity scales with the ambient dimension, by studying function approximation and binary classification when data lie on a low-dimensional manifold. The key insight is that convolutional residual networks (ConvResNets) can exploit intrinsic low-dimensional geometry to overcome the ambient-dimension curse: when data are supported on a d-dimensional manifold embedded in R^D, approximation and learning rates depend on the manifold dimension d and function smoothness s rather than D. The authors show that with a properly chosen ConvResNet architecture one can approximate Besov-class functions on the manifold arbitrarily well, and that empirical logistic-risk minimization yields an excess classification risk scaling as n^{-s/(2s+2(s∨d))}, so the sample complexity is governed by d and s, demonstrating adaptivity of ConvResNets to low-dimensional data structure.

VITA tackles offline Video Instance Segmentation by asking how to leverage object-centric cues from image detectors to assemble temporally consistent instance masks without heavy spatio-temporal backbones. The key insight is that compact object tokens distilled from a Transformer-based image instance detector can capture object-specific context sufficient to associate instances across frames, so video-level reasoning can be done by linking these tokens rather than propagating dense backbone features. Methodologically, VITA extracts per-frame object tokens from an off-the-shelf image instance segmentation model, builds token associations across frames to form object tracks, and predicts instance masks for the sequence—yielding state-of-the-art results on VIS benchmarks while enabling efficient processing of long or high-resolution videos and reuse of frozen image-trained detectors.

The paper addresses improving encoder architectures for automatic speech recognition to be faster, more memory-efficient, and more accurate than the popular Conformer while retaining both local and global context modeling. The key insight is that combining a U-Net-like multi-resolution encoder (reducing frame rates in middle layers), a restructured block design that reuses attention computations, a modified LayerNorm (BiasNorm) to preserve some length information, novel activation functions (SwooshR/SwooshL) and a scale-aware optimizer (ScaledAdam) yields better trade-offs between speed, memory, and accuracy. The method implements these changes in a new transformer variant called Zipformer—stacking more, smaller blocks with attention reuse, applying down/up-sampling in the encoder, replacing normalization and activations, and training with ScaledAdam—and validates the approach with experiments on LibriSpeech, Aishell-1, and WenetSpeech showing faster convergence and improved ASR performance.

The paper tackles protein-conditioned RNA design, where existing diffusion-based generative models struggle with RNA’s conformational flexibility and the high cost of jointly training large structure predictors. Its key insight is to integrate an inverse folding model into a flow-matching denoising network and fix a pre-trained structure prediction backbone (RosettaFold2NA), thereby offloading sequence-structure coupling to inverse folding and avoiding expensive fine-tuning of the predictor. The method uses flow matching to generate RNA sequences and structures by denoising through a network that combines an inverse folding module—enhanced to condition on inferred conformational ensembles to capture dynamic RNA behavior—with the frozen RosettaFold2NA to steer structural fidelity. Experiments on protein-conditioned RNA generation show that this hybrid inverse-folding–flow approach outperforms prior RNA design methods.

The paper tackles the challenge that unlike supervised learning, reinforcement learning (RL) often fails to benefit from larger model parameter counts and can even degrade as size increases. Its key insight is that Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), especially soft MoE routing, can unlock meaningful parameter scaling in value-based RL by sparsely activating specialized expert sub-networks so the overall capacity grows without overwhelming training or causing destructive interference. The authors integrate Soft MoE modules into value networks and empirically evaluate across multiple training regimes and model sizes, showing consistent performance improvements and enabling larger models to improve rather than deteriorate, thereby providing strong evidence toward establishing scaling laws for RL.

The paper addresses the trade-off in neural solvers for Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs) between high-quality but slow autoregressive (AR) models and fast but lower-quality non-autoregressive (NAR) models, aiming to obtain NAR solvers that match AR performance while retaining low inference latency. The key insight is that pivotal learned components of AR architectures can be preserved and transferred into NAR counterparts via a guided knowledge distillation process, removing the sequential generation constraint yet retaining decision-making quality. The authors propose Guided Non-Autoregressive Knowledge Distillation (GNARKD), which distills trained AR models into NAR architectures by aligning intermediate representations and outputs while adapting the network to parallel generation. Applied to three popular AR VRP models and evaluated on synthetic and real instances, GNARKD yields NAR solvers that run 4–5× faster with only a 2–3% performance drop, demonstrating an effective balance of speed and solution quality.

The paper addresses the lack of efficient algorithms for learning synaptic transmission delays in discrete-time feedforward spiking neural networks (SNNs), which are important because spike-timing and coincidence strongly affect SNN expressivity and performance on temporal tasks like speech recognition. The key insight is to represent inter-layer delays as sparse 1D temporal convolution kernels with a single nonzero weight per synapse whose position encodes delay, and to learn these positions jointly with synaptic weights using Dilated Convolutions with Learnable Spacings (DCLS). Methodologically, the authors implement this approach in PyTorch/SpikingJelly by replacing delay simulation with DCLS-based convolutions in networks of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons and train end-to-end with backpropagation; experiments on SHD, SSC and GSC show learned delays outperform fixed or random delays and achieve state-of-the-art results without recurrence and with fewer parameters.

ChronoR addresses temporal link prediction on temporal knowledge graphs, a challenging problem due to non-stationary, heterogeneous data and complex temporal dependencies. Its key insight is to model relation- and time-conditioned interactions as k-dimensional rotations so that applying a learned rotation to a head-entity embedding moves it close to the corresponding tail embedding, thereby naturally encoding temporal and multi-relational dynamics. The method jointly learns dense embeddings for entities, relations, and time and parameterizes a rotation operator in high-dimensional space for each (relation, time) pair; training minimizes distance between rotated heads and tails so the model captures rich temporal–relational interactions and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on benchmark temporal KG link prediction tasks.

result.text: The paper tackles efficient, symmetry-preserving prediction of quantum Hamiltonian matrices for molecular systems, where maintaining SE(3) equivariance typically conflicts with computational and memory efficiency. The key insight is an architectural design that enforces SE(3)-equivariance while drastically reducing costly tensor-product operations and preventing exponential channel growth as atom types increase. The authors propose QHNet, an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network that restructures equivariant message passing to cut tensor products by 92%, streamlines channels to limit dimensional blowup, and uses this lightweight equivariant circuitry to predict Hamiltonian entries. On four MD17 molecular datasets QHNet matches state-of-the-art accuracy with much faster runtimes and about 50% lower memory consumption.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of choosing layerwise sparsity for magnitude-based neural network pruning, where prior work relies on heuristics or costly hyperparameter searches and performance depends critically on per-layer sparsity allocation. Their key insight is that pruning decisions should account for each layer’s contribution to the model-level ℓ2 distortion, so weight magnitudes can be rescaled into an importance score that reflects the global impact of removing parameters. They propose LAMP (layer-adaptive magnitude-based pruning), a simple, hyperparameter-free scoring scheme that rescales magnitudes by layer-level statistics to produce layerwise sparsities for global pruning, and show empirically on image classification tasks (including weight-rewinding setups) that LAMP consistently outperforms popular baselines. The method is lightweight to compute and requires no expensive tuning while yielding better sparsity–performance tradeoffs than existing layerwise allocation strategies.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of designing practical, high-performing active learning algorithms that work with deep neural networks by revisiting Fisher-information–based selection objectives. Its key insight is that bounds on maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) error expressed via the Fisher information can guide selection of informative batches, and that this classic criterion can be made tractable and efficient for neural models by exploiting linear-algebraic structure. The authors propose BAIT, an algorithm that selects batches by optimizing a Fisher-information–based bound on MLE error and implements this optimization with scalable matrix computations suited to modern hardware. Empirically, BAIT consistently outperforms prior active learning methods on both classification and regression tasks and is adaptable to different model architectures.

The paper tackles the problem of making neural architecture search (NAS) fast and broadly applicable to diverse, under-explored domains beyond computer vision, where AutoML could have the most impact. The key insight is that fixing a standard CNN topology but searching only over operation choices—specifically kernel sizes and dilations—gives rich multi-resolution feature extraction while dramatically reducing the search space, and that leveraging the Fourier diagonalization of convolution lets one efficiently compute mixtures of these operations. Building on this, the authors propose DASH, a differentiable NAS algorithm that uses Fourier-based diagonalization to perform weight-sharing over operation mixtures with improved asymptotic complexity, yielding up to 10× faster search in practice; they evaluate DASH on ten varied tasks (e.g., PDE solving, protein folding, heart disease detection) and show it outperforms state-of-the-art AutoML on most tasks while keeping search-plus-retraining overhead low (often under 2× the training time of a baseline CNN).

result.text: The paper addresses the slow and memory-intensive training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for large-scale scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis. Its key insight is that scene decomposition combined with a distributed consensus optimization—specifically using ADMM—lets multiple local 3DGS models cooperate to learn a single high-quality global model while reducing per-node load and improving convergence stability. Methodologically, DOGS splits a scene into K spatial blocks, runs K local 3DGS trainings on slave nodes that periodically enforce consensus on shared Gaussian parameters with a global model on the master via ADMM, discards the local models after training, and uses only the global model for inference; this yields over 6× faster training on large scenes while maintaining or improving rendering quality.

result.text: The paper tackles the tension in offline reinforcement learning between conservatism—necessary to avoid overestimation under distribution shift—and robustness to observation deviations (e.g., sensor noise or adversarial perturbations), which excessive conservatism can undermine. The key insight is that introducing a conservative smoothing regularizer that enforces consistency and lowered value estimates not only at dataset states but also for nearby perturbed states can simultaneously preserve safety under distribution shift and improve robustness to observation errors. Methodologically, RORL augments standard offline RL by applying regularization on both the policy and value function for states in a neighborhood around dataset states, coupled with conservative value estimation for those neighborhoods; the authors provide tighter suboptimality bounds in linear MDPs and empirically show improved benchmark performance and resilience to adversarial observation perturbations.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between state space models (SSMs) and Transformers for language modeling by targeting efficient long-range contextualization without sacrificing short-term representational power. Its key insight is that combining an SSM sublayer—which excels at capturing long-range dependencies with subquadratic complexity—with a block-wise Transformer sublayer—which handles local, short-term interactions—yields a hybrid that leverages the strengths of both families. The authors propose the Block-State Transformer (BST), present three fully parallelizable variants that integrate SSMs and block attention, and empirically show BST outperforms comparable Transformer architectures on language modeling perplexity, generalizes to longer sequences, and achieves over an order-of-magnitude layer-level speedup versus block-recurrent baselines under model parallelism.

result.text: The paper tackles catastrophic overfitting in single-step adversarial training, a sudden collapse where models become vulnerable to multi-step attacks (PGD) despite appearing robust to single-step attacks (FGSM). The key insight is that using only maximal-perturbation single-step examples concentrates training on boundary points and ignores the continuum of adversarial directions, which distorts the decision boundary and creates a highly curved loss surface that single-step updates cannot reliably defend. The authors analyze this mechanism and propose a simple remedy—augmenting or modifying single-step training to include non-maximal or diversified adversarial examples (thereby sampling the adversarial direction more broadly) to regularize curvature and preserve robustness—showing this prevents catastrophic overfitting and enables single-step procedures to resist multi-step attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between the likelihoods produced by diffusion ODEs (probability flow ODEs of diffusion models) and those of leading likelihood-based generative models, aiming to improve maximum likelihood estimation for deterministic diffusion-based flows. The key insight is that reparameterizing the vector field (velocity parameterization), reducing variance during training, applying a high-order flow matching fine-tuning objective with error bounds, and using a training-free truncated-normal dequantization at evaluation can jointly close the training–evaluation gap and produce smoother, more accurate ODE trajectories. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of reliably estimating confidence for large language model (LLM) predictions, noting that many LLMs are poorly calibrated and resist standard post-hoc calibration techniques. Its key insight is that calibration can be derived from the model’s own behavior by measuring consistency across multiple stochastic generations: agreement among sampled answers serves as a proxy for true confidence. The authors propose three consistency-based measures computed from random generations, evaluate them across eleven models (open and closed) and nine reasoning datasets, and show these measures reduce calibration error compared to prior approaches; they also find that factors like intermediate explanations, model scale, and larger sample sizes improve calibration while instruction-tuning hinders it, and that consistency-derived confidence can even boost downstream performance, with practical guidance on picking metrics based on model traits such as instruction-tuning and RLHF exposure.

The paper examines the vulnerability of recent safety-aligned large language models to simple adaptive jailbreaking attacks, showing that even top models can be reliably coerced into violating safety constraints. Its key insight is that modest adaptivity—tailoring prompt templates to the target model, leveraging available signals like token logprobs, and restricting/random-searching over token suffixes—greatly increases jailbreak success by exploiting model- and API-specific weaknesses. Methodologically, the authors implement random-search-driven attacks that maximize target token logprobs (with multiple restarts) or use transfer and prefilling strategies when logprobs are unavailable, demonstrate 100% success across a wide range of models (including GPT-4 variants, Claude via transfer/prefill, and many open models), and apply a similar restricted-token search to find trojan strings in poisoned models, releasing code and artifacts for reproducibility.

result.text: The paper tackles improving online knowledge distillation, which traditionally transfers only class probabilities between simultaneously trained networks and thus overlooks rich spatial and intensity cues in feature maps. The key insight is that adversarial learning can transfer feature-map-level knowledge more effectively than direct alignment losses (e.g., L1) by matching feature distribution rather than forcing pixelwise correspondence. The method trains multiple networks jointly with per-network discriminators that treat the network’s own feature maps as fake and others’ as real, so each network is trained to fool its discriminator and thereby learn the feature distribution of its peers, and introduces a cyclic learning scheme to scale this to more than two networks. Experiments on classification across architectures show substantial performance gains, particularly when pairing small and large networks.

Its key insight is to recast continuous pose generation as a discrete sequence modeling problem by learning a compact, quantized latent codebook for poses and then modeling that discrete prior with a diffusion-based denoising process suited to variable-length sequences. result.text: The paper examines whether differentiable simulators—which provide first-order gradients—actually yield better policy gradient estimates than traditional zeroth-order (likelihood-ratio) methods for long-horizon, physically realistic control tasks; it identifies the problem that system properties like stiffness and discontinuities can make first-order estimators biased or high-variance and thus worse in practice. The key insight is that exact simulator gradients are not universally superior: depending on system dynamics and noise, pure first-order estimates can suffer from structural bias or variance issues, so a hybrid that interpolates between zero- and first-order information can capture the best of both worlds. Concretely, the authors analyze bias and variance trade-offs, introduce an α-order gradient estimator parameterized by α∈[0,1] that blends zeroth- and first-order terms to adaptively exploit exact gradients when helpful and fall back to robust zeroth-order behavior otherwise, and validate the approach on numerical examples showing scenarios where traditional estimators fail and the α-estimator improves performance.
