result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently and precisely evaluating video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), where existing benchmarks are costly to build and often conflate multiple skills. Its key insight is to synthetically decouple video content from query-responses by inserting unrelated visual “needles” into diverse videos and generating rule-based queries that target specific skills, enabling scalable, controlled, and skill-specific assessment. The method, VideoNIAH, automates creation of video-query-response pairs by programmatically planting needles and applying predefined query templates to produce VNBench, a suite of retrieval, ordering, and counting tasks designed to probe temporal perception, chronological ordering, and spatio-temporal coherence across varied video lengths. Using VNBench to evaluate proprietary and open-source MLLMs, the authors reveal pronounced differences in model capabilities, analyze failure modes, and offer recommendations for improving video MLLM training.

result.text: The paper addresses protecting publicly shared data from unauthorized model training by creating “unlearnable” perturbed examples, noting that prior methods produce perturbations that fail to transfer across different training settings and datasets. Its key insight is that enhancing class-wise linear separability of perturbed data via a Classwise Separability Discriminant (CSD) objective yields perturbations whose unlearnable effects generalize better to unseen training configurations and datasets. The method generates imperceptible additive perturbations optimized to increase class separability penalties (using CSD) so that models trained on the poisoned data learn features that do not generalize, and the authors validate through extensive experiments that these CSD-based unlearnable examples transfer more effectively across varied training settings and datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles improving GAN performance by refining consistency regularization on the discriminator, addressing the problem that naive consistency constraints can introduce visual artifacts and suboptimal synthesis quality. The key insight is that careful design of the consistency loss—avoiding alignment of augmented and unaugmented discriminator outputs in ways that force the generator to produce artifacts, and modifying how augmentations, perturbation magnitudes, and loss targets are applied—yields better training signals without degrading sample fidelity. result.text: The paper addresses how to adapt few-shot object detection (FSOD) to the era of large vision-language models (VLMs), noting that off-the-shelf zero-shot VLMs already outperform SOTA few-shot detectors but can misalign with target application concepts. Their key insight is that few-shot recognition should be reframed as aligning foundation models to target concepts using a small set of multi-modal exemplars (text plus images), since examples and brief instructions can define category semantics more precisely than class names alone. To operationalize this, they introduce Foundational FSOD, a benchmark and protocol that fine-tunes pre-trained VLMs on K-shot multi-modal examples per class (repurposing nuImages), evaluate several open-source VLMs, analyze method performance, and run a community competition demonstrating large gains from tailored adaptation.

result.text: The paper addresses PPO's sample inefficiency stemming from its inability to leverage off-policy data. Its key insight is that a suitably designed clipped surrogate objective can safely incorporate off-policy samples while constraining policy updates to avoid instability, yielding update distances comparable to on-policy PPO. The method derives and analyzes this off-policy clipped surrogate, proves that its policy update distance remains consistent with PPO’s stability properties, and implements an iterative policy optimization algorithm that uses past experience to improve sample efficiency. Empirical results on continuous control benchmarks show the proposed Off-Policy PPO outperforms or matches state-of-the-art baselines on most tasks.

The key insight is that letting roles emerge as learnable stochastic embeddings and conditioning individual policies on these roles encourages specialization and shared behavior among similarly-abled agents without prior domain knowledge. Methodologically, ROMA builds a role embedding space trained with two novel regularizers—one promoting identifiability of roles from behavior and another encouraging specialization by linking roles to task-specific utility—and conditions each agent’s policy on sampled role embeddings so agents with similar roles share learning and specialize on subtasks; empirical results on StarCraft II micromanagement tasks show the approach yields dynamic, identifiable roles and improved performance.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of finding hidden input parameters that produce desired observations in generic inverse problems and argues that inverse methods should be evaluated by how solution quality improves over time rather than by a single best guess. The key insight is that many deep-learning–based inverse methods act as stochastic samplers of the solution space, so benchmarking should treat them as time-dependent search processes and that combining a learned forward model with gradient-based search can exploit this viewpoint. Methodologically, the authors introduce time-to-solution benchmarking across four tasks (two prior benchmarks, one toy visualization, and a new metamaterial design task), compare state-of-the-art inverse models under this metric, and propose the “neural-adjoint” approach which trains a neural network surrogate of the forward process and then uses backpropagation through that surrogate to iteratively optimize inputs, demonstrating superior performance in several settings.

Its key insight is to treat novel-category discovery as a self-labeling clustering problem over the entire target set and to use self-supervised representation learning combined with a mutual-information objective so that labels and inputs become highly predictive of each other, enabling simultaneous identification of seen and unseen categories. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of detecting post-training backdoor attacks on classifiers when the defender lacks the training data or clean reference models, focusing particularly on challenging two-class settings and cases with multiple simultaneous attacks. The key insight is that reverse-engineered candidate backdoor patterns can be evaluated by an expected transferability (ET) statistic that quantifies how consistently a recovered pattern causes inputs from other classes to be misclassified to the same target, and that this ET score yields a domain- and attack-configuration–agnostic separation between attacked and clean models. The method reverse-engineers potential backdoor patterns from the deployed classifier, computes the ET statistic for these candidates (using the classifier’s responses on held-out inputs rather than any training labels), and flags models as backdoored when ET exceeds a fixed threshold; experiments on six benchmarks show the approach reliably detects both two-class and multi-attack scenarios across different reverse-engineering algorithms.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited expressiveness of Neural Processes (NPs), whose reliance on a single global latent variable hinders modeling complex, multimodal data-generating processes and restricts their applicability in meta-learning and few-shot settings. Its key insight is that augmenting NPs with a mixture-of-experts mechanism yields a richer, more flexible meta-representation by allowing multiple specialized latent components to capture diverse modes and local structure across tasks while preserving exchangeability. The method, Mixture of Expert Neural Processes (MoE-NPs), integrates a gating network and multiple expert NPs so that for each context the model infers a mixture over expert latents and aggregates expert predictions to produce task-conditional outputs; this architecture is trained end-to-end and applied to few-shot supervised and meta-reinforcement learning benchmarks, where it shows improved generalization to unseen tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap in understanding why AlphaZero-style Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) heuristics work and how to improve them by framing them as optimization rather than ad-hoc rules. Its key insight is that common MCTS selection rules (including AlphaZero's PUCT and UCT) can be interpreted as approximate solutions to a specific regularized policy optimization problem, so replacing the approximation with the exact optimizer should yield better search policies. Methodologically, the authors derive the underlying regularized optimization formulation, design a variant of AlphaZero that computes the exact solution to that optimization at each node (instead of using the heuristic selection formula), and empirically demonstrate that this principled variant consistently outperforms the original AlphaZero across multiple domains.

result.text: The paper investigates how commonly used baselines in policy gradient methods affect optimization beyond merely reducing gradient variance, showing that baseline choice can change the optimization dynamics and even harm learning despite lower variance. The key insight is that baselines influence the update direction and curvature of the expected update—so two baselines with identical variance can lead to different trajectories and convergence properties, and some baselines can cause natural policy gradient to converge to suboptimal policies for any stepsize when sampling is tied to the current policy. The authors analyze simple illustrative examples and theoretical conditions, and propose decoupling the sampling policy from the current policy to restore robust convergence for a much broader set of baselines, arguing for treating stochasticity in updates more carefully than by variance reduction alone.

result.text: The paper addresses improving out-of-sample generalization by incorporating causal structure into neural-network regularization, motivated by evidence that predicting effects from causes yields lower test error than anti-causal learning. Its key insight is to jointly learn an input-layer-embedded adjacency matrix that represents a causal DAG and use that discovered causal graph to guide regularization, focusing reconstruction only on features with causal neighbors rather than reconstructing all inputs. The method, CASTLE, embeds a differentiable DAG adjacency matrix into the network, enforces acyclicity, and adds a reconstruction-based regularizer that reconstructs only causally connected features while training the predictor end-to-end; the authors prove a generalization bound and empirically show consistent out-of-sample improvements over standard regularizers on synthetic and real datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles how to enable frozen large language models (LLMs) to both understand and generate non-linguistic modalities (e.g., images, videos) without changing the LLM weights. Methodologically, SPAE trains an encoder–decoder that converts images into sequences of interpretable lexical tokens aligned with the LLM’s vocabulary and reconstructs images from those tokens using multiscale latent representations, then uses in-context prompting with frozen PaLM 2 and GPT-3.5 to perform and evaluate multimodal understanding and generation tasks. This approach yields the first demonstration of frozen LLM image generation and substantially improves image understanding performance (over 25% relative) under the same frozen-LM setting.

result.text: The paper addresses composed image retrieval with iterative text feedback, noting that users search from coarse to fine-grained descriptions but existing pairwise training focuses only on fine-grained one-to-one matches and harms recall. The key insight is to model retrieval as a multi-grained matching problem by treating coarse-grained queries as allowing larger uncertainty (fluctuations) in feature space and fine-grained queries as smaller fluctuations, so the model should not force away plausible candidates early. Methodologically, they introduce uncertainty modeling that simulates multi-grained queries via identically distributed feature perturbations and uncertainty regularization that adapts the matching objective to the fluctuation range, which preserves candidate sets during early stages and yields consistent Recall@50 improvements on FashionIQ, Fashion200k, and Shoes.

result.text: The paper tackles automated EEG-based seizure detection and classification, focusing on three gaps in prior work: modeling EEG's non-Euclidean spatiotemporal structure, improving performance on rare seizure types, and providing quantitative interpretability for seizure localization. The key insight is that graph neural networks (GNNs) can better capture electrode geometry or dynamic brain connectivity in EEGs and that self-supervised pre-training—predicting the next time period’s preprocessed signals—boosts downstream detection/classification performance and helps rare-class learning. The method builds EEG graphs (geometry- or connectivity-based), trains GNNs with a self-supervised next-step signal prediction objective before supervised fine-tuning, and introduces a quantitative interpretability metric to evaluate localization ability. Evaluated on a large public dataset, the approach outperforms prior methods on detection (AUROC 0.875) and classification (weighted F1 0.749), notably improving rare seizure classification and precise localization of focal seizures.

result.text: The paper tackles the need for faster and more accurate deep learning on 3D point clouds by revisiting and improving the Set Abstraction (SA) building block from PointNet++; its goal is to reduce computation while boosting accuracy for tasks like classification and segmentation. The key insight is that the original SA mixes channel-wise feature learning and spatial aggregation in a single step, and separating these concerns lets each be learned more efficiently—further enhanced by an Anisotropic Reduction that captures direction-dependent (anisotropic) spatial correlations. result.text: The paper tackles the limitation in tool-augmented LLM training where only successful decision-tree (inference-tree) trajectories are used for supervised fine-tuning, neglecting failed explorations that could inform better tool-usage policies. Its key insight is that failed paths in expert inference trees contain actionable preference signals that, when converted into stepwise preference data and used to directly optimize the model’s policy, can expand the learning signal beyond successful trajectories and improve generalization. result.text: The paper tackles the gap between rapid systems-level advances (in compilers, networking, and hardware) and the slow uptake of those advances within large machine learning frameworks, which hampers prototyping of novel computational paradigms and systems research. Its key insight is that enabling systems researchers requires a library designed with open, modular, and easily customizable internals—alongside research-ready models—so that new ideas can be implemented and evaluated with low friction and realistic workloads. To realize this, the authors present Flashlight, an open-source ML library that emphasizes modularity and performance, offering state-of-the-art models and training setups while keeping overhead low so it competes with or outperforms mainstream frameworks. By making it simple to iterate on computational primitives and tooling, Flashlight aims to accelerate systems-driven innovation that can be adopted by larger frameworks downstream.

The paper tackles the problem of imputing missing values in tabular datasets by extending masked autoencoding to this domain. The key insight is that, beyond treating naturally missing entries as masks, intentionally re-masking a random subset of observed values during training forces the autoencoder to learn representations that are invariant to missingness and better generalize to unobserved entries. result.text: The paper addresses learning the underlying temporal dynamics of physiological signals—specifically ECG heartbeats—by combining data-driven modeling with physical priors rather than relying solely on hand-crafted ODEs. Its key insight is to cast the generator of a GAN as a neural ordinary differential equation: the generator takes a state at a given time (and optional physical parameters) and outputs the state derivative, thereby learning continuous-time dynamics that can be integrated to synthesize realistic trajectories. The method, called ODE-GAN and specialized to ECG-ODE-GAN when incorporating physiological parameters, trains this derivative-producing generator adversarially against a discriminator on real ECG beats and demonstrates that samples produced by integrating the learned ODEs improve downstream heartbeat classification.

result.text: The paper addresses the overlooked availability threat in autonomous driving camera perception—specifically attacks that increase perception latency to create dangerous system-level effects—rather than merely causing misclassification. The key insight is that by crafting adversarial inputs optimized not just for incorrect outputs but for increasing execution time across the entire camera-based perception pipeline, an attacker can amplify downstream safety failures (e.g., crashes) far beyond prior object-detection–focused latency attacks. The authors propose SlowTrack, a two-stage attack framework with three novel loss functions that jointly target perception runtime and imperceptibility, and they evaluate it across four popular perception pipelines as well as on the Baidu Apollo stack and LGSVL simulator. Results show SlowTrack substantially increases perception latency and system-level harm—raising crash rates to about 95% on average—while maintaining comparable visual stealth to existing attacks.

The paper addresses improving Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting for large language models by tackling the problem that current unsupervised CoT selection methods, which pick demonstrations based on question semantics, can be noisy and uninterpretable. The key insight is that demonstrations should be chosen for their reasoning patterns—the distinct procedural routes models use to arrive at answers—so selecting diverse patterns yields clearer, more robust guidance than semantic similarity alone. The method constructs task-specific sets of reasoning patterns using prior knowledge and prompt-based extraction from large models, then selects diverse demonstrations covering those patterns to form CoT prompts, which reduces noise, adds interpretability, and empirically improves performance across multiple reasoning benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of data-driven design where a learned regression model (an oracle) guides in silico search for high-performing designs but is then asked to make predictions far outside its training distribution, leading to poor guidance. The key insight is to treat design and modeling as a coupled, non-zero-sum game in which the oracle should be adaptively updated as the design algorithm explores novel regions, even when no new ground-truth labels are acquired. The authors propose "autofocusing," a principled retraining strategy that adjusts the oracle during the design loop by reweighting or resampling training examples to better reflect the evolving query distribution induced by the optimizer. Empirical results across tasks in protein, small-molecule, and materials design show that autofocusing yields more reliable guidance and improves the quality of discovered candidates compared to static oracles.

result.text: The paper addresses active protection of deep neural network intellectual property by preventing unauthorized model use beyond passive watermarking. Its key insight is that selectively obfuscating a tiny fraction of model weights can catastrophically degrade model performance while storing the original weight indices and values as a compact “secret” that authorized users can restore inside a trusted execution environment. The proposed NNSplitter method automatically identifies and modifies a very small set of critical weights to create an obfuscated model that yields near-random outputs, while keeping the secret weights separately and securely delivered so authorized executions reconstruct full accuracy; experiments show extreme effectiveness (e.g., flipping 275 of ~11M weights reduces ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 to 10%) and robustness to countermeasures like fine-tuning and norm clipping.

The paper addresses the gap in depression detection research by creating a realistic multimodal dataset and model for identifying depression from non-verbal behavior in the wild, noting prior work’s reliance on constrained lab settings. The key insight is that large-scale, naturalistic vlogs contain informative acoustic and visual cues whose cross-modal interactions are critical for reliable depression detection. To this end the authors introduce D-Vlog, a 961-vlog (≈160-hour) YouTube-derived dataset, and propose a multimodal deep model that extracts acoustic and visual features and fuses them with a cross-attention mechanism to capture inter-modal relationships and produce discriminative representations. Experiments show the cross-attention multimodal model substantially outperforms baseline approaches, demonstrating the dataset’s value and the efficacy of modeling acoustic-visual interactions for in-the-wild depression detection.

result.text: The paper tackles detecting training-set backdoor attacks, where poisoned examples cause a learned model to respond to a trigger, and questions whether such examples can be distinguished from benign data. Its key insight is that without prior structural knowledge of the data distribution, backdoor patterns can be indistinguishable from legitimate predictive features—making general-purpose detection impossible—and thus defenses implicitly rely on latent assumptions. Leveraging an alternative, explicit assumption that the backdoor corresponds to the single strongest feature in the training data, the authors formalize this setting and derive a detection primitive and algorithm with theoretical guarantees. Empirically, this method proves effective, and the analysis clarifies which assumptions underpin prior defenses and when they succeed or fail.

result.text: The paper addresses how to optimally scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models to minimize compute for a given performance by expanding the variables considered in scaling analysis to include a new hyperparameter, granularity, that controls expert size. result.text: The paper addresses the failure of Simple Graph Convolution (SGC), a shallow, fast graph method, on heterophilous graphs where connected nodes tend to be dissimilar. Its key insight is that a light-weight, non-deep approach can be made robust to both homophily and heterophily by adaptively choosing how neighborhood information is aggregated, so that the model neither blindly smooths features (harmful under heterophily) nor forgoes useful propagation (harmful under homophily). result.text: The paper studies how lack of transparency about a principal’s decision rule (e.g., loan or college admissions) affects agents who must learn strategically by observing peers with heterogeneous information, addressing whether and when population subgroups can improve their true quality under such information disparities. result.text: The paper addresses how to design policies for Markov decision processes when both the objective and constraints are expressed as dynamic coherent risk measures, which complicates standard constrained MDP solution techniques. The key insight is that if the risk objectives and constraints admit a Markov risk transition mapping, the constrained risk-averse control problem can be cast in a Lagrangian form whose policy-synthesis subproblems admit a difference-of-convex structure. The authors propose an optimization-based method that constructs Markovian policies by solving these DCPs using the disciplined convex-concave programming (DCCP) framework, thereby generalizing the linear-program approach for expected-cost constrained MDPs. They validate the approach numerically on a rover navigation task using CVaR and EVaR measures, demonstrating tractable policy synthesis and effective risk control.

The paper tackles the limited scale of training data for open-vocabulary object detection by enabling web-scale weak supervision; while vision–language pretraining has improved recognition, detectors still lack the vast box-level annotations needed to generalize to many classes. The key insight is that self-training—using a competent detector to generate pseudo-box labels on large collections of image–text pairs—can effectively expand detection datasets if one carefully designs the label space, filters pseudo-annotations, and makes training efficient. The authors introduce OWLv2 (a strong baseline detector) and OWL-ST (a scalable self-training recipe) that produce high-quality pseudo-boxes and scale from ~10M to over 1B examples, yielding large gains on rare LVIS classes (e.g., boosting AP from 31.2% to 44.6% for classes with no human boxes) and demonstrating that web-scale training can unlock open-world localization akin to advances in classification and language models.

result.text: The paper studies the computational complexity of finding envy-free (and sometimes proportional) allocations of indivisible resources when agents observe only neighbors in a given social network, focusing on parameterized complexity with respect to structural parameters of the network and similarities among agents/items. The key insight is that restricting the network structure (e.g., bounded treewidth or bounded clique-width) or exploiting bounded similarity measures can render otherwise hard allocation problems tractable, while these tractability gains are essentially tight. Methodologically, the authors develop fixed-parameter algorithms that leverage dynamic programming over decompositions (treewidth, clique-width) and parameter-aware reductions to solve broad fragments of the envy-free allocation problem, and they match these positive results with lower-bound reductions showing no substantially faster algorithms exist under standard complexity assumptions.

The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently approximating the Pareto set for NP-hard multiobjective combinatorial optimization (MOCO) problems without expensive per-instance search. Its key insight is that a single, preference-conditioned neural model can directly generate high-quality approximate Pareto solutions for any trade-off preference, thereby learning a continuous mapping from preferences to solutions instead of producing a finite set of discrete solutions. Methodologically, the authors train this model with a tailored multiobjective reinforcement learning algorithm inspired by decomposition-based MOEA/D, conditioning the policy on preference vectors and optimizing it to cover the Pareto front; experiments on multiobjective TSP, VRP, and knapsack problems show superior solution quality, inference speed, and model efficiency compared to baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses how differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DPSGD), while protecting privacy, can amplify disparate impact across groups in trained models. result.text: The paper tackles efficient computation of the Projection Robust Wasserstein (PRW) distance, a max–min formulation over the Stiefel manifold designed to mitigate the curse of dimensionality in high-dimensional optimal transport. Its key insight is a novel reformulation of the entropy-regularized max–min PRW problem that enables a Riemannian block coordinate descent (RBCD) strategy with much lower per-iteration cost than prior Riemannian gradient-ascent-plus-Sinkhorn schemes. The proposed RBCD alternately updates blocks on the Stiefel manifold using closed-form or cheaply computed steps while solving simpler transport subproblems, and the authors prove an arithmetic complexity of O(ε−3) to reach an ε-stationary point—vastly improving on the O(ε−12) bound for RGAS. Empirical results on synthetic and real datasets confirm the method’s scalability and superior efficiency, particularly when the sample size is very large.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of reducing computation for short, trimmed video classification by selecting a small subset of informative frames that both speeds up models and can improve accuracy. result.text: DecodingTrust addresses the insufficient and fragmented evaluation of GPT model trustworthiness by proposing a broad, systematic benchmark targeting real-world risks such as toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial and out-of-distribution robustness, privacy leakage, ethics, and fairness. Its key insight is that universal, stealthy trigger tokens and poisoned discrete prompts can be discovered and optimized solely through API queries and few-shot examples, enabling reliable, transferable manipulation without white-box access. The proposed TrojLLM framework combines a trigger-discovery algorithm that searches for universal input-level triggers via black-box queries and a progressive Trojan poisoning algorithm that iteratively crafts poisoned prompts to maximize attack efficacy and transferability across models. Experiments show TrojLLM can successfully implant Trojans in real-world LLM APIs such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 while preserving performance on clean inputs, highlighting practical risks and suggesting avenues for defense.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of crafting adversarial point clouds for 3D deep learning models in a way that preserves surface continuity and realism, rather than applying non-manifold pointwise perturbations. The key insight is that deforming the underlying 2D parameterization of a surface (the parameter plane) via a learned stretching field can produce smooth, realistic adversarial examples with minimal geometric distortion while effectively fooling classifiers. Their method learns a generative mapping from a 2D parameter plane to the 3D surface, then optimizes a stretch field in the parameter domain to maximize classifier loss subject to regularization that preserves surface smoothness; the resulting adversarial point clouds are sampled from the deformed manifold. Experiments demonstrate these manifold-based attacks yield more transferable, less detectable, and higher-success adversarial examples than prior non-manifold perturbation techniques.

The paper tackles data-free quantization of deep neural networks, aiming to reduce bit-widths for weights and activations without access to training data or specialized hardware while preserving accuracy. Its key insight is that restricting quantizers to uniform maps limits performance, but non-uniform quantization must preserve the network’s algebraic operations, so viable transforms are continuous automorphisms of (R+*, ×), i.e., power functions x ↦ x^a. The method, PowerQuant, therefore searches a single exponent per layer by minimizing layer-wise reconstruction error—an optimization the authors show is locally convex with a unique solution—and implements the learned power-law quantization by simple, low-overhead modifications to activation functions at inference, yielding substantial accuracy gains over prior data-free schemes.

result.text: The paper addresses tabular scenario-based question answering (TSQA), where systems must answer questions grounded in mixed-format scenarios that include both text and structured tables—a common and challenging setting for tasks like high-school exam questions that require synthesizing multiple table cells and integrating domain knowledge. The key insight is that converting useful parts of tables into natural-language sentences and selectively feeding those sentences into strong machine reading comprehension (MRC) models can make TSQA more tractable. To this end the authors introduce GeoTSQA, a 1k-question geography dataset with tabular scenarios, and propose TTGen, a table-to-text generator that synthesizes candidate sentences from tables and uses a ranking model conditioned on the scenario, question, and domain knowledge to select the most informative sentences for a downstream MRC solver. Their TTGen-augmented MRC approach significantly outperforms several strong baselines on GeoTSQA.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of inferring the objective (cost) functions that underlie human sensorimotor behavior when motor noise is signal-dependent, rather than assuming a cost a priori and merely comparing predicted to observed actions. Its key insight is to frame this as an inverse optimal control problem within a partially observable Markov decision process that separates the agent’s and experimenter’s inference problems and explicitly models the probabilistic evolution of states and beliefs under signal-dependent noise. Methodologically, the authors derive a probabilistic formulation and an approximate belief-propagation equation for the linear–quadratic Gaussian setting with signal-dependent noise, extend the framework to cases where the experimenter has partial observability of state variables, and validate the approach on synthetic and real experimental data. This enables recovering the implicit costs and benefits guiding sequential sensorimotor behavior, unifying normative optimal-control explanations with descriptive data-driven inference.

result.text: The paper examines channel pruning for CNNs and identifies two overlooked problems in existing pruning criteria: many widely-used criteria produce nearly identical filter importance rankings (Similarity), and some criteria yield scores so close they cannot reliably distinguish redundant filters (Applicability). The key insight is that these issues stem from underlying statistical properties of trained convolutional weights—specifically that filter weights per layer approximately follow a Gaussian-like distribution (Convolutional Weight Distribution Assumption)—which explains why different metrics correlate and fail to separate importance. Methodologically, the authors validate this assumption with extensive statistical tests and then empirically analyze and compare layer-wise and global pruning behaviors across diverse criteria, showing how similarity and score indistinguishability lead to similar pruned structures and limited discrimination of redundancy.

The paper addresses the tradeoff between expressivity and scalability in permutation-equivariant graph learning: standard message-passing GNNs are insufficiently expressive to represent all permutation-equivariant functions, while higher-order architectures that are universal require tensorial or subgraph enumerations that scale exponentially and ignore graph sparsity. The key insight is that by using sparsity-aware heuristics inspired by graph isomorphism techniques, one can design permutation-equivariant networks whose computational cost adapts to the number of edges and local structure, yielding a continuum of models that interpolate between efficient message-passing and fully expressive higher-order schemes. Concretely, the authors introduce SpeqNets, a class of architectures that build higher-order representations only over selected node tuples determined by sparsity-sensitive selection rules and then apply permutation-equivariant aggregation and transformation, achieving universality while drastically reducing memory and time compared to full k-order methods. Empirically, SpeqNets retain much of the predictive power of expressive higher-order networks and outperform standard GNNs and graph kernels on node- and graph-level supervised tasks while scaling to larger, sparse graphs.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of robust RGBT (RGB and thermal) visual tracking, where existing methods struggle to perform cross-modal feature interactions across all network layers because full-layer fusion incurs prohibitive computational cost. To realize this, the authors propose AINet which incorporates a Difference-based Fusion Mamba (DFM) that fuses RGB and thermal features with linear complexity by leveraging their feature discrepancies, and an Order-dynamic Fusion Mamba (OFM) that adaptively changes the scan order of layer tokens to efficiently perform interactions across all layers; combined in a progressive fusion framework, this approach yields state-of-the-art performance on four public RGBT tracking benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses fairness and proportionality in approval-based committee elections, noting that existing strong axioms like priceability and the core still permit committees that can be seen as unfair. The key insight is that market-based explanations—modeled after Lindahl-like personalized prices and contributions—can be strengthened to guarantee more robust fairness by ensuring stability and balance of these price assignments. The authors introduce two solution concepts, stable priceability and balanced stable priceability, which require that voters’ payments and candidate prices form a stable market outcome (akin to a Lindahl equilibrium) so that no group can profitably deviate, and they provide constructive methods to test and produce such committees, arguing these select arguably fairer outcomes with intuitive economic justifications.

result.text: The paper addresses how to empirically verify whether observed sequential decision-making data satisfy the Markov assumption, which underlies reinforcement learning methods. The key insight is that by comparing predictive performance moving forward (using past and present information) versus backward (conditioning additionally on future information), one can nonparametrically detect violations of the Markov property without assuming a specific form for the data-generating distribution. The authors develop a Forward-Backward Learning test that constructs and compares conditional models to assess whether the present state suffices for future prediction, and they demonstrate its effectiveness on synthetic examples and a mobile health dataset to show when higher-order or partially observable models are needed to identify optimal policies.

result.text: The paper addresses blind omnidirectional image quality assessment (BOIQA), where existing methods fail to model how human observers browse 360° images, leading to poor perceptual fidelity predictions. The key insight is to mimic the multi-assessor viewing process by generating multiple plausible viewport sequences and modeling both spatial distortion/semantic features and their temporal transitions, thereby capturing how local degradations and viewing order jointly affect perceived quality. The proposed Assessor360 framework creates pseudo-viewport sequences using a generalized Recursive Probability Sampling (RPS) that combines content and detail cues, processes each viewport with a Multi-scale Feature Aggregation (MFA) module containing Distortion-aware Blocks (DAB) to fuse distorted and semantic features, and feeds sequences into a Temporal Modeling Module (TMM) to learn viewport transitions, yielding state-of-the-art performance across multiple OIQA datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of sampling from a target distribution known up to normalization by designing a particle-based deterministic flow that minimizes a discrepancy to the target. Its key insight is to follow the Wasserstein gradient flow of the Kernel Stein Discrepancy (KSD), yielding a tractable, differentiable loss functional whose gradients can be evaluated without knowing the normalization constant and which admits efficient, parameter-free optimization like L-BFGS. The resulting method, KSD Descent, updates a set of particles by directly minimizing empirical KSD via gradient-based quasi-Newton steps (or other deterministic optimizers), and the authors analyze its convergence properties and empirically demonstrate competitive performance while also identifying situations where the nonconvex loss produces spurious local minima that trap the algorithm.

result.text: The paper addresses community discovery and link prediction on graphs by proposing a probabilistic latent-variable model that yields interpretable, sparse node embeddings. The key insight is to combine a ladder variational autoencoder hierarchy with gamma-distributed latent variables so that multi-layer stochastic representations are non-negative and sparse—making each dimension naturally interpretable as membership strength in a community or topic—while a novel recognition model enables fast inference. Concretely, the method models each node with a deep hierarchy of gamma latent variables, decodes link probabilities from the bottom-layer embeddings via a nonlinear function, and trains the model end-to-end (optionally incorporating node features/labels) using the gamma ladder VAE framework with a modular GNN-based encoder for scalability and empirical gains on benchmarks.

The paper addresses the problem of removing bias from already-trained machine learning models—including large-scale deep neural networks—via a practical post-processing procedure that provably preserves accuracy. Its key insight is that a carefully designed post-processing transformation can be shown to have provably small excess Bayes risk (i.e., be near-optimal), meaning one can correct fairness violations after training without much sacrifice in classification performance. The authors propose a scalable algorithm that applies this theoretically justified adjustment to model outputs, prove bounds on its excess Bayes risk, and empirically demonstrate on standard benchmarks that it outperforms prior post-processing methods and matches in-processing approaches, especially for models trained at scale.

result.text: The paper tackles the mismatch between standard transformer architectures and the iterative nature of many learning algorithms, asking how transformers can more efficiently emulate iterative computation when doing in-context learning on data-fitting tasks. Its key insight is that introducing an explicit recurrent "loop"—re-running a smaller transformer multiple times with shared weights and preserved hidden state—injects iterative structure that lets the model perform multi-step computation without a large parameter budget. The method trains a looped transformer that shares parameters across iterations and feeds back latent states between passes, and evaluates it on a suite of synthetic and real data-fitting problems to compare accuracy and efficiency. Experiments show the looped transformer matches or approaches the performance of a much larger standard transformer while using under 10% of the parameters, indicating iterative recurrence is an effective way to learn learning algorithms.

result.text: The paper studies the vulnerability of counterfactual explanations—used to give recourse to individuals affected by algorithmic decisions—by showing they can be manipulated via small perturbations, so ostensibly similar inputs yield drastically different recommended changes. The key insight is that lack of robustness in counterfactuals enables an attacker or model designer to create classifiers that appear fair under standard audits yet, under slight perturbations, produce much lower-cost recourse for targeted subgroups. Methodologically, the authors formalize a vulnerability framework, introduce an objective to train models that exploit this instability to reduce recourse cost for chosen groups, and empirically demonstrate on loan and violent-crime prediction datasets that certain subgroups can receive up to 20× lower-cost recourse under perturbation. These findings highlight a new failure mode for counterfactual explanations and motivate research into robust, manipulation-resistant recourse methods.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of efficient, generalizable trajectory similarity computation, noting that existing deep-learning methods require heavy preprocessing and produce immature trajectory embeddings with limited generality. The key insight is that embedding map grids with a knowledge-graph–inspired GRot method and then using a prompt-based trajectory embedding trained with unsupervised contrastive learning can better capture grid neighborhood relations, trajectory structure, and point order while avoiding costly supervised preprocessing. The method first learns robust grid representations via GRot, feeds those into a prompt trajectory embedding network that aligns grid and trajectory spaces through a customized prompt paradigm, and trains the whole model with contrastive learning using novel positive-sample generation strategies to provide generality. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets show KGTS outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

result.text: The paper tackles non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM), i.e., decomposing an aggregate household power signal into per-appliance consumption, with a focus on accurately modeling appliances that operate in multiple discrete states and transition between them. The key insight is that explicitly separating state estimation from per-state power regression—and enforcing temporal consistency of state sequences—improves disaggregation accuracy and generalization to unseen appliances. To realize this, the authors propose MSDC, a dual-CNN architecture where one convolutional branch predicts a distribution over discrete appliance states and the other predicts the power level associated with each state, and they couple these outputs with a conditional random field (CRF) that models state transitions; evaluated on REDD and UK-DALE, MSDC yields substantial MAE and SAE improvements over prior methods.

The paper tackles the often-overlooked bottleneck of parallel environment execution in reinforcement learning systems, which limits overall training throughput despite advances in other system components. The key insight is that a carefully designed, highly parallel execution engine—separating environment simulation from Python and exploiting efficient multithreading and batching—can dramatically increase environment step throughput across hardware tiers. The authors implement EnvPool, an open-source C++/multi-threaded environment pool with language bindings and compatibility layers for existing RL libraries, demonstrating orders-of-magnitude speedups (e.g., up to 1M frames/s on Atari and 3M frames/s on MuJoCo on a DGX-A100, and 2.8× faster than Python subprocesses on a laptop). By providing a plug-and-play, high-throughput environment backend, EnvPool enables much faster iteration and scaling for RL research and training pipelines.

result.text: The paper investigates why Adam, which blends adaptive learning rates and momentum, often converges faster but generalizes worse than SGD by disentangling the separate effects of adaptive learning rate and momentum in a diffusion-theoretic framework. The key insight is that adaptive learning rates help escape saddle points effectively but do not bias optimization toward flat minima, whereas momentum induces a drift that aids saddle escape while leaving flat-minimum selection largely unchanged—explaining SGD’s superior generalization when combined with momentum. Based on this analysis the authors propose Adaptive Inertia, a novel optimizer that applies parameter-wise adaptive inertia (momentum) to retain fast saddle escape while incorporating a bias toward flat minima similar to SGD, and they provide theoretical support plus empirical results showing improved generalization over both SGD and conventional adaptive methods.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of generative commonsense reasoning, where pre-trained text generation models often produce implausible sentences because they do not explicitly use structured commonsense relations. result.text: The paper addresses the gap between deep learning’s empirical success on high-dimensional data and statistical theories whose sample complexity scales with the ambient dimension, by studying function approximation and binary classification when data lie on a low-dimensional manifold. result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

result.text: The paper studies why fast single-step adversarial training with FGSM can suddenly fail—“catastrophic overfitting”—losing robustness during training, and questions whether the commonly used random initialization fixes the issue. The key insight is that randomness only helps by shrinking effective perturbation size and that catastrophic overfitting arises from local nonlinearity (even in tiny networks or a single filter) which makes the FGSM linear approximation invalid. To address this, the authors introduce GradAlign, a regularizer that maximizes alignment of input gradients within the perturbation set so the FGSM perturbation better matches multi-step solutions, thereby preventing overfitting and enabling effective fast adversarial training for larger ℓ∞ radii. Experiments show GradAlign narrows the robustness gap to multi-step methods while keeping training efficient.

result.text: The paper examines whether adaptive test-time defenses—methods that adjust a classifier at inference to resist adversarial attacks—actually improve robustness, addressing concerns that such defenses might offer gains beyond static, pre-trained models. The key insight is that, despite theoretical promise, many adaptive strategies fail in practice: when subjected to rigorous, attack-aware evaluation they do not meaningfully outperform well-tuned static defenses and can even degrade performance or increase inference cost. The authors categorize adaptive defenses, implement and stress-test a representative set on image classification benchmarks using stronger, adaptive attacks and careful threat modeling, and find no substantive robustness gains, then provide an expanded, concrete evaluation checklist extending Carlini et al. (2019) tailored to the unique failure modes and evaluation pitfalls of adaptive test-time defenses.

result.text: The paper tackles the trade-off in deep ensembles between increasing member diversity (which improves ensemble performance) and preserving individual network accuracy, noting that many diversity-boosting regularizers harm single-model performance. The key insight is that useful diversity should eliminate spurious, conditionally redundant information between members’ features while preserving class-relevant shared information, formalized via conditional mutual information: members may share predictive signal but should not be able to predict each other’s features beyond what the label explains. The method, DICE, augments a classification loss with an information-bottleneck term and an adversarial conditional mutual information estimator that penalizes conditional predictability between pairs of feature extractors, thereby reducing simultaneous errors without degrading class information; this yields state-of-the-art ensemble accuracy and improved calibration, uncertainty and OOD detection (e.g., 5 DICE-trained networks match 7 independently trained ones on CIFAR-10/100).

result.text: The paper addresses how to extend denoising diffusion probabilistic models to discrete data, where existing approaches (like multinomial diffusion) use simplistic, often uniform corruption that limits performance on text and images. The key insight is that discrete diffusion need not be restricted to uniform transitions: by designing structured transition matrices—e.g., Gaussian-like kernels over discrete indices, nearest-neighbor moves in an embedding space, or transitions with absorbing states—one can better mimic meaningful corruptions and thereby improve generation and likelihood. The method, called D3PM, defines flexible discrete-state corruption processes parameterized by these transition matrices, trains models with a novel loss that augments the usual variational lower bound with an auxiliary cross-entropy term, and uses corresponding denoising conditionals to sample; this yields strong character-level text results at scale and image performance on CIFAR-10 that rivals continuous DDPMs while improving likelihood.

result.text: The paper addresses how to optimally scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models to minimize compute for a given performance by expanding the variables considered in scaling analysis to include a new hyperparameter, granularity, that controls expert size. The key insight is that fine-grained control over expert size fundamentally changes scaling behavior: MoE models obey predictable power-law scaling with respect to model size, training tokens, and granularity, and these relationships show that MoEs outperform dense Transformers increasingly as compute and model size grow. Methodologically, the authors derive analytic scaling laws incorporating granularity, validate them empirically, and use the laws to compute optimal allocations of parameters, experts, and tokens under fixed compute budgets, revealing that matching expert size to feed‑forward layer width is suboptimal across most budgets.

result.text: The paper introduces PlasticineLab, a differentiable physics benchmark for soft-body manipulation that fills the gap left by existing simulators which focus on rigid bodies and provide no gradients for planning and control. The key insight is that enabling differentiable elastic and plastic deformation in a soft-body engine exposes new challenges but also allows gradient-based optimization to directly exploit physics gradients for control, offering a complementary pathway to reinforcement learning. Methodologically, the authors implement a suite of plasticine-deformation tasks on top of DiffTaichi, evaluate standard RL algorithms and gradient-based open-loop control optimization using the engine’s gradients, and compare their performance across tasks. Results show that RL struggles to learn efficient policies for most tasks, while gradient-based optimization converges quickly on short-horizon problems but still fails on multi-stage, long-horizon tasks, motivating hybrid approaches that combine differentiable physics with learning.

The PC-PG algorithm alternates between constructing a policy cover that ensures sufficient state-action coverage (via exploration objectives and ensemble updates) and performing policy-gradient optimization restricted to that cover, yielding polynomial sample and runtime guarantees for tabular and linear/RKHS MDPs and providing robustness results under average-case and distribution-shift approximation errors. Empirical results illustrate that PC-PG improves exploration and learning across both reward-free and reward-driven tasks.

result.text: BEVFusion addresses the problem that current LiDAR-camera fusion methods for 3D object detection break catastrophically when LiDAR malfunctions, because they treat point clouds as mandatory queries for image features. The key insight is to decouple the camera stream from LiDAR input so the image-derived bird’s-eye-view (BEV) representation can be produced independently, enabling robust fusion even if LiDAR fails. The method constructs separate BEV feature streams from images and LiDAR and then fuses them in BEV space, allowing the camera-only branch to produce predictions when LiDAR is absent or degraded; this simple design not only outperforms prior fusion approaches in standard settings but also yields large mAP gains (15.7%–28.9%) under simulated LiDAR malfunction.

result.text: Muse addresses efficient, high-quality text-to-image generation by replacing costly pixel-space diffusion and sequential autoregressive decoding with a masked token prediction paradigm in discrete image-token space. The key insight is that conditioning a Transformer on rich text embeddings from a pre-trained large language model and training it to reconstruct randomly masked image tokens yields parallel, high-fidelity generation that captures fine-grained language-conditioned visual concepts (objects, relations, pose, cardinality) while requiring far fewer sampling steps. Methodologically, Muse tokenizes images into discrete tokens, encodes text with a frozen LLM, and trains a Transformer to predict masked image tokens in parallel (masked modeling), which yields state-of-the-art FID/CLIP results with models from 900M to 3B parameters and naturally supports editing tasks like inpainting and outpainting without additional fine-tuning.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of training GANs when available training images are scarce, which typically causes the discriminator to overfit and destabilize adversarial training. The key insight is that applying adaptive, online data augmentations to discriminator inputs prevents overfitting without altering loss functions or network architectures, and that the augmentation strength can be tuned automatically during training. Their method augments only the discriminator with a learned probability schedule for various transformations, enabling stable GAN training from scratch or via fine-tuning on small datasets; experiments show realistic image synthesis with only a few thousand images and substantially improved FID scores (e.g., lowering CIFAR-10 record from 5.59 to 2.42).

The method is to pretrain a very large transformer-based autoregressive model and evaluate it across numerous benchmarks by providing task descriptions and a handful of demonstrations in-context (few-shot) or none (zero-shot), showing competitive results on translation, QA, cloze, and some reasoning and domain-adaptation tasks while also noting limitations, failure modes, and societal risks.

result.text: This paper tackles image-goal navigation without relying on simulators, reinforcement learning, or ground-truth maps, motivated by the expense and sim-to-real gap of existing methods. The key insight is that passive video of an agent roaming through environments contains sufficient self-supervised signals to learn navigation policies without active interaction or explicit rewards. The method, called No RL, No Simulator (NRNS), trains a policy purely from offline roaming videos using self-supervised objectives that learn correspondences between images and actions (e.g., predicting visual goal-directed progress or relocalization) to guide navigation at test time. NRNS is simple, scalable, and empirically outperforms prior RL-based approaches on image-goal navigation, offering a strong baseline for future work.

result.text: The paper tackles composed image retrieval, where a user provides a reference image plus textual instructions to specify how to shift to a target image, and argues that prior work treats text merely as description and thus often ignores the reference image’s visual cues. The key insight is to view the text as an instruction that induces a structured semantic shift which can be explicitly decomposed into two complementary operations—degradation (mapping the reference image to an intermediate visual prototype) and upgradation (transforming that prototype into the target representation). The proposed Semantic Shift Network (SSN) implements this decomposition by parsing text into degradation and upgradation components and applying them sequentially to generate enriched target features, and experiments on CIRR and FashionIQ show substantial gains (5.42% and 1.37%) and new state-of-the-art results.

result.text: The paper addresses learning solution operators of partial differential equations (PDEs) using convolution-based neural architectures, challenging the prevailing belief that convolutional networks are inconsistent for function-to-function maps. The key insight is that by adapting convolutional networks to respect the underlying continuous function space—preserving translation equivariance and continuity even when discretized—one can obtain architectures that are universal approximators of PDE operators. The authors introduce Convolutional Neural Operators (CNOs), prove a universality theorem showing CNOs can approximate operators from PDEs to arbitrary accuracy, and demonstrate empirically on a diverse benchmark suite (including multi-scale solutions) that CNOs outperform prior baselines, offering a robust, accurate alternative for operator learning.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of understanding and preventing overfitting in meta-learning—especially when the number of meta-training tasks is small—by providing rigorous generalization guarantees for Bayesian base learners under unbounded loss. Its key insight is that PAC-Bayesian analysis can be extended to the meta-learning setting to yield novel generalization bounds that guide the design of a PAC-optimal hyper-posterior and a principled meta-regularizer, thereby linking Bayesian optimality with PAC-style guarantees. The method derives these PAC-Bayes bounds and uses them to define and optimize a PAC-optimal hyper-posterior (PACOH), which when instantiated with Gaussian process base learners yields a meta-learning algorithm that jointly learns hyperposteriors for task-level Bayesian predictors; this approach improves predictive accuracy and calibrated uncertainty compared with several popular baselines.

result.text: The paper tackles the apparent gap between classical PointNet++ and more recent point-cloud networks, arguing that much of the observed improvement in newer models arises from better training recipes and larger models rather than fundamentally superior architectures. Its key insight is that revisiting training, augmentation, and scaling can unlock substantial untapped performance in PointNet++ and that modern architectural tweaks—specifically an inverted residual bottleneck and separable MLPs—allow efficient scaling without sacrificing simplicity. Methodologically, the authors first develop a suite of improved training and optimization strategies that boost vanilla PointNet++ accuracy dramatically (e.g., ScanObjectNN OA from 77.9% to 86.1%), then incorporate the inverted-bottleneck and separable-MLP design to produce PointNeXt, a family of scalable models that deliver state-of-the-art classification and segmentation results while being much faster at inference.

result.text: Chameleon addresses the limitations of large language models (LLMs) in accessing up-to-date information, using external tools, and performing precise mathematical or logical reasoning by enabling plug-and-play compositional reasoning. The key insight is to synthesize executable programs that compose heterogeneous modules—LLMs, vision models, web search, Python functions, and heuristics—so that an LLM acts as a planner that assembles and sequences tools tailored to each task. Concretely, Chameleon uses a planner powered by an LLM (e.g., GPT-4) to infer constraints from instructions, select and order appropriate tool calls, and execute the resulting program to produce final answers; this approach yields large gains on multi-modal, knowledge-intensive benchmarks (e.g., +11.37% on ScienceQA and +17.0% on TabMWP) and demonstrates more consistent, rational tool selection when using a stronger planner model.

result.text: This paper tackles the problem of crafting transferable adversarial perturbations for complex natural scenes containing multiple semantically related objects, where prior attacks have largely focused on single-object images and single-object classifiers. The key insight is that leveraging joint image-text representations from a pre-trained vision-language model (CLIP) allows modeling inter-object semantics and yields stronger, more transferable perturbations than image-only generative attacks. The method, called GAMA, trains a generative perturbation network adversarially using CLIP’s joint image-text features as the objective (rather than only visual logits), so the generator learns to produce perturbations that disrupt semantic alignment across objects and transfer to unknown victim classifiers and data distributions. The method, wav2vec 2.0, uses a convolutional feature encoder to map raw audio to latent vectors, a Transformer context network over masked latent sequences, and a quantization module that produces discrete targets for a contrastive prediction task; after large-scale self-supervised pretraining the model is fine-tuned end-to-end on transcribed speech, delivering state-of-the-art WERs even with minutes or hours of labeled data.

result.text: The paper examines whether commonly-used (first-order) influence functions, which estimate how individual training samples affect test predictions using gradients and the Hessian, remain reliable for non-convex deep neural networks. The key insight is that influence estimates are not generally robust in deep learning: their accuracy depends strongly on architecture, depth/width, degree of overparameterization, regularization (notably weight decay), and even which test point is analyzed, so methods that work for convex linear models can fail widely in non-convex settings. The CaPC method implements a protocol in which each party retains and improves its own local model: encrypted and MPC-protected computations aggregate teacher outputs privately, produce distilled signals for local training, and enforce differential-privacy-style protections to prevent inference attacks, all while supporting heterogeneous architectures and non-IID data. The proposed method, Neural Attention Distillation (NAD), obtains a teacher by independently fine-tuning on a small clean subset and then distills its intermediate attention maps into the backdoored student during further fine-tuning on that same clean data, using attention-alignment losses to guide the student toward the teacher’s behavior. result.text: The paper tackles scalable Bayesian inverse reinforcement learning, aiming to infer a posterior over latent reward functions without relying on costly inner-loop MDP solvers or environment interaction, which limits prior Bayesian IRL to small tabular problems and makes non-Bayesian scalable methods unsafe for high-stakes offline settings. Its key insight is to represent GNN computations as expressions in a procedural tensor language whose syntax (number of indices and nesting depth of summations) directly controls expressive power relative to Weisfeiler-Leman (WL) tests, making WL-based separation bounds immediate. Using this tensor-language view the authors define higher-order message-passing neural networks (k-MPNNs) as a natural extension of MPNNs, derive separation-power bounds and universality results by simple index/summation counting, and show how architectural choices map to WL strength. The method, SwAV, jointly learns cluster prototypes and assigns views to prototypes so that the assignment predicted from one view matches the assignment computed from another, enabling training without pairwise comparisons, momentum encoders, or large memory buffers; it also introduces multi-crop augmentation (mixing different-resolution views) to improve efficiency and performance. result.text: The paper addresses how well deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can approximate functions with Sobolev regularity and the implications for classification risk, especially in high-dimensional settings where curse-of-dimensionality is a concern. The key insight is a new non-asymptotic approximation error bound for CNNs that includes an explicit prefactor which, for Sobolev-regular functions embeddable in Hölder spaces, depends only polynomially on the ambient dimension (rather than exponentially), and can be further improved when the target is supported near a lower-dimensional manifold. Methodologically, the authors construct CNN approximators with controlled depth and filter lengths to prove these bounds, derive corresponding approximation results for manifold-supported functions, and then translate the approximation guarantees into excess risk bounds for classification with common convex surrogate losses (cross-entropy, hinge, logistic, exponential, least squares), showing that CNN-based classifiers can avoid the curse of dimensionality under manifold assumptions.

result.text: Squeezeformer addresses inefficiencies and suboptimal design choices in the Conformer backbone for automatic speech recognition, aiming to reduce computation on long sequences while improving accuracy. The key insight is that both macro-architecture (overall block ordering and downsampling) and micro-architecture (activation functions, normalization placement, and convolutional simplifications) of Conformer can be streamlined to cut cost and redundancy without sacrificing representational power. Squeezeformer implements a Temporal U-Net macro-structure to lower multi-head attention cost on long inputs, replaces Conformer's Macaron ordering with simpler attention/convolution followed by feed-forward blocks, and refines micro-components by simplifying convolutional activations, removing redundant LayerNorms, and adding an efficient depthwise down-sampling layer. result.text: The paper addresses the gap between the community standard of "adaptive attacks" for evaluating adversarial defenses and the reality that many such evaluations are incomplete, leaving purported defenses vulnerable. Its key insight is that failures to fully adapt attacks often stem from methodological oversights—such as not modeling the defense's transformations, gradient masking, randomized or non-differentiable components, or incorrect threat models—rather than from genuine robustness, so systematically constructing stronger adaptive strategies can break many published defenses. The authors analyze thirteen recent defenses and distill practical techniques (e.g., white-box modeling of all defense components, gradient estimation or proxy gradients for non-differentiable parts, expectation over transformation for randomness, careful loss/attack selection, and verification-style checks) to craft complete adaptive attacks, demonstrating how to modify attacks to account for each defense’s specifics. Their method is less a single algorithm than a prescriptive evaluation methodology for designing and documenting adaptive attacks so defenses are tested against the strongest feasible adversary.

Methodologically, the authors derive these rates by proving Łojasiewicz-type inequalities for the softmax parametrization, bounding optimal-action probabilities during optimization, analyzing the entropy-regularized objective to obtain exponential contraction, and complementing upper bounds with Ω(1/t) lower bounds to explain the improvement from entropy via a non-uniform Łojasiewicz degree.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of detecting seizure events and the specific EEG channels involved without relying on scarce, costly labeled seizure data by formulating anomalous channel and clip detection as a self-supervised problem. Its key insight is that local structural and contextual patterns in EEG can be captured via sub-graphs, and contrasting positive (normal) and negative sub-graphs lets a model learn discriminative representations of normal brain activity so anomalies (seizures) stand out at test time. The method builds EEG graphs from channel relationships, samples local sub-graphs as positive and negative pairs, and trains a model with a combination of contrastive and generative losses to learn normal EEG dynamics; at inference, deviations from the learned normal manifold identify seizure channels and clips. result.text: The paper tackles long-horizon visual planning for complex robotic tasks by generating detailed multimodal (video + language) plans that bridge high-level instructions and low-level actions. The key insight is to treat a pretrained text-to-video model as a learned dynamics simulator and vision-language models as both policy and value estimators, enabling search over imagined video trajectories to evaluate and refine plans. The method, called Video Language Planning (VLP), runs a tree search that proposes candidate video continuations with a text-to-video model, scores them with learned vision-language value/policy models, and iteratively expands and selects high-value video-language plans; these generated videos can then be converted into executable goals for goal-conditioned controllers. Empirically, VLP scales with computation budget and yields substantially higher long-horizon task success on diverse simulated and real-robot domains (including multi-object and bi-arm manipulation) than prior approaches.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of domain generalization—training models on multiple source domains so they perform well on unseen target domains—by focusing on the role of image “style” (domain-specific low-level statistics) captured in early CNN layers. The key insight is that mixing instance-level feature statistics (mean and variance) across samples creates novel, realistic style variations that implicitly synthesize new domains and thereby increase source-domain diversity. The proposed method, MixStyle, stochastically mixes batch-normalization–style statistics between feature maps of different examples during training (implemented within mini-batch SGD at shallow layers), which is simple to integrate and requires no extra parameters. Empirically, MixStyle improves generalization across tasks including classification, instance retrieval, and reinforcement learning by making learned features more robust to domain shifts.

result.text: The paper addresses why large language models can perform in-context learning—adapting to a downstream task solely by conditioning on example prompts—despite not being explicitly trained to learn. The key insight is that when pretraining data exhibit long-range coherence governed by latent document-level concepts, the model implicitly learns to perform Bayesian inference over those latent variables, and at test time it applies the same inference to infer a shared concept across prompt examples, producing in-context learning behavior. result.text: The paper addresses the risk of backdoor attacks when training is outsourced, arguing that existing work has focused on data poisoning but overlooked supply-chain threats that directly alter model parameters. The key insight is that handcrafted weight manipulations give an attacker greater degrees of freedom than poisoning, enabling stealthier, higher-fidelity backdoors that can evade many existing detection and removal defenses. The authors demonstrate a method for injecting backdoors by directly modifying network weights of trained models—designing and applying targeted perturbations across multiple architectures and datasets—to achieve high attack success rates (above 96%) while preserving overall accuracy. Their results highlight the need to broaden research on backdoor defenses to cover weight-level, supply-chain manipulations in addition to data poisoning.

result.text: The paper addresses defending against poisoning-based backdoor attacks when training data or models come from untrusted sources by identifying and removing poisoned samples. The key insight is that feature representations of poisoned (triggered) samples are more sensitive to input transformations than clean samples, so measuring feature consistency towards transformations (FCT) reliably distinguishes poisoned from clean data. Methodologically, they compute the FCT metric to separate samples, then either train a secure model from scratch via a two-stage secure training module that excludes or downweights flagged poisons, or apply a backdoor removal procedure on an existing backdoored model that alternates unlearning the distinguished poisoned samples and relearning the clean ones; experiments on three benchmarks across eight attack types show state-of-the-art defense performance.

result.text: The paper addresses dataset distillation: how to compress large training sets into a tiny synthetic dataset that still trains models well, which is increasingly important as models and data grow. The key insight is that infinitely wide convolutional neural networks can be analyzed via their corresponding kernel (the neural tangent/kernel regime), and that performing distillation in this kernel/meta-learning framework yields more faithful and transferable synthetic examples than prior methods. result.text: The paper tackles overfitting when fine-tuning large pretrained language models on low-resource target tasks by addressing the problem that many pretrained features are irrelevant for specific tasks. Its key insight is to apply the Variational Information Bottleneck (VIB) to force the model to compress representations and discard task-irrelevant information, which both reduces overfitting and yields sentence encodings less sensitive to dataset biases. The method integrates a VIB objective into fine-tuning: it learns a stochastic bottlenecked latent representation of inputs via a variational encoder and optimizes a trade-off between task predictive likelihood and mutual information penalty (KL regularizer) to constrain information flow from the pretrained encoder to the classifier. Empirically, this VIB-enhanced fine-tuning improves performance across seven low-resource tasks and boosts out-of-domain generalization on most of 15 NLI benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses optimization for performative prediction, where deploying a model changes the future data distribution through agents' responses, distinguishing deployment from mere parameter updates. The key insight is that performativity creates a trade-off between updating frequently (which causes repeated distribution shifts) and updating lazily (which accumulates optimization error under a fixed distribution), and that this trade-off depends on the strength of performative effects. Under smoothness and strong convexity assumptions, the authors analyze two strategies—greedy deploy (deploy after every stochastic update) and lazy deploy (perform multiple updates per deployment)—and derive non-asymptotic convergence rates that interpolate to the standard O(1/k) rate as performativity vanishes, identifying regimes where each strategy is preferable; they validate these theoretical findings with synthetic and strategic-classification experiments.
