result.text: The paper addresses fine-grained visual classification, where subtle inter-class differences make it hard to locate and exploit the truly discriminative object parts. The key insight is that a vision transformer's self-attention between the class token and patch tokens naturally indicates the importance of patches, so aggregating raw attention can guide selection of the most discriminative parts without complex region-detection pipelines. The authors propose TransFG, which augments a ViT with a Part Selection Module that fuses attention weights into an attention map to select informative patch tokens and model their relations, and they add a contrastive loss to push apart representations of confusing classes. Experiments on five fine-grained benchmarks show that this attention-guided patch selection and relational modeling yields state-of-the-art performance.

result.text: The paper addresses why large models trained with SGD often follow neural scaling laws—test error falling as a power law with model and data size—despite classical bias–variance intuition that variance should grow with model size. The key insight is that in an infinite-dimensional linear regression model with a power-law eigenvalue spectrum and Gaussian prior on the optimal parameters, the variance term that would increase with parameter count is suppressed by SGD’s implicit regularization, so the reducible test error is dominated by approximation and data-limited terms. result.text: The paper tackles the computational intractability of the Projection Robust Wasserstein (PRW) distance—a robust variant of the Wasserstein distance designed to compare high-dimensional probability measures but hindered by a non-convex, non-smooth optimization formulation. Its key insight is that, despite theoretical minimax hardness results, the original PRW/WPP formulation can be practically and efficiently optimized by exploiting the low-dimensional search structure through Riemannian optimization on the Grassmann manifold, often outperforming convex relaxations. The authors propose three simple Riemannian algorithms (with provable complexity bounds for each) that directly optimize the projection subspace and transport plan, and validate their approach with extensive synthetic and real-data experiments showing improved robustness and computational efficiency. This work thus establishes a practical computational framework linking optimal transport and Riemannian optimization and provides the first concrete complexity guarantees for computing PRW.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of poor and noisy geometry reconstruction in neural volume rendering, where prior methods model geometry indirectly via a generic density field and extract surfaces from arbitrary density level sets. result.text: The paper tackles the inconsistent evaluation and lack of strong, easy-to-use baselines in the literature on deep learning for tabular data, where diverse novel architectures are reported on different benchmarks and protocols making fair comparison difficult. The authors systematically reimplement and compare major families of tabular DL models, introduce these two baseline architectures, and run extensive experiments against many existing methods and Gradient Boosted Decision Trees across diverse tasks with unified training and tuning; their results show the Transformer variant frequently leads while no approach is universally dominant.

result.text: The paper addresses generative modeling of 3D point clouds with the goal of producing not just point representations but an explicit parametrization of object surfaces. The key insight is to use a hypernetwork that, given a latent code, outputs the weights of a smaller “target” network which maps samples from a simple 3D prior (a unit ball) into the object’s surface, so the target network’s weights become a continuous surface parametrization rather than a discrete point set. Methodologically, the authors train an autoencoder-style hypernetwork to reconstruct 3D shapes by producing target-network weights for each shape; at generation time they sample latent codes and produce target networks that transform uniform samples into point clouds (and implicitly meshes), yielding mesh-capable generative models with point cloud quality comparable to state-of-the-art.

The paper addresses improving post-training quantization (PTQ)—quantizing neural networks without end-to-end retraining—whose accuracy typically lags behind quantization-aware training (QAT) and struggles at very low bitwidths. The key insight is to treat PTQ as a block-wise reconstruction problem and use a second-order error analysis to balance cross-layer dependency and generalization error, enabling aggressive quantization down to INT2 while selectively using mixed precision where sensitivity demands. The method, called BRECQ, reconstructs and quantizes network building blocks one-by-one using block-wise optimization informed by second-order approximations of quantization error, and integrates inter- and intra-layer sensitivity estimates to assign mixed precisions; extensive experiments show BRECQ produces 4-bit ResNet and MobileNetV2 models comparable to QAT and dramatically speeds up quantization.

result.text: The paper addresses improving stochastic local search (SLS) for the (Weighted) Partial MaxSAT problem, where current clause-weighting strategies inadequately handle the interplay of hard and soft clauses and are sensitive to initial weight settings. The key insight is that (a) the initial soft-clause weights substantially affect SLS performance and (b) hard and soft clauses should be treated with different update conditions, rather than using a single uniform weighting rule. The authors introduce NuWLS, which combines a principled weight-initialization method for soft clauses with a novel clause-weighting scheme that applies distinct update criteria to hard versus soft clauses, and integrate these into an SLS framework. Empirical evaluation on six benchmarks from MaxSAT Evaluations 2019–2021 shows NuWLS substantially improves over existing SLS and even SAT-based incomplete solvers, and a hybrid combining NuWLS with a SAT-based solver won all incomplete-track categories at MSE 2022.

result.text: The paper tackles improving neural network pruning beyond standard magnitude-based methods, which decide pruned weights solely by individual magnitude and can be short-sighted when multiple layers interact. The key insight is that magnitude pruning optimizes Frobenius-norm distortion only for a single layer, so extending this objective across multiple consecutive layers—i.e., looking ahead to how pruning in earlier layers affects downstream layers—yields better global fidelity. The authors propose "lookahead pruning," a simple algorithm that jointly selects weights to remove by minimizing multi-layer Frobenius distortion (effectively solving a small multi-layer optimization instead of independent per-layer thresholds) and demonstrate empirically that it consistently outperforms magnitude pruning on architectures like VGG and ResNet, especially at high sparsity.

To realize this, TAILOR first uses an adversarial multi-modal refinement module to separate and enhance common versus private modality signals, then applies a BERT-like cross-modal encoder to progressively fuse those representations, and finally employs a label-guided decoder that leverages label semantics to generate customized representations per label. Experiments on CMU-MOSEI in aligned and unaligned settings show that this approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

result.text: The paper tackles reducing discrimination in deep neural networks without expensive sensitive-attribute labels or fully debiased encoders by asking whether fairness can be achieved by only modifying the classification head while leaving biased representations intact. The key insight is that forcing the classifier to ignore spurious correlations between encoded sensitive information and class labels—by training it on "neutralized" representations derived from samples that share the same ground-truth label but differ in sensitive attributes—can yield fairer decisions without reworking the encoder. The method, Representation Neutralization for Fairness (RNF), constructs neutralized inputs from paired examples (same label, different sensitive attribute) and trains the task head to produce consistent predictions for these neutralized representations; when sensitive annotations are unavailable, RNF generates proxy attribute labels using a bias-amplified model. result.text: The paper addresses fairness in algorithmic recourse—recommendations given to individuals to change an unfavorable classifier outcome—pointing out that prior measures ignoring causal feature relationships can miss disparate downstream effects. They validate their approach theoretically and empirically, including a case study on the Adult dataset, and argue that some fairness issues revealed by their criteria may warrant societal interventions rather than solely classifier constraints.

result.text: This paper tackles trajectory similarity computation for trajectories constrained by road networks, noting that prior methods designed for Euclidean trajectories ignore network topology and multi-relation semantics of points. result.text: The paper investigates why some neural networks become effectively linear as their width grows, equivalently why their neural tangent kernel (NTK) becomes constant, and whether this is necessary for successful training. The key insight is that constancy of the NTK and transition-to-linearity follow from the way the operator norm of the network Hessian scales with width: when the Hessian norm vanishes with increasing width, higher-order terms in the network’s Taylor expansion disappear and the network behaves like its linearization; conversely, if the last layer is nonlinear or the Hessian norm does not shrink, the NTK need not become constant. Methodologically, the authors develop a general Hessian-scaling framework that bounds second-order contributions across common architectures, prove conditions under which the NTK is asymptotically constant (or not), and use this analysis to show that constant NTK is neither universal for wide nets nor required for gradient-descent optimization.

result.text: The paper addresses whether sparse transformer attention—designed to reduce the quadratic O(n^2) pairwise attention cost—can retain the universal approximation power of dense transformers and how sparsity pattern and level affect expressivity. The key insight is that surprisingly few connections suffice: under simple sufficient conditions on the sparsity graph, attention layers with only O(n) nonzero connections per layer can still approximate any sequence-to-sequence function that a dense transformer can. The authors formalize a unifying framework capturing many existing sparse attention schemes, prove universality results for families of sparsity patterns (identifying the connectivity properties required), and construct architectures and proofs showing O(n)-connected layers achieve the same function class as dense attention. They validate these theoretical findings with experiments comparing different sparsity patterns and levels on standard NLP tasks, illustrating practical tradeoffs between efficiency and performance.

result.text: The paper addresses why large models trained with SGD often follow neural scaling laws—test error falling as a power law with model and data size—despite classical bias–variance intuition that variance should grow with model size. Concretely, for M learned parameters and N samples the reducible error scales as Θ(M^{-(a−1)} + N^{-(a−1)/a}) when the covariance spectrum decays with exponent a>1, a result derived for one-pass SGD on sketched covariates and validated by simulations.

The key insight is that using lengthy, multi-shot YouTube videos with free-form, human-annotated questions aligned to a detailed ability taxonomy, and leveraging GPT-4 for automated scoring, yields a more faithful and robust measure of LVLMs’ practical video comprehension. result.text: The paper examines whether practical approximate machine unlearning techniques—designed to comply with data deletion requests—can also remove the effects of poisoned training examples, a desirable property for mitigating data poisoning attacks. The key insight is empirical: across a range of poisoning types (indiscriminate, targeted, and a new Gaussian poisoning attack), model architectures (image classifiers and large language models), and generous compute budgets, existing unlearning methods often fail to erase poisoning effects even when they appear effective by standard metrics. result.text: The paper investigates the robustness of safe reinforcement learning (RL), showing that policies trained to satisfy safety constraints can be vulnerable to carefully crafted observational perturbations that induce unsafe behavior. The key insight is that adversarial attacks tailored for standard RL do not transfer well to safe RL and that attacks which maximize reward can paradoxically be both potent and stealthy by keeping task performance high while causing safety violations. The authors formally analyze attacker objectives in the safe RL context, propose two new attack strategies—one maximizing accumulated safety cost and one maximizing reward—and introduce a robust training framework to defend against such perturbations. They validate their findings with comprehensive experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of the attacks and the benefits of their robustness approach.

result.text: The paper addresses optimization for performative prediction, where deploying a model changes the future data distribution through agents' responses, distinguishing deployment from mere parameter updates. The key insight is that performativity creates a trade-off between updating frequently (which causes repeated distribution shifts) and updating lazily (which accumulates optimization error under a fixed distribution), and that this trade-off depends on the strength of performative effects. result.text: The paper addresses defending machine learning models against model inversion (MI) attacks, which try to infer sensitive training-data attributes from model outputs, noting existing defenses either harm utility or are model-specific. The key insight is that preventing MI attacks can be framed as limiting the mutual information between model inputs and outputs—if predictions reveal less information about inputs, adversaries have less to reconstruct—leading to a model-agnostic regularization principle. The authors propose MID (Mutual Information Regularization based Defense), derive tractable approximations of the mutual information regularizer for linear regression, decision trees, and neural networks, and formalize MI attacks via a game-based leakage definition to analyze why differential privacy can be ineffective; empirical results show MID achieves better utility-privacy trade-offs than prior defenses across multiple attacks, models, and datasets.

The paper introduces StressID, a large multimodal dataset aimed at improving automatic stress identification by providing synchronized high-quality video, audio, and physiological recordings (ECG, EDA, respiration) from 65 participants across 11 stress-inducing tasks. The key insight is that combining behavioral (facial and vocal) and physiological signals collected under diverse stimuli—emotional clips, cognitive challenges, and public speaking—yields richer, more generalizable indicators of stress than unimodal sources. The authors describe a standardized data-collection protocol and annotation of perceived relaxation, stress, arousal, and valence, resulting in over 39 hours of labeled data, and present baseline pipelines that include signal cleaning, feature extraction, and classification for each modality as well as multimodal fusion models. By releasing the dataset and benchmarks, StressID enables development and evaluation of improved stress-detection systems that leverage complementary modalities.

result.text: The paper addresses how to design decision policies and counterfactual explanations when individuals can strategically change features in response to explanations to improve their chances of favorable decisions. The key insight is that while optimizing explanations for a given policy is NP-hard, the utility objective is nondecreasing and submodular (and the joint policy-plus-explanations objective is a non-monotone submodular maximization), which enables efficient approximation via greedy and recent randomized algorithms with provable guarantees. The authors therefore cast explanation selection as a submodular optimization problem, apply a greedy algorithm for the constrained (monotone) case and a randomized algorithm for the joint (non-monotone) case, and introduce matroid constraints to promote diversity of explanations across the population. Experiments on synthetic and real lending and credit-card datasets confirm that their algorithms produce explanation sets and policies that yield higher utility than several baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses few-shot fine-grained recognition, where the challenge is to learn discriminative part-level representations from very few labeled examples of closely related subordinate categories. The proposed Dual Attention Network builds two parallel branches—one that selects and aggregates a small set of informative deep descriptors via multi-instance learning and another that produces a soft-attended activation map—and fuses their outputs into a holistic image embedding that is trained via meta-learning in a metric space to generalize to novel classes. result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of deploying high-performing hyperspectral image (HSI) reconstruction models for snapshot compressive imaging (SCI) on resource-constrained devices by dramatically reducing model size and computation while retaining accuracy. Its key insight is that a carefully redesigned base network can be binarized without large performance loss if activations are adaptively redistributed before binarization and the gradient approximation during training closely matches the sign function. Concretely, the authors propose the Binarized Spectral-Redistribution Network (BiSRNet) built from a novel Binarized Spectral-Redistribution Convolution (BiSR-Conv) that adaptively reshapes HSI representations, employs a scalable hyperbolic tangent surrogate for Sign in backpropagation, and integrates four specialized binarized convolutional modules to handle dimensional mismatches and propagate full-precision information. Extensive experiments show BiSRNet outperforms existing binarization approaches and achieves reconstruction quality comparable to full-precision methods while being far more efficient and hardware-friendly.

result.text: The paper addresses why differentially private (DP) learning sometimes avoids the expected degradation in utility as model dimension grows, a phenomenon at odds with classical bounds that worsen with model size. The key insight is that performance depends not on raw parameter dimensionality but on the magnitudes of gradients when projected onto low-dimensional subspaces—if gradients concentrate in a few principal directions then privacy noise has much less harm. Methodologically, the authors formalize this via a "restricted Lipschitz continuity" condition for convex objectives, prove improved excess empirical and population risk bounds that can be independent of ambient dimension under additional assumptions, and empirically validate that gradients during private fine-tuning of large language models are dominated by a few principal components, explaining why large pretrained models can be privately fine-tuned effectively.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of high quantization error in post-training quantization (PTQ) for large language models by expanding the class of allowed transformations beyond simple per-weight scalings. Its key insight is that optimizing an equivalent affine transformation between pre- and post-quantized weights (and applying the inverse to preserve outputs) enlarges the optimization space and can substantially reduce quantization-induced error while retaining PTQ’s efficiency. The method, AffineQuant, directly optimizes an affine matrix for each layer subject to invertibility constraints enforced via a gradual mask optimization that starts with diagonal entries and progressively frees off-diagonal elements—leveraging the Levy–Desplanques theorem to maintain invertibility—and applies the corresponding inverse to keep pre- and post-quantization outputs equivalent. Empirically, this approach yields consistent improvements across LLMs and settings (e.g., better perplexity and zero-shot accuracy in 4/4-bit quantization) without runtime overhead.

result.text: The paper tackles the computational challenge of approximating the Shapley value—an axiomatic measure of player contribution whose exact computation is exponential in the number of agents—without relying on the usual marginal-contribution sampling schemes. Its key insight is a novel representation of the Shapley value that is detached from marginal contributions, enabling estimation strategies that avoid the variance and sampling inefficiencies inherent to marginal-based approaches. Building on this representation, the authors introduce two parameter-free, domain-independent algorithms (SVARM and Stratified SVARM) with provable approximation guarantees and demonstrate through theory and experiments on synthetic games and explainability tasks that these methods outperform or match state-of-the-art approximators.

result.text: The paper addresses the high communication cost in federated learning by eliminating frequent weight updates from clients to server. Its key insight is that useful models can be obtained not by training weights but by learning a sparse subnetwork (a binary mask) within a randomly initialized dense network, so only mask updates—far smaller than full-weight gradients—need to be communicated. The method freezes random initial weights and has clients collaboratively train a stochastic binary mask via federated rounds to identify and converge to an optimal sparse random subnetwork, yielding a final compact model with random weights and a learned sparsity pattern; experiments on MNIST, EMNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 show improved accuracy, faster convergence, and drastic communication reduction (under 1 bit per parameter) compared to baselines in low-bitrate settings.

result.text: The paper tackles building a single scalable model that can jointly understand and generate across vision and many languages, addressing limitations of prior work that scaled language far more than vision and lacked a unified multilingual multimodal interface. The key insight is that jointly scaling both vision and language components and leveraging large pretrained encoder–decoder LMs together with much larger vision backbones improves multimodal capabilities, so a balanced increase in visual capacity yields substantial gains. The method constructs PaLI by combining large pretrained language models with a newly trained 4B-parameter Vision Transformer (ViT-e), training on a massive multilingual image–text mixture (≈10 billion image–text pairs across 100+ languages) with a unified text-generation interface for tasks like captioning, VQA, and scene-text understanding. The resulting model is simple and modular yet achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple vision–language benchmarks while demonstrating the importance of joint scaling.

result.text: SmartPlay addresses the lack of a systematic benchmark for evaluating large language models as interactive, goal-directed agents by providing a suite of game-based tasks that probe agentic capabilities. Its key insight is that a small, diverse set of games—each designed to stress different cognitive skills—lets evaluators isolate and measure distinct agent abilities (e.g., planning, spatial reasoning, dependency reasoning, learning from history, handling randomness) across many variations. The method constructs six games (e.g., Rock-Paper-Scissors, Tower of Hanoi, Minecraft) with up to 20 evaluation settings and potentially infinite environment instances, maps each game to subsets of nine targeted capabilities, and uses performance across these controlled tasks to analyze strengths and gaps in LLM-agent behavior. By combining fine-grained capability attribution with broad, scalable task generation, SmartPlay provides both a rigorous testbed and a roadmap for improving LLM-based agents.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of applying large-scale self-supervised learning to music audio, where conventional speech/audio SSL struggles to capture musical properties like pitch and tonality. The key insight is that MLM-style acoustic pretraining benefits from teacher-generated pseudo-labels tailored to music: combining an acoustic teacher (RVQ-VAE) that captures timbral and temporal structure with a musical teacher based on Constant-Q Transform (CQT) that encodes pitched/tonal information yields better supervision than speech-focused teachers. Methodologically, MERT trains masked acoustic language models at scale (95M–330M parameters) using those dual teacher pseudo-labels and extensive stability and hyperparameter explorations, and demonstrates broad generalization by achieving state-of-the-art results across 14 music understanding tasks.

result.text: This paper tackles learning in stochastic shortest path (SSP) problems where an agent minimizes expected cost to reach a goal under unknown dynamics and costs, aiming for tight regret guarantees without prior knowledge of problem-dependent horizons. The key insight is that carefully skewing empirical transition estimates and adding a targeted exploration bonus to costs yields both optimism and stable convergence of value iteration, enabling minimax-optimal performance while being parameter-free. The authors develop EB-SSP, a model-based algorithm that perturbs empirical models to ensure optimistic planning and prove a minimax regret bound of Õ(B* sqrt(SAK)), matching lower bounds and not requiring knowledge of B* or the optimal time-to-goal T*; they also show variants and settings (e.g., positive costs or when T* is roughly known) where regret only depends logarithmically on T*, giving one of the first horizon-free guarantees beyond finite-horizon MDPs.

result.text: This paper investigates which positions in Transformer self-attention are truly important during pre-training and finds the surprising result that diagonal elements (i.e., positions attending to the same token) are the least important. The key insight is that many commonly visualized attention patterns from pre-trained models can mislead importance analysis, and that some attention entries—particularly diagonals—can be removed without harming model expressivity or downstream performance. To support this, the authors prove that removing diagonal attention elements does not deteriorate model performance, introduce a Differentiable Attention Mask (DAM) algorithm to learn which attention positions can be pruned, and use DAM to design SparseBERT, validating via extensive experiments that learned sparse masks yield efficient models with comparable effectiveness to dense attention.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of existing Trojan reverse-engineering defenses, which assume triggers are static input-space patterns and thus miss feature-space triggers like style transformations. The key insight is that both input-space and feature-space Trojans correspond to separable hyperplanes in the model’s feature space, so constraining reverse-engineering in feature space rather than input space can reveal a much broader class of triggers. The authors design a method that searches for feature-space perturbations (hyperplane constraints) that induce the backdoor behavior and then maps these constraints to effective triggers for detection and mitigation; evaluated on four datasets and seven attacks, it detects Trojaned models with about 93% accuracy and reduces attack success rate to 0.26% while keeping benign accuracy nearly unchanged.

result.text: The paper tackles the failure of post-training quantization (PTQ) when compressing networks to extremely low-bit widths, showing that naively quantizing activations during reconstruction harms final accuracy. The key insight is that incorporating activation quantization into the PTQ reconstruction objective—specifically by promoting flatness of the optimized low-bit model across calibration and test data—improves generalization and robustness to aggressive quantization. Based on this, the authors propose QDrop, a simple method that randomly drops activation quantization during PTQ reconstruction (i.e., stochastically using either quantized or full-precision activations during calibration) to encourage flat minima and reduce sensitivity to quantization noise. Experiments across vision and NLP tasks demonstrate that QDrop substantially extends PTQ to 2-bit activations, yielding large accuracy gains (up to ~51.5%) and setting new state-of-the-art PTQ results.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of modeling very long-range dependencies in sequence data (tens of thousands of steps) where standard RNNs, CNNs, and Transformers either fail mathematically or are computationally infeasible. Its key insight is that state space models (SSMs) with carefully structured state matrices can provably capture long-range behavior, and that by parameterizing the state matrix as a diagonalizable base plus a low-rank correction one can both retain those theoretical strengths and enable dramatically more efficient computation. result.text: The paper addresses inconsistent and sometimes poor-quality samples produced by deep generative models by proposing a post-generation refinement procedure that improves individual outputs rather than discarding them. The key insight is to view refinement as following the gradient flow of an entropy-regularized f-divergence between the generated and real data distributions, which yields a non-linear Fokker–Planck PDE whose particle dynamics are given by a McKean–Vlasov process driven by the discriminator (critic) gradients. The method, called Discriminator Gradient flow (DGflow), simulates this process via discretized stochastic updates on generated samples using gradients from vector-valued critics (and applicable to VAEs and flows as well as GANs), thereby nudging poor samples toward higher-density regions of the data distribution without rejection sampling. Empirically, DGflow consistently improves sample quality across synthetic, image, and text benchmarks and outperforms prior refinement approaches like DOT and DDLS.

The paper addresses the problem of training deep reinforcement learning agents that are robust to adversarial perturbations of state observations, noting that prior defenses break down as perturbation magnitude grows. The key insight is to use an adversarial curriculum that both conservatively bootstraps each phase with the best solutions from multiple prior runs and opportunistically skips forward when agents are ready, thereby stabilizing learning and exposing agents to gradually harder adversarial conditions. The proposed method, Bootstrapped Opportunistic Adversarial Curriculum Learning (BCL), constructs a sequence of adversarial training phases, selects high-quality policies across runs to initialize each phase, and allows adaptive progression through the curriculum to efficiently reach stronger perturbations. Empirically BCL yields substantially improved robustness—e.g., on Pong tolerating adversarial noise up to 25/255 versus 5/255 for prior methods.

result.text: The paper addresses how to define and achieve proportional outcomes in approval-based participatory budgeting when voters’ satisfaction can be measured either by number of approved projects or by total cost, noting ambiguity over which measure reflects true utility. result.text: The paper tackles the problem of “unlearning” undesirable behaviors in large language models—such as toxicity, unwanted sentiment, or repetition—by fine-tuning them on signals of what not to produce while staying close to the original model. The proposed method, Quantized Reward Konditioning (Quark), iteratively samples outputs from the current model, sorts them into reward-based quantiles, prepends a token indicating each quantile, and fine-tunes the model with a standard language modeling loss plus a KL-divergence penalty to keep it near the base model; at inference time, prepending a high-reward token steers generation away from the unwanted property. result.text: The paper addresses the "multiple manifold problem," a binary classification task in which a deep fully-connected network must separate two low-dimensional submanifolds on the unit sphere, and asks when randomly-initialized gradient descent can rapidly and perfectly learn this separation. The key insight is that depth and width play complementary roles—depth provides a fitting resource making networks smoother and more capable of separating class manifolds, while width supplies a statistical resource that concentrates the random network and its gradients—so that in an overparameterized NTK regime training succeeds with high probability when width and sample size scale polynomially with depth. Methodologically, the authors analyze a one-dimensional manifold configuration using the neural tangent kernel to give nonasymptotic concentration and generalization guarantees, proving essentially optimal uniform concentration rates for the initial NTK of deep networks (width n ≳ L·poly(d0)) via martingale concentration to control layerwise dependencies, and then showing gradient descent learns to classify the manifolds under these conditions.

result.text: The paper addresses molecular conformation generation—predicting stable 3D atomic coordinates from 2D molecular graphs—where prior methods first predict interatomic distances and then reconstruct coordinates, a pipeline that compounds errors from noisy distance predictions. The key insight is to bypass explicit distance-to-coordinate reconstruction by directly learning the gradient field of the log density (the score) of atomic coordinates, which lets one sample stable conformations via Langevin dynamics; to handle the roto-translation equivariance of coordinate scores, the authors show this is equivalent to estimating score fields over interatomic distances. The method, ConfGF, adapts score-based generative modeling to estimate these distance-based gradient fields and then integrates them to produce coordinate samples using equivariant Langevin dynamics, yielding significantly improved performance over prior state-of-the-art models across multiple benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles the limited data efficiency and expressivity of graph neural networks for predicting molecular and tensorial properties, which arises in part from using rotation-invariant representations that discard directional information. Its key insight is that enforcing rotational equivariance in message passing—so node features transform appropriately under rotations—retains essential geometric information and boosts learning efficiency and accuracy while allowing compact models. The authors introduce PaiNN, a polarizable atom interaction neural network that uses equivariant atom-wise features and equivariant message and update functions to predict scalar and tensorial quantities, demonstrating improved benchmark performance, smaller/faster models, and leveraging the learned representations to predict tensor properties and molecular spectra. Applied to spectrum simulation, PaiNN achieves 4–5 orders of magnitude speedup over electronic structure calculations while maintaining accuracy.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of extreme pruning at initialization, where existing skeletonization methods degrade sharply beyond ~95% sparsity and can even underperform random pruning. The key insight is to choose a subnetwork with maximum foresight connection sensitivity (FORCE): select connections whose perturbation would have the largest impact on loss, and update importance progressively so previously unimportant weights can become important later. Methodologically, the authors propose an efficient approximate FORCE maximization algorithm that progressively prunes a network at initialization rather than one-shot removing, enabling iterative re-evaluation of connection importance and preserving trainability. Empirically, this progressive skeletonization lets networks retain accuracy at very high sparsities (up to 99.9%) and outperforms recent initialization-pruning baselines across many tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses whether convolutional neural networks can regain competitiveness with transformers by scaling convolutional kernels far beyond the common 31x31 limit without incurring performance saturation or prohibitive costs. The key insight is that sparsity and factorization can be used to compose extremely large receptive fields efficiently: by representing large kernels as sparse, factorized blocks (mixing dense center regions with sparse outer rings and channel-wise factorization) one can maintain expressivity while controlling parameter and compute growth. Methodologically, the authors develop a recipe for sparse large kernels and implement it in a pure-CNN architecture called Sparse Large Kernel Network (SLaK), which uses sparse factorized 51x51 (and up to 61x61) convolutions within a hierarchical backbone and demonstrate parity or improvements over state-of-the-art transformers and modern ConvNets across ImageNet classification and downstream detection/segmentation benchmarks.

result.text: FreeSplat addresses the challenge of enabling generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting for free-view synthesis of indoor scenes from long image sequences, overcoming prior methods’ limitations to narrow-range interpolation and heavy backbones that hinder accurate Gaussian localization. The key insight is that efficient cross-view feature aggregation and redundancy-aware fusion can both improve geometric consistency across wide view ranges and reduce unnecessary Gaussians, enabling scalable, feed-forward reconstruction without depth priors. Methodologically, FreeSplat builds a Low-cost Cross-View Aggregation module that constructs adaptive cost volumes among nearby views and aggregates multi-scale features, pairs this with a Pixel-wise Triplet Fusion to remove redundant Gaussians in overlapping regions while merging multi-view observations, and employs a free-view training strategy to make synthesis robust across broad view variations. Empirically, this design yields state-of-the-art novel-view color and depth quality, faster inference, and significant reduction of redundant Gaussians, enabling efficient large-scene reconstruction.

The key insight is that controlling a policy’s Lipschitz constant yields robustness guarantees and that, under mild conditions, there exist Lipschitz policies that remain close to optimal. The key insight is that the cheap fast gradient sign method (FGSM), when paired with random input initialization and standard efficiency tricks, can produce robustness comparable to PGD-based training at a fraction of the cost, provided a specific failure mode is avoided. The authors develop and evaluate FGSM-based adversarial training protocols, demonstrate dramatic speedups (e.g., robust CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classifiers trained in minutes–hours with competitive robust accuracy), and diagnose “catastrophic overfitting” as the reason prior FGSM attempts failed, offering practical recommendations and code to reproduce their results.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap in LLM evaluation regarding their ability to quantify uncertainty for unrealizable prediction tasks rather than merely predict correct answers; existing benchmarks focus on accuracy and thus miss whether model probabilities reflect true outcome risk. The key insight is that LLMs can produce useful risk scores but that standard multiple-choice and instruction-tuned setups distort calibration—base models tend to be over-uncertain, instruction tuning drives overconfidence and polarized answer distributions, while chat-style verbalized risk queries improve calibration. To demonstrate this, the authors introduce folktexts, a flexible software toolkit that generates and evaluates LLM-derived risk scores across customizable census-based prediction tasks, compare 17 recent models under diverse prompting schemes (zero-shot multiple-choice vs. verbalized queries), and show systematic miscalibration patterns that conventional realizable benchmarks would not reveal.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of LLMs being vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks that manipulate prompts to elicit unsafe or undesired outputs, noting that prior defenses struggle against new or adaptive attacks. Its key insight is to model the adversary explicitly within the defensive objective and optimize a compact, transferable suffix that hardens the model against worst-case adaptive jailbreaks. The method, Robust Prompt Optimization (RPO), formulates an optimization-based defense that searches for system-level prompt suffixes by iteratively simulating adversarial attacks during training and minimizing attack success rates. Empirically and theoretically, RPO substantially improves robustness—dropping ASR on JailbreakBench to 6% for GPT-4 and 0% for Llama-2—while remaining lightweight and transferable.

result.text: The paper tackles gloss-free sign language translation, where scarce annotated sign data and long video sequences make end-to-end learning difficult. Its key insight is that large pretrained vision and language models can be adapted for sign translation using lightweight adapters and a pseudo-gloss pretraining objective, enabling transfer from abundant spoken-language resources without relying on manual gloss annotations or gloss order. The method inserts efficient adapters into frozen pretrained encoders and decoders, pretrains the visual encoder to predict automatically extracted pseudo-glosses (derived from unsupervised tokenization of sign videos) to learn sign-specific representations, and fine-tunes the combined model end-to-end on target sign-to-text datasets. Evaluated on RWTH-PHOENIX-Weather 2014T and CSL-Daily, Sign2GPT substantially improves state-of-the-art gloss-free translation performance.

result.text: Deep Generative Networks often inherit non-uniform sampling biases from training data, producing over- or under-represented regions on the learned manifold that hurt fairness and downstream use; MaGNET addresses how to draw samples uniformly across a pre-trained DGN’s manifold without retraining. The key insight is to view the generator as a smooth map from latent space to a data manifold and correct for the induced non-uniform density by estimating and compensating for the manifold’s volume element (Jacobian determinant) so that samples are weighted to achieve uniform coverage on the manifold. Methodologically, MaGNET estimates local manifold densities via the generator’s Jacobian (using efficient approximations) and then constructs a sampler that reweights or resamples latent vectors according to the inverse of that density, yielding uniform manifold sampling applicable to any frozen DGN; experiments (e.g., StyleGAN2 on FFHQ) show improved precision/recall and reduced gender bias without labels or retraining, while also analyzing how semantic attributes shift under uniform manifold sampling.

result.text: The paper examines why state-of-the-art large language models remain vulnerable to "jailbreak" attacks despite safety training, attributing persistent failures to two core problems: competing objectives (where capability to follow harmful instructions conflicts with imposed safety goals) and mismatched generalization (where safety training does not generalize to domains the model can handle). The key insight is that these failure modes explain why adversarially crafted prompts can reliably elicit unsafe behavior even from heavily red‑teamed models, and that designing attacks around these modes yields far stronger jailbreaks than ad hoc methods. result.text: The paper addresses scalable learning on large text-attributed graphs (TAGs), where each node has associated text and jointly leveraging powerful language models and graph neural networks (GNNs) is computationally prohibitive at scale. Its key insight is that alternating, variational EM-style updates can decouple training of the language and graph modules while still allowing them to interact and reinforce one another, avoiding the cost of end-to-end joint optimization. The proposed method, GLEM, formulates a variational EM framework in which the E-step updates the language model (or its text representations) conditioned on current graph beliefs and the M-step updates the GNN parameters given the updated text embeddings, iterating these steps to convergence; this enables separate, efficient training of each module yet yields mutually improved representations. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets show GLEM achieves strong performance and efficiency gains compared to jointly trained baselines.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of learning useful feature representations from unlabeled 3D medical images to reduce reliance on costly expert annotations for downstream tasks. Its key insight is that popular self-supervised proxy tasks can be extended from 2D to fully volumetric 3D formulations to better capture spatial structure in medical scans, yielding richer semantic features than 2D slice-based pretraining or training from scratch. The authors implement 3D versions of five methods—Contrastive Predictive Coding, Rotation prediction, Jigsaw puzzles, Relative patch location, and Exemplar networks—and show via experiments on brain MRI and pancreas CT segmentation (and transfer to 2D fundus images) that 3D pretraining improves data efficiency, accuracy, and convergence speed, and transfers well from large unlabeled 3D corpora to small task-specific datasets. They also release an open-source library containing their 3D and 2D implementations to facilitate adoption.

result.text: The paper tackles hyperspectral image (HSI) denoising, aiming to remove noise while preserving fine spatial structures and spectral correlations, a challenge for convolutional methods that struggle to model long-range, non-local dependencies without heavy computation. The key insight is that treating spatial and spectral dimensions with dedicated non-local attention mechanisms captures intrinsic similarities more effectively: window-based spatial self-attention models spatial similarity beyond local neighborhoods, while global spectral self-attention captures long-range dependencies across highly correlated bands. The proposed Spatial-Spectral Transformer (SST) integrates these two Transformer-based attentions to jointly exploit spatial and spectral non-local information for denoising, and experiments show it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in quantitative metrics and visual quality.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of accurate post-training quantization (PTQ) for large language models, where activation outliers in certain channels cause large quantization error and degrade low-bitwidth performance. The key insight is to mitigate outlier effects by redistributing their large magnitudes across channels—reducing peak activation ranges—while preserving model structure and efficiency. QLLM implements this via adaptive channel reassembly: disassembling outlier channels into multiple sub-channels to balance activation magnitudes, then reassembling similar channels to restore the original channel count with an adaptive rule to choose the number of splits; additionally, it applies a lightweight low-rank tuning step that trains a small set of parameters (which can be fused back into the frozen quantized weights) to recover accuracy. Experiments on LLaMA-1/2 show QLLM yields substantially better low-bit (e.g., 4-bit) results and practical efficiency (e.g., quantizing LLaMA-2-70B in ~10 hours on one A100) compared to prior PTQ methods.

result.text: The paper addresses channel pruning for network compression in architectures with complex, coupled structures (e.g., residual links, group/depthwise convolutions, FPNs) where multiple layers’ channels must be removed jointly. The key insight is to automatically group coupled channels and evaluate their joint importance using a Fisher-information-based metric, while recognizing that practical GPU speedup correlates better with memory reduction than with FLOPs so importance should be normalized by per-channel memory savings. The method therefore (1) applies a layer-grouping algorithm to identify coupled channels, (2) computes unified Fisher-based importance scores for single and grouped channels, normalizes these scores by expected memory reduction, and (3) prunes channels accordingly to produce compact models that empirically yield real inference speedups across diverse backbones and tasks without significant accuracy loss.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of combining client-level differential privacy with communication-efficient federated learning, noting that existing compression techniques and privacy mechanisms have not been jointly optimized. Its key insight is that by unifying compression operators with a flexible family of local gradient estimators (including variance-reduced methods and shifted compression schemes), one can design algorithms that preserve local differential privacy while improving communication complexity without degrading utility. The proposed method, SoteriaFL, first analyzes the pitfalls of naively compressing differentially private SGD and then introduces a general framework that integrates noise-adding for local differential privacy with tailored compressed gradient estimators and variance-reduction/shift strategies. The authors provide theoretical characterizations of the trade-offs among privacy, utility, and communication, showing SoteriaFL attains strictly better communication complexity than prior private federated learning methods that do not use compression while maintaining comparable privacy and utility.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of training generalist embodied agents that can learn a wide spectrum of open-ended tasks rather than narrow, manually specified objectives learned tabula rasa. Its key insight is that combining a richly varied environment, internet-scale multimodal knowledge about that environment, and scalable agent architectures enables language-specified, open-ended skill acquisition without handcrafted dense rewards. To demonstrate this, the authors present MineDojo: a Minecraft-based simulation suite with thousands of diverse tasks plus a large corpus of videos, tutorials, wiki pages, and forum posts, and they train agents using a novel algorithm that uses large pretrained video–language models as learned reward functions to optimize behavior from free-form language goals. The result is agents that can solve varied open-ended tasks specified in natural language, and the project, including data, code, and models, is released to stimulate further research.

result.text: The paper addresses the safety risk that LLM agents—especially those relying on long-term memory or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) knowledge bases—can be stealthily manipulated by poisoned memories or KB entries that cause malicious behavior when specific inputs occur. The key insight is that one can craft backdoor “triggers” not by changing model weights but by optimizing example texts so their embeddings map to a unique region of the retrieval space, ensuring those poisoned demonstrations are returned only when the trigger appears while leaving benign behavior intact. The method, AgentPoison, formulates trigger generation as a constrained optimization that selects or modifies poisoning instances to align their embeddings, injects them into the agent’s memory or RAG store at a very low poison rate, and then validates that triggered user instructions reliably retrieve the malicious entries; experiments show >80% attack success across varied real-world agents with <1% impact on benign performance and <0.1% poisoning.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of incorporating domain knowledge and semantic context into automated feature engineering for tabular AutoML, where current systems often ignore dataset descriptions and human-understandable features. result.text: The paper tackles fast, differentiable surface reconstruction from point clouds, addressing the drawbacks of neural implicit representations (slow inference and tricky initialization) and limitations of existing explicit representations. The key insight is to make Poisson Surface Reconstruction differentiable and GPU-accelerated so an oriented point cloud can be converted into an implicit indicator field within an end-to-end learnable pipeline, enabling optimization of surface-level losses. Methodologically, they implement a differentiable point-to-mesh layer by formulating a solvable Poisson equation for the indicator function on the GPU, which bridges explicit oriented points and watertight manifold meshes and permits training from unoriented inputs via orientation and surface losses. The resulting Shape-As-Points (SAP) representation is lightweight, interpretable, topology-agnostic, yields watertight surfaces, and achieves an order-of-magnitude faster inference than neural implicit baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses fast, dataset-free post-training quantization of deep networks for privacy-sensitive inference devices, where existing data-free methods either lose accuracy, require synthetic data or are slow. The key insight is that the second-order (Hessian) loss around weights can be decomposed into three diagonalizable components aligned with weight-tensor dimensions (element-wise, kernel-wise, output-channel-wise), enabling a tractable discrete optimization objective that does not rely on data or architecture specifics. result.text: The paper addresses how to scale language models when the amount of unique training text is limited, examining how data repetition interacts with compute and model size in data-constrained regimes. The key insight is that modest repetition (up to about four epochs) has little impact on loss at fixed compute, but beyond that repeated data yields diminishing returns and eventually nullifies the benefit of extra compute or parameters—so optimal scaling must account for the reduced value of repeated tokens. result.text: The paper tackles the gap between parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA and full fine-tuning, which often leads to underperformance on complex or domain-specific tasks. The key insight is that standard LoRA’s symmetric, uniform low-rank adapters are both training- and parameter-inefficient for challenging datasets, and that an asymmetric allocation of adapter capacity can better capture task-specific complexity without needing domain expertise. The authors propose HydraLoRA, an asymmetric LoRA architecture that redistributes low-rank components across layers and projection directions to match representational needs, and they validate it through experiments showing consistent gains over existing PEFT methods—including those that incorporate domain knowledge—while maintaining parameter efficiency.

The paper tackles numerical reasoning over hybrid inputs (tables plus long texts) by addressing the limitation that static retrieval in retriever-generator pipelines cannot account for the fact that different generation steps need different supportive sentences. The key insight is to make retrieval dynamic: after an initial retrieval, a reranker is invoked at each generation step to reorder retrieved sentences so the generator attends to the most relevant evidence for the current substep of program construction. The proposed DyRRen framework implements this retriever–reranker–generator loop, where the reranker conditions on the partially generated program (or generation context) to produce step-specific reranks that guide the generator to produce executable multi-step reasoning programs; this approach achieves superior performance on the FinQA benchmark.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of choosing layerwise sparsity for magnitude-based neural network pruning, where prior work relies on heuristics or costly hyperparameter searches and performance depends critically on per-layer sparsity allocation. Their key insight is that pruning decisions should account for each layer’s contribution to the model-level ℓ2 distortion, so weight magnitudes can be rescaled into an importance score that reflects the global impact of removing parameters. They propose LAMP (layer-adaptive magnitude-based pruning), a simple, hyperparameter-free scoring scheme that rescales magnitudes by layer-level statistics to produce layerwise sparsities for global pruning, and show empirically on image classification tasks (including weight-rewinding setups) that LAMP consistently outperforms popular baselines. The method is lightweight to compute and requires no expensive tuning while yielding better sparsity–performance tradeoffs than existing layerwise allocation strategies.

result.text: The paper addresses inconsistent and sometimes poor-quality samples produced by deep generative models by proposing a post-generation refinement procedure that improves individual outputs rather than discarding them. The key insight is to view refinement as following the gradient flow of an entropy-regularized f-divergence between the generated and real data distributions, which yields a non-linear Fokker–Planck PDE whose particle dynamics are given by a McKean–Vlasov process driven by the discriminator (critic) gradients. The method, called Discriminator Gradient flow (DGflow), simulates this process via discretized stochastic updates on generated samples using gradients from vector-valued critics (and applicable to VAEs and flows as well as GANs), thereby nudging poor samples toward higher-density regions of the data distribution without rejection sampling. Empirically, DGflow consistently improves sample quality across synthetic, image, and text benchmarks and outperforms prior refinement approaches like DOT and DDLS.

result.text: The paper tackles the inefficiency and limited parameter budgets of applying State Space Models (SSMs) to vision tasks, where standard multi-scan strategies improve long-range dependency capture but incur significant redundancy and cost. result.text: MinVIS addresses video instance segmentation (VIS) by asking whether strong VIS can be achieved without video-specific architectures or video-based training, thereby reducing labeling and memory costs. The key insight is that queries learned by a query-based image instance segmentation model to discriminate objects within a single frame are temporally consistent across frames and thus can serve as identity signals for tracking without any handcrafted tracking heuristics or video training. The method trains only on independently treated annotated frames (even heavily sub-sampled, e.g., 1% of frames) with a query-based image mask head, runs per-frame instance segmentation at inference, and then performs online tracking by bipartite matching of query representations between consecutive frames to link masks into tracks. This minimal pipeline achieves state-of-the-art VIS results (notably +10% AP on Occluded VIS) while drastically cutting annotation needs and memory footprint.

The key insight is that fixing a standard CNN topology but searching only over operation choices—specifically kernel sizes and dilations—gives rich multi-resolution feature extraction while dramatically reducing the search space, and that leveraging the Fourier diagonalization of convolution lets one efficiently compute mixtures of these operations. result.text: The paper tackles the problem of automatically discovering jailbreak prompts for black-box large language models (LLMs), aiming to expose and bypass safety guardrails without access to model internals. result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of predicting human perceptual image quality without relying on costly supervised labels or ratings, aiming for a tractable, biologically informed metric that rivals supervised learned models. Its key insight is that information-theoretic objectives applied to an architecture inspired by human visual physiology can learn perceptually meaningful representations from unlabeled natural video frame pairs. result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of decoding natural images from noisy, non-invasive EEG recordings to enable object recognition directly from brain signals. Its key insight is that self-supervised contrastive learning can align representations learned from paired image stimuli and EEG responses, allowing useful image features to be inferred from EEG despite low signal-to-noise ratios. The method uses separate image and EEG encoders trained with a contrastive objective to pull matching image–EEG pairs together in feature space, augmented by attention modules to capture spatial correlations and extensive analyses across temporal, spatial, spectral, and semantic EEG dimensions. Evaluated on a large EEG–image dataset, the approach achieves substantially above-chance zero-shot recognition (15.6% top-1, 42.8% top-5 on 200-way tasks) and offers biologically plausible insights for neural decoding and BCI applications.

result.text: The paper addresses the high computational cost of drawing samples from Gaussian process (GP) posteriors, which traditionally scale cubically with the number of test locations and thus hinder downstream Monte Carlo integration and uncertainty quantification in large-scale applications. The key insight is a factorization that cleanly separates the prior component of a GP from the data-dependent update, enabling posterior sample paths to be formed by combining cheap prior draws with a low-rank, data-driven correction; this decoupling allows accurate posterior sampling without the full cubic cost. result.text: The paper addresses the overlooked problem of evaluating the efficiency (not just functional correctness) of code generated by large language models, proposing a rigorous benchmark to measure whether LLMs produce expert-level, performance-minded implementations. The authors introduce ENAMEL, centered on a generalized eff@k metric (extending pass@k to efficiency) and an unbiased, variance-reduced Rao–Blackwellized estimator with a numerically stable implementation, alongside expert-designed optimal algorithms/implementations and curated test-case generators to filter incorrect solutions and surface suboptimality. result.text: The paper addresses the practical challenge of imputing missing values in tabular data, balancing the simplicity and flexibility of iterative conditional modeling against the scalability and capacity of deep generative methods. Its key insight is that iterative imputation can be both robust and performant if the per-column models and their hyperparameters are selected and tuned automatically, thereby avoiding manual specification while retaining conditional modeling advantages. The proposed method, HyperImpute, is a generalized iterative imputation framework that adaptively configures column-wise learners, optimizers, and simulation strategies via automated model/hyperparameter selection and provides an extensible implementation with out-of-the-box components. Empirical evaluation across many public datasets shows HyperImpute produces accurate imputations compared to strong benchmarks, supporting an automated iterative-imputation approach as a competitive alternative to deep generative methods.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of severe performance degradation when merging multiple single-task model checkpoints into a single multi-task model and the related storage inefficiency of keeping many task-specific checkpoints. The key insight is that task information is largely localized: different tasks predominantly use non-overlapping subsets of weights, so the essential task-specific parameters remain preserved after naive merging but are diluted or interfered with by other tasks’ parameters. The authors introduce TALL-masks, a method that identifies per-task supports from task vectors and shows that applying these masks to the merged multi-task vector recovers >99% of single-task accuracy, and they analyze mask intersections to identify “selfish” and “catastrophic” weights that harm fusion; based on this they propose Consensus Merging, which removes such detrimental weights to improve merging quality. Empirically across vision and NLP benchmarks with up to 20 tasks, Consensus Merging consistently boosts existing merging methods and enables a compression scheme that reduces storage dramatically (e.g., from 57GB to 8.2GB) while preserving ~99.7% performance.

result.text: The paper addresses Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), where a dataset has both labeled and unlabeled images and the goal is to cluster the unlabeled images into both known and novel classes consistent with the taxonomy implied by the labeled set. The key insight is that existing benchmarks often admit a single natural partition, so models can succeed by unsupervised grouping rather than by extrapolating the labeled taxonomy; to reveal this, the authors introduce Clevr-4, a synthetic dataset with four equally valid mutually orthogonal partitions (shape, texture, color, count) that forces methods to follow the labeled taxonomy. They show strong unsupervised methods fail on Clevr-4 and identify weaknesses in prior GCD algorithms, then propose μGCD, a simple mean-teacher–based method that leverages consistency regularization from representation learning to align unlabeled clustering with the labeled taxonomy; μGCD substantially outperforms baselines on Clevr-4 and achieves state-of-the-art results on the real-data Semantic Shift Benchmark.

The method incrementally approximates transition probabilities as intervals, updates or revises these intervals as new (possibly inconsistent or changing) data arrive, and at any interruption computes a robust policy over the current uMDP; experimentally the approach adapts to environment changes and outperforms robust policies derived from uMDPs learned via UCRL2 on several benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles source-free domain adaptation (SFDA), asking whether existing SFDA methods generalize beyond typical computer-vision shifts to challenging, naturally-occurring distribution changes in bioacoustics where only an off-the-shelf model and unlabeled target data are available. The key insight is that current SFDA techniques, benchmarked mainly on vision datasets, can behave very differently or even degrade performance on markedly different modalities, so robustness across diverse domains is not guaranteed. Methodologically, the authors evaluate a suite of existing SFDA algorithms on new bioacoustic shifts, diagnose their failures, and introduce a simple new adaptation approach that empirically outperforms prior methods on the bioacoustic benchmarks while remaining competitive on standard vision datasets, arguing for broader modality consideration when designing SFDA methods.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that graph neural networks trained on graphs of one size often fail to generalize to graphs of different (typically larger) sizes, without access to test-domain graphs or strong generative assumptions. Its key insight is that size shifts can be simulated at training time by coarsening graphs to mimic smaller-to-larger size differences, and that enforcing robustness to these simulated shifts via a regularizer improves size generalization for generic GNNs. The proposed method, SizeShiftReg, applies graph coarsening to create perturbed versions of training graphs and adds a regularization term that encourages the model’s predictions or representations to be consistent across original and coarsened views, so any GNN can be trained with this extra loss to become more size-robust. Experiments show substantial gains (up to ~30%) when models are trained on the smallest 50% of graphs and tested on the largest 10%, demonstrating the effectiveness of the regularizer without using test data or specialized generative models.

result.text: The paper tackles one-shot medical image segmentation, where only a single labeled atlas and a few unlabeled MRIs are available, by addressing the challenge of generating sufficient realistic training data without costly annotations. The key insight is to model the probabilistic distribution of unlabeled-image deformations relative to the atlas—capturing both shape and intensity variations—so synthetic yet authentic examples can be drawn that reflect real inter-subject variability. Concretely, the authors train 3D variational autoencoders on unlabeled images to learn deformation and intensity latent distributions conditioned on the atlas, sample from these distributions to synthesize new labeled MRIs by warping the atlas, and then use the augmented dataset to train a segmentation network, demonstrating superior one-shot cross-dataset generalization.

result.text: The paper tackles the gap between standard composition-based differential privacy (DP) analyses for iterative learning algorithms—which assume an adversary sees the algorithm’s internal state and therefore yield privacy loss growing linearly with epochs—and the more realistic setting where the internal state is hidden. The key insight is that hiding state enables strong privacy amplification by subsampling and randomized post-processing, so the cumulative privacy loss for noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD) need not diverge but can instead converge rapidly. Concretely, for strongly convex smooth losses and commonly used mini-batch schemes (“shuffle and partition” and “sample without replacement”), the authors derive R\'enyi-DP bounds that decay exponentially with iterations and are much tighter than composition bounds after a few epochs. The result implies that either DP algorithms must converge very quickly to match composition-based guarantees or practitioners should exploit hidden-state analyses to obtain substantially stronger privacy-preserving learning.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately and efficiently applying post-training quantization to large language models (LLMs), where activations exhibit outliers that make simultaneous 8-bit quantization of weights and activations (W8A8) both inaccurate and hardware-inefficient. The key insight is that weights are generally easier to quantize than activations, so one can mathematically transfer—i.e., "smooth"—the quantization difficulty from activation tensors into adjacent weight matrices without retraining, reducing activation dynamic range while preserving exact model computation. The method performs an offline, layer-wise transformation that rescales activations and compensates by inversely scaling corresponding weights, then applies standard INT8 quantization to both, enabling W8A8 for all matrix multiplications in many LLMs; this yields up to 1.56x inference speedup and 2x memory reduction with negligible accuracy loss, allowing even very large models to be served on a single node.

Its key insight is to combine adapter-style task-specific weights with low-rank and hypercomplex (Kronecker-product) structure so that many layer-specific parameters can be generated from a small set of shared components. The proposed Compacter method inserts compact task-specific weight matrices into a pretrained model, where each such matrix is formed as a sum of Kronecker products between shared "slow" tensors and per-layer "fast" rank-one factors, enabling efficient computation and extreme parameter reduction. result.text: The paper tackles few-shot tabular learning by addressing the challenge of leveraging large language models (LLMs) for feature engineering without incurring heavy per-sample inference costs or prompt-size constraints. Its key insight is that LLMs can be used once, in-context, to automatically synthesize high-quality predictive features or rules from a small labeled dataset, and those features can then power a simple downstream model at inference time. The method, FeatLLM, prompts an LLM to generate candidate features and transforms for the entire dataset, selects and encodes the most informative ones, and trains a lightweight predictor (e.g., linear regression) on those engineered features; this eliminates the need to call the LLM per test sample, requires only API-level access, and scales across domains. Empirically, FeatLLM produces robust rule-like features that improve few-shot performance on diverse tabular benchmarks, outperforming prior LLM-based approaches by roughly 10% on average.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of reconstructing accurate continuous surfaces from 3D point clouds by learning signed distance functions (SDFs). Its key insight is to supervise the network not by direct SDF regression alone but by a differentiable “pulling” operation that moves arbitrary query points toward their closest surface neighbors using the network-predicted signed distance and its gradient, thereby tightly coupling value and gradient learning. The method trains a neural network that, for each query 3D location, predicts an SDF value and gradient and then applies a stride equal to that predicted distance (forward or backward along the gradient depending on the sign) to pull the query onto the surface; the pulling loss between pulled points and real surface samples is backpropagated to update both SDF values and gradients, yielding improved surface reconstruction and single-image reconstruction performance.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of high quantization error in post-training quantization (PTQ) for large language models by expanding the class of allowed transformations beyond simple per-weight scalings. Its key insight is that optimizing an equivalent affine transformation between pre- and post-quantized weights (and applying the inverse to preserve outputs) enlarges the optimization space and can substantially reduce quantization-induced error while retaining PTQ’s efficiency. The method, AffineQuant, directly optimizes an affine matrix for each layer subject to invertibility constraints enforced via a gradual mask optimization that starts with diagonal entries and progressively frees off-diagonal elements—leveraging the Levy–Desplanques theorem to maintain invertibility—and applies the corresponding inverse to keep pre- and post-quantization outputs equivalent. Empirically, this approach yields consistent improvements across LLMs and settings (e.g., better perplexity and zero-shot accuracy in 4/4-bit quantization) without runtime overhead.

result.text: The paper addresses how to improve fairness of machine learning models when protected group labels (e.g., race, gender) are unavailable due to privacy or regulation, so conventional fairness interventions cannot be applied. Its key insight is that non-protected features and task labels contain enough signal to identify and upweight instances from groups that suffer the worst outcomes, enabling fairness improvements without explicit demographic information. The proposed method, Adversarially Reweighted Learning (ARL), jointly trains a predictor and an adversary that learns a reweighting over training examples to maximize a fairness-aware objective (e.g., Rawlsian max–min performance), so the predictor is trained on adversarially emphasized examples from worst-off implicit groups. Empirically, ARL yields significant gains in worst-group AUC and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across multiple datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of adapting vision-language models at test time to improve robustness on challenging, unlabeled images without costly online fine-tuning. Its key insight is that a near-optimal episodic test-time adaptation procedure can be obtained simply by taking multiple augmentations, keeping only the most confident predictions, and marginalizing with a zero-temperature (argmax) softmax—an approach they call ZERO—which dispenses with gradient updates and heavy prompt tuning. Methodologically, ZERO performs N augmentations per test image, runs a single batched forward pass through the vision encoder, selects the top-confidence class predictions across augmentations, and aggregates them via zero-temperature marginalization to produce a final label. Empirically, ZERO matches or outperforms prior prompt-tuning TTA methods while being about an order of magnitude faster and significantly more memory-efficient, making it a strong, simple baseline for future TTA work.

result.text: The paper investigates how Transformers perform in-context learning (ICL) for linear regression, challenging the view that they emulate Gradient Descent (GD) and asking whether they can realize faster, second-order optimization behavior. The key insight is that Transformer layers empirically and theoretically approximate Iterative Newton’s Method rather than GD, yielding exponentially faster convergence: successive layers' predictions linearly match Newton iterations (with each middle layer roughly implementing three Newton steps), enabling effective learning even on ill-conditioned data where GD fails. Methodologically, the authors combine empirical experiments comparing layer-wise outputs to Newton and GD trajectories and show faster convergence and robustness on challenging datasets, and they provide a constructive proof that a Transformer can implement k Newton iterations using k + O(1) layers, formalizing the capacity for second-order in-context optimization.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of existing graph contrastive learning methods that depend on handcrafted graph augmentations and homophily assumptions, which hurt performance on heterophilic graphs where neighbors can have different labels and features. Its key insight is that an asymmetric view of neighboring nodes—treating a node and its neighbors differently in contrastive pairs—can capture both one-hop local information and two-hop monophily similarity without any augmentations. The proposed method, GraphACL, constructs asymmetric contrastive objectives between a node and an aggregated neighbor view (rather than symmetric augmented views), is simple to implement, and theoretically and empirically shown to learn useful representations for both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. Experiments demonstrate that GraphACL significantly outperforms prior graph contrastive and self-supervised methods across diverse graph types.
