result.text: The paper tackles the limitation of unsupervised Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) in capturing global structural and semantic relationships among nodes that are not locally proximate, which harms the quality of learned node representations. The key insight is that explicit structural and semantic contrastive objectives can inject global graph knowledge into representations even when using a much simpler encoder than a graph neural network. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of domain adaptation when the target domain exhibits relaxed label shift—i.e., changes in label marginals possibly alongside changes in class-conditionals—which existing benchmarks and methods do not systematically evaluate, leaving many heuristics vulnerable to degraded performance. Its key insight is that many popular domain-adaptation heuristics fail under substantial label-proportion shifts, but a simple, broadly compatible two-step correction—pseudo-balancing training data each epoch and then adjusting the final classifier using an estimate of the target label distribution—can substantially recover accuracy. The authors introduce RLSbench, a large-scale benchmark of over 500 shift pairs across vision, tabular, and language tasks with varying label proportions, use it to evaluate 13 methods revealing widespread failures, and show that their meta-algorithm improves accuracy by typically 2–10 points under large shifts while minimally affecting performance when proportions do not shift.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of making large-scale reinforcement learning experiments accessible without massive distributed infrastructure by improving single-machine efficiency for training agents from pixels in complex 3D environments. Its key insight is that careful system and algorithm co-design — specifically an asynchronous, GPU-based sampler combined with off-policy correction — can produce extremely high environment frame throughput without degrading sample efficiency. The authors implement this as Sample Factory, a high-throughput training system that uses lock-free, asynchronous actors feeding a shared GPU policy, along with importance-weighted off-policy updates, and extend the framework to support self-play and population-based training. Using this approach they demonstrate training of egocentric 3D control agents (including multiplayer first-person shooter bots) at over 100,000 environment frames per second on a single machine.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of answering complex questions that require reasoning over both textual context and latent world knowledge, observing that pretrained language models alone poorly capture structured relationships while knowledge graphs are hard to fuse effectively with language. Its key insight is to replace direct feature comparisons with a swapped prediction objective that enforces consistency between cluster assignments of different augmentations of the same image, effectively turning contrastive learning into online clustering. The approach scales to large datasets and batches, is more memory-efficient, and achieves strong results (e.g., 75.3% top-1 on ImageNet with ResNet-50) and superior transfer performance.

result.text: The paper studies why gradient clipping—used in differentially private SGD to bound per-example gradients—can both impede convergence and yet still work well in practice; it shows clipping can prevent SGD from reaching stationary points by introducing bias. result.text: The paper tackles dense video captioning for long, untrimmed videos, aiming to generate accurate, temporally localized event descriptions while drastically reducing computational cost from processing all frames. Its key insight is that a learned frame-selection agent can watch only informative frames—watching more when content is rich and skipping redundant segments—thus simplifying event proposal and captioning and lowering false proposals. Methodologically, they train an actor-critic reinforcement learning agent to select frames, use the agent’s encoded state to guide event proposal and caption generation, and apply knowledge distillation to boost accuracy; experiments on ActivityNet Captions show this selective-watching framework preserves caption quality while cutting processing overhead.

The paper addresses the problem that jailbreak research frequently overstates attack effectiveness because there is no standard, high-quality benchmark for measuring whether a model actually yields harmful, specific information when prompted to do so. The key insight is that prior benchmarks and evaluators inflate success rates and miss a novel effect whereby jailbreaks that circumvent safety fine-tuning often degrade the victim model’s capabilities, so accurate assessment requires prompts demanding concrete forbidden outputs and an evaluator that correlates with human judgments. The authors introduce StrongREJECT: a dataset of forbidden prompts requiring specific harmful answers and an automated evaluator that measures how much useful forbidden information a response provides, showing state-of-the-art agreement with human ratings and revealing that many existing evaluation methods substantially overstate jailbreak success.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of designing linear bandit algorithms that automatically adapt to stochastic, corrupted, and adversarial environments, achieving both instance-optimal and minimax-optimal regret guarantees with high probability. The key insight is to plug a novel loss estimator into the optimization problem that characterizes the instance-optimal strategy and then combine this estimator with an adversarial component and carefully designed tests to detect and react to nonstochastic behavior. Methodologically, the authors build a primary algorithm using the new estimator to attain near instance-optimal regret in stochastic settings and additive regret proportional to corruption in corrupted settings, and then augment it with an adversarial module plus switching tests to obtain minimax-optimal guarantees in fully adversarial environments. All results are high-probability bounds, improving over prior work that lacked instance-optimality, optimal corruption dependence, or high-probability guarantees.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of effective tabular data augmentation in ultra low-data regimes, where conventional synthetic generators fail to produce sufficiently diverse and utility-preserving samples. The key insight is that pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) encode rich prior knowledge that can produce plausible new tabular examples, but LLM outputs must be selectively curated because not all synthetic samples aid downstream learning. The authors propose CLLM, a pipeline that generates candidate augmentations with LLMs and then applies a principled curation stage using learning dynamics together with confidence and uncertainty metrics to filter for high-utility samples. Empirical results across multiple real-world datasets show that CLLM yields superior downstream performance in low-data settings and analysis of the generation/curation steps identifies feature patterns associated with high-quality augmentations.

result.text: The paper addresses how to reliably predict the benefits of increasing model, dataset, or compute scale by revisiting empirical neural scaling laws and correcting weaknesses in prior fitting practices. Its key insight is that fitting scaling laws should minimize extrapolation loss—performance on held-out, larger-scale regimes—rather than merely optimizing interpolation to observed points, because that yields more trustworthy forecasts of performance at scales beyond the data. The authors propose a practical recipe for estimating scaling-law parameters from learning curves (including procedures for model selection, data splitting, and loss computation) and show across image classification, NMT, language modeling, and BIG-Bench tasks that their method extrapolates more accurately than previous approaches; they also release a 90-task benchmark to standardize future evaluations.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of efficiently and reliably certifying solver outputs when solvers use advanced reasoning like parity (XOR) handling, where existing DRAT proof formats become impractically large or inexpressive. Its key insight is that pseudo-Boolean (PB) inequalities augmented with extension variables can naturally and compactly capture XOR deductions and other richer constraints, forming a strict generalization of DRAT that supports concise proof traces. The method implements XOR reasoning within a SAT solver by emitting PB-inequality-based proof steps (with extensions) to justify derived clauses, and experimentally demonstrates orders-of-magnitude reductions in proof logging and verification time compared to DRAT encodings. This approach not only enables practical certification of parity reasoning but also extends to 0-1 and constraint programming encodings, pointing toward a unified, machine-verifiable proof framework for richer combinatorial paradigms.

result.text: The paper addresses why the Structured State Space (S4) model—an SSM-based architecture that empirically handles very long sequences—works despite using a seemingly ad-hoc “HiPPO” initialization whose theoretical role was unclear. The key insight is a generalized HiPPO framework that interprets S4 as projecting input histories onto an orthogonal basis of exponentially-warped polynomials (specifically Legendre polynomials) and shows that different orthogonal bases (e.g., Fourier) yield different long-range behaviors, thereby explaining S4’s ability to represent long dependencies and guiding principled choices like timescale initialization. Methodologically, the authors derive this generalized class of HiPPO matrices, connect them to time-invariant SSM parameterizations, propose alternative S4 variants based on other bases, and use these theoretical prescriptions to initialize and train improved SSMs, empirically boosting long-range performance on benchmarks like Long Range Arena.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of making fine-tuning large pre-trained language models efficient in parameters as model sizes and task counts grow, noting many recent approaches fine-tune only a small set of extra parameters but lack a unifying explanation. Its key insight is that diverse parameter-efficient methods can be reinterpreted as applying computed modifications to specific hidden states of a pre-trained model, which lets them be characterized along shared design dimensions (e.g., how the modification is computed and where it is injected). Methodologically, the authors propose a unified framework that decomposes and connects existing approaches, perform extensive empirical studies across machine translation, summarization, language understanding, and classification to identify important design choices, and leverage the framework to transfer design elements between methods to create new, more parameter-efficient yet equally effective fine-tuning schemes. The resulting instantiations tune fewer parameters than prior techniques while achieving performance comparable to full fine-tuning across all evaluated tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the classic non-identifiability problem in inverse reinforcement learning (IRL), where multiple reward functions can explain the same observed optimal behavior, making the true reward unrecoverable from demonstrations alone. args.text: Streaming Equal Shares via Pacing (SESP): We study participatory budgeting with arbitrary project costs in a streaming setting where projects arrive online and must be irrevocably funded, seeking proportional guarantees over time. SESP maintains per-voter pacing multipliers that throttle equal-share contributions to currently arriving approved projects and funds a project once its paced contributions meet cost; the multipliers are updated to equalize spend rates, yielding Lindahl-like personalized prices and a dynamically stable priceable outcome. Under i.i.d. arrivals from a stationary distribution, the time-averaged funded bundle converges to the static Equal Shares (and, when applicable, balanced-stably-priceable) solution for the underlying distribution, implying PJR and EJR-up-to-one-project guarantees in the limit along with per-prefix approximate group no-deviation bounds. Further, by leveraging strengthened priceability across satisfaction measures, SESP simultaneously preserves proportionality under both cardinal-by-cost and cardinal-by-count satisfactions, while running in polynomial time per arrival.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of scaling convolution-based Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to large graphs without losing global-context information or slowing inference, problems that sampling-based methods struggle with. Its key insight is that a small set of learned, quantized reference vectors can compactly represent global node messages so that the full message passing can be approximated via a low-rank factorization of the huge graph convolution matrix, avoiding neighbor explosion while retaining expressive power. result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of learning robust region embeddings from diverse urban data to better capture both intra-region and inter-region correlations for downstream smart-city tasks. The HREP framework implements this by building a heterogeneous region graph with multiple edge types, applying relation-aware graph embedding and self-attention to learn region and relation embeddings, using an attention-based fusion module to combine correlation types, and employing prefix-tuning as a lightweight prompt mechanism during downstream training; experiments on real-world datasets show it outperforms prior methods.

The paper addresses Graph Domain Adaptation (GDA), where graph-structured training and testing data differ, causing shifts in node features, labels, and especially graph connectivity that break usual graph-based label inference. Its key insight is that adapting pairwise relationships—by reweighting edges to correct conditional structure shift (how neighbor labels relate given node features) and reweighting label losses to correct label shift—directly mitigates the core causes of poor generalization across graphs. The method implements a graph denoising diffusion process where the protein backbone and node-wise physicochemical and local-environment features condition the reverse denoising, while the forward noising uses amino acid replacement matrices to encode biologically meaningful priors and reduce the effective sampling space. Empirically, this approach attains state-of-the-art sequence recovery against popular baselines and demonstrates strong potential to generate diverse candidate sequences consistent with a target backbone.

result.text: The paper addresses active learning for deep neural networks in realistic streaming scenarios where data arrive sequentially and labels must be requested on the fly rather than from an offline pool. Its key insight is that effective streaming active learning can be achieved by balancing per-sample uncertainty with diversity among a small group of recently seen points, thereby matching a target query rate without hand-tuned hyperparameters. The proposed method, VeSSAL, examines incoming data in small batches, scores candidates by a combined uncertainty-diversity objective, selects a subset to query immediately to satisfy the query budget, and updates the model incrementally; this streaming sampling scheme enables practical batch active learning for DNNs on large, fragmented, or human-in-the-loop datasets.

The paper tackles the inefficiency of FFT-based long convolutions on modern hardware, where poor utilization of matrix-multiply units and high memory I/O make FFT convolutions slower in wall-clock time than optimized Transformers despite their favorable O(N log N) complexity. The key insight is that the FFT can be reframed as a block matrix decomposition that maps naturally onto specialized matrix-multiply units (e.g., tensor cores) and enables kernel fusion, and that sparsity patterns in this decomposition can be exploited to skip work and reduce I/O. The authors introduce FlashFFTConv, which implements the FFT via fused matrix-multiply kernels and two sparse variants—partial convolutions (skipping blocks to prune spatial work) and frequency-sparse convolutions (skipping blocks in the frequency domain)—to save compute and memory; this yields up to ~8× speedups over PyTorch for exact FFTs, substantial end-to-end gains, and model-quality improvements (e.g., better perplexity, GLUE, vision accuracy, and the ability to handle ultra-long DNA sequences).

result.text: The paper studies the “modality gap,” a geometric phenomenon where different data modalities (e.g., images and text) occupy distinct, arm’s-length regions in the shared embedding space of multi-modal contrastive models like CLIP, which can hinder downstream performance and fairness. args.text: BB-NPG: a bilevel approach that learns the state-value baseline to explicitly shape the natural gradient’s preconditioning so that per-state update aggressiveness respects a trust-region-like constraint on the minimum optimal-action probability. The algorithm decouples data collection via a policy-cover behavior mixture to guarantee coverage, while performing on-policy NPG updates with the learned baseline and reusing off-policy data through clipped importance weights derived from off-policy policy-improvement bounds; gradient estimation leverages a triple-robust estimator to control bias. We show that optimizing the baseline to minimize an upper bound on probability-collapse risk yields global O(1/t) convergence with improved constants and, with entropy regularization, a linear rate; decoupled sampling restores robustness across a broad class of baselines. Empirically, this should stabilize updates without sacrificing sample efficiency, outperforming fixed-baseline NPG and PPO-like variants on sparse-reward and distribution-shifted tasks.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of multimodal fake news detection, where prior approaches that inject external knowledge often introduce noisy, irrelevant entities and fail to model complex interactions between text, images, and knowledge. Its key insight is that selecting a compact, content-relevant subgraph of knowledge for each news item and then learning cross-modal relations over that refined graph yields more reliable, discriminative signals than using all candidate entities statically. The method, AKA-Fake, uses reinforcement learning to adaptively extract a subset of entities and their contextual neighbors from a knowledge graph per news instance, then applies a heterogeneous graph learning module with topology refinement and modality-attentive pooling to capture trustworthy cross-modality correlations for final detection. Experimental evaluation on three benchmark datasets shows the approach outperforms existing knowledge-enhanced and multimodal baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap in current multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs), which struggle to unify image comprehension and generation within a single autoregressive Transformer and thus lack open-world emergent abilities. The key insight is that images must be tokenized into a 1D sequence of semantically rich, causally ordered tokens that mirror the left-to-right autoregressive structure of text and are optimized to balance discriminativeness and reconstructability. The authors propose SEED, an image tokenizer that produces position-independent, high-level visual tokens trained for both reconstruction and semantic separation, and integrate these tokens into LLaMA to train SEED-LLaMA via standard next-token prediction and instruction tuning on interleaved text–image data. The resulting model performs scalable multimodal autoregression and demonstrates strong unified comprehension and generative capabilities, including emergent multi-turn in-context multimodal generation.

result.text: The paper addresses the tendency of GANs to produce poor-quality samples in low-density regions of the data manifold—e.g., minority or underrepresented groups—without sacrificing diversity. The key insight is that underrepresented data points can be identified by statistics of the discrepancy between the empirical data distribution and the model distribution at each instance: such samples exhibit high average discrepancy or high variability in discrepancy. The method uses these per-instance discrepancy statistics to upweight or emphasize underrepresented samples during GAN training, thereby guiding the generator to allocate more capacity to those regions. Experiments show this simple diagnostic-and-emphasis scheme improves both quality and diversity, particularly for minor groups, across multiple datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles automated EEG-based seizure detection and classification, focusing on three gaps in prior work: modeling EEG's non-Euclidean spatiotemporal structure, improving performance on rare seizure types, and providing quantitative interpretability for seizure localization. The key insight is that graph neural networks (GNNs) can better capture electrode geometry or dynamic brain connectivity in EEGs and that self-supervised pre-training—predicting the next time period’s preprocessed signals—boosts downstream detection/classification performance and helps rare-class learning. The method builds EEG graphs (geometry- or connectivity-based), trains GNNs with a self-supervised next-step signal prediction objective before supervised fine-tuning, and introduces a quantitative interpretability metric to evaluate localization ability. Evaluated on a large public dataset, the approach outperforms prior methods on detection (AUROC 0.875) and classification (weighted F1 0.749), notably improving rare seizure classification and precise localization of focal seizures.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap that standard Bayesian optimization (BO) cannot incorporate a practitioner's prior beliefs about where the optimum lies, which wastes useful information in hyperparameter optimization and other black-box tuning tasks. The key insight is that acquisition functions can be augmented by multiplying them with a user-provided probability density over the input space (a prior belief π), thereby biasing search toward regions the user considers promising while retaining BO’s principled exploration–exploitation tradeoff. The authors introduce πBO, a simple, library-friendly modification that applies this reweighting to many common acquisition functions (analytically studying Expected Improvement), prove regret bounds and convergence rates that hold regardless of the prior, and empirically demonstrate improved performance across benchmarks— including a 12.5× time-to-accuracy speedup on a deep learning task—versus competing methods.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that existing iterative preference-optimization methods improve general instruction following but fail to substantially boost multi-step reasoning performance; the authors aim to better select and refine Chain-of-Thought (CoT) traces that lead to correct answers. Their key insight is to directly optimize preferences over competing CoT candidates by emphasizing the winning versus losing reasoning steps that causally lead to the correct answer, and that combining a DPO-style preference loss with an additional negative log-likelihood term is crucial to steer the model toward correct reasoning trajectories. Methodologically, they iteratively generate multiple CoT samples, label winners and losers according to answer correctness, and train the model with a modified DPO objective plus an NLL term to increase probability of winning steps and decrease that of losing steps; repeated iterations yield steady reasoning improvements. Empirically, this procedure—applied to Llama-2-70B-Chat using only in-dataset examples—substantially raises accuracy on GSM8K, MATH, and ARC-Challenge (e.g., GSM8K from 55.6% to 81.6%, and 88.7% with 32-sample majority voting).

result.text: The paper addresses the difficulty LLMs have in solving complex programming problems due to generating monolithic solutions rather than modular, reusable code. Its key insight is that iteratively extracting, clustering, and feeding back representative sub-modules into the model encourages reuse and yields more modular and correct programs. The proposed method, CodeChain, first prompts the LLM to produce modular code via chain-of-thought style guidance, then repeatedly extracts and clusters generated sub-modules, selects cluster representatives as generic implementations, augments the prompt with these representatives, and asks the model to regenerate solutions; this chain of self-revisions substantially improves pass@1 on challenging benchmarks and generalizes across both proprietary and open-source LLMs.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of applying self-supervised representation learning to tabular data, where common augmentation strategies used in images or text are not applicable and designing effective augmentations is difficult. Its key insight is to treat tabular features as multiple complementary views by partitioning features into subsets and learning to reconstruct full data from these subsets, which encourages learning robust latent factors without relying on corruption-based augmentations. The proposed method, SubTab, trains autoencoder-style encoders on feature subsets and aggregates their latent representations at test time via "collaborative inference," enabling reconstruction and downstream predictions from partial feature sets. Experiments show SubTab yields strong representations, achieving SOTA performance on MNIST in a tabular setting and outperforming baselines on several real-world datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of inaccurate and inefficient model editing in Transformers, where existing methods treat Transformer layer (TL) hidden states as FFN-specific key-value memories despite those states mixing signals from MHSA, FFN, and residual connections. The key insight is that MHSA primarily encodes general knowledge-extraction patterns (and stores little factual knowledge), so updating MHSA is unnecessary and can contaminate FFN-targeted edits. The proposed method, PMET, jointly optimizes MHSA and FFN component hidden states but uses only the optimized FFN hidden states to update FFN weights, thereby isolating and precisely injecting new factual knowledge; experiments on CounterFact and zsRE show state-of-the-art editing performance and ablations confirm MHSA’s limited role in factual storage.

Its key insight is that naive permutation-and-average merging fails when networks have task-specific, non-overlapping features, so merging should allow selective combination of features and support partial merging to preserve task-specific heads. The proposed method, ZipIt!, introduces a general "zip" operation that merges corresponding features across models (rather than simply averaging entire weights) and permits partial zipping up to a chosen layer to produce a shared backbone with separate heads. The method, LayoutNUWA, uses Code Instruct Tuning with three modules: Code Initialization converts numerical layout conditions into HTML-like code with masks, Code Completion uses an LLM to fill the masked code portions leveraging its formatting and contextual knowledge, and Code Rendering converts the completed code into a visual layout; this approach yields large SOTA improvements across multiple datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles improving CLIP’s zero-shot accuracy without incurring extra training or parameter overhead, addressing the deployment and data-cost limitations of prior fine-tuning approaches. Its key insight is that pretraining already aligns image and text embeddings closely enough to enable a parameter-free cross-modal attention mechanism to enrich each modality with informative signals from the other, boosting alignment without learning new weights. The method, CALIP, constructs a bidirectional, weightless attention operation that updates visual and textual features by computing cross-modal interactions and blending visual-aware text and text-aware image representations at inference time; this plug-in, training-free module yields consistent zero-shot gains across 14 2D and 3D benchmarks, and a lightweight variant with a few linear layers further improves few-shot robustness.

The paper addresses the challenge of translating wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) into clinically useful electrocardiography (ECG) for continuous, low-cost cardiac monitoring, where standard diffusion models struggle to capture fine-grained ECG temporal features. The key insight is that indiscriminate noise injection across an entire signal hinders modeling of critical ECG regions (e.g., QRS complexes), so selectively treating regions of interest (ROI) during the forward and reverse diffusion processes can disentangle and preserve diagnostically important structure. They propose the Region-Disentangled Diffusion Model (RDDM), which applies targeted noise addition to ROIs in the forward process and performs separated denoising for ROI and non-ROI regions in the reverse steps, enabling high-fidelity PPG-to-ECG translation in as few as 10 diffusion steps. To validate clinical utility, they introduce CardioBench, a comprehensive benchmark of cardiac tasks, and show RDDM achieves state-of-the-art performance across heart rate and blood pressure estimation, stress classification, and detection of atrial fibrillation and diabetes.

result.text: The paper addresses slow and sometimes brittle inference in pretrained language models by enabling dynamic early stopping to save computation while maintaining or improving accuracy. The key insight is that attaching simple internal classifiers to each layer and stopping when their predictions stop changing for a fixed number of consecutive layers (a “patience” threshold) prevents overthinking and unnecessary deeper computation. The method—Patience-based Early Exit—therefore runs the model sequentially, checks intermediate predictions at each layer, and halts inference once the same class is predicted for a preset number of steps, yielding fewer average layers evaluated; experiments with ALBERT show this plug-and-play approach improves efficiency and robustness and gives a better accuracy-speed trade-off than prior early-exit strategies.

result.text: The paper addresses the vulnerability of deep neural networks to backdoor attacks, where a small number of poisoned training samples cause malicious behavior only when a trigger is present. The key insight is that end-to-end supervised training causes poisoned samples to cluster in feature space, so decoupling representation learning from label-driven fitting can reduce this clustering and mitigate backdoors. The proposed method trains the backbone with self-supervised learning (ignoring labels) to obtain robust feature representations, then freezes the backbone and trains the classifier head on labeled data, and finally identifies low-credibility samples (likely poisoned), removes their labels, and performs semi-supervised fine-tuning of the whole model. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show this three-stage decoupling substantially reduces backdoor effectiveness while maintaining high benign accuracy.

result.text: The paper addresses improving transferability of adversarial examples in black-box attacks by rethinking why ensemble-based attacks work, noting prior methods merely average model outputs without analyzing underlying causes. The key insight is that ensemble transferability hinges on exploiting a "common weakness" across models, characterized by two properties: flatness of the loss landscape around adversarial examples and their closeness to each model’s local optima, both of which correlate with stronger cross-model transfer. The authors propose Common Weakness Attack (CWA), a method that explicitly promotes these two properties when generating adversarial perturbations across an ensemble, and provide empirical and theoretical evidence—on image classification, object detection, adversarially trained models, and a black-box vision-language system—that CWA yields more transferable attacks than prior ensemble averaging approaches.

result.text: The paper investigates whether algorithmic monoculture—decision-makers reusing the same models or training data—causes outcome homogenization, meaning the same individuals or groups consistently receive negative decisions across multiple decision-makers. Its key insight is the component-sharing hypothesis: sharing components like training data or pre-trained models increases the likelihood that harmful outcomes concentrate on the same people, potentially entrenching exclusion beyond what group-level fairness metrics reveal. Methodologically, the authors formalize outcome homogenization, then empirically test the hypothesis on standard fairness benchmarks by measuring individual- and group-level overlap of adverse outcomes under varying degrees of data and model sharing, and they further study how adaptation methods for foundation models affect homogenization in vision and language tasks. They find that sharing training data reliably increases homogenization—especially at the individual level—while model sharing’s effect depends strongly on adaptation technique, and they discuss the philosophical and societal risks this pattern poses for deployed ML systems.

args.text: We propose Gradient-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Token Selection for fine-grained recognition: a ViT that prunes and refines tokens hierarchically while enforcing sub-pixel, gradient-based spatial-semantic consistency. Concretely, a quadtree-style coarse-to-fine attention selects promising regions, while a CAP-like regularizer aligns each retained token’s saliency with local image gradients to preserve subtle, discriminative part boundaries; in parallel, a dual-branch design maintains a dense soft-attention stream to retain context and a sparse hard-attention stream for selected parts, fusing them for classification. A confusion-aware contrastive loss focuses supervision on visually similar classes by pulling together same-class part tokens and pushing apart easily-confused inter-class parts. This yields accuracy gains on FGVC (and improved data efficiency in few-shot regimes) while reducing compute via early token pruning.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of principled, per-prediction feature attributions for kernel methods by bringing Shapley values (SVs) into the kernel setting. The key insight is that SVs can be formulated and computed in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) via kernel mean embeddings, enabling both Interventional and Observational Shapley values to be derived functionally and computed efficiently while offering robustness to local perturbations. Methodologically, the authors develop RKHS-SHAP to estimate SVs using kernel embeddings of conditional and marginal distributions, prove stability properties, and introduce a Shapley regulariser that can be added to empirical risk minimisation to control feature contributions—enabling robustness to covariate shift and fairness by constraining sensitive features’ attributions during learning.

result.text: The paper tackles semi-supervised learning on ImageNet, aiming to achieve high accuracy with very few labeled examples by leveraging large amounts of unlabeled data. Its key insight is that task-agnostic unsupervised pretraining with very large (deep and wide) networks yields representations that become increasingly beneficial as labeled data decreases, and that a second, task-specific use of unlabeled data via distillation can transfer that knowledge into a smaller model with little accuracy loss. The method combines three steps: unsupervised pretraining of a big ResNet using SimCLRv2, supervised fine-tuning on the few available labels, and then distillation using unlabeled examples to refine and compress the model; this yields, for example, 73.9% ImageNet top-1 accuracy with only 1% of labels and outperforms fully supervised baselines with 10% of labels.

result.text: The paper addresses how to provide differentially private noise for federated learning with secure aggregation and limited communication by using a discrete mechanism that is practical to implement and composes well across users. The key insight is that the Skellam distribution—the difference of two independent Poisson variables—yields a discrete analogue to the Gaussian with comparable privacy-accuracy trade-offs, is closed under summation (so user-level noise aggregates cleanly), and can be sampled efficiently via standard Poisson samplers even at low precision. The authors analyze privacy by deriving a sharp bound on the Rényi divergence between shifted Skellam distributions and numerically evaluating the privacy loss distribution, and they demonstrate empirically in federated learning setups (with secure aggregation and communication constraints) that Skellam matches the Gaussian mechanism’s accuracy while offering practical advantages over the discrete Gaussian.

result.text: The paper addresses inductive representation learning for temporal graphs, where embeddings must handle evolving topology, new nodes, and temporal node/edge features so that representations are functions of time. The method, TGAT, stacks temporal graph attention layers that aggregate temporally-aware neighbor features using attention scores computed over time-augmented representations, allowing inductive inference of time-conditioned embeddings for both seen and unseen nodes and supporting tasks like temporal link prediction and node classification. Evaluation on two benchmark and one industrial dataset shows TGAT outperforms prior temporal and static baselines and naturally incorporates temporal edge features.

result.text: DeVRF addresses slow training of Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) methods for dynamic, non-rigid scenes by dramatically accelerating convergence while retaining high-fidelity novel-view synthesis. The key insight is to represent both the 3D canonical appearance and the 4D non-rigid deformation field with explicit, discrete voxel grids and to regularize the large parameter space by transferring knowledge from a separately learned multi-view static canonical volume. Methodologically, DeVRF first captures and trains a volumetric canonical radiance field from multi-view static images, then learns a voxelized 4D deformation field from few-view dynamic sequences under a static-to-dynamic learning paradigm and several implementation strategies to avoid overfitting; this yields comparable quality to prior dynamic NeRFs but trains roughly 100× faster.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that existing adversarial attacks on 3D point-cloud classifiers use global distance losses that fail to accurately measure and constrain fine-grained local geometric structure, leading to perturbations that distort local topology and are either detectable or ineffective. The key insight is that explicitly capturing and preserving multi-scale local topology through geometry-aware spectral filtering lets an attack better measure and constrain point-wise perturbations while maintaining imperceptible local geometry. The method, called Multi-grained Geometry-aware Attack (MGA), builds multi-scale spectral local filter banks tailored to object shapes and stacks them in multi-layer, coarse-to-fine banks to highlight local topology in filter coefficients, then enforces similarity of these coefficients between benign and adversarial samples during optimization to produce small, topology-preserving perturbations that remain effective against diverse 3D classifiers and defenses.

result.text: The paper addresses the memory bottleneck of fine-tuning very large language models, where backpropagation’s activation storage makes training impractical on typical hardware. The key insight is that a carefully adapted zeroth-order optimization—estimating gradients via only forward passes—can be made memory-efficient and practical for large LMs when combined with appropriate pretraining and prompting, contrary to pessimistic classical ZO theory. The authors introduce MeZO, an in-place adaptation of ZO-SGD that operates with the same memory footprint as inference and supports full-parameter and parameter-efficient schemes (LoRA, prefix tuning), and show it can fine-tune models up to 66B parameters on a single 80GB GPU. Empirically and theoretically, MeZO matches backprop fine-tuning across classification, multiple-choice, and generation tasks, outperforms in-context and linear probes, reduces memory by up to 12x (and GPU time up to 2x), and can optimize non-differentiable objectives like accuracy or F1.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of standardized benchmarks for evaluating Automatic Curriculum Learning (ACL) methods in deep reinforcement learning, which makes fair comparison across approaches difficult due to varying experimental setups. Its key insight is that a benchmark combining focused unit-test environments for specific ACL challenges with a more complex, procedurally generated composite environment can reveal strengths and weaknesses of ACL algorithms and expose open problems. To realize this, the authors introduce TeachMyAgent (TA): a suite of procedural environments including challenge-specific Box2D bipedal walker variants and a novel procedural Parkour task, and they implement or re-implement a range of ACL teachers and DRL student agents to run comparative studies. Using TA, they demonstrate that some ACL methods without expert priors are competitive, identify remaining failure modes in the Parkour environment, and provide an open-source package to standardize future ACL evaluation.

result.text: The paper tackles zero-shot robotic manipulation in unstructured environments where robots must handle novel objects and scenarios not seen during training by decomposing tasks into achievable subgoals. The key insight is that pretrained image-editing diffusion models, which have broad visual and semantic knowledge from Internet-scale data, can be finetuned to predict plausible future “subgoal” observations from a current camera view and a language command, and these visual subgoals can guide a separate low-level goal-conditioned policy more effectively than end-to-end language-conditioned controllers. The method, called SuSIE, finetunes InstructPix2Pix on mixed human and robot video data to generate hypothetical next-view images conditioned on instructions, and trains a robot-specific goal-conditioned policy on robot rollouts to realize those generated subgoal images; at runtime the diffusion model proposes intermediate visual goals that the controller tracks sequentially. Empirically, SuSIE leverages large-scale visual pretraining to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the CALVIN benchmark and strong real-world generalization, outperforming baselines that use privileged information or far more compute and data.

args.text: We propose Uncertainty-Guided Order-Dynamic Fusion Mamba (UG-OFM) for RGBT tracking: augment difference-based cross-modal fusion with per-token, per-modality uncertainty (heteroscedastic heads and cross-modal disagreement) to modulate the selective SSM input/forget gates and to choose a scan order that writes reliable tokens first while attenuating or deferring unreliable ones. To maintain efficiency while preserving long-range context, we integrate multi-scale Mamba scanning, running full-resolution passes only in regions/timesteps flagged as high-uncertainty and delegating global context capture to downsampled branches elsewhere. This quality-aware, order-dynamic fusion unifies theoretical robustness of uncertainty-weighted multimodal fusion with the mechanics that make Mamba effective, yielding resilience to noisy thermal/RGB frames and occlusion without prohibitive compute. We anticipate state-of-the-art robustness on RGBT benchmarks, with ablations showing uncertainty-guided ordering outperforms naive ordering and static gating.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of removing fairness-utility tradeoffs in pre-processing for supervised learning, aiming to eliminate discrimination without degrading predictive accuracy. Its key insight is that assigning uniform weights to demographic subgroups is suboptimal; instead, the influence of each individual training sample on both a fairness metric (e.g., equal opportunity) and predictive utility can be estimated and used to set granular, individualized weights. The proposed method computes per-sample weights by optimizing under constraints that enforce a fairness target while preserving utility, using influence-based measurements to guide reweighting during training. Empirically, this influence-driven reweighing yields “cost-free” fairness for equal opportunity across standard classifiers on multiple real-world tabular datasets, outperforming baseline reweighing methods that sacrifice accuracy.

result.text: The paper tackles learning interactive recommender systems from logged user feedback without any opportunity for online exploration, aiming to maximize cumulative user rewards despite distributional mismatch between logging and target policies. Its key insight is to cast recommendation as a probabilistic generative model and perform offline stochastic policy inference, combined with multiple principled mechanisms to constrain or correct for the gap between the logging policy and the learned policy. The method develops an inference algorithm for discrete stochastic policies from logged data and introduces five complementary strategies—support constraints, supervised regularization, explicit policy constraints, dual constraints, and reward extrapolation—to reduce distributional shift during offline training. Experiments on two public real-world datasets show these techniques yield better cumulative-reward performance than standard supervised and prior offline RL approaches for recommendation.

result.text: The paper investigates what learning algorithm transformer-based in-context learners implement, focusing on whether they implicitly encode and update smaller models when given sequences of labeled examples, using linear regression as a testbed. The key insight is that transformers can and do recover standard estimation procedures—such as gradient descent, ridge regression, and exact least-squares—and can transition between these behaviors depending on architecture depth, width, and dataset noise, even converging to Bayesian estimators in large models. Methodologically, the authors prove by construction that transformers can implement closed-form and iterative linear learners, empirically train transformers on linear tasks to show their predictions match those classical algorithms, and analyze internal representations to find nonlinear encodings of weight vectors and moment matrices in late layers. Together, these results support an algorithmic interpretation of in-context learning whereby transformers rediscover and execute familiar estimation algorithms within their activations.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of providing reliable algorithmic recourse when the true structural causal model is unknown, showing that without correct structural equations one cannot guarantee recourse. Its key insight is that instead of assuming perfect causal knowledge, one can treat causal uncertainty probabilistically—either by placing a distribution over structural equations and using Bayesian model averaging under additive Gaussian noise, or by foregoing functional assumptions entirely and estimating the average interventional effect of actions on a relevant subpopulation. Methodologically, the authors formalize these two probabilistic recourse notions, derive a gradient-based optimization to select actions that maximize the probability (or expected effect) of achieving recourse given limited causal information, and empirically demonstrate that these approaches produce more reliable recommendations than deterministic, non-probabilistic baselines.

result.text: Megaverse tackles the bottleneck of slow, resource-limited 3D embodied simulation for reinforcement learning by providing an extremely high-throughput engine that can run physics-based, egocentric, fully-shaded scenes at over one million actions per second on a single 8‑GPU node. The key insight is that batching many simulator instances and executing physics, rendering, and interaction logic on GPUs unlocks massive parallelism and amortizes overheads, yielding up to 70× speedups over prior platforms like DeepMind Lab while still supporting complex interactive objects and multi-agent scenarios. Methodologically, the authors build a GPU-centric simulator that performs batched physics and rendering pipelines, design a diverse benchmark of single- and multi-agent cognitive tasks, and validate the platform by running model-free RL baselines to demonstrate feasibility and provide open-source tools and data for future research.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of enabling large language models to perform deep, complete, and faithful reasoning on knowledge-intensive tasks where standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) often returns shallow or incomplete evidence. The key insight is that tightly coupling retrieval over unstructured documents with retrieval over structured knowledge graphs—using the graph to link and deepen document contexts while using documents to ground and guide graph traversal—yields iterative, knowledge-guided searches that surface in-depth clues for reasoning. The proposed Think-on-Graph 2.0 (ToG-2) framework alternates between graph retrieval (querying entities and relations in a KG) and context retrieval (pulling relevant document passages linked to those entities), feeding the combined, iteratively refined evidence into an LLM to generate answers without additional training. Experiments show ToG-2 is plug-and-play with various LLMs, achieves SOTA results on most evaluated knowledge-intensive datasets with GPT-3.5, and substantially improves smaller models (e.g., LLaMA-2-13B) toward GPT-3.5-level reasoning.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of preserving and mining local geometric information in deep networks that operate on the Riemannian manifold of Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) matrices, where existing SPD networks largely lack mechanisms analogous to Euclidean local convolutions. The key insight is that convolution’s role in capturing locality can be abstracted categorically and adapted to SPD manifolds, enabling principled definition of local information in Riemannian geometry rather than naively porting Euclidean filters. Based on this view the authors design a multi-scale submanifold block that constructs and processes local SPD submanifolds to extract multi-scale geometric features while respecting manifold structure and SPD constraints. Experiments across several visual tasks demonstrate that incorporating this Riemannian local mechanism improves representation quality and task performance compared to prior SPD network designs.

result.text: The paper addresses how to jointly satisfy communication and (ε,δ)-differential privacy constraints while minimizing estimation error in distributed mean and frequency estimation problems common in federated learning and analytics. The key insight is that communication-efficient compression can itself amplify privacy: by having each client send only a randomly selected partial sketch of its data, the effective privacy loss per client is reduced, allowing optimal privacy-accuracy trade-offs with far fewer bits than uncompressed protocols. Concretely, the authors prove that optimal error under (ε,δ)-DP can be achieved when each client transmits Θ(n·min(ε,ε^2)) bits for mean estimation and Θ(log(n·min(ε,ε^2))) bits for frequency estimation, yielding substantial savings whenever n·min(ε,ε^2)=o(d). Their method constructs randomized compression schemes and sampling-based communication protocols that integrate with noise addition to meet (ε,δ)-DP while exploiting privacy amplification from partial, randomly selected transmissions.

result.text: The paper addresses the apparent dichotomy between particle-based deep generative models (like gradient flows and score-based diffusion) and generator-based methods (GANs), questioning whether pushforward generators and differential-equation particle dynamics are fundamentally different paradigms. The key insight is that training a generator can be interpreted as a generalized particle transport: generator-driven pushes are just one optional mechanism to move an empirical distribution, so adversarial training and score-based dynamics can be unified under a common generative-particle framework. Methodologically, the authors formalize this view by casting generator learning as a continuum of particle displacement processes, derive variants that embed a generator into score-based diffusion and conversely remove the generator from GAN training, and validate these constructions with empirical proofs of concept showing the feasibility of the unified approaches.

The paper studies how instruction tuning of large language models can be maliciously manipulated via data poisoning: an adversary injects crafted instruction-following examples into the instruction-tuning dataset to steer downstream model behavior toward attacker-desired outputs. The key insight is that because instruction-tuned models heavily weight instruction-following examples, a small, coherent set of poisoned examples—generated with the help of an oracle LLM—can reliably induce targeted behaviors (e.g., content injection or over-refusal) while remaining linguistically natural and stealthy. The authors present AutoPoison, an automated pipeline that uses an oracle to create versatile poisoned examples conditioned on specific attack goals, and they empirically benchmark attack strength and stealth, showing that minimal poisoning can substantially change model behavior without obvious detection.

result.text: The paper addresses efficient channel pruning for convolutional neural networks by improving layer-by-layer methods that focus only on reconstructing next-layer features without directly considering final task performance. Its key insight is that pruning should be guided both by the downstream classification loss and by feature importance across subsequent pruning stages, since many reconstructed features will be discarded later and thus need not be faithfully reconstructed. The proposed CPLI method combines a loss-aware channel selection criterion with a strategy to identify and suppress unimportant features that are likely to be removed in future pruning, enabling more targeted reconstruction and pruning decisions. Experiments on CIFAR-10, ImageNet and UCF-101 show CPLI yields better accuracy-compression trade-offs than prior layer-wise reconstruction-only approaches.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of understanding and improving subgraph-enhanced graph neural networks (GNNs), whose varied designs lack a unifying theory and either exhaustively, randomly, or heuristically select subgraphs rather than learning which to use. result.text: We propose Uncertainty-Guided Order-Dynamic Fusion Mamba (UG-OFM) for RGBT tracking: augment difference-based cross-modal fusion with per-token, per-modality uncertainty (heteroscedastic heads and cross-modal disagreement) to modulate the selective SSM input/forget gates and to choose a scan order that writes reliable tokens first while attenuating or deferring unreliable ones. To maintain efficiency while preserving long-range context, we integrate multi-scale Mamba scanning, running full-resolution passes only in regions/timesteps flagged as high-uncertainty and delegating global context capture to downsampled branches elsewhere. This quality-aware, order-dynamic fusion unifies theoretical robustness of uncertainty-weighted multimodal fusion with the mechanics that make Mamba effective, yielding resilience to noisy thermal/RGB frames and occlusion without prohibitive compute. We anticipate state-of-the-art robustness on RGBT benchmarks, with ablations showing uncertainty-guided ordering outperforms naive ordering and static gating.

result.text: Streaming Equal Shares via Pacing (SESP): We study participatory budgeting with arbitrary project costs in a streaming setting where projects arrive online and must be irrevocably funded, seeking proportional guarantees over time. SESP maintains per-voter pacing multipliers that throttle equal-share contributions to currently arriving approved projects and funds a project once its paced contributions meet cost; the multipliers are updated to equalize spend rates, yielding Lindahl-like personalized prices and a dynamically stable priceable outcome. Under i.i.d. arrivals from a stationary distribution, the time-averaged funded bundle converges to the static Equal Shares (and, when applicable, balanced-stably-priceable) solution for the underlying distribution, implying PJR and EJR-up-to-one-project guarantees in the limit along with per-prefix approximate group no-deviation bounds. Further, by leveraging strengthened priceability across satisfaction measures, SESP simultaneously preserves proportionality under both cardinal-by-cost and cardinal-by-count satisfactions, while running in polynomial time per arrival.

result.text: The paper tackles the shortage of large, diverse datasets for data-driven short-term load forecasting (STLF), which has limited progress on pretrain-then-fine-tune approaches for predicting building energy use. Its key insight is that a very large synthetic dataset can enable pretrained models that generalize well to real buildings, especially commercial ones, and that increasing synthetic data size and diversity yields diminishing improvements following a power-law. The authors introduce BuildingsBench, comprising Buildings-900K (900K simulated U.S. buildings) plus an evaluation suite of ~1,900 real residential and commercial buildings, and benchmark zero-shot STLF (no fine-tuning) and transfer learning (fine-tuning) tasks. They show synthetically pretrained models transfer effectively to many real targets and that fine-tuning further improves performance for most buildings, providing a public dataset and codebase to accelerate generalizable STLF research.

result.text: The paper addresses slow, resource-intensive training of deep reinforcement learning agents in visually complex 3D environments by making simulation the primary bottleneck to scale. Its key insight is that organizing the renderer and simulator around "batch simulation" — accepting and executing very large batches of simulation requests at once — lets the system amortize scene asset storage, rendering, data loading, and synchronization costs across many agents, massively increasing frames-per-second throughput. Methodologically, the authors implement a batch-oriented 3D renderer and embodied navigation simulator, pair it with a computationally efficient policy network, and adapt training algorithms to preserve sample efficiency with large mini-batches; together these changes yield two-orders-of-magnitude speedups (e.g., >19k fps on one GPU, up to 72k fps on eight GPUs) and enable near-state-of-the-art navigation performance with far fewer resources.

result.text: The paper addresses the computational bottleneck of performing tensor products of irreducible representations (irreps) in E(3)-equivariant neural networks, whose cost grows prohibitively with higher-order tensors. The key insight is that Clebsch–Gordan coefficients used for these tensor products are mathematically equivalent to Gaunt coefficients—integrals of three spherical harmonics—so that tensor products can be reframed as pointwise multiplications of spherical functions and thus re-expressed in a 2D Fourier basis. Methodologically, the authors define the Gaunt Tensor Product which converts spherical-harmonic representations to a 2D Fourier basis and uses the convolution theorem with Fast Fourier Transforms to compute products efficiently, reducing complexity from O(L^6) to O(L^3). Empirically, this approach yields substantial speedups and performance gains on molecular benchmarks such as the Open Catalyst Project and 3BPA.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of limited length generalization in Mamba models for long-range sequence processing, where despite Mamba’s efficiency and strong performance, models trained at a given context length fail to extrapolate to much longer inputs. The key insight is that this limitation stems from a restricted effective receptive field determined by the training sequence length, and that exploiting a hidden filtering mechanism in the S6 layer can extend receptive range without retraining. The authors propose DeciMamba, a context-extension method that modifies the hidden filtering within S6 to permit longer-context aggregation at inference time, and demonstrate empirically on real-world long-range NLP tasks that DeciMamba enables substantial extrapolation to much longer contexts while providing faster inference.

result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of calibrating predictive probabilities for domain-adapted models, where domain shift and absence of target labels make uncertainty estimation unreliable and existing DA methods often trade calibration for higher accuracy. The key insight is that this trade-off can be resolved by explicitly optimizing a transferable calibration mapping that reduces both bias and variance of calibration errors across domains, rather than relying on source-only or naive target-proxy approaches. The proposed method, TransCal, is a hyperparameter-free, post-hoc recalibration framework that learns a calibration transformation transferable from source to target using theoretical criteria that guarantee lower bias and variance, and can be applied on top of any DA model. Empirical and theoretical results show TransCal consistently improves calibration on target data while preserving or improving accuracy compared to prior calibration and DA baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of standardized, reproducible evaluation for jailbreak attacks that coax large language models into producing harmful or policy-violating outputs, noting inconsistent metrics and inaccessible artifacts in prior work. Its key insight is that a shared, open, and evolving benchmark—combining a curated repository of adversarial prompts, a representative behavior dataset, and a unified evaluation protocol—can make jailbreak research comparable, transparent, and reproducible while enabling systematic tracking of defenses. The authors present JailbreakBench, which packs (1) an evolving collection of jailbreak artifacts, (2) a 100-behavior dataset aligned with OpenAI policies drawn from prior literature and new cases, (3) a standardized threat model, chat templates, system prompts, and scoring functions implemented in an open evaluation framework, and (4) a public leaderboard to record attack and defense performance across models.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of capturing long-range spatio-temporal interactions for continuous sign language recognition (CSLR) from video, where fine-grained motion (e.g., finger and hand trajectories) and relevant region dynamics must be modeled efficiently. The key insight is to decompose spatio-temporal modeling into trajectory-aligned token streams that preserve continuous motion patterns and a correlated-region attention mechanism that dynamically selects and assigns relevant key-value tokens, thereby focusing computation on informative moving regions while filtering irrelevant background. TCNet implements this by converting frames into aligned trajectories of continuous visual tokens and applying self-attention along each trajectory to capture region-specific motion patterns, while a correlation module uses dynamic attention to prune irrelevant regions and supply adaptive key-value tokens for each query, yielding lower memory/computation and state-of-the-art accuracy on multiple CSLR benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses inefficient and imbalanced token-to-expert routing in sparsely-activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where fixed top-k routing can leave experts under- or over-trained and tokens unfairly limited in expert access. The key insight is to reverse the selection direction—have experts choose the top-k tokens to serve rather than forcing tokens to pick a fixed number of experts—so each expert maintains a fixed bucket size while tokens can be routed to a variable number of experts, improving load balance and utilization. The method implements this “expert choice” routing within heterogeneous MoEs, compares it to prior top-1 and top-2 gating schemes under equal computational budgets, and demonstrates that expert choice yields over 2× faster pretraining convergence and better downstream fine-tuning performance on GLUE/SuperGLUE tasks, and even outperforms a dense T5 baseline on several tasks at lower activation cost.

result.text: The paper addresses understanding long-form videos with LLM-based approaches and probes why such models perform well even when video-specific information is limited. The key insight is that much of the strong performance comes from the LLMs' world knowledge and reasoning, so augmenting them with targeted, object-centric video information—rather than raw frames—can more effectively improve accuracy. result.text: The paper tackles the problem of removing backdoor triggers implanted in deep neural networks—poisoned training-time manipulations that leave clean accuracy intact but force targeted misclassification when a trigger appears. Its key insight is that backdoored models exhibit altered intermediate-layer attention patterns that can be corrected by aligning the compromised model’s attention with that of a cleanly fine-tuned teacher, thereby erasing the trigger’s effect without degrading normal performance. The proposed method, Neural Attention Distillation (NAD), obtains a teacher by independently fine-tuning on a small clean subset and then distills its intermediate attention maps into the backdoored student during further fine-tuning on that same clean data, using attention-alignment losses to guide the student toward the teacher’s behavior. args.text: Bayesian Router for Zero-Shot Adapter Composition: instead of learning a controller to fuse many task adapters, compute per-input (optionally per-token/per-channel) adapter weights from a Laplace-approximated predictive marginal likelihood, using each adapter’s local curvature (Fisher/precision) around a shared base to score how well it explains the input. These evidence scores drive a training-free mixture over adapter deltas or selection among masked supports, yielding dynamic composition akin to a MoE router without additional data. To reduce interference and cost, restrict routing to task supports discovered by mask-based merging or lightweight modulators and fall back to the base when no adapter has sufficient evidence. We hypothesize this Bayesian gating closes much of the gap to learned multi-adapter routers while preserving the simplicity and robustness of Fisher/Laplace-based merging.

result.text: The paper tackles video-to-audio generation, aiming to produce high-quality, temporally synchronized audio from silent video while being efficient at sampling. Its key insight is to model conditional generation as rectified flow matching—regressing a transport vector field that maps noise straight to spectrogram latents—rather than using autoregressive or score-based diffusion models, which yields better audio quality and alignment. Methodologically, Frieren uses a non-autoregressive feed-forward transformer with channel-level cross-modal fusion to estimate the vector field, solves an ODE for sampling, and applies reflow plus one-step distillation with a guided vector field to enable very fast (few- or single-step) generation. Empirically, this approach achieves state-of-the-art quality and temporal alignment on VGGSound, notably 97.22% alignment accuracy and a 6.2% inception score improvement over a strong diffusion baseline.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of learning robust representations for remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) signals from facial videos when labeled data are scarce and conventional contrastive augmentations fail to capture subtle, periodic physiological cues amid noise. result.text: The paper tackles scalable detection of backdoor attacks in deep neural networks, where existing optimization-based defenses become prohibitively slow as the number of classes grows because they try to find minimal triggers for every possible target label. The key insight is to frame label selection as a K‑arm optimization problem akin to multi‑armed bandits: by stochastically and iteratively focusing optimization effort on a small set of promising target labels guided by an objective, the method both cuts complexity and reduces uncertainty about which labels are likely poisoned. The proposed K‑Arm scanning algorithm alternates between selecting candidate labels according to estimated rewards and running trigger‑finding optimizations on those labels, refining selections over iterations; this yields much faster scanning and higher detection accuracy, outperforming prior techniques on thousands of IARPA TrojAI models.

args.text: We propose Gradient-Guided Subpatch Refinement (GSR) for fine-grained visual classification, which expands only ambiguous image regions into higher-resolution tokens to capture subtle part cues without part annotations. Starting from a ViT, we compute per-patch ambiguity from class–patch attention and a learned head, then spawn TNT-style subpatch tokens only for the top-K regions and process them with an inner transformer in a quadtree-like coarse-to-fine schedule to keep compute near-linear. A context-aware consistency loss enforces spatial–semantic coherence between refined subpatch groups and their parent patch, while a part-level contrastive loss on selected (sub)patch tokens pushes apart confusing classes. This targeted subpatch refinement recovers within-patch detail where it matters, yielding better fine-grained discrimination at modest computational cost.

result.text: The paper tackles autoformalization: automatically converting natural-language mathematics into formal specifications and proofs, a task important for formal verification and AI but long considered out of reach. The key insight is that large language models (LLMs) can already translate a substantial fraction (~25.3%) of competition-style math problems exactly into Isabelle/HOL formal statements, providing useful training data for downstream theorem proving. The authors use LLM-generated formalizations to augment training of a neural theorem prover and thereby improve performance on the MiniF2F benchmark, raising the proof success rate from 29.6% to 35.2%. This demonstrates that LLM-driven autoformalization can both produce high-quality formal statements and materially advance automated theorem proving.

args.text: Recent work shows jailbreaks that bypass safety can also degrade model capabilities, but defenses rarely monitor this shift. We propose Sentinel Probes: interleaving lightweight, content-agnostic micro-probes (e.g., quick reasoning, calibration, and consistency checks) during a conversation to estimate real-time capability drift and trigger recovery (state reset, safety re-grounding, or conditional routing) when a jailbreak-induced mode shift is detected. We evaluate across standardized jailbreak suites and forbidden-information metrics, extend to agentic and code-completion settings with context-specific probes, and quantify both detection AUC and retained helpfulness on capability testbeds. This turns capability degradation from a hidden side-effect into a detectable signal for robust, low-latency jailbreak mitigation.

Its key insight is that Transformers, various attention mechanisms, and SSMs can be unified through decompositions of structured semiseparable matrices, revealing a state-space duality (SSD) that exposes equivalent computational primitives across these model families. Leveraging SSD, the authors derive generalized models and efficient algorithms that blend selective SSM behavior with attention-like operations, and they instantiate this as Mamba-2: a refinement of the Mamba selective SSM that implements the dual formulations to achieve 2–8× speedups while retaining competitive language-modeling performance.

The paper tackles the challenge of pre-training language models for table understanding despite the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality tabular datasets by proposing to teach models to execute SQL on tables. Its key insight is that synthetic, executable SQL queries paired with their execution results can serve as a diverse and scalable supervision signal that trains a model to mimic a neural SQL executor, thereby instilling table-specific reasoning abilities. TAPEX implements this by automatically synthesizing a large corpus of SQL queries and outputs over tables and pre-training a transformer-based model to predict execution results and intermediate representations, then fine-tuning on downstream table reasoning tasks. This approach yields substantial gains and new state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks (WikiSQL, WikiTableQuestions, SQA, TabFact), demonstrating the effectiveness of synthetic executable programs for table pre-training.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of accurately estimating belief states in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), especially for high-dimensional continuous and unknown environments where existing deep learning approaches yield limited, inflexible posterior approximations. Its key insight is to combine the expressive power of normalizing flows with recurrent variational inference so that the learned belief can represent complex, continuous, and multimodal distributions over hidden states. result.text: The paper tackles the problem of accurately perceiving and reasoning about human emotions from real-world, multimodal signals, addressing limitations of prior models that use single modalities or struggle to integrate audio and subtle facial micro-expressions. Its key insight is that learning emotion-specific representations across audio, visual, and textual modalities and aligning them into a shared embedding space enables a language model to both recognize nuanced emotional cues and perform higher-level emotion reasoning when instruction tuned. args.text: We propose Quantized Explanation-Quality Conditioning (QEQC) for LLM-based explainable recommendation, replacing RLHF-style optimization with discrete control tokens derived from automatic explanation-quality reward (EQR) scorers. result.text: The paper addresses whether and how one can unsupervisedly factorize (disentangle) the latent symmetry factors of a data manifold—i.e., recover a Lie-group-induced decomposition—solely from observations of its orbit. result.text: MinVIS addresses video instance segmentation (VIS) by asking whether strong VIS can be achieved without video-specific architectures or video-based training, thereby reducing labeling and memory costs. The key insight is that queries learned by a query-based image instance segmentation model to discriminate objects within a single frame are temporally consistent across frames and thus can serve as identity signals for tracking without any handcrafted tracking heuristics or video training. The method trains only on independently treated annotated frames (even heavily sub-sampled, e.g., 1% of frames) with a query-based image mask head, runs per-frame instance segmentation at inference, and then performs online tracking by bipartite matching of query representations between consecutive frames to link masks into tracks. This minimal pipeline achieves state-of-the-art VIS results (notably +10% AP on Occluded VIS) while drastically cutting annotation needs and memory footprint.

The key insight is that for a fixed agent policy one can compute (and therefore learn) an optimal adversary that provably minimizes the agent’s return, and that alternatingly training the agent against such a learned adversary produces stronger robustness than prior heuristic attacks. result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of providing formal safety guarantees for neural network dynamic models (NNDMs), which predict system trajectories via iterative noisy NN outputs but lack reliable safety analysis. The key insight is that stochastic barrier functions can certify safety probabilities for NNDMs in a manner analogous to Lyapunov functions for stability, and that recent convex approximation techniques for neural networks enable tractable synthesis of such barriers. The method constructs piecewise-linear bounds on the NN dynamics using convex approximations, formulates barrier synthesis as a sum-of-squares convex optimization that yields a lower bound on safety probability, and—if the bound is insufficient—computes minimally invasive controllers by exploiting barrier convexity to cast safety-maximizing control synthesis as a linear program. result.text: Video-LaVIT tackles the challenge of scaling image-text multimodal LLMs to real-world videos by addressing the difficulty of modeling spatiotemporal dynamics in large-scale video-language pre-training. Evaluations show the approach yields competitive performance across 13 multimodal benchmarks for image/video understanding and generation.
