args.text: We propose a bidirectional auxiliary-task distillation framework for LiDAR–camera 3D detection that couples lightweight point↔pixel association with symmetric geometric pretext losses: the image branch learns normalized local coordinate maps while the LiDAR branch predicts per-point local surface attributes, and each loss backpropagates through the cross-modal links to sharpen the other modality’s backbone features. To ensure robustness when a sensor degrades, we decouple per-modality BEV streams and train with stochastic modality dropout while distilling from a joint BEV teacher so that either camera-only or LiDAR-only branches can produce strong predictions. The interaction module preserves modality-specific representations but exchanges them selectively via the auxiliary gradient routes rather than heavy fusion, reducing compute while improving geometric alignment. This yields stronger point features under sparse point clouds and markedly better camera-only performance under LiDAR malfunction, without adding inference cost when both sensors are present.

The authors introduce ProgramPort, which uses a semantic parser to convert instructions into a program of functional modules grounded in vision and action; each module combines deterministic operations and learnable neural components, and program execution yields parameters for general manipulation primitives for the end-effector, with the whole modular network trained end-to-end via imitation learning. result.text: We propose Gradient-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Token Selection for fine-grained recognition: a ViT that prunes and refines tokens hierarchically while enforcing sub-pixel, gradient-based spatial-semantic consistency. Concretely, a quadtree-style coarse-to-fine attention selects promising regions, while a CAP-like regularizer aligns each retained token’s saliency with local image gradients to preserve subtle, discriminative part boundaries; in parallel, a dual-branch design maintains a dense soft-attention stream to retain context and a sparse hard-attention stream for selected parts, fusing them for classification. A confusion-aware contrastive loss focuses supervision on visually similar classes by pulling together same-class part tokens and pushing apart easily-confused inter-class parts. This yields accuracy gains on FGVC (and improved data efficiency in few-shot regimes) while reducing compute via early token pruning.

Its key insight is that these three beneficial strategies can be unified into a single integrated-gradients-based objective that captures input attribution along a path, thereby encouraging perturbations that both align with model saliency and traverse smoothed decision boundaries. The proposed method, Transferable Attack based on Integrated Gradients (TAIG), computes integrated gradients along either a straight-line path or a random piecewise linear path from a baseline to the input and uses this single-term gradient signal to generate transferable adversarial perturbations. Empirically, both TAIG variants achieve stronger transferability than prior state-of-the-art attacks and can be combined with existing techniques to further improve black-box attack success.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of making complex model predictions interpretable without the faithfulness issues and scalability limits of post-hoc explanations or traditional per-feature Generalized Additive Models (GAMs). Its key insight is that shape functions for many features can be efficiently represented as linear combinations of a small, shared set of learned basis functions, so interpretability is preserved while parameter count and computation scale far better. The proposed Neural Basis Model (NBM) implements this by training a single neural network to learn a compact basis dictionary and per-feature coefficients (and optionally higher-order interaction terms) that combine those bases into feature-wise shape functions, yielding a scalable, accurate, and compact GAM-like model. Empirically, NBMs match or beat prior interpretable models on tabular and image tasks in accuracy, model size, and throughput while retaining clear per-feature explanations.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning compact, interpretable representations of graph-structured data when individual graphs are unregistered and may live in different metric spaces with varying numbers of nodes, which makes standard linear dictionary learning inapplicable. result.text: We propose Quantized Explanation-Quality Conditioning (QEQC) for LLM-based explainable recommendation, replacing RLHF-style optimization with discrete control tokens derived from automatic explanation-quality reward (EQR) scorers. result.text: This paper tackles the problem of efficient filter pruning for compressing convolutional neural networks without the cumbersome multi-stage training and many hyperparameters typical of prior work, and it also addresses uneven pruning needs across layers. args.text: We propose Conformally-Weighted Self-Consistency (CWSC), a black-box uncertainty method that turns LLM agreement patterns into prediction sets or risk thresholds with PAC-style guarantees under distribution shift. CWSC defines nonconformity from both intra-prompt self-consistency and cross-prompt stability (via paraphrases/rationale variants), then conformalizes these scores using importance-weighted calibration to target the shifted prompt distribution, while refining quantiles per embedding-clustered subgroups to avoid residual subgroup miscalibration. This marries practical black-box elicitation with self-consistency and multicalibration, yielding finite-sample target-domain coverage and tighter failure prediction than marginal consistency alone. We will evaluate on unrealizable census-style benchmarks and across base vs. instruction-tuned models to test coverage, set size, and failure detection, hypothesizing robustness to instruction-tuning overconfidence and improved fine-grained calibration.

args.text: Safety Subspace Projection for VLMs: learn a shared, low-dimensional safety latent across image and text encoders, plus a projection that removes unsafe components from visual embeddings before fusion with the LLM. At inference, we (i) project visual features through the learned safety nullspace and (ii) gate generation with a calibrated safety score, regularized by OCR cycle-consistency so image-rendered text yields the same safety decision as its transcription. result.text: The paper addresses the problem that standard GAN discriminators lose sensitivity to high-frequency image content—largely due to downsampling layers—causing generators to produce images with deficient spectral detail and a notable spectrum discrepancy from real data. result.text: We propose a bidirectional auxiliary-task distillation framework for LiDAR–camera 3D detection that couples lightweight point↔pixel association with symmetric geometric pretext losses: the image branch learns normalized local coordinate maps while the LiDAR branch predicts per-point local surface attributes, and each loss backpropagates through the cross-modal links to sharpen the other modality’s backbone features. To ensure robustness when a sensor degrades, we decouple per-modality BEV streams and train with stochastic modality dropout while distilling from a joint BEV teacher so that either camera-only or LiDAR-only branches can produce strong predictions. The interaction module preserves modality-specific representations but exchanges them selectively via the auxiliary gradient routes rather than heavy fusion, reducing compute while improving geometric alignment. This yields stronger point features under sparse point clouds and markedly better camera-only performance under LiDAR malfunction, without adding inference cost when both sensors are present.

args.text: We propose Continual EM-Contrastive Distillation (CECD) for streaming dynamic text-attributed graphs, extending variational EM co-training to the temporal setting with parameter-efficient, structure-aware adapters. result.text: The paper tackles interactive image retrieval where a user provides a reference image and a natural language modification and the system must find the target image that matches the requested change. result.text: The paper addresses the practical failure modes of Expected Improvement (EI) and its variants in Bayesian optimization, where acquisition values often underflow to zero in many regions as observations, dimensionality, constraints, or parallel evaluations increase, leading to poor and inconsistent optimization performance. The key insight is that these failures are largely numerical rather than conceptual: taking a numerically stable transformation (logarithm) of the EI-style acquisition functions preserves their optima (exactly or approximately) while avoiding vanishing values and other pathologies that hinder optimization algorithms. The authors introduce the LogEI family—log-domain reformulations of EI, Expected Hypervolume Improvement (EHVI), and their constrained, noisy, and parallel extensions—derive analytic and approximate expressions that maintain equivalent maximizers, and implement them within standard optimization routines. Empirically, LogEI variants substantially improve optimization reliability and performance over canonical EI formulations and surprisingly match or surpass several recent state-of-the-art acquisition functions, underscoring the critical role of numerical stability in acquisition optimization.

args.text: We propose Union-of-Product Manifolds Disentangling (UPMD): a representation learner that jointly clusters data into components with variable intrinsic dimensionality and, within each component, recovers a product-of-submanifolds factorization. An isometry-regularized encoder first makes the latent space approximate the data manifold’s metric; then, inside each cluster, a diffusion-based de Rham decomposition extracts factor-aligned axes, while weak paired-sample constraints align coordinates for shared factors across pairs. Cluster assignments are driven by local intrinsic-dimension estimates and by violations of product structure, enabling different components to host different numbers and types of factors. This unifies the union-of-manifolds view with weakly supervised factorization and yields identifiable, controllable latents on datasets with disconnected supports and heterogeneous factor sets.

result.text: The paper studies how full-batch gradient descent behaves when training neural networks and challenges common optimization assumptions by showing that training typically occurs in an "Edge of Stability" regime. The key insight is that the largest Hessian eigenvalue repeatedly hovers just above 2/(step size), causing short-term non-monotonic loss dynamics while still producing steady long-term loss decrease, so standard analyses based on smoothness and monotonic descent do not describe practical neural network training. The authors support this claim with extensive empirical investigations across architectures, datasets, and step sizes, tracking Hessian spectra, loss trajectories, and optimization dynamics to show the persistent Edge of Stability phenomenon and discuss its implications for theoretical understanding of gradient-based training.

result.text: This paper tackles open-vocabulary object detection—enabling detectors to recognize categories unseen during training by specifying novel classes at inference—by integrating language and visual exemplars into a two-stage detector. The key insight is that large language model–generated class descriptions provide powerful, complementary signals to image exemplars, and fusing both modalities yields stronger classifiers than either alone or than fully supervised detectors. Methodologically, the authors prompt an LLM to produce informative textual class descriptions to build text-based classifiers, design a visual aggregator that ingests any number of exemplar images to form vision-based classifiers, and introduce a simple fusion scheme to create multi-modal classifiers within a standard two-stage detection pipeline. Evaluated on LVIS, their text classifiers outperform prior OVOD work, vision classifiers match previous text-based methods, and the multi-modal approach achieves the best results, surpassing fully supervised baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of crafting adversarial examples that transfer well across models for black-box attacks, noting that prior work separately optimizes loss, manipulates attention maps, or smooths decision surfaces. Its key insight is that these three beneficial strategies can be unified into a single integrated-gradients-based objective that captures input attribution along a path, thereby encouraging perturbations that both align with model saliency and traverse smoothed decision boundaries. The proposed method, Transferable Attack based on Integrated Gradients (TAIG), computes integrated gradients along either a straight-line path or a random piecewise linear path from a baseline to the input and uses this single-term gradient signal to generate transferable adversarial perturbations. Empirically, both TAIG variants achieve stronger transferability than prior state-of-the-art attacks and can be combined with existing techniques to further improve black-box attack success.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of improving segmentation on a target medical imaging modality that lacks annotations by leveraging annotated data from an assistant modality despite large appearance differences. Its key insight is that modality-shared anatomical knowledge (e.g., shape priors) can be more effectively transferred if the appearance gap is reduced and if two modality-specific segmentors mutually distill knowledge to each other online, allowing implicit cross-modality learning beyond direct supervision. The method applies an Image Alignment Module to narrow appearance discrepancies between modalities and trains two segmentors jointly in a Mutual Knowledge Distillation (MKD) framework where each network learns from its own annotations and the peer’s predictions, with an ensemble of both segmentors producing the final segmentation; experiments on MM-WHS 2017 show substantial gains in CT segmentation when using MRI as the assistant modality.

The paper addresses how to get privacy amplification for iterative DP-SGD-style learning when data is distributed across many devices (federated learning) and central sampling or shuffling assumptions are infeasible. The key insight is that independent, randomized client “check-ins” (local participation decisions) suffice to amplify privacy in a way comparable to classical subsampling or shuffling, yet require no server-driven uniform sampling, global permutation, or even knowledge of total population size. The authors propose a random check-in protocol where each client independently decides whether to participate in each round and applies a local DP randomizer; they prove amplification bounds for this protocol (including a strengthened analysis of amplification by shuffling for (ε,δ)-DP local randomizers that gives exponential improvements), and show the method achieves similar privacy–utility trade-offs while greatly relaxing coordination requirements.

args.text: Temporal graph models and benchmarks often treat timestamps as precise, yet blockchain networks batch many interactions at identical block times, include intra-block execution order, mempool delays, and occasional reorgs—making models brittle and evaluations optimistic. We propose Block-aware Temporal Benchmarking: paired datasets and protocols that expose block height and intra-block transaction indices, add controlled time-warp perturbations (within-block shuffles, timestamp jitter, reorg simulation), and report a clock-invariance robustness metric alongside standard scores on live NFT and other on-chain graphs. We further introduce hierarchical time encodings that fuse block-relative positional features with intra-block order embeddings, drop-in compatible with TGAT/TGN layers, decoupling learning from wall-clock artifacts. This suite aligns temporal-graph evaluation with blockchain microstructure, mitigating memorization biases and enabling more reliable cross-domain comparisons.

result.text: The paper tackles both generic and query-focused video summarization by enabling customizable, language-guided selection of salient scenes rather than relying solely on fixed, visual-only importance models. Its key insight is that large pretrained language–vision priors (via dense captions or user queries) can guide frame saliency and that a unified multimodal transformer can score frames based on relative importance and alignment with language to serve both tasks. The method, CLIP-It, encodes video frames and text (user queries or auto-generated dense captions) into a shared multimodal transformer that learns pairwise frame importance and query–frame correlation and can be trained supervised or unsupervised; this yields strong gains on TVSum, SumMe and QFVS and particularly improves cross-dataset transfer.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of systematic evaluation for jailbreak attacks on large language models (LLMs), noting prior work often focuses narrowly on model vulnerabilities and ignores diverse attack factors and defenses. Its key insight is that jailbreak effectiveness depends on multiple configurable factors at both the target and attack level, so meaningful comparison requires a standardized benchmark that tests attacks against defense-enhanced models. The authors present JailTrickBench, a benchmarking suite that defines eight key factors of jailbreak attacks, implements seven representative attacks, and evaluates them across six defense methods and two datasets in roughly 354 experiments (~55,000 GPU hours) to quantify how different settings influence success rates. By providing a common evaluation framework and open-source code, the work establishes baseline results and highlights the need for standardized assessment of jailbreaks on defended LLMs.

args.text: We propose delay-robust adversarial SSP, addressing stochastic shortest path learning with unknown transitions, adversarially chosen per-episode costs, and arbitrary, obliviously chosen delays in revealing trajectory and cost feedback. The algorithm maintains optimism-based confidence sets for transitions as in state-of-the-art SSP learners but updates them through a delayed credit-queue that logs episode models and attributes late-arriving feedback to the correct past planning states; it augments planning with delay-aware step-size schedules and optional skipping of extremely delayed feedback to keep variance controlled. We conjecture high-probability regret O~(sqrt(S^2 A D T* (K + D_tot))) under full-information delays and O~((S^3 A^2 D T*)^{1/3} (K + D_tot)^{2/3}) in the bandit-adversarial case, with horizon-free variants replacing T* by B* via skewed empirical models, and refined bounds when selectively skipping highly delayed episodes. Technically this blends optimistic SSP estimation with occupancy-measure style delayed aggregation and bandit delay adaptivity, yielding the first instance-dependent guarantees for SSP under adversarial costs and unbounded delays.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of prompt injection attacks—malicious user-provided prompts that subvert designers’ intended instructions for LLMs—by collecting and analyzing large-scale, human-generated adversarial examples. Its key insight is that crowd-sourced, game-driven adversaries produce attacks with interpretable structure that reveal common weaknesses (notably prompt extraction and prompt hijacking) and that many of these strategies transfer to real-world LLM deployments. The authors built Tensor Trust, an online game that yielded over 126,000 attacks and 46,000 defensive prompts, used the dataset to characterize attack types, and constructed a benchmark to evaluate model robustness against those attacks, demonstrating broad vulnerability across models; they also release the full dataset and code for further research.

The paper addresses the problem of why deep learning architectures underperform on tabular datasets compared with traditional methods like gradient-boosted trees, and whether plain multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) can be made competitive. Its key insight is that joint, dataset-specific selection and tuning of a large set of modern regularization techniques—rather than novel architectures—can unlock MLP performance on tabular data. The method is to define a “cocktail” of 13 regularizers and jointly optimize which regularizers to apply and their hyperparameters per dataset, then evaluate these well-regularized MLPs on 40 tabular datasets; the empirical result is that properly regularized simple nets outperform recent specialized neural architectures and even strong traditional methods such as XGBoost.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of selecting effective cutting planes for mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs), where current solvers use hand-tuned heuristics that may miss cuts yielding strong bound improvements. Its key insight is that a greedy “lookahead” selection rule which simulates the bound improvement of candidate cuts gives high-quality choices but is too computationally costly to run in practice, so this expert policy can be imitated. The authors introduce NeuralCut, a neural architecture trained via imitation learning to mimic the lookahead expert’s decisions using features of the MILP and candidate cuts, and show it outperforms standard heuristic baselines on synthetic MILP benchmarks. They further demonstrate applicability by integrating NeuralCut into a branch-and-cut solver for neural network verification, where it yields better cut-selection performance while avoiding the prohibitive cost of explicit lookahead.

args.text: We propose a flow-variational inverse sensorimotor control framework that jointly recovers human motor cost functions and the signal-dependent noise law in partially observed tasks. The method fuses POMDP inverse optimal control with a recurrent normalizing-flow belief module that tracks multimodal latent states and noise scales from histories, while optimizing a scalable variational Bayesian IRL objective that co-learns a posterior over rewards and policies without inner-loop planning. To ensure identifiability of both reward and noise, we fit across modest interventions that vary discount/horizon or environment dynamics, and optionally perform active data collection by injecting temporally and actuator-correlated latent perturbations to elicit trajectories diagnostic of noise–effort trade-offs. This yields more accurate counterfactuals and safer assistance than LQG approximations and standard IRL on synthetic and real sensorimotor datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between filter pruning (hardware-friendly but coarse) and weight pruning (fine-grained but less hardware-compatible) by introducing a middle-ground pruning granularity that preserves accelerator friendliness while improving compression. The key insight is that a convolutional filter can be decomposed into K×K "stripes" (1×1 subfilters across channels), and pruning these stripes—i.e., shaping each filter—yields a more important architectural reduction than simply removing whole filters or individual weights. The proposed method, Stripe-Wise Pruning (SWP), learns a compact Filter Skeleton matrix that modulates the K×K stripe importance per filter and is trained to zero out unimportant stripes, producing structured sparsity that accelerates inference; experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show SWP outperforms prior filter-pruning approaches and achieves state-of-the-art compression without significant accuracy loss.

The paper tackles sample-efficient reinforcement learning under partial observability, where worst-case exponential sample complexity motivates identifying structural conditions that permit polynomial-time learning. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning flexible probability distributions on data that lie on Riemannian manifolds (e.g., spheres, tori, hyperbolic spaces), where standard normalizing flows—built for Euclidean (flat) spaces—are misspecified and perform poorly. Its key insight is that continuous normalizing flows can be generalized to Riemannian manifolds by defining the flow as the solution of an ODE whose vector field respects the manifold geometry, allowing exact transformation of densities via the manifold-aware continuity equation rather than flat-space change-of-variable formulas. The method parameterizes a time-dependent tangent-vector field on the manifold, integrates the induced ODE to push a base density along manifold-respecting trajectories, and computes log-density changes using the Riemannian divergence (trace of the covariant derivative) to train the model; experiments show substantial improvements over Euclidean and projected-flow baselines on synthetic and real datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of multi-network (multi-graph) alignment, where finding node correspondences across more than two networks is challenging because the search space grows exponentially and existing measures lack high-order discrepancy modeling. The key insight is to extend fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) geometry to a hierarchical multi-marginal optimal transport formulation that jointly captures high-order relationships among many networks while reducing complexity by decomposing networks into smaller aligned clusters via an FGW barycenter. Methodologically, the authors define a multi-marginal FGW distance to align networks jointly, build a hierarchical clustering/alignment pipeline that leverages FGW barycenters to partition and align substructures, and develop a fast proximal point optimization algorithm with convergence guarantees to compute the multi-marginal transport efficiently. Empirically, this Hierarchical Optimal Transport (HOT) framework yields substantial gains in accuracy and scalability compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA), where a source model must adapt to continuously changing unlabeled target domains without access to source data, a setting in which self-training with noisy pseudo-labels leads to error accumulation and catastrophic forgetting. The key insight is to shift adaptation from altering model parameters to learning lightweight image-layer visual prompts that reformulate inputs for the frozen source model, thereby preserving source knowledge while capturing domain-specific shifts. The method designs two complementary prompt types—domain-specific prompts to encode current-domain characteristics and domain-agnostic prompts to retain shared knowledge—and introduces a homeostasis-based adaptation strategy that suppresses domain-sensitive parameters in the agnostic prompts to better learn invariant features. result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), observing that minimizing the perturbed-loss (maximum loss in a neighborhood) does not necessarily prefer flat minima because different curvature directions can yield similarly low perturbed loss. The proposed method, GSAM, augments SAM with an inexpensive two-step routine—(1) a SAM-like descent to reduce perturbed loss and (2) an ascent (i.e., corrective) step in the gradient-orthogonal direction to explicitly reduce the surrogate gap—yielding provable convergence and improved generalization empirically (notably +3.2% over SAM on ImageNet for ViT-B/32).

result.text: This paper studies how adversarial training changes the loss landscape and hinders optimization, showing that larger adversarial budgets increase curvature, scatter gradients, prevent escape from poor random initializations, sustain non-vanishing gradients, and drive models toward sharper minima. The key insight is that these adverse geometric effects, rather than just stronger perturbations, are what make adversarial training harder and more sensitive to hyperparameters like the learning rate. The authors analyze adversarial loss functions analytically across budgets, validate the detrimental landscape properties with numerical experiments, and propose Periodic Adversarial Scheduling (PAS)—alternating phases with and without adversarial perturbations—to mitigate curvature and gradient scattering, improving performance and robustness to learning-rate choices compared to standard adversarial training.

args.text: We propose Topology-Aware Broken Scaling Laws for MoE: a unifying model that augments granularity-based MoE scaling with an explicit communication model to predict wall-clock loss vs. budget across routing/topology regimes. By expressing step time as compute plus communication (bandwidth, latency, All-to-All degree, and an overlap factor) and training dynamics as functions of parameters, tokens, experts, granularity, and routing scheme, we derive piecewise power laws with topology-induced breaks (e.g., transitions from compute-bound to comm-bound to overlap-dominated). The theory yields compute- and topology-optimal choices of expert count, granularity, routing (e.g., expert-choice vs. token-choice), and overlap scheduling, and predicts phase transitions where different routing/dispatch strategies dominate. We further propose an online controller that adapts expert granularity and routing to cluster load to remain on the optimal branch, validated on heterogeneous interconnects where it outperforms compute-only MoE scaling and static dispatch.

Methodologically, the authors build MotionEpic, an MLLM that grounds video content at the pixel and temporal object-relation level via STSGs, and then wrap it in a Video-of-Thought (VoT) framework that decomposes complex video QA tasks into sequential subproblems solved from perception to interpretation, yielding substantial improvements on multiple complex video QA benchmarks.

result.text: The paper investigates why state-of-the-art GANs produce an excess of high-frequency content compared to real images, a discrepancy that makes generated images easy to detect. The key insight is that spectral artifacts arise from biases in both generator and discriminator architectures—different upsampling methods in generators induce distinct spectral properties and checkerboard patterns alone don’t explain the mismatch, while discriminators struggle not with high frequencies per se but with low-magnitude high-frequency signals because their downsampling can weaken the training signal. The authors systematically study generator and discriminator components, isolating effects of up/downsampling and frequency sensitivity, and evaluate existing mitigation strategies, concluding that improving discriminator design (to better preserve and signal low-magnitude high-frequency differences) is a promising direction since current fixes do not fully eliminate spectral artifacts.

result.text: The paper addresses credit assignment in partially observable cooperative multiagent reinforcement learning under centralized training with decentralized execution, where the challenge is decomposing a global Q-value into individual agent contributions to improve coordination. The key insight is to use an integrated-gradient-style path attribution to directly decompose the joint Q-value along state-action trajectory paths, avoiding restrictive functional form constraints that prior decomposition methods impose. The method, Q-value Path Decomposition (QPD), computes attributions of the global Q to each agent by integrating gradients of the joint Q with respect to agent-specific inputs along interpolation paths, producing individual Q-value estimates used to train decentralized policies; experiments on StarCraft II micromanagement tasks show QPD outperforms existing cooperative MARL approaches in both homogeneous and heterogeneous agent settings.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that neural-operator models for solving PDEs typically learn boundary conditions (BCs) only implicitly from data and therefore may violate essential physics-based BCs (Dirichlet, Neumann, periodic) at evaluation, undermining solution existence, uniqueness, and physical fidelity. The key insight is that BC satisfaction can be enforced structurally by modifying the operator kernel rather than relying solely on data or loss penalties, so the network’s mapping inherently respects boundary constraints. The authors propose Boundary enforcing Operator Network (BOON), a refinement procedure that alters the operator kernel to impose BCs exactly, and they demonstrate across multiple PDEs that BOON guarantees BC satisfaction and substantially reduces domain-wide errors. Empirically, BOON yields dramatic improvements (2×–20×) in relative L2 error compared with baseline operators, achieving very low errors (e.g., 8.4e-5 for Burgers’ equation).

result.text: The paper tackles why domain generalization (DG) methods fail inconsistently across different distribution shifts, especially when multiple attributes shift simultaneously, by arguing that trusting a single fixed regularization constraint is insufficient. Its key insight is that different types of distribution shifts correspond to different causal/independence constraints among observed variables in a canonical data-generating causal graph, so an algorithm must identify and impose the correct constraint for the particular shift to generalize. The authors formalize multi-attribute shifts with causal realizations, prove that no single fixed-constraint method can succeed across all shifts, and propose Causally Adaptive Constraint Minimization (CACM), which uses knowledge of the data-generating process to adaptively select and enforce the appropriate independence constraints; empirical results on synthetic and real datasets show adaptive, dataset-dependent constraints yield the best OOD accuracy while incorrect constraints hurt performance.

Methodologically, POMO modifies REINFORCE by using multiple-optima-aware rollouts (starting from every possible depot/starting point), a low-variance baseline computed across these correlated rollouts, and an augmentation-based inference scheme; together these yield faster, more stable training and substantially improved solution quality and inference speed on TSP, CVRP, and knapsack benchmarks.

result.text: We propose a degradation-aware deep equilibrium reconstructor for CASSI that conditions a learned implicit transformer operator on per-scene estimated degradation parameters (mask, noise level, and ill-posedness) to drive fixed-point inference. Concretely, we embed a Half-Shuffle-style spectral–spatial transformer within a DEQ formulation and interleave it with physics-consistency projections whose step sizes are modulated by the estimated ill-posedness, enforcing non-expansiveness for stable convergence and constant memory. Trained via implicit differentiation, the model inherits degradation guidance and long-range modeling while gaining DEQ stability and generalization across masks; we further explore a spectrally redistributed low-bit variant for on-device deployment. This yields improved robustness to mask/noise variation and faster inference via fewer fixed-point iterations than explicit unrolling.

result.text: The paper tackles the growing memory and loading-time bottleneck of KV caches during batched LLM inference by proposing a practical low-bit quantization strategy that requires no tuning. The key insight is that keys and values have distinct element distributions that call for different quantization granularities: keys benefit from per-channel (along the channel dimension) quantization while values are better quantized per-token. Building on this analysis, the authors design KIVI, a hardware-friendly, tuning-free 2-bit quantization algorithm for KV caches that preserves model quality across Llama, Falcon, and Mistral while reducing peak memory by ~2.6×, enabling up to 4× larger batches and delivering 2.35–3.47× throughput improvements on real inference workloads.

result.text: The paper addresses how to get privacy amplification for iterative DP-SGD-style learning when data is distributed across many devices (federated learning) and central sampling or shuffling assumptions are infeasible. The key insight is that independent, randomized client “check-ins” (local participation decisions) suffice to amplify privacy in a way comparable to classical subsampling or shuffling, yet require no server-driven uniform sampling, global permutation, or even knowledge of total population size. The authors propose a random check-in protocol where each client independently decides whether to participate in each round and applies a local DP randomizer; they prove amplification bounds for this protocol (including a strengthened analysis of amplification by shuffling for (ε,δ)-DP local randomizers that gives exponential improvements), and show the method achieves similar privacy–utility trade-offs while greatly relaxing coordination requirements.

result.text: The paper tackles automatic songwriting—specifically lyric-to-melody and melody-to-lyric generation—where scarce paired data and the need for strict word–note alignments hinder quality. The key insight is that large-scale, modality-specific sequence-to-sequence pre-training at the song level can capture long musical context while attention-based constraints can enforce fine-grained alignment between lyrics and melody. Their method, SongMASS, extends MASS pre-training to song-level data with separate encoders/decoders for lyrics and melody, applies sentence-level attention masks and token-level attention constraints during training, and uses dynamic programming at inference to produce explicit word/syllable-to-note alignments. Pre-training on unpaired lyric and melody corpora yields substantially better objective and subjective generation quality than baselines.

args.text: We study stochastic shortest path (SSP) with unknown transitions and adversarially chosen costs when both costs and next-state observations arrive after arbitrary, unbounded delays, and propose DA2-SSP, a delay-adaptive algorithm. DA2-SSP maintains EB-SSP–style optimistic confidence sets updated upon delayed feedback and runs a barrier-regularized, increasing-stepsize mirror-descent learner over occupancy measures to track adversarial costs, while a delay-aware skipping/tuning mechanism ensures regret scales with the observed total delay. We prove high-probability regret Õ(√(S^2 A D T* (K + D_tot))) under full information and Õ(√(S^3 A^2 D T* (K + D_tot))) with bandit feedback; when costs are i.i.d., the algorithm adapts to attain Õ(B* √(SA (K + D_tot))) without prior knowledge of T*. A lightweight switching test detects nonstochasticity and activates the adversarial module, yielding best-of-both-worlds guarantees across stochastic, corrupted, and adversarial regimes with delays.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of scaling Transformer attention to long sequences while preserving relative positional encoding (RPE), noting that existing linearized/ kernelized attention methods generally cannot incorporate RPE and often suffer training instability. The key insight is that RPE induces a Toeplitz structure in the pairwise positional terms, which permits reinterpreting kernelized attention with RPE as convolution-like operations that can be computed exactly and efficiently via the Fast Fourier Transform. Building on this, the authors derive an O(n log n) algorithm that combines kernelized (linearized) attention with RPE through FFT-based convolution, show that including RPE can also stabilize training of kernelized attention, and empirically demonstrate from-scratch training stability, improved accuracy over many efficient Transformer variants, and faster runtime than standard attention on long sequences.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that transformer activations develop extreme outliers during training—driven by attention heads trying to perform exact “no-op” residual updates—which prevents effective low-bit quantization and forces higher precision or costly workarounds. The authors propose two simple, independent modifications to attention—clipped softmax, which bounds softmax inputs, and gated attention, which allows heads to smoothly scale their updates—showing empirically on BERT, OPT, and vision transformers that models trained with these changes exhibit much smaller activation outliers while preserving or improving float performance. As a result, transformers can be quantized to full INT8 activations without extra fine-tuning or special numeric formats.

result.text: The paper tackles the high compute and energy costs of improving model performance solely by increasing dataset size, challenging the conventional neural scaling law that error decreases as a power law with data. The key insight is that if one had a high-quality data-pruning metric that ranks training examples by importance, then discarding data in that optimal order can break the power-law scaling—potentially yielding much faster (even exponential) error reduction with effective dataset size. To validate this, the authors derive the theoretical improved scaling under optimal pruning, empirically demonstrate better-than-power-law scaling on ResNets for CIFAR-10, SVHN, and ImageNet using pruned datasets, benchmark ten pruning metrics on ImageNet (showing many fail to scale and the best are costly and label-dependent), and introduce a simple, cheap, self-supervised pruning metric that matches top supervised metrics, arguing that better pruning metrics can substantially lower resource costs of deep learning.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of choosing which separators (procedures that generate cutting planes) to activate in branch-and-cut MILP solvers, a combinatorial decision that heavily impacts solver speed but is difficult to learn directly due to the large selection space. Its key insight is that restricting the action space to a smaller, data-driven set of candidate configurations and learning instance-aware, dynamically adjustable selections yields most of the benefit of full optimization while remaining tractable. The authors implement a learning-guided algorithm that first derives a compact set of promising separator configurations from training instances and then predicts and adapts among these configurations during solves, integrating with SCIP to produce instance-specific dynamic policies. result.text: The paper addresses how to automatically generate useful distributions of training environments for reinforcement learning to improve robustness, transfer, and emergent complexity without costly hand-design. The key insight is to introduce a three-player setup—a protagonist (learner), an antagonist agent, and an environment-generator adversary—where the adversary selects environment parameters to maximize the regret (the return gap between antagonist and protagonist), which encourages creation of challenging but solvable environments rather than trivially hard or random ones. Their method, PAIRED, trains the adversary to produce environments that increase protagonist–antagonist regret while the antagonist learns to exploit those environments, resulting in a natural curriculum of increasing difficulty; experiments show this produces structured complexity and yields better zero-shot transfer to novel test environments than domain randomization or minimax adversarial approaches.

args.text: We propose an off-policy evaluation method for partially observable environments that leverages short-memory decodability: by augmenting state with a recent history of length m, the process becomes Markov and the target policy’s value reduces to an expectation under the stationary distribution of this history-Markov chain. Concretely, we learn the stationary density ratio between the behavior-induced and target-induced history chains via a GenDICE-style variational objective that enforces history-level stationarity constraints with flexible function approximation, and use it to reweight logged trajectories for consistent value estimation. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning classifiers that remain fair when the test distribution differs from the training distribution by weighted perturbations, a realistic concern since most fairness work assumes the training and deployment distributions match. The key insight is to cast fairness under distributional shift as a min–max (distributionally robust) objective that simultaneously minimizes worst-case loss over a class of weighted perturbations while enforcing fairness constraints across that same class. result.text: We propose delay-robust adversarial SSP, addressing stochastic shortest path learning with unknown transitions, adversarially chosen per-episode costs, and arbitrary, obliviously chosen delays in revealing trajectory and cost feedback. result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of building graph neural networks that are equivariant to Euclidean transformations (rotations, translations, reflections) and node permutations—crucial for physical and geometric tasks—without the computational burden of high-order representations and with scalability beyond 3D. The key insight is that equivariance can be maintained by designing message-passing updates that couple scalar node features and pairwise relative positional vectors through simple, learnable functions that act only on invariant scalars and produce equivariant vector outputs, avoiding costly tensor-valued intermediate features. The proposed E(n)-Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) uses edge-wise functions of relative distances and node features to update positions and features in an equivariant manner, enabling efficient, scalable message passing applicable to arbitrary dimensional Euclidean spaces. args.text: We propose Semiseparable Associative Retrieval (SSAR): an associative-memory augmentation for selective SSMs that uses the state-space duality of structured semiseparable matrices to realize attention-like retrieval as low-rank corrections to the SSM state. Concretely, SSAR maintains a compact bank of online-updated key/value sketches embedded in the SSM state and learns convolutional gating filters that select a few memory slices per step, yielding O(n) retrieval that approximates nearest-neighbor attention without quadratic cost. This directly targets the observed ICL gap of Mamba on retrieval-heavy tasks while complementing H3-style recall and cross-token comparison primitives, aiming to match hybrid attention–SSM performance at SSM speed. Combined with hidden-filter context extension, SSAR is expected to length-extrapolate without retraining while preserving fast inference.

args.text: We propose DEON-Adaptive Trust-Projected PPO, which safely reuses off-policy data by combining exact per-state trust-region projections for Gaussian policies with a clipping range that adapts to measured off-policyness. Concretely, we insert differentiable projection layers that enforce a per-state KL trust region during forward passes and modulate the surrogate’s clipping bounds as a monotone function of an off-policy metric (e.g., DEON), tightening when data are far from on-policy and relaxing when they are close. The step size and importance weighting are calibrated using generalized off-policy policy improvement bounds, yielding updates whose distances and guarantees mirror PPO’s while expanding the effective data reuse regime. We hypothesize this improves sample efficiency and stability over PPO, Off-Policy PPO, G-PPO-SR, and sigmoid-surrogate variants across continuous-control benchmarks.

result.text: EffiBench addresses the overlooked problem of efficiency in code produced by automatic code-generation models by providing a standardized benchmark to measure runtime and memory performance rather than just correctness. The key insight is that many LLMs produce functionally correct code that is substantially less efficient than top human solutions, so assessing efficiency on a diverse, efficiency-critical suite is necessary for sustainability and practical deployment. The method constructs a 1,000-problem benchmark drawn from LeetCode with executable human-written canonical solutions representing state-of-the-art efficiency, then evaluates 42 LLMs (35 open-source, 7 closed-source) by comparing generated code’s execution time and memory usage against these canonical baselines. Their empirical results show generated code is often much slower and more memory-hungry (e.g., GPT-4’s code averages 3.12× the execution time of canonical solutions and reaches up to 13.89×/43.92× in extreme cases), and the authors release the dataset and a public leaderboard.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning from human preference judgments in sequential decision problems without relying on brittle reward models or adversarial training, and while remaining robust to non-Markovian, intransitive, and stochastic preferences that cause compounding errors in offline methods. The method, Self-Play Preference Optimization (SPO), samples multiple trajectories from the current policy, obtains pairwise preference comparisons (from humans or a teacher model), treats the empirical proportion of wins as a trajectory-level reward, and uses this signal to update the policy with strong convergence guarantees. result.text: Temporal graph models and benchmarks often treat timestamps as precise, yet blockchain networks batch many interactions at identical block times, include intra-block execution order, mempool delays, and occasional reorgs—making models brittle and evaluations optimistic. We propose Block-aware Temporal Benchmarking: paired datasets and protocols that expose block height and intra-block transaction indices, add controlled time-warp perturbations (within-block shuffles, timestamp jitter, reorg simulation), and report a clock-invariance robustness metric alongside standard scores on live NFT and other on-chain graphs. We further introduce hierarchical time encodings that fuse block-relative positional features with intra-block order embeddings, drop-in compatible with TGAT/TGN layers, decoupling learning from wall-clock artifacts. This suite aligns temporal-graph evaluation with blockchain microstructure, mitigating memorization biases and enabling more reliable cross-domain comparisons.

args.text: Compute-Aware Multimodal Frame-Token Routing (CAM-FTR) unifies joint frame selection with modality-agnostic sparse computation to scale LVLMs to long videos under tight budgets. A lightweight router conditions on text queries or auto-generated differential captions to select a complementary, storytelling subset of frames and salient within-frame patches, while jointly gating a shared MoE backbone so only selected tokens are routed to appropriate experts. The router is trained end-to-end with a compute-budget regularizer and alternating gradient updates across modalities and tasks, warm-started via large-scale highlight supervision from user interactions and distilled differential caption signals. This yields substantial compute savings while preserving or improving performance on summarization, captioning, and video QA relative to dense processing, and enhances zero-shot transfer through language-guided, coverage-aware selection.

The key insight is to enforce view consistency through two complementary regularizations: geometric regularization that uses NeRF-derived depth to establish cross-view correspondences, and learned regularization that aligns latent codes in a 2D diffusion model between edited and unedited images so edits on key views diffuse throughout the scene. result.text: The paper tackles the problem of channel pruning for convolutional neural networks to reduce computational cost while preserving accuracy. Its key insight is that a filter whose weights can be well approximated as a linear combination of other filters is effectively redundant and can be removed with minimal impact, and that directly compensating remaining weights can further mitigate output changes. The proposed method, Linearly Replaceable Filter (LRF), identifies replaceable filters by measuring linear representability and prunes them, while the complementary Weights Compensation step adjusts surviving filter weights to reduce output discrepancies caused by removals. Experiments on benchmarks including ImageNet show that LRF with compensation achieves state-of-the-art pruning—e.g., cutting about 56% FLOPs on ResNet-50 without top-5 accuracy loss—supported by extensive analyses.

The paper addresses the problem of "over-squashing" in graph neural networks, where information from distant nodes gets compressed and distorted during message passing, limiting GNN performance on tasks needing long-range interactions; this is commonly attributed to graph bottlenecks but lacked a precise formulation. The key insight is that over-squashing corresponds to negatively curved edges in the graph: such edges act as combinatorial bottlenecks that concentrate and distort many incoming messages, and can be detected via a novel edge-based discrete curvature measure. The authors define this new curvature, prove a formal relationship between negative curvature and the deterioration of information flow in message passing, and propose a curvature-driven graph rewiring algorithm that adds or reweights edges to reduce negative curvature; experiments show that this rewiring alleviates over-squashing and improves GNN performance on long-range tasks.

result.text: Streaming Equal Shares via Pacing (SESP): We study participatory budgeting with arbitrary project costs in a streaming setting where projects arrive online and must be irrevocably funded, seeking proportional guarantees over time. SESP maintains per-voter pacing multipliers that throttle equal-share contributions to currently arriving approved projects and funds a project once its paced contributions meet cost; the multipliers are updated to equalize spend rates, yielding Lindahl-like personalized prices and a dynamically stable priceable outcome. Under i.i.d. arrivals from a stationary distribution, the time-averaged funded bundle converges to the static Equal Shares (and, when applicable, balanced-stably-priceable) solution for the underlying distribution, implying PJR and EJR-up-to-one-project guarantees in the limit along with per-prefix approximate group no-deviation bounds. Further, by leveraging strengthened priceability across satisfaction measures, SESP simultaneously preserves proportionality under both cardinal-by-cost and cardinal-by-count satisfactions, while running in polynomial time per arrival.

result.text: The paper tackles the limited performance of no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) caused by lack of high-quality (HQ) priors and the impracticality of full-reference IQA (FR-IQA) which requires pixel-aligned references. Its key insight is that leveraging easily obtainable, content-variant non-aligned reference (NAR) HQ images to provide HQ–LQ distribution priors and using knowledge distillation from an FR teacher can transfer robust HQ–LQ difference cues to an NAR student, improving quality prediction without strict alignment. The proposed CVRKD-IQA trains an FR-teacher on aligned pairs and distills distribution-difference knowledge into an NAR-student that compares LQ inputs with multiple NAR HQ samples, while the student processes multiple patches via an MLP-Mixer for efficient local–global feature fusion and fast inference. Cross-dataset experiments show the method outperforms state-of-the-art NAR/NR-IQA approaches and approaches FR-IQA performance in some cases, offering a practical, content-variant reference framework for robust IQA.

To further accelerate convergence, precondition the particle updates with a Laplacian-adjusted metric approximated by the particle-graph Laplacian, importing the speedups of LAWGD without requiring a spectral decomposition of the target. We hypothesize well-posedness of the resulting flow and non-asymptotic descent in KSD under Poincaré/LSI conditions, with empirical gains on multimodal targets and conditional inverse problems.

result.text: The paper tackles reducing discrimination in deep neural networks without expensive sensitive-attribute labels or fully debiased encoders by asking whether fairness can be achieved by only modifying the classification head while leaving biased representations intact. The key insight is that forcing the classifier to ignore spurious correlations between encoded sensitive information and class labels—by training it on "neutralized" representations derived from samples that share the same ground-truth label but differ in sensitive attributes—can yield fairer decisions without reworking the encoder. The method, Representation Neutralization for Fairness (RNF), constructs neutralized inputs from paired examples (same label, different sensitive attribute) and trains the task head to produce consistent predictions for these neutralized representations; when sensitive annotations are unavailable, RNF generates proxy attribute labels using a bias-amplified model. Empirical results on benchmarks show RNF substantially reduces discrimination with only minor impact on task performance.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of ensuring agnostic PAC learning guarantees simultaneously for many structured subgroups (e.g., demographic groups): given a benchmark hypothesis class H, a loss function, and a possibly large collection of subgroups G, the goal is to learn a single predictor whose loss on every group g ∈ G is nearly as small as the best loss achievable for that group within H. The key insight is that under natural conditions one can characterize exactly which loss functions admit such a uniform multi-group comparator, and for those losses it is possible to avoid dependence on |G| in sample complexity beyond a logarithmic factor. Methodologically, the authors give this characterization and then construct an algorithm that, for any loss satisfying the condition, produces a predictor with the desired per-group guarantees and has sample complexity scaling logarithmically with |G|, thereby unifying and extending prior positive and negative results for specific losses.

args.text: We propose Language-Calibrated Laplacian Transduction (LCLT) for zero-/few-shot CLIP at test time: jointly infer batch label assignments by minimizing a Laplacian-regularized objective with a language-guided prior. Concretely, we build a kNN graph and use LaplacianShot-style pairwise smoothness, but add a KL/alpha-divergence regularizer that pulls per-sample posteriors toward a multi-prompt, augmentation-marginalized text prior computed via lightweight test-time prompting and zero-temperature marginalization, while also learning a batch-level class-prior variable to accommodate unknown/imbalanced label marginals. We optimize with a block majorize–minimize procedure that alternates closed-form updates of assignments and priors, yielding a plug-and-play transductive head unifying vision structure, language semantics, and label-shift robustness, improving over vision-only transduction and entropy-only prompt tuning.

result.text: The paper tackles online multi-armed bandits with delayed feedback, aiming for a single algorithm that is simultaneously minimax-optimal against adversarial losses and near-optimal in stochastic environments with fixed or arbitrary delays. The key insight is a modified tuning of Zimmert and Seldin’s algorithm combined with delay-aware mechanisms (including a skipping technique and an oracle-assisted extension for arbitrary delays) that balance exploration and robustness to ancient feedback so as to avoid adversarial blow-ups while still exploiting gap structure in stochastic problems. Methodologically the authors adjust learning rates and feedback handling to obtain adversarial regret O(√(TK) + √(dT log K)) (or O(√(TK) + √(D log K) + d_max K^{1/3} log K) with arbitrary delays) and stochastic gap-dependent bounds O(Σ_{i≠i*}( (1/Δ_i) log T + d/(Δ_i log K)) + d K^{1/3} log K) (analogously with σ_max and d_max for arbitrary delays), and they complement these upper bounds with a lower bound matching the skipping-based adversarial regret.

result.text: The paper tackles video moment retrieval (VMR), where existing cross-modal alignment methods falter because videos carry far richer, noisier semantics than short language queries, creating a modality imbalance that degrades retrieval. The key insight is to rebalance semantics by enhancing both modalities: suppress query-irrelevant video content at the fine-grained frame-word level and enrich the short query with segment-relevant knowledge at the coarser segment-sentence level. Their Modal-Enhanced Semantic Modeling (MESM) framework implements frame-word video enhancement via word reconstruction to highlight frame features tied to query words, and augments text representations by learning complementary information from context sentences and ground-truth segments; jointly these two levels produce more balanced cross-modal representations and substantially improve retrieval accuracy and generalization on multiple benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of designing neural networks with provable ℓ∞-bounded Lipschitz constants for certified robustness against adversarial examples, where existing architectures struggle to be both expressive and certifiably robust. The key insight is that standard Lipschitz networks built from norm-bounded affine layers and Lipschitz activations fundamentally lose expressive power—provably failing to represent certain Boolean functions even in low dimensions—unless they incorporate order-statistic operations, which is how recent models like GroupSort and ℓ∞-distance nets circumvent these impossibilities. The authors formalize two impossibility theorems (for robust classification on finite datasets and for Lipschitz function approximation), analyze how order-statistic-based architectures avoid these limits, and then propose a unified Lipschitz network family that generalizes prior methods; they also present a practical, efficiently trainable variant ("SortNet") that makes certified robust training inexpensive and demonstrate improved certified robustness empirically across datasets and perturbation sizes.

result.text: The paper studies whether the Heavy-ball momentum parameter β induces implicit regularization in momentum-accelerated gradient descent (GD+M) and its stochastic variant (SGD+M), beyond the known effect of finite step size h in plain GD. The key insight is that the discrete GD+M updates can be seen as following a continuous trajectory for a modified loss equal to the original loss plus an implicit regularizer, and that this implicit regularizer is amplified relative to GD by a factor (1+β)/(1−β), explaining improved generalization and test accuracy with momentum. Methodologically, the authors derive the modified continuous dynamics corresponding to GD+M and characterize the pointwise continuous trajectory for SGD+M, analyze the form and strength of the implicit regularizer, and validate the theoretical predictions with experiments comparing GD, GD+M, and SGD+M.

args.text: Atlas-ResNets for union-of-manifolds data: we propose to learn a soft atlas of charts over data that occupy a disjoint union of low-dimensional manifolds with varying intrinsic dimension and curvature, and attach a chart-conditioned Riemannian residual block to each chart (optionally pseudo-Riemannian to capture mixed topology). A gating network estimates chart membership and transition weights; within each chart we train a ConvResNet that operates in the learned tangent geometry, with consistency penalties on overlaps to ensure coherent global predictions. We hypothesize and aim to prove that excess classification risk decomposes across components, achieving rates governed by each local dimension d_i and smoothness s (as in manifold-adaptive ConvResNets) plus only a boundary term scaling with chart-transition complexity, thus adapting to unions without prior knowledge of the partition. Empirically, we would test on image datasets with disconnected structure and on graphs with mixed topology, showing gains over single-manifold and purely Euclidean baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses open-vocabulary video instance segmentation (OpenVIS), i.e., detecting, segmenting, and tracking instances of arbitrary categories in video without being limited to training-time classes. Its key insight is that strong open-vocabulary capabilities can be achieved by combining class-agnostic, recall-focused mask proposals with instance-centric open-vocabulary token encoders and a tracking formulation that predicts future instance tokens rather than relying on closed-set identity labels. The proposed InstFormer framework implements this by (1) using an open-world mask proposal network trained with a contrastive instance margin loss to exhaustively propose class-agnostic masks, (2) adapting CLIP into InstCLIP with Instance Guidance Attention to produce compact open-vocabulary instance tokens for classification and tracking, and (3) introducing universal rollout association that casts tracking as next-frame instance token prediction; together these components enable lightweight fine-tuning on limited-category data and achieve state-of-the-art OpenVIS performance while remaining competitive on supervised VIS.

args.text: Zip-SSMformer: replace most fine-scale self-attention in Zipformer/Squeezeformer-style temporal U-Nets with Liquid-S4 state-space blocks to model long context linearly, retaining a small, coarsest-scale attention module for rare cross-span comparisons. A Branchformer-like learned gate adaptively routes between SSM and attention per layer and segment, disabling attention on easy spans to cut compute; at the coarsest scale, use BigBird-style sparse attention for further efficiency on very long utterances. We cache and reuse SSM convolution kernels and recurrent states across adjacent blocks and up/down-sampling boundaries (analogous to Zipformer’s attention reuse), and keep BiasNorm-like length-aware normalization to preserve timing cues under multirate processing. We hypothesize lower latency/memory and stronger robustness on long/noisy speech with comparable or better WER, validated on LibriSpeech, AIShell-1, WenetSpeech, and SRB streaming/robustness suites.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of training deep spiking neural networks (SNNs) with backpropagation: existing methods struggle with the discontinuous, event-driven nature of spikes and require many time steps (high latency) to reach competitive performance. The key insight is to decompose error backpropagation into two complementary dependency types—inter-neuron dependencies via presynaptic firing times (capturing the all-or-none spike events) and intra-neuron dependencies via the continuous temporal evolution of each neuron’s internal state—so gradients more accurately reflect temporal spike causality. The proposed Temporal Spike Sequence Learning Backpropagation (TSSL-BP) explicitly models and backpropagates through both dependency classes, enabling precise temporal credit assignment and efficient training of deep SNNs in only a few time steps. Empirically, TSSL-BP shortens required temporal windows and improves accuracy on image classification benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR-10), making spike-based deep learning more scalable and practical.

args.text: We propose Fractional Fourier Neural Operators (FrFNO), which replace the fixed Fourier basis in FNO layers with a learned mixture of fractional Fourier transforms (FRFTs) at multiple, potentially spatially varying, orders. args.text: I propose Input Sharpness-Aware Fast Adversarial Training (iSAFAT): augment single-step adversarial training with a lightweight penalty that explicitly reduces input-space sharpness within the adversarial ball. Concretely, estimate a surrogate of the dominant eigenvalue of the input Hessian by generating two FGSM-like perturbations in approximately orthogonal directions and measuring a small-radius perturbed-loss gap, then penalize this gap while aligning input gradients across these perturbations to regularize curvature without leaving the single-step regime. By directly targeting the high curvature that grows with adversarial budgets, iSAFAT mitigates the decision-boundary distortion implicated in catastrophic overfitting and stabilizes training at large epsilons. This is complementary to strong-noise FGSM variants, offering a principled curvature control mechanism at similar cost.

result.text: We propose Likelihood-Aware Rectified Multisample Flow Matching: train the probability-flow ODE with a stochastic-interpolant/flow-matching velocity loss augmented by explicit second–third order matching terms that directly target ODE NLL bounds, plus curvature-and-length regularization via OT-style path penalties and minibatch couplings to straighten flows and reduce variance. Per-time trust regions monitor local acceleration and divergence to adapt coupling strength and regularization so higher-order errors remain below bound while maintaining near-straight, fast-to-integrate trajectories. This yields a single deterministic ODE that achieves strong likelihoods with truncated-normal dequantization at evaluation and requires fewer NFEs due to low-curvature paths. The method unifies high-order likelihood-aware objectives with rectified/OT-regularized and multisample-coupled flow matching, improving both NLL and sampling speed.

args.text: We propose a Joint Transfer–Consistency Subspace (JTCS) detector that explicitly assumes backdoor triggers induce a shared low-dimensional activation subspace that is both highly transferable across source classes yet inconsistent under input augmentations. Concretely, we reverse-engineer a small set of candidate patterns per putative target on unlabeled inputs, then (i) quantify expected transferability across sources to that target and (ii) extract penultimate-layer subspaces spanned by triggered activations across augmented views; we score models by the affinity of these subspaces versus the augmentation-consistency gap between triggered and clean features. Attacked models exhibit a compact, high-affinity “trigger subspace” with strong ET but markedly lower feature-consistency than clean data, yielding a domain-agnostic statistic that works in two-class and multi-attack settings and remains effective against input-aware triggers whose visuals vary but converge in representation. This design sidesteps general impossibility by making its assumption explicit and testable (low-rank backdoor subspace), integrating transferability and transformation-consistency into one post-training, data-light procedure.

args.text: Performative Bayesian design with oracle-aware acquisition: instead of optimizing candidates under a static oracle, choose queries that maximize expected improvement under the next-iterate oracle obtained by an autofocusing reweighting step. We approximate the one-step effect of a candidate (or batch) on the oracle via influence functions or implicit differentiation, yielding a tractable, lookahead acquisition that explicitly trades off objective gain and calibration in the optimizer’s target region. Practically, we implement the query policy as a generative optimizer or RL design policy and backpropagate through the surrogate oracle-update, driving the system toward a performatively stable fixed point while mitigating the greedy-versus-lazy deployment trade-off. result.text: The paper addresses the overlooked supply-chain risk that pretrained models downloaded from untrusted repositories can be tampered with to compromise the privacy of downstream finetuning data. Its key insight is that subtle weight corruptions in a pretrained model can act as "privacy backdoors" that, once the model is finetuned on private data, enable an attacker to deterministically or highly reliably recover individual finetuning samples—even against models trained with differential privacy if the attacker controls the pretrained initialization. The authors demonstrate concrete constructions of such backdoors across architectures (including transformers), show attack algorithms that reconstruct training examples from the finetuned weights or outputs, and empirically and theoretically analyze their effectiveness and limitations, highlighting how loose DP guarantees do not protect against untrusted pretrained initializations.

args.text: Learned invariance probing for backdoor detection: Learn a semantic-preserving augmentation group by training a contrastive model on auxiliary clean data, then probe each untrusted training sample’s representation for invariance across these learned transforms using multiple backbones trained with differing inductive biases. Clean samples should maintain near-invariant, full-rank feature statistics, whereas poisoned/triggered samples—including feature-space backdoors—exhibit anisotropic, low-rank deviations that are unstable across backbones; a multi-backbone invariance-variance score can flag and downweight or remove such samples and guide alternating unlearning/relearning. This approach operationalizes the explicit structure required by impossibility results via learned semantic invariances, uses memorization-capacity insights to set detection thresholds, and advances fixed-transform FCT by replacing hand-crafted transforms with learned ones and adding representation-space checks. We expect improved robustness in pretrain–finetune regimes and black-box transfer to new tasks via portability of the learned invariance group.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of "narrow vision" in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, where the gating mechanism routes inputs so strictly that individual experts see limited data and underfit their sub-tasks, constraining overall generalization. The proposed method, MoDE, implements mutual distillation regularization across experts during training—encouraging them to mimic useful aspects of each other’s outputs while preserving gating-driven specialization—and is validated across tabular, NLP, and CV benchmarks, with an "expert probing" analysis that empirically shows distilled knowledge improves per-expert and overall MoE performance.

args.text: I propose a closed-loop weight-decay controller that jointly targets a constant intrinsic learning rate and a scale-invariant sharpness setpoint, while balancing per-layer rotational equilibria, to keep normalized networks near the productive Edge of Stability without recurring destabilization cycles. Concretely, the controller estimates intrinsic LR from step size and current weight norms on scale-invariant parameters, tracks sharpness via a lightweight top-eigenvalue surrogate, and normalizes updates in a modular norm so its gains transfer across width/depth, then adjusts decay each step to hold these targets. This should suppress BN+WD feedback-driven spikes, reduce or eliminate LR warmup, and outperform fixed or gradient-norm–scheduled decay on image models. We will ablate rotation-balancing versus sharpness-tracking components and compare against scaling-law–guided L2 schedules.

result.text: The paper addresses whether natural language explanations produced by large language models (LLMs) actually let humans predict how the model would behave on counterfactual inputs—i.e., whether explanations are counterfactually simulatible. Its key insight is that explanations should be judged not by plausibility or human approval alone but by two operational metrics—precision (how often humans’ predictions from the explanation match the model’s actual outputs) and generality (how broadly those predictions hold across diverse counterfactuals)—because an explanation that sounds good can still mislead about the model’s behavior. The method automatically generates diverse counterfactuals using LLMs, elicits human inferences from model explanations, and computes precision and generality to evaluate state-of-the-art models on multi-hop factual reasoning and reward modeling, finding that explanations often have low precision and that plausibility does not predict simulatability, implying that optimizing for human approval (e.g., RLHF) is insufficient to ensure truthful, usable explanations.

The key insight is that any filter defined on the normalized Laplacian spectrum can be uniformly approximated by a finite-order Bernstein polynomial, whose nonnegative basis and coefficient structure enable controlled spectral shapes and stable learning. args.text: I propose an online control framework for CMDPs whose objectives and constraints are dynamic coherent risk measures under uncertain, potentially drifting transition dynamics. We maintain interval-valued uncertainty sets for transitions via Bayesian evidence accumulation and, at each update, compute policies by solving a robust dynamic-risk Bellman problem that leverages a Markov risk transition mapping while approximating worst-case evaluation through a risk-regularized surrogate operator, inheriting the computational tractability of regularized MDPs. This yields anytime policies with monotone tightening of risk bounds as data accrue, and admits analysis of bounded suboptimality under piecewise-stationary drift by coupling uncertainty shrinkage with stability of the regularized operator. Empirically, we target CVaR/EVaR objectives on navigation and continuous-control benchmarks, showing faster adaptation and tighter risk control than static DCCP synthesis and standard robust baselines.

result.text: We propose Intrinsic Shapley Interaction Networks: extend Shapley-as-latent representations to any-order interactions by implementing SHAP-IQ’s cardinal interaction indices as differentiable, permutation-invariant modules inside the network. These modules produce layer-wise interaction tensors whose aggregations satisfy symmetry, dummy/missingness, and efficiency for each interaction order, and are trained jointly with the predictor using sparsity and low-order-promoting regularizers plus variance-aware weighting from SHAP-IQ’s estimators. This yields interaction-aware explanations at training time and enables direct control over which interactions the model may use (e.g., bounding total k-way mass), while retaining competitive accuracy.
