result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of cross-modal alignment in sign language translation (SLT), where the modality gap between continuous sign videos and spoken-language text hinders direct video-to-text translation and prior work often relies on gloss intermediates. Its key insight is to use a conditional variational autoencoder with dual paths—a visual-only prior and a visual+text posterior—tied by two KL divergences so that the encoder is regularized and the posterior distills knowledge into the prior, yielding better cross-modal consistency. The method implements this by training a prior path that predicts text from visual features and a posterior path that reconstructs text from combined visual and textual inputs, enforcing one KL term for C-VAE regularization and a second KL for self-distillation, and further improving integration via a shared Attention Residual Gaussian Distribution that models the posterior’s textual info as a residual to the prior. Experiments on public SLT datasets show the approach reduces representation discrepancy and achieves state-of-the-art translation performance.

result.text: The paper addresses the high-variance, slow-convergence problem of single-point zeroth-order optimization (SZO) in online black-box and time-varying control settings, where only one function query per time step is allowed. Its key insight is that concepts from extremum seeking control—specifically high-pass and low-pass filters—map naturally to variance-reduction and acceleration mechanisms in discrete-time SZO: the high-pass filter corresponds to residual feedback and the low-pass filter to momentum. The authors implement these ideas in a novel algorithm, HLF-SZO, which integrates residual-feedback-style high-pass filtering with momentum-style low-pass filtering to reduce estimator variance and speed convergence, and they empirically demonstrate that HLF-SZO attains substantially lower variance and faster convergence than vanilla SZO and outperforms existing residual-feedback SZO across extensive numerical experiments.

result.text: LongVideoBench addresses the lack of public benchmarks for evaluating large multimodal models (LMMs) on long, interleaved video-language inputs by introducing a question-answering dataset that tests long-term multimodal understanding up to hour-long videos. args.text: We propose Role-Tensor Q-Decomposition (RTQD), which learns soft role embeddings and assignments to group agents into a small set of roles, and represents the joint Q as a low-rank tensor whose modes correspond to role action spaces so that inter-role factors capture coordination and intra-role sharing yields scalability and sample efficiency. Roles are discovered via mutual-information and stochastic-embedding objectives and attended by the global state, while a lightweight contrastive identity-aware loss preserves agent-level distinctiveness within each role to avoid homogenization. During training, Q-value Path Decomposition attributes role-level values down to individual agents to stabilize credit assignment and train decentralized policies; variable team sizes are handled by permutation-invariant pooling over agents per role. We hypothesize RTQD improves coordination under heterogeneity and dynamic team composition, outperforming pure role or pure decomposition baselines on SMAC and GRF, and generalizing to unseen team sizes.

result.text: The paper tackles the high computational cost and limited flexibility of existing neural operators for solving forward and inverse PDE problems defined on large geometric domains. Its key insight is that mapping input functions into a learned latent space, performing the operator learning there, and decoding back to the geometric space via a physics-aware cross-attention yields a compact, efficient representation that still permits continuous-space decoding for interpolation and extrapolation. The proposed Latent Neural Operator (LNO) implements this by introducing a Physics-Cross-Attention (PhCA) module to transform geometric representations into latent tokens, learning the operator entirely in latent space, and applying the inverse PhCA to recover values at arbitrary spatial locations; this architecture reduces memory and training time while improving accuracy, achieving substantial speedups and competitive or state-of-the-art results on multiple forward and inverse PDE benchmarks.

args.text: We propose an operator-conditioned diffusion solver for inverse lithography that jointly learns a fast, differentiable neural operator to emulate the optical+resist forward map and a conditional score model over manufacturable masks, trained and evaluated on LithoBench. At inference, we generate masks by solving the probability-flow ODE with a neural-operator sampler that maps noise to the full trajectory in one pass (DSNO-style), while enforcing target-print and manufacturability consistency via projection steps inspired by DDRM but generalized to the nonlinear forward map. To handle process variability (e.g., NA, illumination, resist curves) without retraining, we wrap the score model within a Neural Inverse Operator composition so conditioning on operator changes is explicit and stable. This aims to deliver state-of-the-art ILT quality with orders-of-magnitude speedups over PDE-constrained optimization and a standardized, benchmarkable pipeline on LithoBench.

result.text: The paper tackles universal domain adaptation, where labeled source and unlabeled target domains differ in both data distribution and category sets, making it hard to align shared classes while isolating private ones without knowing overlap a priori. The key insight is to rely less on potentially source-biased classifier outputs and more on intrinsic target structure via mutual nearest-neighbor contrast at the instance level and on hybrid prototype-driven self-training to produce reliable target labels. Methodologically, MATHS is a two-stage framework: stage one uses mutual nearest neighbor contrastive learning to align features and a bimodality-based statistical test on maximum class probabilities to separate likely target-private samples from common ones; stage two builds an incremental pseudo-classifier trained only on target data using hybrid representative prototypes and a confidence-guided prototype contrastive loss for self-training to reduce category allocation uncertainty. Extensive experiments show this combination yields superior performance across standard UniDA benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses whether expressive neural networks can learn structural causal models (SCMs) and make valid causal inferences from data, pointing out the gap between function approximation and causal learnability. Its key insight is that universal approximability does not overcome fundamental limits from the causal hierarchy—neural nets, no matter how expressive, cannot identify effects of interventions from purely observational data without additional structural constraints. To resolve this, the authors define neural causal models (NCMs) that embed an inductive bias encoding SCM-style structural constraints, and they derive and implement an algorithm that characterizes when a causal effect is identifiable from available data and, when identifiable, provides a neural estimation procedure; simulations validate that the method is both necessary and sufficient for identifiability and effective for estimation.

args.text: Rather than pruning low-density real instances before GAN training, we propose Density-Gated MoE-GAN: a mixture-of-experts generator whose routing is conditioned on estimated local data density in a robust, frozen feature space. We compute per-instance densities from multi-scale pretrained embeddings and define neighborhoods around anchors (instance-conditioned), then train a gating network to route latents to experts specialized for different density regimes while mildly upweighting underrepresented neighborhoods during adversarial training. This converts static capacity redirection into dynamic, train-time allocation that preserves rare modes yet prevents wasting capacity on clear off-manifold outliers. We hypothesize improved fidelity–coverage trade-offs on complex or limited-data settings versus pruning-only or uniform training.

result.text: We propose Delta-aware Continual Graph Distillation for dynamic text-attributed graphs, which explicitly models change by feeding a TAG-tuned LLM with textual and structural deltas between consecutive snapshots to produce event embeddings (and optional rationales) that a temporal GNN ingests via time-decayed message passing. Training alternates EM-style between updating the LLM (to better summarize deltas given current graph beliefs) and the GNN (to predict future links/labels given event embeddings), while using multi-granularity contrastive distillation at node/edge/subgraph levels to align both state and delta channels. args.text: We propose a disease-conditioned multi-lead ECG generator that models a latent 3D cardiac dipole trajectory with a neural ODE and projects it to 12 leads through a fixed or patient-calibrated lead-field matrix, enforcing cross-lead physical consistency. args.text: Active information-gain CoT selection: treat the target problem’s reasoning pattern as a latent variable and choose in-context demonstrations that maximally disambiguate it. Build a library of patterns and exemplar traces (mined from prior tasks or auto-generated), fit a lightweight surrogate that estimates a posterior over patterns given the question, and then greedily select demos that maximize expected reduction in posterior entropy via a submodular objective over pattern coverage. At inference, combine the selected pattern-targeted demos with self-consistency decoding to robustly aggregate across sampled chains. This Bayesian experimental-design view of ICL aligns with latent-concept inference theory and yields more interpretable, task-aligned prompts than semantic or naive diversity heuristics at comparable cost.

A low-SNR–tolerant rPPG extractor combining state-space modeling with physiology-aware self-supervised augmentations is pretrained on large unlabeled vlog corpora to produce heart/respiration traces, segment-level HRV features, and a learned signal-quality score; a quality-gated cross-modal attention then fuses these signals with audio–visual encoders to emphasize reliable physiological evidence. Multi-task training jointly predicts depression while reconstructing the rPPG waveform to regularize periodicity, and pretraining/calibration against lab-quality multimodal stress data transfers physiological semantics and improves generalization. result.text: Learned invariance probing for backdoor detection: Learn a semantic-preserving augmentation group by training a contrastive model on auxiliary clean data, then probe each untrusted training sample’s representation for invariance across these learned transforms using multiple backbones trained with differing inductive biases. Clean samples should maintain near-invariant, full-rank feature statistics, whereas poisoned/triggered samples—including feature-space backdoors—exhibit anisotropic, low-rank deviations that are unstable across backbones; a multi-backbone invariance-variance score can flag and downweight or remove such samples and guide alternating unlearning/relearning. This approach operationalizes the explicit structure required by impossibility results via learned semantic invariances, uses memorization-capacity insights to set detection thresholds, and advances fixed-transform FCT by replacing hand-crafted transforms with learned ones and adding representation-space checks. We expect improved robustness in pretrain–finetune regimes and black-box transfer to new tasks via portability of the learned invariance group.

The method, SIC-CADS, trains a multi-modal multi-label recognition (MLR) module to produce image-level category scores from CLIP and uses those scores to re-weight or refine instance-level detection confidences from existing OVOD models, boosting detection of hard objects; experiments on OV-LVIS, OV-COCO, Objects365 and OpenImages show consistent improvements across different OVOD baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of existing spectral graph neural networks, which typically use scalar-to-scalar, fixed-order polynomial filters that ignore global spectral patterns and thus lack expressiveness and flexibility. Its key insight is to treat the entire set of graph eigenvalues as a sequence and apply self-attention in the spectral domain to learn set-to-set filters that capture global spectrum structure while maintaining permutation equivariance. The proposed Specformer implements this by encoding eigenvalues, applying transformer-style self-attention to produce learned spectral responses, and decoding with learnable bases to enable non-local graph convolution; stacking these Specformer layers yields a powerful spectral GNN that more accurately recovers ground-truth filters in synthetic tests and outperforms state-of-the-art GNNs on node- and graph-level benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles the high computational cost of Vision Transformers (ViTs) at inference and training time by reducing the number of tokens processed without retraining or with minimal training. The key insight is that many tokens are redundant (e.g., multiple tokens representing parts of the same object or across frames) and can be merged into representative tokens with little accuracy loss, so selectively combining similar tokens yields large speedups. The proposed method, Token Merging (ToMe), uses a lightweight, general matching algorithm to pair and merge similar token embeddings during forward passes (optionally applied during training), thereby cutting token count and compute while preserving information; empirically ToMe doubles throughput for large ViTs on images, videos, and audio with only ~0.2–0.4% accuracy/mAP drops and can also accelerate MAE fine-tuning.

result.text: The paper addresses overfitting in deep neural networks caused by large numbers of parameters and limitations of conventional binary dropout in reducing neuron co-adaptation. Its key insight is that controlling intermediate-layer complexity via targeted perturbations informed by empirical Rademacher complexity can yield better generalization than simple random masking. The proposed method randomly replaces selected feature-map elements during training with specific values chosen using a generalization-error bound derived from Rademacher complexity (instead of setting them to zero), thereby distorting feature maps in a principled way to regularize the network. Experiments on benchmark image datasets show this feature-map distortion improves test performance compared with standard dropout strategies.

The key insight is that reparameterizing the network and convexifying the inner optimization via a frozen finite-width neural tangent kernel (NTK) makes implicit-gradient calculations more accurate and tractable, and that analytically solving for final-layer parameters given the body parameters reduces bias in those implicit gradients. args.text: We propose web-scale video-text self-training for open-vocabulary detection by generating temporally consistent pseudo-track labels from narrated videos rather than per-frame boxes. Class-agnostic mask/box tracks are produced with an open-world proposal+tracking module, aligned to time-localized narration via vision–language matching to assign soft category labels, and distilled into a frame-level detector with certainty-aware weighting that combines alignment confidence, localization stability, and temporal consistency. Segment-level multi-label priors reweight detections to boost small/occluded objects and reduce false positives, while the vast diversity of video-text data improves long-tail coverage. This spatio-temporal self-training should surpass image-only web-scale self-training on rare and small objects and transfer to both image OVOD and OpenVIS.

result.text: The paper tackles black-box adversarial attacks when only the target model’s confidence scores are accessible, aiming to reduce query counts while maintaining high attack success. The key insight is that surrogate models capture transferable visual saliency and gradients that, when combined with query-based adjustments and periodic surrogate updates using query feedback, yield far more effective attacks than either approach alone. Methodologically, the authors introduce SimBA++, a simple transferability-boosted query attack that leverages a surrogate, and HOGA (High-Order Gradient Approximation), a novel scheme that uses a constructed high-order gradient computation graph to update the surrogate so it better matches the victim in both forward and backward passes; together forming LeBA, which achieves near-100% success with substantially fewer queries on ImageNet and defended models.

result.text: This paper tackles offline multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL), where an agent must learn a single, preference-agnostic policy from a finite dataset of demonstrations so it can generalize to arbitrary user preferences at test time. The key insight is that by conditioning a decision-making model on both preferences and returns, one can train a transformer-based policy that reproduces diverse behavior seen in offline data and interpolates along the Pareto front to produce Pareto-efficient solutions. To that end the authors introduce D4MORL, a large benchmark of 1.8M annotated demonstrations across 6 MuJoCo tasks with 2–3 objectives, and propose Pareto-Efficient Decision Agents (PEDA), which extend Decision Transformers with preference-and-return conditioning and are empirically shown to closely match behavioral policies and approximate Pareto fronts effectively as measured by hypervolume and sparsity.

result.text: The paper addresses the inefficiency and suboptimality of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), which applies dense adversarial weight perturbations to improve generalization but doubles computation and can perturb parameters unnecessarily. args.text: MaskDiff-Select proposes a diffusion model over binary frame-selection masks conditioned on video features and optional text queries. By denoising masks with a coarse-to-fine temporal schedule, the sampler proposes complementary, distributed frame subsets for long videos, unifying joint subset selection and selective watching. We train the mask generator with a hybrid objective that distills rewards from downstream heads (classification/captioning) via reinforcement learning and optionally supervises with large-scale highlight labels; at inference, we sample a small set of diverse masks and pick one via a cheap proxy (e.g., CLIP-style alignment) to control compute. This generative, arbitrarily conditioned selector supports text-guided summarization and improves the accuracy–compute Pareto frontier across tasks.

result.text: The paper tackles the gap in evaluating and attacking moderation guardrails in large language models (LLMs), noting that many jailbreak benchmarks ignore prompts that trigger input- or output-level moderation filters; this leaves both evaluation and red-teaming incomplete. The key insight is that effective jailbreaks must target both input filters (via crafted prefixes) and output filters (by encoding harmful content using non-standard “cipher characters” produced by a surrogate model that mimics the guardrail), enabling harmful content to evade detection and decoding back into readable form. The authors introduce JAMBench, a 160-instruction benchmark spanning four risk categories and multiple severity levels designed to reliably trigger guardrails, and propose JAM, a two-part attack combining jailbreak prefixes to bypass input-level defenses with a fine-tuned shadow model that generates cipher-character outputs to slip past output-level filters; experiments on four LLMs show JAM substantially increases jailbreak success and reduces filtering compared to baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the unexplored safety problem of backdoor attacks on LLM-based agents, which are increasingly used in real-world tasks like shopping and tool use. Its key insight is that agent backdoors are more diverse and covert than traditional LLM backdoors: they can either corrupt the final output distribution or inject malicious behavior only into intermediate reasoning steps while leaving the final answer correct, and triggers can reside not only in user queries but also in intermediate observations from the environment. Learned cut-selection policies in MILP solvers often optimize solve time but ignore the downstream cost of producing verifiable certificates, leading to bloated or impractical proofs. result.text: We propose Semiseparable Associative Retrieval (SSAR): an associative-memory augmentation for selective SSMs that uses the state-space duality of structured semiseparable matrices to realize attention-like retrieval as low-rank corrections to the SSM state. Concretely, SSAR maintains a compact bank of online-updated key/value sketches embedded in the SSM state and learns convolutional gating filters that select a few memory slices per step, yielding O(n) retrieval that approximates nearest-neighbor attention without quadratic cost. This directly targets the observed ICL gap of Mamba on retrieval-heavy tasks while complementing H3-style recall and cross-token comparison primitives, aiming to match hybrid attention–SSM performance at SSM speed. Combined with hidden-filter context extension, SSAR is expected to length-extrapolate without retraining while preserving fast inference.

result.text: We propose an off-policy evaluation method for partially observable environments that leverages short-memory decodability: by augmenting state with a recent history of length m, the process becomes Markov and the target policy’s value reduces to an expectation under the stationary distribution of this history-Markov chain. Concretely, we learn the stationary density ratio between the behavior-induced and target-induced history chains via a GenDICE-style variational objective that enforces history-level stationarity constraints with flexible function approximation, and use it to reweight logged trajectories for consistent value estimation. To select m and guard against misspecification, we embed a forward–backward sufficiency diagnostic on histories and adaptively increase m until the test accepts. Finally, we pair the estimator with a deeply debiased doubly robust correction to deliver tight, reliable confidence intervals.

args.text: We propose Gaze-Comparative BOIQA, a 360° quality assessor that replaces heuristic viewport sampling with a gaze-conditioned policy learned from AR/VR eye-tracking and aggregates human-like comparative judgments along sampled trajectories. For each visited viewport, an LMM trained for discrete-level quality alignment and comparative reasoning is used to score the patch via soft preferences against severity anchors and a small set of retrieved, content-variant high-quality non-aligned references, converting the resulting probability matrix to a continuous score. A temporal aggregator weights viewport scores by fixation duration and transition dynamics to yield sequence-aware overall quality and an explainable spatiotemporal defect map. By unifying gaze-guided browsing, LMM-based comparison-to-score conversion, and NAR priors, the method aims to improve human-aligned BOIQA robustness under diverse panoramic distortions.

The method, called Isometric Diffusion, augments a standard diffusion objective with a regularization term that enforces approximate isometry between latent and image spaces (measuring and penalizing distortion of local pairwise or neighborhood distances) and is evaluated via image interpolation, inversion, and linear attribute editing to demonstrate smoother transitions, improved reconstruction accuracy, and more precise latent manipulations.

args.text: Krylov-ICL: implement conjugate-gradient-style in-context learning in a looped, weight-shared transformer that incrementally builds a small orthogonal basis of task-specific directions across recurrent passes. Each pass computes residuals for the current predictor on the prompt, uses attention plus fast-weight delta-rule updates to store and orthogonalize a new direction, and updates predictions by projecting queries into the learned Krylov subspace, yielding condition-number-robust convergence with few iterations. Compared to depth-based Newton-like ICL, looping decouples compute from parameters and enables budget-adaptive halting; compared to preconditioned-GD linear attention, the explicit basis memory targets ill-conditioned and noisy regimes with stronger sample efficiency. Evaluate on linear and kernel regression and long-context streaming settings, measuring error vs iterations and examining learned bases.

args.text: We propose a manipulation-resistant recourse fairness audit that certifies subgroup disparities under small input perturbations and plausible model updates, closing the loophole where nominal counterfactuals can be exploited to appear fair while delivering cheaper recourse to targeted subgroups. For each individual, we compute low-cost actions that satisfy a target invalidation-probability constraint and carry moment-based guarantees of validity across model shifts, then aggregate subgroup-level worst-case (or high-quantile) recourse costs to form certified disparity metrics. A hierarchical semi-supervised estimator produces posterior intervals for these certified disparities, and the audit reports a "manipulation gap" (nominal vs. certified disparity) as an explicit risk indicator. For linear and differentiable models we provide convex/bi-level relaxations building on robust-recourse and local-smoothness tools to keep computation practical, and we scope actions to causal pathways to align with recourse fairness notions.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of learning generalizable, transferable, and robust unsupervised representations for graph-structured data, where self-supervised pretraining methods are less developed than for images. Its key insight is that contrastive learning applied to graphs can be made effective by designing and combining diverse graph augmentation operators that inject useful invariances and perturbations, enabling representations that transfer across tasks and resist adversarial perturbations. Methodologically, the authors introduce GraphCL, a framework that defines four types of graph augmentations, applies contrastive objectives to maximize agreement between differently augmented views of the same graph, and systematically evaluates augmentation combinations and augmentation extents across semi-supervised, unsupervised, transfer learning, and adversarial settings. Empirically, GraphCL yields comparable or superior generalizability, transferability, and robustness to state-of-the-art methods even with simple GNN backbones, and further gains can be achieved by tuning parameterized augmentation patterns.

args.text: We propose Learnable Non-Uniform Spectral Convolution (L-NSC): instead of applying FFTs on a fixed grid or truncating to lowest modes, each layer learns a sparse set of complex frequency locations and gains (per channel/group) and performs convolution via a differentiable non-uniform FFT, yielding anisotropic, task-adaptive receptive fields with minimal parameters. This generalizes learnable spacings in dilated convolutions to the frequency domain and replaces fixed mode selection with learned, non-uniform spectral sampling; we further develop fused block-NUFFT kernels and sparsity-aware layouts inspired by recent FFT-on-accelerator designs to achieve competitive wall-clock efficiency. Compared to continuous kernel parameterizations, L-NSC directly controls spectral support and can allocate capacity to sharp features or oscillations, improving operator learning on PDEs with discontinuities and long-context vision tasks while maintaining O(N log N) complexity with small constants. result.text: Communication-aware MoE scaling with overlap–granularity control: We augment granularity-based MoE scaling laws with explicit system terms for expert-parallel all-to-all communication and a measured overlap factor that quantifies how much of communication can be hidden behind computation. args.text: Projection-Resistant Unlearnable Examples (PRUE): a defender-in-the-loop minimax objective that crafts imperceptible perturbations to simultaneously mislead supervised and contrastive learners across training checkpoints (self-ensembled) while surviving common decontamination steps (orthogonal projection, linear reweighting, PCA whitening) that can recover signal from prior unlearnable datasets. Concretely, the inner loop trains both supervised and MoCo/SimCLR-style encoders with standard augmentations and momentum, while the outer loop spreads perturbation energy across many random, approximately orthogonal feature subspaces and induces augmentation-invariance conflicts, preventing concentration in any linearly removable direction. This unifies and strengthens prior UE/CSD/OPS approaches by optimizing for transfer across objectives and checkpoints and by adversarially anticipating projection-based recovery. We hypothesize PRUE will sustain near-chance performance even under projection-style defenses that re-enable learning on existing unlearnable baselines, and will degrade contrastive representations despite momentum encoders, echoing contrastive poisoning insights.

result.text: The paper tackles open-vocabulary object detection, where models must detect novel categories but struggle because popular weak supervision sources—CLIP image-text pretraining and image-level labels—are misaligned with object-level localization. The key insight is that bringing language embeddings into an object-centric space and automatically grounding image-level labels to high-quality object proposals can close the gap between image- and object-level representations, yielding better transfer to novel categories. Methodologically, the authors perform object-centric alignment of CLIP embeddings and generate pseudo-labeled object proposals from image-level supervision to visually ground categories, then combine these complementary signals with a learned weight-transfer function that aggregates their strengths during detector training. This combined strategy substantially improves open-vocabulary detection, raising novel-class AP on COCO by 8.2 points and boosting LVIS rare and overall mask AP versus prior state-of-the-art.

args.text: We propose Partially Equivariant Mixture-of-Expert Neural Processes (PE-MoE-NP), where each expert NP implements a different degree and range of group equivariance and a context-conditioned router selects mixtures based on symmetry evidence in the observed data. Concretely, experts instantiate Conv/Steerable NP encoders/decoders parameterized to interpolate between no, partial, and full equivariance over relevant (sub)groups, while the gating network infers a task-specific equivariance profile and softly aggregates expert predictions. args.text: We propose Meta-Causal Regularization: a predictor that meta-learns a small library of candidate causal invariance constraints and sparse DAGs during training, then adaptively selects which constraint to impose at test time to match the observed shift. The library is learned by a scalable differentiable causal discovery module trained on mixed observational and interventional data (including unknown targets), using a stable log-det acyclicity penalty to recover candidate graphs. At inference, a lightweight selector estimates which constraint best explains current domain statistics (following the insight that different shifts correspond to different causal/independence relations) and applies CASTLE-style causal reconstruction regularization under the selected graph. We hypothesize this adaptive scheme outperforms fixed-constraint and single-graph regularizers on heterogeneous shifts and yields stronger OOD generalization.

We propose Active Perception Tokens (APT), an LLM-in-the-loop visual tokenization scheme for unified autoregressive multimodal models. Decoding begins from a compact set of semantically grouped, coarse visual tokens; at each step the language model monitors its predictive uncertainty and cross-modal attention to request localized, hierarchical refinements from the tokenizer, yielding variable-length, targeted token updates over time. Training jointly optimizes next-token likelihood with a token-cost regularizer and uses differentiable soft routing or straight-through estimators so the refinement policy learns to spend tokens where they most reduce entropy. This closes the loop between perception and generation for efficiency and alignment, and naturally extends to video by budgeting refinements across keyframes and motion tokens.

Current retrieval-augmented idiom translation systems handle known idioms but still miss novel figurative usages and metaphors. I propose a reasoning-augmented figurative translation pipeline that unifies an idiom knowledge base with interpretable concept-mapping for metaphors and RAG-style evidence retrieval: the model first flags figurative spans, retrieves idiom entries and candidate source→target concept mappings, then uses evidence-aware self-reasoning to select or induce a context-appropriate paraphrase with verifiable citations. The chosen paraphrase is injected as a controllable intermediary into the MT decoder (e.g., as constraints or retrieved prompts), and when no entry fits, the induced paraphrase plus provenance is added back to the KB with calibrated uncertainty for continual improvement. This should improve both fidelity and traceability when translating idioms and novel metaphors across languages.

args.text: We propose a density- and discrepancy-aware curriculum for GAN training that reconciles the gains of instance pruning with rare-mode coverage. Early in training, we embed images in a frozen perceptual feature space to estimate local density and temporarily downweight the extreme low-density tail to stabilize the discriminator and boost fidelity; as the generator improves, we switch to upweighting instances with persistently high data–model discrepancy to steer capacity toward underrepresented regions. A scheduler modulates per-instance sampling weights and augmentation strength over training, leveraging differentiable augmentations and a projected-feature discriminator to maintain stable gradients while emphasizing rare modes. Compared to static pruning or static reweighting, this staged curriculum improves FID and minority recall on long-tailed datasets and can be combined with instance-conditioned GANs by applying the schedule within each neighborhood.

args.text: We propose Rational Spectral Neural Operators (RaSNO), which replace unconstrained learned weights on truncated spectral modes with learnable, stable rational multipliers expressed as Padé-like functions of frequency or Laplacian eigenvalues. This rational parameterization yields smooth, low-complexity approximations to PDE solution operators with built-in stability (via positivity/H∞ constraints) and improved cross-resolution generalization; on irregular domains we apply the same multipliers through rational–Krylov evaluations on graph/mesh Laplacians, removing the need for FFTs or equispaced grids. By explicitly matching spectral responses across discretizations, RaSNO mitigates operator aliasing and preserves the intended continuous-operator behavior, while pointwise stages can use rational nonlinearities to compactly capture stiff local physics. Empirically, RaSNO targets FNO-style performance on regular grids and surpasses it on irregular meshes, maintaining stability under resolution changes at comparable compute to direct non-equispaced spectral methods.

result.text: The paper addresses the practical failure modes of Expected Improvement (EI) and its variants in Bayesian optimization, where acquisition values often underflow to zero in many regions as observations, dimensionality, constraints, or parallel evaluations increase, leading to poor and inconsistent optimization performance. The key insight is that these failures are largely numerical rather than conceptual: taking a numerically stable transformation (logarithm) of the EI-style acquisition functions preserves their optima (exactly or approximately) while avoiding vanishing values and other pathologies that hinder optimization algorithms. The authors introduce the LogEI family—log-domain reformulations of EI, Expected Hypervolume Improvement (EHVI), and their constrained, noisy, and parallel extensions—derive analytic and approximate expressions that maintain equivalent maximizers, and implement them within standard optimization routines. Empirically, LogEI variants substantially improve optimization reliability and performance over canonical EI formulations and surprisingly match or surpass several recent state-of-the-art acquisition functions, underscoring the critical role of numerical stability in acquisition optimization.

args.text: Circuit-Targeted Memory-Space Prompting (CT-MSP) injects per-instance visual knowledge into only those FFN sublayers most likely to mediate the current text query, avoiding long visual token prefixes and unnecessary MHSA perturbations. To make the adapter compact and robust, the image is first passed through frozen LLM transformer blocks used as information filters to distill salient visual slots, and a semi-parametric memory retrieves and composes adapters from similar past contexts to amortize compute. result.text: Bayesian Router for Zero-Shot Adapter Composition: instead of learning a controller to fuse many task adapters, compute per-input (optionally per-token/per-channel) adapter weights from a Laplace-approximated predictive marginal likelihood, using each adapter’s local curvature (Fisher/precision) around a shared base to score how well it explains the input. These evidence scores drive a training-free mixture over adapter deltas or selection among masked supports, yielding dynamic composition akin to a MoE router without additional data. To reduce interference and cost, restrict routing to task supports discovered by mask-based merging or lightweight modulators and fall back to the base when no adapter has sufficient evidence. We hypothesize this Bayesian gating closes much of the gap to learned multi-adapter routers while preserving the simplicity and robustness of Fisher/Laplace-based merging.

A robust rPPG estimator is first tuned on a lab dataset with ground-truth physiology and affect labels to learn physiologically meaningful representations, then used to extract heart-rate/HRV and respiration proxies from vlog faces; these proxies are fed as auxiliary tokens and privileged distillation targets into a cross-attention audio–visual depression model. A temporal consistency loss aligns pseudo-physiology with AV features over long windows so that, at test time, the model relies only on AV cues enriched by physiology-informed tokens, improving robustness to covariate shift. We expect gains on D-Vlog and stronger cross-dataset generalization versus AV-only baselines.

result.text: Learned invariance probing for backdoor detection: Learn a semantic-preserving augmentation group by training a contrastive model on auxiliary clean data, then probe each untrusted training sample’s representation for invariance across these learned transforms using multiple backbones trained with differing inductive biases. Clean samples should maintain near-invariant, full-rank feature statistics, whereas poisoned/triggered samples—including feature-space backdoors—exhibit anisotropic, low-rank deviations that are unstable across backbones; a multi-backbone invariance-variance score can flag and downweight or remove such samples and guide alternating unlearning/relearning. This approach operationalizes the explicit structure required by impossibility results via learned semantic invariances, uses memorization-capacity insights to set detection thresholds, and advances fixed-transform FCT by replacing hand-crafted transforms with learned ones and adding representation-space checks. We expect improved robustness in pretrain–finetune regimes and black-box transfer to new tasks via portability of the learned invariance group.

args.text: We propose staggered stochastic transparency for multi-principal ecosystems that reuse models or data: each institution randomizes and staggers partial disclosures (e.g., counterfactual exemplars or coarse decision-rule signals), decorrelating agents’ learned manipulation gradients across institutions while preserving robustness from noisy agent responses. We formalize a coupled performative game with opaque, peer-learning agents and define a cross-institution information-overlap proxy to target universal improvement across subpopulations and to provably reduce individual-level outcome homogenization relative to monoculture baselines. Analytically, we derive regimes where staggered stochastic transparency lowers the price of opacity by aligning disclosure noise with stability conditions from smoothed-response microfoundations and by coordinating disclosure schedules across principals. args.text: We propose RobustBoost-GNN, a multi-scale graph neural network trained under a boosting-like framework for robust risk that explicitly accounts for worst-case perturbations to node features and edges. args.text: Fixed-kernel convexification in RCIG can mis-specify the small but crucial feature-learning that occurs even in the first few steps; theory shows a single update induces a low-rank spike that alters the effective kernel. result.text: The paper addresses privacy guarantees in federated/distributed learning when only a random subsample of clients participates each round and clients apply local randomization before their messages are shuffled, aiming to quantify how subsampling and shuffling amplify privacy. Its key insight is that Renyi Differential Privacy (RDP) can be analyzed for the subsampled shuffle model to yield tighter, composition-friendly privacy bounds than prior (ε,δ)-DP analyses, enabling a clearer privacy-utility trade-off for discrete local randomizers. Methodologically, the authors develop a new theoretical technique to bound the RDP of the combined subsampling-plus-shuffle mechanism for discrete-valued outputs, derive composition results for iterative learning, and validate numerically that their RDP-based bounds give substantially stronger privacy guarantees and improved privacy-utility operating points on real datasets compared with state-of-the-art approximate DP bounds.

args.text: We propose Sequence-Adaptive Orthogonal Codebooks for PTQ: instead of a single global rotation, learn a tiny codebook (e.g., 2–4 entries) of hardware-friendly orthogonal preconditioners per layer (Hadamard/permutation/Householder products) optimized on calibration clusters that capture token-dependent outlier patterns. At inference, a lightweight selector uses statistics from the first few tokens of a sequence to pick one codebook entry per layer for the whole sequence, applying the corresponding rotations to residual streams and attention/MLP intermediates before low-bit quantization; transforms are cheap and fixed per sequence, so they can be implemented with butterfly-style kernels without per-token overhead. Jointly co-designing loss-aware quantization grids for each codebook entry further reduces error, yielding better W4A4 (and KV) robustness than a single fixed rotation while keeping PTQ practicality. This bridges learned-rotation smoothing with outlier-aware token effects and grid learning, targeting the main failure modes of ultra-low-bit LLM PTQ.

args.text: We propose Fisher-Transposable Sparse Updates (FTSU): select and update only a subset of parameters under a hardware-friendly, transposable N:M sparsity pattern while capturing most task-relevant curvature. Concretely, we initialize a transposable N:M mask by maximizing accumulated Fisher information mass under the transposability constraint (via a min-cost flow solver), then train only those weights to obtain end-to-end sparse forward/backward speedups. To mitigate suboptimality of a fixed mask, we periodically refine the structure using a bounded-variance policy-gradient estimator that proposes local N:M-preserving swaps using only forward passes, maintaining full sparsity throughout. FTSU aims to match or surpass unstructured fixed-Fisher sparse-update accuracy while delivering practical training and inference acceleration and reduced memory/communication costs for PEFT and distributed settings.

We propose a Distributional Projection-Robust Wasserstein (DPRW) distance that replaces the hard max over k-dimensional subspaces in PRW with an optimized probability distribution on the Grassmann manifold, yielding a smooth expectation of projected entropic OT costs that interpolates between PRW (Dirac/low-temperature) and distributional sliced families. Algorithmically, we alternate between (i) estimating energies by sampling subspaces and solving entropic OT per sample using efficient PRW-style inner solvers, and (ii) updating the Grassmann distribution via mirror descent with KL regularization over measures; a Riemannian corrected extragradient can be used for the joint min–max to match Euclidean rates up to curvature. This energy-based, parameter-free slicing on subspaces mirrors DSWD/EBSW but with multi-dimensional projections, offering reduced variance versus max and improved statistical stability while retaining robustness to high-dimensional structure. Practically, importance sampling or MCMC on the Grassmann provides scalable estimators, and the framework subsumes prior SW/DSW/EBSW and PRW as limits to trade off information and compute for generative modeling and robust comparison.

We propose BIMS, a co-designed private training pipeline that composes a banded lower-triangular matrix-mechanism factorization for multi-epoch SGD with a client-side sparse JL sketch and randomized check-in participation, all operated in an integer domain with Skellam noise and secure aggregation. Each client clips and sketches its update with a sparse projection, adds integer Skellam noise in the sketch domain, and participates independently; the server aggregates sketches via secure modular summation, de-sketches, and applies the online inverse of the banded factorization. The privacy analysis treats the end-to-end operator as a single linear mechanism M = (check-in mask) × (sketch) × (banded factorization), yielding RDP bounds governed by the banded sensitivity and the sketch’s spectrum, thereby capturing amplification from both sketching and random participation while significantly reducing per-client bits. We give parameter-selection rules for sketch sparsity and band width to meet a target (ε, δ) and bit budget, aiming near the known communication lower bounds while matching or improving DP-SGD utility in federated settings.

result.text: The paper addresses shortcomings in current evaluation practices for graph neural network (GNN) based link prediction—namely inconsistent baselines and splits, underestimated baseline performance, and overly easy negative sampling that inflates results. Its key insight is that fair, unified benchmarking and harder, more realistic negatives are required to accurately assess models and drive progress toward practical link prediction. Methodologically, the authors re-evaluate prominent GNN and non-GNN baselines under unified data splits and hyperparameter searches and introduce HeaRT (Heuristic Related Sampling Technique), a negative-sampling protocol that generates hard negatives using multiple heuristics to better mimic real-world difficulty. Their empirical results and released code/data demonstrate that prior comparisons were often misleading and that HeaRT produces a more challenging, informative benchmark for future work.

args.text: We propose Event-Structured Sparse Conditioning for long-horizon video diffusion: a learned, budgeted frame-selection policy chooses a small, complementary set of keyframes (optionally language/query-conditioned) to serve as conditioning masks for arbitrary-mask video diffusion. Unlike uniform or heuristic schedules, the selector is trained end-to-end to maximize temporal coherence and content fidelity of completions over long durations, using a differentiable subset sampler (e.g., Gumbel-Top-k with a DPP prior) and a distillation signal from a densely conditioned teacher plus perceptual/consistency rewards. We warm-start the selector with large-scale highlight/importance supervision and transfer joint selection priors from short-video classification, then fine-tune with task-specific prompts. This yields controllable, compute-efficient long-video generation and completion that concentrates conditioning around predicted event boundaries and salient moments.

args.text: We propose Smooth-RAG, a certified-robust retrieval layer for LLM agents that reduces and detects backdoor memory triggers. At query time, we apply randomized smoothing in embedding space and return only documents that win a majority-vote top-k across many Gaussian-perturbed embeddings, yielding per-query certificates that within a calculable L2 radius the retrieved set cannot flip to any specific poisoned memory—directly countering AgentPoison’s reliance on trigger-unique embedding regions. We further learn feature-space separating hyperplanes that characterize candidate backdoor clusters from historical retrievals and downweight or quarantine those entries during the smoothed vote. Evaluated against black-box prompt-trigger attacks and RAG leakage setups, Smooth-RAG should significantly cut attack success with small recall loss and modest latency.

Introduce a retrieval-augmented closed loop for LLM-based feature engineering on tabular data by building a cross-dataset "feature memory" that stores engineered-feature code, natural-language rationales, dataset schema/statistics signatures, and measured lifts (including subgroup-wise) from prior runs. For a new dataset, retrieve semantically/structurally similar feature templates and prompt the LLM to adapt/compose them, then apply a two-stage selector—fast coarse filtering with cheap learners followed by precise marginal-contribution scoring via feature boosting—to keep only high-value candidates. To ensure reliability, gate acceptance on robustness metrics: subgroup-consistent gains via Data-IQ-style stratification and stability under time-split/shift stress tests, pruning features that deliver brittle or spurious improvements. This reuses experience beyond per-dataset loops like OCTree/CAAFE and complements one-shot approaches (e.g., FeatLLM) by reducing search cost while improving trustworthiness.

result.text: The paper addresses how to scale language models when the amount of unique training text is limited, examining how data repetition interacts with compute and model size in data-constrained regimes. The key insight is that modest repetition (up to about four epochs) has little impact on loss at fixed compute, but beyond that repeated data yields diminishing returns and eventually nullifies the benefit of extra compute or parameters—so optimal scaling must account for the reduced value of repeated tokens. Methodologically, the authors run 400 controlled training experiments across up to 9B-parameter models and 900B training tokens, measure loss under varying repetition and compute budgets, derive and validate a modified scaling law that discounts repeated data and excess parameters, and test mitigation strategies like adding code data or relaxing filters to improve effective dataset size.

result.text: Samba tackles the challenge of building language models that can handle effectively unlimited context without quadratic cost or poor length extrapolation by combining state-space compression with local attention. The key insight is to layer-wise hybridize a selective State Space Model (Mamba) that compresses and carries long-range recurrent hidden states with a Sliding Window Attention (SWA) that precisely recalls recent context, yielding both efficient long-term memory and exact short-term retrieval. result.text: Zero-Backprop Banked Bypass Tuning: attach an unbound ladder/bypass side network to a frozen backbone, but parameterize all its per-layer tuners from a single shared vector bank and select them with fine-grained multi-head routing. Train only the vector bank and routing via zeroth-order, forward-only updates so training memory equals inference, while reusing a single backbone forward pass to optimize multiple task heads simultaneously. This marries no-backbone-backprop side-tuning with extreme adapter storage sharing and expressive routing, yielding scalable multi-task adaptation that supports cheap task arithmetic and even zero-shot composition by averaging or fusing pre-trained routed bank selections. We expect large activation/memory savings and stronger cross-task generalization than standard LoRA/adapters at comparable or lower parameter/storage budgets.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of retrieving accurate answers for complex real-world queries that require jointly using unstructured textual descriptions and structured relational data from semi-structured knowledge bases—scenarios underexplored because prior work typically treats textual and relational retrieval separately. The key insight is that realistic, challenging retrieval tasks arise from queries that integrate diverse relational constraints and nuanced textual properties, so a unified benchmark spanning multiple domains is needed to evaluate and drive progress on such semi-structured retrieval problems. The authors introduce STaRK, a large-scale benchmark covering product search, academic paper search, and precision medicine, created via a pipeline that synthesizes realistic user queries combining relational and textual conditions, validated through human evaluation and supplemented with high-quality human-written queries; experiments on LLM-driven retrieval systems show current methods struggle on STaRK, demonstrating the benchmark’s difficulty and utility.

args.text: We propose disagreement-aware self-contrast distillation for Mixture-of-Experts that bakes inference-time self-contrast gains into training while preserving specialization. For each batch, we run a weak-activation pass (small k) and a strong-activation pass (larger, adaptively chosen k), compute per-token expert disagreement, and for high-uncertainty tokens construct a teacher distribution by contrasting the two passes; routed experts are then updated toward this teacher while applying moderate cross-expert distillation to prevent collapse. To maintain load balance with variable activation, we pair this with expert-choice routing (fixed expert buckets) and adaptive k, and restrict contrast to the most informative off-route experts. We hypothesize improved generalization, calibration, and sample efficiency over standard MoE, achieving SCMoE-like benefits without added inference cost.

result.text: This paper tackles the problem of efficient filter pruning for compressing convolutional neural networks without the cumbersome multi-stage training and many hyperparameters typical of prior work, and it also addresses uneven pruning needs across layers. The key insight is to learn structured sparsity directly from scratch by dynamically allocating layer-wise pruning ratios and progressively increasing a sparsity-inducing penalty so the network becomes sparse gradually rather than being forced abruptly. Methodologically, DPFPS imposes a novel structured sparsity regularizer on expected pruning parameters, uses a Taylor-series-based channel sensitivity criterion to identify pruneable channels, and solves the resulting pruning-ratio optimization with an iterative soft-thresholding (ISTA) procedure under dynamic sparsity, producing a final pruned model that requires no fine-tuning. Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet demonstrate competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods, e.g., compressing ResNet-101 to cut 44.97% of FLOPs while slightly improving Top-5 accuracy.

args.text: We propose Learnability-Constrained Behavioral Optimal-Transport Curricula (L-BOT): learn a behavioral embedding of task instances via an adversarial trajectory discriminator and compute a Wasserstein-geodesic curriculum from an easy source distribution to the target in that space. The geodesic’s ground metric is adapted online with learnability estimates (e.g., probability-of-success variance or failure-conditioned regret), detouring around regions that provide little learning signal. At each waypoint we train with a PAIRED-style antagonist to keep challenges solvable-yet-informative, pace progression with a self-paced update based on agent capability, and within-waypoint select levels via Prioritized Level Replay. We hypothesize this yields smoother transfer and stronger zero-shot generalization than standard UED or fixed-metric OT curricula.

We propose Token-Adaptive Mixed-Precision for LLM inference: a budgeted per-token bitwidth scheduler that allocates precision across layers and attention heads based on lightweight features such as pre-LN norms, attention entropy, and KV-similarity drift, directly targeting the memory-bandwidth bottleneck in single-batch generation. The scheduler is learned with differentiable bitwidth parameters and a bit-sparsity regularizer to yield discrete per-layer/head bit windows, and we co-train a representation-aware fine-tuning objective so quantized weights are robust to the distribution of token-conditioned precisions; at inference, a tiny LUT enforces a global per-step bit budget for predictable latency. Unlike static mixed precision or per-activation bit skipping, this approach adapts precision where it matters most for each token while keeping KV-cache formats stable to avoid thrashing, promising substantial bandwidth reduction at near-4-bit accuracy. We hypothesize 1.3–1.7× bandwidth savings on LLaMA-style models with <0.5 perplexity degradation by combining token-aware scheduling with end-to-end learnable quantization choices.

result.text: The paper addresses robust multimodal emotion recognition when one or more modalities (language, vision, acoustic) are missing in real-world settings, which degrades performance of conventional MER systems. Its key insight is to treat modality imputation as a generative recovery problem and use score-based diffusion to map noise into realistic modality-specific distributions while conditioning on available modalities to enforce semantic consistency. The method, called IMDer, trains a score-based diffusion model to recover missing modality features by gradually denoising Gaussian noise into samples that match the original modality distribution, with conditioning embeddings from present modalities to reduce semantic ambiguity between recovered and observed data; experiments and visualizations show the recovered features are both distributionally consistent and semantically aligned, yielding state-of-the-art MER performance across various missing-modality patterns.

result.text: The paper tackles long-horizon visual planning for complex robotic tasks by generating detailed multimodal (video + language) plans that bridge high-level instructions and low-level actions. The key insight is to treat a pretrained text-to-video model as a learned dynamics simulator and vision-language models as both policy and value estimators, enabling search over imagined video trajectories to evaluate and refine plans. The method, called Video Language Planning (VLP), runs a tree search that proposes candidate video continuations with a text-to-video model, scores them with learned vision-language value/policy models, and iteratively expands and selects high-value video-language plans; these generated videos can then be converted into executable goals for goal-conditioned controllers. Empirically, VLP scales with computation budget and yields substantially higher long-horizon task success on diverse simulated and real-robot domains (including multi-object and bi-arm manipulation) than prior approaches.

args.text: We propose group-free conformal fairness under shift: for a black-box model deployed on an unlabeled, shifted target domain without sensitive-attribute labels, we discover latent subgroups in the model’s representation using bias-sensitive directions (estimated via post-hoc filters or proxy-attribute predictors), then learn distributionally robust, subgroup-specific nonconformity thresholds that equalize calibrated coverage across these subgroups. Concretely, we pair split conformal calibration with a worst-case reweighting objective over weighted perturbations of the target distribution and optimize per-cluster thresholds post-hoc on target data, yielding fairness guarantees that hold under covariate shift while preserving accuracy. The same idea extends to retrieval by coupling robust calibration with post-hoc re-ranking to bound demographic skew in top-k results without retraining. This unifies shift-robust fairness, group-agnostic representation discovery, and model-agnostic threshold adaptation in a single deployable pipeline.

result.text: The paper investigates how Transformers perform in-context learning (ICL) for linear regression, challenging the view that they emulate Gradient Descent (GD) and asking whether they can realize faster, second-order optimization behavior. The key insight is that Transformer layers empirically and theoretically approximate Iterative Newton’s Method rather than GD, yielding exponentially faster convergence: successive layers' predictions linearly match Newton iterations (with each middle layer roughly implementing three Newton steps), enabling effective learning even on ill-conditioned data where GD fails. Methodologically, the authors combine empirical experiments comparing layer-wise outputs to Newton and GD trajectories and show faster convergence and robustness on challenging datasets, and they provide a constructive proof that a Transformer can implement k Newton iterations using k + O(1) layers, formalizing the capacity for second-order in-context optimization.

The key insight is that both low- and high-frequency signals can be informative depending on the graph and task, so a GNN should adaptively weigh and integrate multiple frequency components rather than assuming low-frequency dominance. They propose Frequency Adaptation Graph Convolutional Networks (FAGCN), which uses a self-gating mechanism within message passing to learn adaptive coefficients for combining different spectral (frequency) components, and provide theoretical analysis explaining how these components affect representation learning; experiments on six real-world graphs show FAGCN reduces over-smoothing and outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

args.text: We propose Expansion-Calibrated Balanced Poisson Propagation (EC-BPP) for source-free domain adaptation under subpopulation and label-proportion shift. EC-BPP selects reliable target seeds via early-time training from a source-pretrained teacher, estimates target label proportions, and then performs Poisson label propagation on a target graph with class-size priors while reweighting edges to enforce a lower bound on local expansion estimated in the teacher’s representation. By coupling expansion-based guarantees for label propagation with explicit label-shift correction, EC-BPP aims to provably improve upon the teacher without source data; theory links errors to expansion and proportion-estimation accuracy, and practice iterates seed selection, proportion refinement, and propagation. This unifies expansion-driven transfer with robust pseudo-labeling and balancing, addressing common failures on relaxed label-shift and SFDA benchmarks.

We propose SM-SSM-NILM, a duration-aware state-space pretraining framework for non-intrusive load monitoring. The model augments MSDC-style disaggregation with a semi-Markov switching head that jointly predicts discrete appliance states and dwell-times atop a long-range Linear State-Space backbone, and attaches a per-state power regressor for calibrated consumption estimates. We pretrain this architecture on massive synthetic appliance- and circuit-level traces (in the spirit of BuildingsBench) using masked event/duration prediction and cross-home contrastive objectives to learn cross-appliance transferable features as in PowerPM while capturing regime-dependent dynamics as in RED-SDS. We hypothesize substantially better zero/few-shot disaggregation and more accurate state segmentation on REDD/UK-DALE, especially for rare multi-state appliances.

We propose GraphFuse-RL, an accelerator-native runtime that fuses environment stepping and policy inference into a single persistent-kernel execution graph. The system compiles environment dynamics (C++/CUDA or JAX) and buckets env instances by control-flow fingerprints to reduce warp divergence, then uses CUDA Graphs/XLA to capture end-to-end step→policy→update pipelines with zero-copy ring buffers. An adaptive co-scheduler tunes micro-batch sizes and overlaps kernels to sustain high occupancy while bounding action-staleness via lightweight importance correction, preserving sample efficiency at extreme throughput. This unifies vectorized CPU envs, GPU-native simulators, and GPU-based sampling into one in-graph workflow, targeting board games, multi-agent driving, and 3D navigation.

Existing approaches to generative commonsense either fuse static knowledge graphs into seq2seq models or generate auxiliary symbolic graphs before reasoning, but they rarely let graph structure act as hard constraints during decoding. We propose graph-conditioned constrained decoding: interleave text generation with on-the-fly construction of a local, context-specific commonsense subgraph and compile that subgraph’s type, relation, and path constraints into a subword-aligned finite-state controller that prunes implausible continuations in the decoder. The subgraph is updated after each span, and when it is sparse we augment it by alternating lightweight KG traversal and entity-linked passage retrieval to enrich constraints without retraining the LM. This closed-loop graph–text co-decoding should yield more plausible, faithful, and interpretable generations on CommonGen and knowledge-intensive QA while matching the inference speed of recent constraint decoders.

result.text: We propose Algebraic-Diffusion IP-IRM, which augments iterative partition-based invariance with unsupervised discovery of continuous symmetries. We learn a small set of Lie-algebra generators in feature space from local view pairs, build a diffusion operator to estimate invariant subspaces and orbits, and alternate between (i) partitioning by orbit components to enforce subset-invariance and (ii) sparsifying cross-subspace interactions while applying a factorized-support regularizer to decouple correlated factors. This yields modular, approximately group-equivariant latents without prespecified groups, and ties downstream predictors to sparse subsets of generators/subspaces to enhance identifiability and OOD transfer. We hypothesize that the learned generators converge to true data symmetries when present and to approximate stabilizers otherwise, improving disentanglement and transfer on correlated-factor benchmarks while enabling plug-and-play equivariant layers.

Per-frame object tokens from a frozen image instance segmenter initialize observations (as in tokenized image-to-video linking), while a lightweight dynamical model extrapolates next-frame instance tokens (inspired by next-token rollout) and then fuses them with detector tokens via a Kalman-style update; association is performed by bipartite matching in token space. args.text: We propose a Fractional Fourier Neural Operator (FrFNO) that replaces the global Fourier multipliers in FNO with learnable multi-order fractional Fourier transforms, allowing the model to operate in intermediate space–frequency domains that better capture non-stationary, chirp-like PDE phenomena while retaining resolution-agnostic operator learning. result.text: EdgeDecentGS: a fully decentralized, fault-tolerant training framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting on heterogeneous, intermittently connected devices. It adopts DOGS-style spatial decomposition but replaces the master-driven ADMM with boundary-only consensus performed via scheduled one-peer exponential graphs and Moshpit-style averaging, enabling near-exact model alignment without a reliable high-speed fabric. Communication is further reduced by Grendel’s sparsity—nodes gossip only Gaussians whose screen-space footprints intersect neighbors’ pixel shards—and by LEAD-style compressed exchanges with error-corrected tracking, stabilizing optimization under heavy quantization. This yields city-scale 3DGS that scales beyond single clusters, preserving quality while improving wall-clock convergence under churn and load imbalance.

result.text: Propose a hardware-aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scaling law that augments granularity-based MoE analysis with explicit communication topology and overlap terms, predicting regime switches (broken scaling) when interconnects saturate. We derive a parametric compute–performance model linking tokens T, parameters P, experts E, and granularity g to step time and throughput under topology-aware dispatch and communication–computation overlap, and account for routing variants (e.g., expert-choice) that alter activation sparsity and load balance. The model yields compute-optimal allocations {P,E,g,T} and a training-time controller that adapts granularity and routing to remain in compute-bound rather than comm-bound regimes, producing predictable piecewise power laws akin to a broken scaling curve. We validate by fitting exponents on a small cluster and extrapolating across network topologies, showing that topology-aware routing plus adaptive granularity tracks the compute-optimal frontier better than fixed-g MoE.

args.text: We propose Video Landmark Memory (VLM), a random-access attention architecture for long-video LMMs that adapts landmark-based infinite context to the spatio-temporal domain. Videos are partitioned into blocks, each distilled into a few query-conditioned spatio-temporal landmark tokens that summarize objects, motions, and subtitles; at inference, language queries first attend to landmarks to pick relevant blocks, then perform fine-grained attention within selected blocks, while a lightweight streaming update maintains landmarks online for hour-long inputs. We train landmarks with segment-level supervision and referring-reasoning signals so they become keys to the correct temporal neighborhoods, yielding large accuracy and latency gains on long-video QA versus dense tokenization. This design preserves native attention compatibility, enables constant-memory retrieval over very long videos, and aligns with referring-context evaluation protocols.

result.text: The paper addresses invisible data poisoning attacks that add small adversarial perturbations to training examples to force targeted misclassification at test time, noting that existing defenses either hurt generalization, are slow, or are attack-specific. The key insight is that poisons create local sharp regions of high training loss which, when minimized, cause models to learn the adversarial perturbations; thus blunting those sharp regions prevents the attack from succeeding. The proposed method crafts an optimized "friendly" perturbation that maximally perturbs training examples without degrading performance, and combines it with a randomly varying noise component to smooth loss landscapes and add unpredictability; this lightweight defense thwarts a range of triggerless targeted and hidden-trigger backdoor attacks, transfers across architectures, and resists adaptive attacks due to its randomization.

args.text: We propose Frequency-Balanced Gradient Regularization (FBGR) for limited-data GANs: decompose each input into multiple frequency bands and explicitly match the discriminator’s input-gradient energy on real vs. fake within each band, closing the gradient gap not only in aggregate but per-frequency. A lightweight spectral head supplies band-specific real/fake feedback and stabilizes gradients in high-frequency regions, complementing the main spatial pathway. To avoid consistency-induced artifacts, we apply band-conditioned consistency regularization only across perturbations that preserve band structure (e.g., mild magnitude jitter or phase-preserving transforms), aligning predictions within bands rather than between augmented and unaugmented outputs. By equalizing gradient flow across frequencies, FBGR addresses the discriminator’s insensitivity to low-magnitude high-frequency signals and reduces spectrum mismatch, improving fine detail without destabilizing training.

The authors introduce OWLv2 (a strong baseline detector) and OWL-ST (a scalable self-training recipe) that produce high-quality pseudo-boxes and scale from ~10M to over 1B examples, yielding large gains on rare LVIS classes (e.g., boosting AP from 31.2% to 44.6% for classes with no human boxes) and demonstrating that web-scale training can unlock open-world localization akin to advances in classification and language models.

result.text: The paper addresses the mismatch between scalable deep reinforcement learning algorithms (like PPO and TRPO) and the classic theoretical frameworks—generalised policy iteration (GPI) and trust-region learning (TRL)—which are either unscalable or require heuristics that break their assumptions. Its key insight is that both practical algorithms and the classical frameworks can be unified under a broader theoretical construct called Mirror Learning, which subsumes GPI and TRL as special, overly restrictive cases and directly explains why PPO/TRPO-like methods work. The method formalises a family of policy optimisation objectives and updates that obey a mirror-like regularisation principle, derives theoretical performance and stability guarantees for this family, and shows that many existing algorithms fall into or can be interpreted within this family. By reframing policy optimisation through Mirror Learning, the paper provides principled justification for current heuristics and a foundation for designing new scalable, theoretically sound RL algorithms.

result.text: The paper investigates whether few-shot learning (FSL) is vulnerable to backdoor attacks, addressing observed failures of existing backdoor methods in FSL due to overfitting to either benign or trigger features and easy detection of visible triggers in tiny support sets. The method, Few-shot Learning Backdoor Attack (FLBA), optimizes these perturbations to convert all support examples into a hidden poisoned support set and fine-tunes the model on it, yielding high attack success rates across FSL paradigms while preserving clean accuracy and stealthiness.

args.text: We propose Symmetry-Adaptive Neural Diffusion Processes that model function-valued posteriors with a mixture of equivariant diffusion score networks, enabling the degree and type of symmetry to vary across tasks and input regions. Each expert score enforces a (sub)group or partial equivariance via steerable/partial-equivariant architectures, while a permutation-invariant gating network over the context set predicts input-dependent mixture weights that are used to combine scores during the reverse diffusion to sample finite marginals. This unifies Neural Diffusion Processes with equivariant Neural Processes and Mixture-of-Experts, yielding exchangeable, non-stationary function priors that recover fixed-symmetry and stationary models as special cases and improve calibration and sample fidelity on data with approximate or locally varying symmetries. We train end-to-end with the diffusion loss plus a diversity regularizer on experts and evaluate on spatio-temporal and image-like tasks where symmetries drift or hold only approximately.

result.text: I propose I-P MCTS for continuous actions: each node maintains a lightweight local action policy and alternates two operators—(i) an exact entropy/KL-regularized improvement step over the continuous action space that maximizes the node’s backup objective, and (ii) a projection step that selects a small, diverse action set for progressive widening via determinantal coresets or an expected-improvement acquisition using ensemble uncertainty. This replaces heuristic PUCT with the exact optimizer, exploits local smoothness via gradient refinement of candidate actions, and scales by sampling only a few actions per node. Compared to VOOT/BOMCP, the novelty is treating action-set growth as a principled projection coupled to an exact improvement operator, unifying optimization-based MCTS with progressive widening. We amortize local policies across similar states to warm-start the improvement step and hypothesize tighter regret bounds under mild smoothness and diversity conditions.
