args.text: I propose Active Token Querying (ATQ), an LLM-driven perceptual loop that begins from a coarse, low-cost visual token summary and inserts explicit REFINE(region, scale, modality) actions into the autoregressive sequence to request only the most informative fine-grained tokens. A queryable tokenizer exposes uncertainty and expected information-gain maps over spatial regions and motion segments, and the LLM learns a budget-aware policy to trade task reward (e.g., VQA accuracy, editing fidelity) against compute via imitation of oracle gains followed by RL fine-tuning. Training couples masked/token-reconstruction and round-trip multimodal objectives with a budgeted loss so the same mechanism also prioritizes where to render higher-fidelity content first during generation, improving quality under fixed decoding steps. ATQ unifies and extends dynamic semantic tokenization and autoregressive visual tokens with cross-modal token merging and video keyframe/motion tokens, but introduces explicit query/action tokens and budget-aware planning that prior unified multimodal models lack.

We propose Reasoned Concept-Mapping for Idiomatic and Metaphorical MT (RCM-IMT): a retrieval- and reasoning-augmented translator that unifies idiom sense resolution with novel metaphor handling by grounding spans in a multilingual concept–mapping graph plus an idiom knowledge base. At inference, a RAG-style retriever surfaces candidate idiom senses and source→target concept mappings; a lightweight self-consistency chain-of-thought module then decides literal vs figurative usage, selects a mapping, and emits a short rationale that doubles as a verifiable citation trace. The generator is a prompt-tuned MT model conditioned on (a) the selected mapping’s human-aligned paraphrase and examples and (b) multilingual KG neighborhoods fused across languages to bridge lexical gaps, yielding faithful yet natural translations. We expect gains on idiom- and metaphor-heavy test sets, with ablations showing complementary benefits of retrieval, KG fusion, and reasoning; evaluation reports both standard MT scores and explanation quality via citation correctness and human judgments.

result.text: The paper addresses multi-modality 3D object detection by providing a single unified voxel-space representation that supports both single- and cross-modality inputs without collapsing geometric detail. The key insight is that preserving a full 3D voxel feature space (avoiding height compression) and bringing modality-specific inputs into that shared voxel space enables richer spatial connections and reduces semantic ambiguity, while transformer-based object queries can efficiently sample and reason over this unified representation. Methodologically, UVTR constructs modality-specific voxel spaces for images and point clouds, applies cross-modality interaction via knowledge transfer and fusion to combine geometry-aware and context-rich features, and uses a transformer decoder with learnable sampling positions to perform object-level feature sampling and detection, yielding state-of-the-art results on nuScenes for detection and tracking.

From videos, estimate egomotion and camera pose to derive pseudo-rewards for viewpoint novelty, anticipated field-of-view coverage along candidate paths, and goal-image progress; train the camera policy with conservative offline RL to avoid out-of-distribution optimism, and condition it on planned motion primitives so sensing actions anticipate near-future movement. The key insight is that DPO, despite strong empirical results on some benchmarks, has fundamental theoretical limitations, while PPO's apparent poor performance often stems from suboptimal implementation choices rather than inherent algorithmic weakness. The authors analyze algorithmic properties of DPO, dissect the factors that enable PPO to perform well when properly tuned for LLM fine-tuning, and conduct comprehensive empirical comparisons across diverse RLHF testbeds from dialogue to code generation. Their experiments show that PPO, when configured appropriately, consistently matches or outperforms other alignment methods and achieves state-of-the-art results on challenging code tasks.

args.text: We propose a PMU-guided self-optimization loop for LLM-generated code that augments coarse runtime/memory feedback with fine-grained hardware performance counters (e.g., cache/TLB miss rates, branch mispredicts, vectorization utilization, IPC) collected from brief profiled runs. args.text: We propose a VCG-guided, disease-conditioned ROI diffusion model that jointly synthesizes 12-lead ECGs and translates PPG to ECG while enforcing cross-lead physiological consistency. The core idea is to embed a differentiable vectorcardiogram source model (with fixed/learned lead-field mapping) inside a region-disentangled diffusion process, so denoising is applied separately to diagnostically critical segments (e.g., QRS/ST) while a shared low-dimensional dipole trajectory guarantees coherent morphology across leads. Disease conditioning is injected at localized temporal regions to imprint label-specific changes, and a neural ODE prior regularizes the latent dipole dynamics to remain physiologically plausible. We expect improved rFID, new lead-consistency metrics (e.g., VCG reconstruction error), and state-of-the-art PPG→ECG translation in few diffusion steps on CardioBench, with clearer disease localization and cross-lead agreement.

result.text: The paper addresses robust non-contact heart-rate estimation from facial videos when subject distance and head motion cause large, time-varying face resolution and motion artifacts that break existing rPPG models tuned to constant-distance inputs. The key insight is that decoupling resolution- and motion-related degradations via two plug-and-play modules—a physiological feature extraction (PFE) block that maps arbitrary-resolution facial frames to a fixed-resolution facial-structure representation guided by representative-area information, and a temporal face alignment (TFA) block that uses estimated optical flow to undo head-motion–induced signal confusion—yields more stable rPPG features. They implement these blocks within a two-stream dual-resolution training framework with a cross-resolution constraint so PFE learns resolution-robust features, and show by integrating PFE and TFA into spatio-temporal rPPG models that HR estimation improves across UBFC-rPPG, COHFACE and PURE benchmarks under varying resolution and severe head movement.

result.text: Propose a hardware-aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scaling law that augments granularity-based MoE analysis with explicit communication topology and overlap terms, predicting regime switches (broken scaling) when interconnects saturate. We derive a parametric compute–performance model linking tokens T, parameters P, experts E, and granularity g to step time and throughput under topology-aware dispatch and communication–computation overlap, and account for routing variants (e.g., expert-choice) that alter activation sparsity and load balance. The model yields compute-optimal allocations {P,E,g,T} and a training-time controller that adapts granularity and routing to remain in compute-bound rather than comm-bound regimes, producing predictable piecewise power laws akin to a broken scaling curve. We validate by fitting exponents on a small cluster and extrapolating across network topologies, showing that topology-aware routing plus adaptive granularity tracks the compute-optimal frontier better than fixed-g MoE.

args.text: We propose Adversarial Dual-Domain Masking (ADM), which jointly learns a spatial masker and a frequency masker that adversarially select complementary regions/components to maximize the encoder’s representation gap, while the encoder is trained to minimize this gap across original and jointly masked views. The spatial masker is regularized by attention priors from the encoder to preserve a controllable fraction of high-saliency patches, and the frequency masker targets band-limited components under a shared masking budget, preventing trivial background-only or narrow-band strategies and forcing invariance to both structural and textural cues. To stabilize training and avoid dimensional collapse under heavy dual-domain invariance pressure, we add a uniformity-encouraging term to the representation objective. We hypothesize ADM yields faster, architecture-agnostic pretraining with improved robustness and dense-task transfer versus single-domain adversarial masking.

args.text: We propose Counterfactual-Simulatability–Aware NLE Selection for NLI: for each candidate explanation, we automatically synthesize diverse, causally-controlled counterfactuals of the premise/hypothesis and score the explanation by how precisely and generally it lets a lightweight simulator predict the model’s outputs on those counterfactuals. To robustly estimate this score, we aggregate over paraphrases of the explanation using semantic-entropy pooling, and use either LLM-guided counterfactual edits or an efficient training-time matching proxy to hold confounders fixed. These simulatability scores drive an instance selector that weights or filters NLEs during augmentation and adds a counterfactual-consistency regularizer, yielding rationale-grounded training akin to LIREx but optimized for predictive faithfulness rather than plausibility. We hypothesize this improves out-of-domain NLI accuracy and produces explanations with higher counterfactual simulatability than existing NLE-augmented methods.

args.text: Separation-aware adaptive domain randomization (ADR-ID): model the simulator as a latent mixture of MDPs and train two-phase memory policies that begin with brief probing trajectories chosen via OOM/PSR-style spectral criteria to maximally separate candidate dynamics, then switch to control while hedging residual ambiguity using TV-robust regularization implemented through regularized (R^2) MDP updates. result.text: We propose a mechanism-based predictor for Broken Neural Scaling Law breakpoints: breaks occur when training crosses optimizer and architecture regime boundaries, specifically when the step-size–to–curvature ratio and effective SGD noise exceed Edge-of-Stability/unstable-convergence thresholds, or when MoE granularity/routing reallocations shift the compute–error tradeoff. Leveraging analyses of EOS dynamics and high-dimensional SGD, and MoE granularity scaling, we specify a multi-axis piecewise power law whose break locations are explicit functions of η·λ_max, batch-size/data-reuse noise scale, and expert granularity/load variance; this yields conditions for when compute-optimal policies switch from “add steps” to “add parameters/experts.” We outline experiments that jointly track sharpness, noise scale, and routing imbalance across scales to fit these breakpoint predictors and validate their extrapolations, enabling proactive curricula (step size, batch, and granularity schedules) that avoid suboptimal pre-break regimes.

args.text: We propose a spatiotemporal sketched matrix-mechanism for user-level DP in cross-device FL that jointly optimizes privacy, communication, and multi-participation. Each participating client multiplies its clipped gradient by a shared sparse sketch (e.g., CountSketch/JL) and adds discretized Skellam noise in the sketched domain; across rounds, the server (via secure aggregation) only sees sums of banded lower-triangular temporal combinations of these sketches, chosen to inherit the privacy amplification guarantees of banded MF while accommodating randomized client check-ins. Random partial sketching further amplifies privacy and reduces per-round communication to near the central-DP lower bound (up to log factors), while preserving accuracy via de-sketching and band-limited temporal smoothing. The analysis uses RDP for Skellam noise composed with linear sketches and the banded temporal operator, yielding end-to-end guarantees and demonstrating DP-SGD-level utility at substantially fewer bits per client.

result.text: The paper tackles weakly supervised 3D segmentation where sparse ground-truth labels force methods to rely on selective pseudo-labeling (e.g., confidence thresholding), which wastes unlabeled data and limits performance. The key insight is that noisy pseudo-labels create large discrepancies with model predictions that confuse training, so regularizing pseudo-label distributions to reduce this gap enables use of all points. The authors propose ERDA, combining an entropy regularization loss to encourage confident predictions and a KL-based distribution alignment loss (implemented as a cross-entropy formulation) that jointly optimizes the pseudo-label generator and segmentation network to align their output distributions. This simple yet effective strategy is validated across baselines and large-scale datasets, yielding state-of-the-art results and even surpassing fully supervised models when only 1% of annotations are available.

The paper tackles the problem of LLMs being vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks that manipulate prompts to elicit unsafe or undesired outputs, noting that prior defenses struggle against new or adaptive attacks. Its key insight is to model the adversary explicitly within the defensive objective and optimize a compact, transferable suffix that hardens the model against worst-case adaptive jailbreaks. The method, Robust Prompt Optimization (RPO), formulates an optimization-based defense that searches for system-level prompt suffixes by iteratively simulating adversarial attacks during training and minimizing attack success rates. Empirically and theoretically, RPO substantially improves robustness—dropping ASR on JailbreakBench to 6% for GPT-4 and 0% for Llama-2—while remaining lightweight and transferable.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of accurate post-training quantization (PTQ) for large language models, where activation outliers in certain channels cause large quantization error and degrade low-bitwidth performance. The key insight is to mitigate outlier effects by redistributing their large magnitudes across channels—reducing peak activation ranges—while preserving model structure and efficiency. QLLM implements this via adaptive channel reassembly: disassembling outlier channels into multiple sub-channels to balance activation magnitudes, then reassembling similar channels to restore the original channel count with an adaptive rule to choose the number of splits; additionally, it applies a lightweight low-rank tuning step that trains a small set of parameters (which can be fused back into the frozen quantized weights) to recover accuracy. Experiments on LLaMA-1/2 show QLLM yields substantially better low-bit (e.g., 4-bit) results and practical efficiency (e.g., quantizing LLaMA-2-70B in ~10 hours on one A100) compared to prior PTQ methods.

result.text: We propose CoreConCut: a core-contraction–guided cut-selection policy for core-guided pseudo-Boolean MaxSAT that learns to pick and order PB cuts to maximally shrink the current multiset of unsatisfiable cores. The key signal is a core-contraction reward defined as the predicted reduction in a weighted minimum hitting set objective over recent cores; we train a hierarchical policy (first predict how many cuts, then select an ordered subset) to imitate a lookahead expert that evaluates true contraction via short rollouts. The policy featurizes core structure (literal/relaxation-variable frequencies and co-occurrence motifs) and candidate cuts, and is integrated into the PB bound-refinement loop to alternate contraction- and bound-oriented phases for faster convergence. We further adapt sample-complexity guarantees for cut-selection to this reward by showing that small perturbations of cut parameters induce stable changes in the contraction metric, yielding learnability bounds tailored to core-guided PB optimization.

args.text: Confidence-Adaptive Expert Expansion (CAEE) is an inference-time policy for MoE models that starts with a minimal expert set and incrementally activates additional experts for a token only when predicted uncertainty or cross-expert disagreement is high. A small marginal-utility head on the router is trained to estimate the expected gain in log-likelihood from adding the next expert, using targets formed by contrasting outputs under weak versus strong activation during training, with a monotonicity regularizer to encourage diminishing returns as k grows. This yields per-token, compute-aware routing that adapts activation size at inference without retraining and complements expert-choice load balancing. We expect improved calibration and accuracy at a fixed average FLOP budget compared to static top-k or globally tuned k, validated on language and vision MoEs.

result.text: The paper tackles sample-efficient reinforcement learning in partially observable settings by focusing on undercomplete POMDPs—models where the observation space is higher-dimensional than the latent state space—thereby avoiding known hardness results for general POMDPs while still requiring exploration and memory. Building on this, the authors propose OOM-UCB, an episodic algorithm that leverages observable operator model (OOM)-style spectral estimation together with optimism in the face of uncertainty to control exploration, and they prove it attains optimal O(1/ε^2) sample complexity (polynomial in other parameters) for finding an ε-optimal policy, with a specialized efficient procedure for deterministic-transition POMDPs.

args.text: I propose Uncertainty- and Diversity-Aware Channel Pruning (UDCP) to directly address the Similarity and Applicability issues in channel-pruning criteria. UDCP estimates each channel’s functional importance and its uncertainty via repeated mini-batch perturbations or MC-dropout, then applies an upper-confidence bound (UCB) to avoid pruning channels that have low mean importance but high uncertainty. To break ties among near-identical scores and reduce redundancy, it performs diversity-aware selection by whitening feature maps and penalizing correlated channels (e.g., via a DPP or orthogonal matching pursuit), ensuring pruned sets remove representationally replaceable channels. By combining UCB-based caution with redundancy-aware selection, UDCP yields more robust and discriminative pruning decisions under high sparsity.

args.text: We propose a Wasserstein-Regret UED curriculum that traces a smooth path over environment parameters from an easy seed distribution to a frontier of adversarially generated, high-regret tasks. The frontier is discovered via a PAIRED-style protagonist–antagonist adversary, while the geodesic is computed in a behavior-embedding metric induced by a discriminator so adjacent curriculum waypoints preserve policy occupancy continuity. At each waypoint, we prioritize training on high-learnability instances and within-waypoint levels are sampled via TD-error–based level replay to concentrate updates where they most improve the policy. This hybrid aims to retain adversarial pressure without brittle jumps, yielding stable progression and stronger transfer than either pure regret-driven UED or pure optimal-transport curricula alone.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of preserving accuracy in post-training quantization (PTQ) for large language models while keeping hardware-friendly efficiency, addressing the shortcomings of uniform-precision schemes that degrade performance at very low bit-widths. The key insight is that important weights exhibit a structured, group-wise distribution of salience, so allocating precision nonuniformly at the group level and incorporating element-level salience into quantizer calibration can capture critical information without sacrificing implementation efficiency. Their method, SliM-LLM, partitions weights into groups within each layer, uses a Salience-Determined Bit Allocation to assign group-wise bit-widths adaptively, and applies a Salience-Weighted Quantizer Calibration to optimize quantizer parameters by weighting elements by salience; an extended SliM-LLM+ adds gradient-based optimization for further gains. Experiments show this structured mixed-precision approach matches the speed and hardware friendliness of uniform quantization while significantly improving accuracy at low bits (e.g., 2-bit LLaMA-7B with ~6× memory reduction and large perplexity reductions compared to prior PTQ methods).

args.text: We propose Traj-GPF: pre-train a single heterogeneous region–road–POI–time graph encoder with structural- and semantic-contrastive objectives to capture global topology and attributes, then adapt it to diverse trajectory similarity notions by attaching small, learnable Graph Prompt Features to the nodes/edges touched by a query trajectory. Unlike prior trajectory encoders that learn standalone sequence embeddings or bespoke prompt modules, we condition the shared graph encoder via feature-space prompts localized along the path, producing a trajectory-conditioned graph readout that serves as the trajectory embedding. We train prompts with contrastive objectives using route-alternative positives and temporally perturbed replays, freeze the backbone for cross-city transfer, and use a lightweight residual sequence unit only to synthesize prompt features from ordered GPS points. This design aims to match or exceed prior road-network-aware similarity while offering few-shot, zero-shot, and definition-flexible adaptation through prompt-only tuning.

result.text: The paper tackles graph domain adaptation (GDA), where models trained on graph-structured source data must generalize to target graphs with distributional shifts—particularly when graph structure and node attributes change, as in applications like high energy physics. Its key insight is that beyond marginal shifts in node representations, there exists a conditional structure shift (CSS)—changes in graph connectivity conditioned on labels—that shared-encoder alignment methods are provably ill-suited to correct. The authors propose structural re-weighting (StruRW), which detects and compensates for structural mismatches by reweighting structural contributions during training so that node representation learning accounts for conditional connectivity differences; they validate StruRW on synthetic graphs, four benchmarks, and an HEP dataset, showing substantial gains under large structural shifts and modest improvements when attribute shifts prevail.

args.text: We propose MiFSim: uncertainty-gated mixed-fidelity batched simulation for accelerator-native RL. Most steps run in a fast, coarse GPU path (batched physics/rendering), while a lightweight classifier flags rare, high-contact/interaction states for promotion to a high-fidelity micro-simulator (CPU or fine-grained GPU) that executes asynchronously in micro-batches and writes back corrected states/rewards via event queues. We keep transitions in on-device ring buffers and use importance weighting plus delayed credit assignment to debias learning under heterogeneous simulators, preserving sample efficiency and stability while achieving large throughput gains. This unifies batch-simulation and GPU-native engines with off-policy, asynchronous pipelines for embodied 3D and multi-agent driving tasks.

result.text: We propose Algebraic-Diffusion IP-IRM, which augments iterative partition-based invariance with unsupervised discovery of continuous symmetries. We hypothesize that the learned generators converge to true data symmetries when present and to approximate stabilizers otherwise, improving disentanglement and transfer on correlated-factor benchmarks while enabling plug-and-play equivariant layers.

The key insight is that distillation can improve aggregate accuracy while degrading performance on specific classes that exceed the student’s capacity to reproduce, and that the prevalence of such classes correlates with the capacity gap between teacher and student. The authors propose a simple Teach Less, Learn More (TLLM) framework that detects and discards these undistillable classes during student training, effectively preventing the student from being misled by teacher outputs it cannot emulate. Empirical results across datasets and architectures show that TLLM consistently improves student performance over standard and state-of-the-art distillation methods.

args.text: We propose MoLAK: a hardware-aware pruning method that fuses layer-adaptive magnitude rescaling with multi-layer distortion modeling and fine-tuning movement cues to select structured sparsity under strict latency budgets. The key idea is to compute group-wise importance by combining LAMP-style global rescaling with a lookahead multi-layer Frobenius distortion proxy, then adapt these scores during a brief fine-tuning window using movement-based signs, and finally select groups via a latency-knapsack solver. Concretely, we partition parameters into dependency-aware groups, score each group as (LAMP-rescaled multi-layer sensitivity) multiplied by an exponential-moving-average of positive update directions, normalize by per-group latency from a lookup table, and solve a constrained selection every few epochs while distilling to stabilize accuracy. args.text: We propose CertGuard, a certified prompt-level defense that turns robust prompt optimization into a randomized-smoothing scheme over a distribution of semantically equivalent guard prefixes, enabling probabilistic guarantees against bounded prompt edits and suffix-based jailbreaks. The generator is optimized to maximize the smoothed safety margin under strong black-box attacks and calibrated via Clopper–Pearson bounds on Monte Carlo samples. Plugged into a peer-ensemble/mean-teacher framework, this yields stronger, more stable online teachers and a curriculum over teacher informativeness without extra inference cost. We expect improved convergence and student accuracy, especially for small models, by exploiting the richer dark knowledge of intermediate teachers early and consolidating with the ensemble later.

args.text: Certified neural-adjoint inverse design: augment gradient-based design through learned simulators with stochastic barrier certificates and reachability guarantees, so each candidate design comes with a provable lower bound on safety along long-horizon rollouts. Concretely, at each optimization step we synthesize a stochastic barrier for the NN-driven dynamics of the surrogate and use tight, SLR-style local reachability to bound violation probabilities, backpropagating through these certificates to steer updates toward higher safety margins. This preserves the time-to-solution benefits of neural-adjoint and learned-simulator design while returning solutions with quantified, certified safety under model error, enabling robust fluid–structure and PDE-control designs.

result.text: We propose an operator-conditioned diffusion solver for inverse lithography that jointly learns a fast, differentiable neural operator to emulate the optical+resist forward map and a conditional score model over manufacturable masks, trained and evaluated on LithoBench. At inference, we generate masks by solving the probability-flow ODE with a neural-operator sampler that maps noise to the full trajectory in one pass (DSNO-style), while enforcing target-print and manufacturability consistency via projection steps inspired by DDRM but generalized to the nonlinear forward map. To handle process variability (e.g., NA, illumination, resist curves) without retraining, we wrap the score model within a Neural Inverse Operator composition so conditioning on operator changes is explicit and stable. This aims to deliver state-of-the-art ILT quality with orders-of-magnitude speedups over PDE-constrained optimization and a standardized, benchmarkable pipeline on LithoBench.

args.text: I propose a decoupled, nonparametric prototype framework for universal domain adaptation and generalized category discovery that avoids a monolithic “unknown” bucket. First, we separate target-private from shared samples via mutual-nearest-neighbor contrast and a bimodality-based confidence test, then align shared samples to the labeled taxonomy by bipartite prototype matching with semantic-weighted soft assignments. For private samples, we grow novel clusters on-the-fly with a momentum-teacher mutual-information objective, instantiating new prototypes when local neighbor-consistency density exceeds a threshold, while explicitly minimizing mutual information between low-level domain features and cluster assignments to prevent domain-induced fragmentation. This yields a single head with K known and M dynamic novel prototypes, stabilizing discovery and transfer under UniDA/SFDA with reliable label propagation and domain-robust semantics.

Real-world meta-tasks often exhibit heterogeneous or only partial symmetries across datasets, which fixed-group equivariant Neural Processes cannot capture, while mixture-of-experts NPs improve multimodality but do not discover or calibrate symmetry structure. We propose Symmetry-Adaptive Mixture-of-Equivariant Neural Processes: a mixture where each expert is a steerable, convolutional NP tied to a candidate symmetry group or subgroup, and whose layers include learnable partial-equivariance parameters; a permutation-invariant context encoder infers both the expert mixture and per-expert equivariance strengths for the current task. Training uses the standard NP objective (MLE/ELBO depending on dependency modeling) augmented with a symmetry-consistency regularizer over group-orbit augmentations and a sparsity prior on expert usage, preserving exchangeability while enabling soft, data-driven symmetry selection. This design should yield better calibrated joint predictions and sample efficiency across tasks with varying or approximate symmetries (e.g., weather fields with seasonal anisotropy or rotated-digit variants) than either fixed equivariant NPs or symmetry-agnostic MoE-NPs.

result.text: The paper addresses understanding and improving convergence guarantees for policy gradient (PG), natural policy gradient (NPG), and their variance-reduced variants under general smooth policy parameterizations, aiming to get global optimality guarantees (up to function-approximation error) and better sample complexity. The key insight is that the existing convergence analyses for PG (which yield stationary-point guarantees) and for NPG (which yield global convergence) can be combined: stationary convergence proofs for PG can be transferred to NPG, while NPG’s global analysis can be leveraged to upgrade variance-reduced PG’s guarantees to global convergence, enabling variance reduction for NPG. result.text: I propose Active Token Querying (ATQ), an LLM-driven perceptual loop that begins from a coarse, low-cost visual token summary and inserts explicit REFINE(region, scale, modality) actions into the autoregressive sequence to request only the most informative fine-grained tokens. Training couples masked/token-reconstruction and round-trip multimodal objectives with a budgeted loss so the same mechanism also prioritizes where to render higher-fidelity content first during generation, improving quality under fixed decoding steps. ATQ unifies and extends dynamic semantic tokenization and autoregressive visual tokens with cross-modal token merging and video keyframe/motion tokens, but introduces explicit query/action tokens and budget-aware planning that prior unified multimodal models lack.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of poor depth accuracy in multi-view 3D object detection, which limits detection performance especially in outdoor driving scenarios. Its key insight is that temporal stereo—using successive frames as stereo pairs—can substantially improve depth estimation if the temporal stereo’s center and disparity range are chosen dynamically and robustly rather than fixed for all views. The proposed BEVStereo method finds a most-confident temporal-stereo center per view using an EM-like algorithm and adapts the disparity range accordingly, enabling selective temporal-stereo construction that keeps compute and memory costs low while handling challenging outdoor conditions (e.g., static ego vehicle, moving objects). Evaluated on nuScenes, BEVStereo demonstrates state-of-the-art camera-only 3D detection performance and practical efficiency compared to prior stereo-based and monocular methods.

result.text: We propose Rational Spectral Neural Operators (RaSNO), which replace unconstrained learned weights on truncated spectral modes with learnable, stable rational multipliers expressed as Padé-like functions of frequency or Laplacian eigenvalues. This rational parameterization yields smooth, low-complexity approximations to PDE solution operators with built-in stability (via positivity/H∞ constraints) and improved cross-resolution generalization; on irregular domains we apply the same multipliers through rational–Krylov evaluations on graph/mesh Laplacians, removing the need for FFTs or equispaced grids. By explicitly matching spectral responses across discretizations, RaSNO mitigates operator aliasing and preserves the intended continuous-operator behavior, while pointwise stages can use rational nonlinearities to compactly capture stiff local physics. Empirically, RaSNO targets FNO-style performance on regular grids and surpasses it on irregular meshes, maintaining stability under resolution changes at comparable compute to direct non-equispaced spectral methods.

args.text: We propose a disease-conditioned, multi-lead ECG generator that unifies region-disentangled diffusion with cross-lead consistency and physics priors, targeting both unconditional synthesis and PPG-to-ECG translation. result.text: We propose a Relightable Large Reconstruction Model (R-LRM) that maps a single in-the-wild image to a disentangled, relightable asset: geometry (SDF/mesh), spatially-varying BRDF, and an HDR environment map. Training scales LRM-style feed-forward reconstruction with procedurally generated assets featuring randomized BRDFs and environment maps, and uses a physically based differentiable renderer with Monte Carlo sampling plus learned denoising to keep gradients stable, augmented by a Neural-PIL-like pre-integrator for efficient lighting supervision. Beyond photometric losses, we introduce relighting-consistency distillation: render the predicted asset under random novel lights and use a frozen 2D diffusion prior as a distributional critic to penalize relit views that are inconsistent with input shading/material cues, improving single-image reflectance/illumination separation. R-LRM yields canonical, editable assets that support fast relighting and material editing at test time while retaining LRM-level generalization and speed.

result.text: We propose staggered stochastic transparency for multi-principal ecosystems that reuse models or data: each institution randomizes and staggers partial disclosures (e.g., counterfactual exemplars or coarse decision-rule signals), decorrelating agents’ learned manipulation gradients across institutions while preserving robustness from noisy agent responses. We formalize a coupled performative game with opaque, peer-learning agents and define a cross-institution information-overlap proxy to target universal improvement across subpopulations and to provably reduce individual-level outcome homogenization relative to monoculture baselines. Analytically, we derive regimes where staggered stochastic transparency lowers the price of opacity by aligning disclosure noise with stability conditions from smoothed-response microfoundations and by coordinating disclosure schedules across principals. Practically, we cast disclosure/explanation set selection as a (constrained) submodular objective that trades off accuracy, privacy, and homogenization, enabling efficient approximation algorithms for coordinated anti-monoculture transparency policies.

result.text: The paper addresses the high computational cost of vision transformers (ViTs), particularly the quadratic scaling with token count and limitations of existing token-reduction methods that either break spatial structure or require costly pretraining. Its key insight is to perform dynamic, instance-wise token selection using the transformer’s native global class attention and then treat retained (“informative”) and dropped (“uninformative”) tokens differently through a slow-fast updating scheme that preserves spatial structure and information flow. The method, called Evo-ViT, selects tokens via class-attention-based scoring and routes selected tokens through more frequent, heavier updates while routing unselected tokens through lighter, less frequent updates, enabling compatibility with both flat and deep-narrow ViT architectures from training start. Experiments show Evo-ViT greatly reduces FLOPs and increases throughput (e.g., >60% speedup on DeiT-S) with minimal accuracy loss (~0.4% top-1 on ImageNet-1K), outperforming prior pruning approaches in efficiency and accuracy.

args.text: We propose ADAMFlow, an exact and differentiable meshing layer for ReLU MLP implicit surfaces with controllable topology. It first applies analytic marching over the network’s linear regions to recover the exact piecewise‑planar zero set, then solves a small diffeomorphic flow from a template mesh to project this surface onto a two‑manifold while preserving geometry within a user‑bounded Hausdorff tolerance; the entire pipeline is end‑to‑end differentiable. A bilevel objective softly enforces genus/component priors and supports both SDFs and hybrid UDF+sign fields by locally thickening open sheets during projection. This yields stable physics/rendering training with mesh‑level losses while retaining the fidelity and speed of analytic extraction.

We propose an adversarial transductive generalization theory for GNNs by defining an adversarial transductive Rademacher complexity that accounts for bounded structural perturbations (e.g., up to B edge edits under homophily-preserving constraints). We derive bounds for multi-scale message-passing classes that decompose into (i) a spectral sensitivity term capturing Lipschitzness to adjacency changes and (ii) a scale-aggregation margin term, implying that elastic L1/L2 smoothing and diffusion-based robust aggregation shrink the adversarial complexity. Building on boosting-style transductive training, we introduce a scalable surrogate objective that minimizes an unbiased estimator of this complexity via stochastic edge-perturbation ensembles coupled with weighted truncated adversarial weight perturbation. The framework predicts (and we empirically verify) that robust gains correlate with reduced spectral sensitivity and flatter minima, unifying large-scale graph robustness practice with principled adversarial generalization guarantees.

The proposed method, ProMaC, pairs a prompt generator that uses multi-scale chain-of-thought prompting to deliberately elicit and then distill hallucinated context into candidate instance prompts with a mask generator that enforces mask semantic alignment; masks produced feed back to iteratively refine the prompt generator, suppress irrelevant hallucinations, and converge on better prompts and segmentation. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of spatio-temporal distribution shifts in dynamic graph neural networks (DyGNNs), where learned structural and temporal patterns may be spuriously correlated with labels and thus fail to generalize under changing distributions. The key insight is that separating invariant spatio-temporal patterns (which retain predictive power across shifts) from variant ones, and explicitly intervening to remove the influence of variant patterns, enables robust prediction under distributional changes. The proposed method, DIDA, first uses a disentangled spatio-temporal attention network to extract variant and invariant components of node features and graph structure over time, then generates multiple interventional distributions by sampling and reassembling variant patterns across neighborhoods and timestamps to break spurious correlations, and finally applies an invariance regularization that minimizes prediction variance across these interventions so the model relies on invariant signals. Experimental results on three real-world and one synthetic dataset show DIDA outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under distribution shifts.

args.text: DiGMoE: disagreement-gated selective distillation and activation for MoE. We compute a per-token uncertainty score as the dispersion (e.g., KL variance) among logits from a small pool of candidate experts drawn via expert-choice buckets, and use it to adapt top-k per token—activating extra experts only when disagreement is high. During training, we apply selective mutual distillation that transfers only the disagreeing probability mass from unchosen-but-high-affinity experts to the chosen ones to broaden their vision without collapsing specialization; at inference, a training-free fallback mirrors self-contrast by conditionally invoking a stronger activation only when the uncertainty score exceeds a threshold. This unifies expert-choice balancing, consistency/mutual learning, and dynamic activation to reduce compute while improving generalization.

result.text: The paper tackles parameter inference for stochastic models that are strongly indeterminate—where different parameter combinations produce identical observations—by exploiting auxiliary data that share global parameters. The key insight is that pooling multiple related observations governed by the same global variables resolves indeterminacies, and that normalizing-flow-based neural posterior estimation can be extended to hierarchical Bayesian settings to learn these shared-parameter posteriors. The proposed method, Hierarchical Neural Posterior Estimation (HNPE), incorporates a hierarchical generative model into simulation-based inference: it trains conditional normalizing flows to approximate the joint posterior over local and global parameters given sets of observations, leveraging simulated datasets that reflect the hierarchical structure. The authors validate HNPE on an analytically tractable toy problem and demonstrate its practical utility by inverting a nonlinear computational-neuroscience model on both simulated and real EEG data, showing improved identifiability of global parameters.

args.text: We propose Stability-Adjusted Uncertainty Pruning (SAUP), which estimates channel importance as a selection probability under an ensemble of stochastic views (mini-batch subsampling, augmentation, dropout) and complementary criteria (LAMP-rescaled magnitude and channel independence), then prunes channels with consistently low survival probability under FDR control. Leveraging the approximately Gaussian per-layer weight distribution, we derive closed-form variance calibrations for each score to convert selection frequencies into calibrated confidence bounds—akin to UCB but at the channel level—and defer channels with indistinguishable scores. This explicitly addresses Similarity and Applicability by turning correlated, near-tied scores into uncertainty-aware decisions while prioritizing inter-channel redundancy, yielding safer high-sparsity pruning without costly hyperparameter search. A lightweight one-step lookahead updates probabilities after tentative removals to capture downstream interactions.

result.text: The paper tackles the limitation of standard neural networks on tasks requiring variable, iterative reasoning—where harder problems need more computation—by proposing a framework that lets models flexibly spend extra computation on difficult instances. The key insight is to have a neural network parameterize an energy function over candidate outputs and treat reasoning as minimizing that energy, so iterative optimization steps correspond to deeper reasoning and more complex optimizers can be used when needed. Concretely, the method trains a network to define an energy landscape and implements each reasoning step as an energy-minimization update (e.g., gradient-based or other optimizers) to find low-energy solutions, allowing adjustable computation time and improved generalization on algorithmic tasks in graph and continuous domains, including recursive, nested reasoning problems.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of interpretability and higher-level semantic reasoning in recommendation systems by proposing a method to extract and encode user-specific logical relationships. The key insight is that large language models can be used to generate personalized reasoning graphs that causally and logically link a user's profile and behavioral sequences into interpretable interest representations, which can complement standard recommender inputs without extra user/item data. LLMRG constructs these graphs via four stages—chained graph reasoning to infer stepwise relations, divergent extension to broaden hypotheses, self-verification and scoring to prune and rank graph elements, and knowledge-base self-improvement to refine graph generation—then encodes the resulting graph with graph neural networks and feeds it as auxiliary input to base recommenders. Experiments on benchmarks and real-world scenarios show that augmenting engineered recommendation models with LLM-derived reasoning graphs improves recommendation quality while providing more explainable outputs.

Each block infers gradients from example tokens, updates the curvature memory via fast-weight delta rules, and applies an attention-implemented two-loop recursion to precondition updates, while a learned gating/halting policy controls update count and selective forgetting. This unifies Newton-like in-context learning with architectures that pass state across blocks and segments, yielding robust learning on ill-conditioned, noisy tasks distributed over long contexts at fixed per-token compute. We predict strong gains on streaming regression and program-synthesis benchmarks and propose probes that recover stored curvature and step trajectories from activations to validate the mechanism.

result.text: We propose Traj-GPF: pre-train a single heterogeneous region–road–POI–time graph encoder with structural- and semantic-contrastive objectives to capture global topology and attributes, then adapt it to diverse trajectory similarity notions by attaching small, learnable Graph Prompt Features to the nodes/edges touched by a query trajectory. Unlike prior trajectory encoders that learn standalone sequence embeddings or bespoke prompt modules, we condition the shared graph encoder via feature-space prompts localized along the path, producing a trajectory-conditioned graph readout that serves as the trajectory embedding. We train prompts with contrastive objectives using route-alternative positives and temporally perturbed replays, freeze the backbone for cross-city transfer, and use a lightweight residual sequence unit only to synthesize prompt features from ordered GPS points. This design aims to match or exceed prior road-network-aware similarity while offering few-shot, zero-shot, and definition-flexible adaptation through prompt-only tuning.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of enabling high-throughput generation with very large language models on limited hardware (e.g., a single commodity GPU with 16GB), where standard inference requires multiple high-end accelerators. The key insight is that throughput can be vastly increased for latency-insensitive, batched workloads by flexibly aggregating memory and computation across GPU, CPU, and disk, and by jointly optimizing tensor placement and low-bit compression to expand feasible batch sizes. The method, implemented in FlexGen, formulates tensor storage/access decisions as a linear program to find efficient offloading patterns, applies 4-bit compression to weights and attention caches with negligible accuracy loss, and dynamically schedules computation to exploit the enlarged batch space; this enables running models like OPT-175B on a single 16GB GPU and achieving substantially higher token-per-second throughput than prior offloading systems.

args.text: Tail-Index Adaptive Momentum-and-Clipping (TIAMC) is an optimizer that measures the per-layer tail index α of stochastic gradient noise online (via a robust Hill/QQ estimator over recent per-sample gradient norms) and uses α to co-tune two knobs: (1) a positive–negative momentum split whose difference Δm ≈ k·max(0, 2−α) synthesizes or attenuates anisotropic heavy-tailed noise, and (2) a normalized clipped step with a threshold τ(α) that tightens as α→1. This operationalizes Lévy-SDE insights on escape dynamics and flat-minimum selection by amplifying noise when it is too Gaussian and damping/clipping when it is already heavy-tailed, while leveraging theory that clipping+momentum yields stable last-iterate descent under heavy tails. Implementation adds two EMAs and a small tail-index estimator per layer and sets the base step size to hit a target escape-time budget; we hypothesize improved escape from sharp minima and better generalization over SGD/Adam and PNM across vision and language benchmarks.

result.text: Existing approaches to generative commonsense either fuse static knowledge graphs into seq2seq models or generate auxiliary symbolic graphs before reasoning, but they rarely let graph structure act as hard constraints during decoding. We propose graph-conditioned constrained decoding: interleave text generation with on-the-fly construction of a local, context-specific commonsense subgraph and compile that subgraph’s type, relation, and path constraints into a subword-aligned finite-state controller that prunes implausible continuations in the decoder. The subgraph is updated after each span, and when it is sparse we augment it by alternating lightweight KG traversal and entity-linked passage retrieval to enrich constraints without retraining the LM. This closed-loop graph–text co-decoding should yield more plausible, faithful, and interpretable generations on CommonGen and knowledge-intensive QA while matching the inference speed of recent constraint decoders.

result.text: KalmanTokenVIS represents each track with a probabilistic token-state that jointly models appearance embeddings and 2D motion, enabling efficient, robust video instance segmentation with adaptive compute. Plugging in open-vocabulary instance encoders for the observation tokens yields an OpenVIS-capable variant with strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs without heavy spatio-temporal backbones.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of reliably estimating confidence for large language model (LLM) predictions, noting that many LLMs are poorly calibrated and resist standard post-hoc calibration techniques. Its key insight is that calibration can be derived from the model’s own behavior by measuring consistency across multiple stochastic generations: agreement among sampled answers serves as a proxy for true confidence. result.text: We propose Stein-Variational MCTS (SV-MCTS): at each node, treat child selection as solving the exact regularized policy optimization over a continuous action distribution, and approximate the optimizer by applying a few SVGD updates to a small set of action particles. The network policy serves as the KL reference prior, Q- or model-based critic gradients provide score information, and the repulsive kernel maintains diverse, high-value candidates, yielding implicit progressive widening without hand-tuned samplers. This unifies the optimization view of MCTS with continuous-action gradient refinement and Bayesian action focusing while remaining compatible with sample-based planning loops. result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of designing and learning expressive, well-posed graph spectral filters for graph neural networks, observing that prior approaches either fix filter shapes or learn unconstrained coefficients that can be ill-behaved. The key insight is that any filter defined on the normalized Laplacian spectrum can be uniformly approximated by a finite-order Bernstein polynomial, whose nonnegative basis and coefficient structure enable controlled spectral shapes and stable learning. BernNet implements this idea by parametrizing spectral filters as order-K Bernstein polynomial approximations, mapping learned coefficients to convolutional filter weights via the Bernstein basis applied to powers of the normalized Laplacian, and training those coefficients end-to-end on observed graph signals; experiments show it can recover complex filters (e.g., band-rejection, comb) and yields improved performance on real graph tasks.

result.text: The paper tackles the need for faster and more accurate deep learning on 3D point clouds by revisiting and improving the Set Abstraction (SA) building block from PointNet++; its goal is to reduce computation while boosting accuracy for tasks like classification and segmentation. The key insight is that the original SA mixes channel-wise feature learning and spatial aggregation in a single step, and separating these concerns lets each be learned more efficiently—further enhanced by an Anisotropic Reduction that captures direction-dependent (anisotropic) spatial correlations. Methodologically, the authors design a Separable Set Abstraction module that first learns channel correlations and then spatial correlations, embed an Anisotropic Separable SA (ASSA) variant that uses anisotropic pooling/aggregation, replace PointNet++’s SA modules with ASSA to form ASSANet, and demonstrate via extensive experiments that this architecture yields substantially higher accuracy and much faster inference on benchmarks like S3DIS and part segmentation.

result.text: The paper tackles the limitation in tool-augmented LLM training where only successful decision-tree (inference-tree) trajectories are used for supervised fine-tuning, neglecting failed explorations that could inform better tool-usage policies. Its key insight is that failed paths in expert inference trees contain actionable preference signals that, when converted into stepwise preference data and used to directly optimize the model’s policy, can expand the learning signal beyond successful trajectories and improve generalization. Methodologically, the authors construct step-wise preference pairs from both successful and failed tree branches, first SFT the LLM on successful tool-usage trajectories and then apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) with the derived preference data to produce TP-LLaMA; experiments show this approach improves performance, generalization to unseen APIs, and reasoning efficiency over prior baselines like ToolLLaMA.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of imputing missing values in tabular datasets by extending masked autoencoding to this domain. The key insight is that, beyond treating naturally missing entries as masks, intentionally re-masking a random subset of observed values during training forces the autoencoder to learn representations that are invariant to missingness and better generalize to unobserved entries. The method, called ReMasker, trains a masked autoencoder to reconstruct these re-masked values (while leaving original missing entries masked), then applies the trained model to predict the true missing entries at inference time; empirical results on benchmarks show it matches or outperforms state-of-the-art imputers, especially as missingness increases, and theoretical analysis supports its missingness-invariance property.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of merging multiple finetuned model weights into a single multi-task model without suffering large performance drops or requiring additional data or training. The key insight is that no single model’s weights can simultaneously represent all task-specific solutions, so instead the authors elect a unified base model from the available weights and add extremely lightweight, task-specific modulators that adjust weight direction (via binary masks) and magnitude (via rescalers) to align each task model to the unified base. Their method, EMR-Merging, therefore consists of (a) selecting an elected model as the common backbone and (b) generating and applying per-task masks and rescalers to merge other models into that backbone; this tuning-free approach requires no extra data or training and achieves strong performance across many vision, NLP, PEFT, and multi-modal merging scenarios.

result.text: We propose a shot-aware hierarchical video-to-music system that first plans a long-horizon symbolic score aligned to video—tempo/beat curve, section boundaries, chord/mode trajectory, and motif tokens—then renders audio with a fast rectified-flow spectrogram generator. The planner uses LORIS-like context encoders over minutes of visual rhythm and events, but predicts discrete score tokens with a DanceFormer-inspired beat-first decomposition; the actor conditions on both the plan and CAVP-style visual embeddings, and supports optional text/style prompts via a CoDi-like composable interface. During sampling, we apply lightweight joint discriminator guidance to correct cross-modal misalignment and tighten audiovisual synchronization, yielding high fidelity without training a full multimodal model end-to-end. Trained on in-the-wild video–music pairs with weak labels for harmony/structure, this architecture targets stronger long-term rhythmic alignment and thematic consistency than prior V2A/V2M systems.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap between current visual instruction-tuned vision-language models (VLMs) and the need for effective multi-step, goal-directed decision-making in interactive environments. Its key insight is that prompting VLMs to produce chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning as intermediate, text-based reasoning steps both enables more efficient exploration and yields better parsing into executable actions for environment interaction. The proposed method fine-tunes VLMs end-to-end with reinforcement learning by (1) providing task descriptions and eliciting CoT outputs, (2) parsing the open-ended text into executable actions that interact with the environment to receive task rewards, and (3) using those rewards to update the whole VLM via RL; experiments show this approach substantially improves decision-making and that CoT is critical to the gains, enabling smaller (7B) models to outperform larger commercial baselines.

result.text: Performative Bayesian design with oracle-aware acquisition: instead of optimizing candidates under a static oracle, choose queries that maximize expected improvement under the next-iterate oracle obtained by an autofocusing reweighting step. We approximate the one-step effect of a candidate (or batch) on the oracle via influence functions or implicit differentiation, yielding a tractable, lookahead acquisition that explicitly trades off objective gain and calibration in the optimizer’s target region. Practically, we implement the query policy as a generative optimizer or RL design policy and backpropagate through the surrogate oracle-update, driving the system toward a performatively stable fixed point while mitigating the greedy-versus-lazy deployment trade-off. This equilibrium-aware co-training accelerates discovery and reduces OOD exploitation compared to static acquisitions and post-hoc retraining.

result.text: The paper addresses active protection of deep neural network intellectual property by preventing unauthorized model use beyond passive watermarking. Its key insight is that selectively obfuscating a tiny fraction of model weights can catastrophically degrade model performance while storing the original weight indices and values as a compact “secret” that authorized users can restore inside a trusted execution environment. The proposed NNSplitter method automatically identifies and modifies a very small set of critical weights to create an obfuscated model that yields near-random outputs, while keeping the secret weights separately and securely delivered so authorized executions reconstruct full accuracy; experiments show extreme effectiveness (e.g., flipping 275 of ~11M weights reduces ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 to 10%) and robustness to countermeasures like fine-tuning and norm clipping.

result.text: The paper addresses the gap in depression detection research by creating a realistic multimodal dataset and model for identifying depression from non-verbal behavior in the wild, noting prior work’s reliance on constrained lab settings. The key insight is that large-scale, naturalistic vlogs contain informative acoustic and visual cues whose cross-modal interactions are critical for reliable depression detection. To this end the authors introduce D-Vlog, a 961-vlog (≈160-hour) YouTube-derived dataset, and propose a multimodal deep model that extracts acoustic and visual features and fuses them with a cross-attention mechanism to capture inter-modal relationships and produce discriminative representations. Experiments show the cross-attention multimodal model substantially outperforms baseline approaches, demonstrating the dataset’s value and the efficacy of modeling acoustic-visual interactions for in-the-wild depression detection.

result.text: This paper addresses the scarcity of large, realistic datasets for studying physical backdoor attacks—where real-world objects act as triggers causing targeted misclassification—by proposing a scalable way to find naturally occurring co-locations of potential triggers and target classes inside existing image datasets. The key insight is that many widely used datasets (e.g., ImageNet) already contain images where certain physical objects consistently appear with particular classes, and by systematically identifying and relabeling those subsets one can create realistic “natural backdoor” training sets without manual collection. The method clusters and scores candidate object-class co-occurrences using automated detection and statistical validation to find high-confidence trigger-class pairs, then relabels identified images to simulate backdoor poisoning and demonstrates that resulting models exhibit attack behaviors equivalent to those trained on manually curated physical trigger datasets. The authors validate the approach on common datasets, produce effective natural backdoor subsets, and release code so researchers can generate more realistic benchmarks for studying physical backdoor attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses how to optimally scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models to minimize compute for a given performance by expanding the variables considered in scaling analysis to include a new hyperparameter, granularity, that controls expert size. The key insight is that fine-grained control over expert size fundamentally changes scaling behavior: MoE models obey predictable power-law scaling with respect to model size, training tokens, and granularity, and these relationships show that MoEs outperform dense Transformers increasingly as compute and model size grow. Methodologically, the authors derive analytic scaling laws incorporating granularity, validate them empirically, and use the laws to compute optimal allocations of parameters, experts, and tokens under fixed compute budgets, revealing that matching expert size to feed‑forward layer width is suboptimal across most budgets.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of blackbox transfer attacks on object detectors, which are harder than classifier attacks because detectors reason about whole-scene context and object co-occurrence. The key insight is that leveraging context—specifically object co-occurrence patterns, relative locations, and size relationships—enables creation of adversarial perturbations that better fool detectors in realistic, multi-object scenes. The authors propose a context-aware attack method that conditions perturbation generation on surrounding objects’ presence, positions, and scales to craft targeted mis-categorization examples, and evaluate it across multiple detectors and datasets. Experiments on PASCAL VOC and MS COCO show this context-aware strategy yields up to ~20 percentage points higher blackbox transfer success than prior state-of-the-art methods.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of learning disentangled representations that recover the independent generative factors underlying observed data without strong supervision or restrictive assumptions. Its key insight is to model the unknown low-dimensional data manifold explicitly as a Cartesian product of submanifolds, where each submanifold corresponds to one factor of variation, and to use pairs of samples known to share at least one factor to induce disentanglement. The method implements a weakly supervised product-manifold projection algorithm that trains encoders/decoders to map observations onto and reconstruct from coordinates on these submanifolds, using paired-sample constraints (but no knowledge of transformation types or subspace properties) to align shared factors while letting others vary; experiments on synthetic and real-world image and 3D surface data show competitive or superior performance to prior approaches.

result.text: The paper addresses why training neural networks with batch normalization (BN) and weight decay often exhibits recurring destabilizations rather than smooth convergence or outright divergence. The key insight is that the interplay between scale-invariance introduced by BN and the implicit shrinkage from weight decay creates a feedback loop: weight norms are driven down by decay, which increases effective learning rates for scale-invariant parameters and periodically destabilizes optimization, yet these episodes reset norms and allow training to continue in a new regime. To explain this, the authors combine empirical observations with theoretical analysis of simplified models to characterize when and how these periodic cycles arise, showing the phenomenon unifies and generalizes previous equilibrium- and instability-based perspectives on BN plus weight decay.

result.text: We propose Counterfactual-Simulatability–Aware NLE Selection for NLI: for each candidate explanation, we automatically synthesize diverse, causally-controlled counterfactuals of the premise/hypothesis and score the explanation by how precisely and generally it lets a lightweight simulator predict the model’s outputs on those counterfactuals. To robustly estimate this score, we aggregate over paraphrases of the explanation using semantic-entropy pooling, and use either LLM-guided counterfactual edits or an efficient training-time matching proxy to hold confounders fixed. These simulatability scores drive an instance selector that weights or filters NLEs during augmentation and adds a counterfactual-consistency regularizer, yielding rationale-grounded training akin to LIREx but optimized for predictive faithfulness rather than plausibility. We hypothesize this improves out-of-domain NLI accuracy and produces explanations with higher counterfactual simulatability than existing NLE-augmented methods.

args.text: We propose p-VarBasisNet, a spectral GNN that filters in a learned, spatially varying p-Laplacian domain to match local heterophily. Concretely, we learn node-/edge-wise p to control simultaneous low- and high-pass behavior, learn an orthonormal spectral polynomial basis via Favard recurrence instead of fixing it, and parameterize filter coefficients in the Bernstein simplex for stable, expressive responses. We further decouple terminal diffusion strength from propagation depth, enabling many propagation steps without over-smoothing. The result is a region-specific frequency response that unifies heterophily-robust filtering with stable basis learning and deep propagation.

The method trains this end-to-end Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) on about one million multi-view objects drawn from Objaverse and MVImgNet, producing a NeRF in seconds and yielding detailed reconstructions for in-the-wild photos and generative-model outputs.

result.text: We propose staggered stochastic transparency for multi-principal ecosystems that reuse models or data: each institution randomizes and staggers partial disclosures (e.g., counterfactual exemplars or coarse decision-rule signals), decorrelating agents’ learned manipulation gradients across institutions while preserving robustness from noisy agent responses. We formalize a coupled performative game with opaque, peer-learning agents and define a cross-institution information-overlap proxy to target universal improvement across subpopulations and to provably reduce individual-level outcome homogenization relative to monoculture baselines. Analytically, we derive regimes where staggered stochastic transparency lowers the price of opacity by aligning disclosure noise with stability conditions from smoothed-response microfoundations and by coordinating disclosure schedules across principals. Practically, we cast disclosure/explanation set selection as a (constrained) submodular objective that trades off accuracy, privacy, and homogenization, enabling efficient approximation algorithms for coordinated anti-monoculture transparency policies.

result.text: The paper tackles the inefficiency of Vision Transformers (ViT) that use a fixed, dense grid of image patches (tokens) for every input, noting that many images are "easy" and don't require high token density while a few "hard" images do. The key insight is that token resolution should be dynamic per image: by starting with few coarse tokens and progressively refining only when needed, one can retain accuracy for difficult cases while saving computation on easy ones. The authors implement this as a cascaded Dynamic Transformer that sequentially activates Transformers with increasing token counts and stops inference early when confidence is sufficient, along with feature-reuse and relationship-reuse mechanisms to avoid redundant computation across stages. Experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR datasets show substantial reductions in FLOPs and inference latency with minimal accuracy loss compared to fixed-token baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of step-by-step, heuristics-driven neural theorem proving methods that get stuck on short-sighted or distracting subgoals and thus struggle to find longer proofs. The key insight is to prove theorems recursively by searching for verifiable high-level proof sketches and deferring detailed subproofs with a placeholder tactic, so the system can outline an entire proof first and then recursively fill in intermediate conjectures. Their method, POETRY, implements this level-by-level strategy in Isabelle: at each level it finds a sketch where unresolved intermediate lemmas are replaced by a “sorry” placeholder, then in subsequent levels it replaces those placeholders by proving the conjectures, iterating until the full proof is verified. Experiments on miniF2F and PISA show that POETRY improves success rates over prior methods (e.g., a 5.1% gain on miniF2F) and substantially increases the maximum proof lengths discovered.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of converting continuous deep implicit signed distance fields (SDFs) into explicit mesh representations in a way that is differentiable with respect to the underlying implicit field, enabling end-to-end training for tasks that require meshes rather than implicit volumes. The key insight is that local perturbations of the implicit field induce predictable changes in the iso-surface geometry, so one can compute gradients of surface vertex positions (and thus mesh outputs) with respect to the SDF by analytically relating field changes to surface sample displacements. The method, MeshSDF, instantiates this idea by deriving differentiable mappings from SDF values to 3D locations of surface samples and connectivity, producing an explicit mesh whose vertex positions and topology can be backpropagated through; the approach is validated on single-view reconstruction with differentiable rendering and physically-driven shape optimization, outperforming prior non-differentiable conversion pipelines.

result.text: The paper addresses why multi-scale graph neural networks (GNNs) empirically mitigate the over-smoothing problem and how transductive learning with such architectures can be optimized and generalized. The key insight is that transductive training of multi-scale GNNs can be framed in a boosting-like procedure where weak-learning conditions guarantee training-error convergence, and transductive Rademacher complexity can be used to bound the generalization gap so that certain multi-scale designs yield test-error bounds that improve with depth. Methodologically, the authors develop optimization guarantees via boosting theory applied to transductive settings, derive generalization bounds by estimating transductive Rademacher complexity for the multi-scale hypothesis class, and validate the theory by implementing boosting-based training for multi-scale GNNs on node-prediction benchmarks, showing empirical behavior consistent with the theoretical predictions.

result.text: Separation-aware adaptive domain randomization (ADR-ID): model the simulator as a latent mixture of MDPs and train two-phase memory policies that begin with brief probing trajectories chosen via OOM/PSR-style spectral criteria to maximally separate candidate dynamics, then switch to control while hedging residual ambiguity using TV-robust regularization implemented through regularized (R^2) MDP updates. We derive sim-to-real gap bounds that decompose into an identification error term (governed by the achieved separation/reachability of latent models) plus a Lipschitz transfer term in an MDP metric between the inferred and true dynamics, yielding improved guarantees with active domain selection. Practically, the DR curriculum is adapted to maximize projected separation among latent models (to ease per-episode identification) while using TV-based uncertainty sets for favorable sample complexity, and entropy-style regularization to retain robustness at training-time cost similar to non-robust methods. This yields memory-efficient probe-then-control policies with provable transfer in partially observed or mildly nonstationary settings where naive DR fails.

To control variance, use RCIG’s convexified inner problem with closed-form final-layer solves as a control variate and antithetic perturbations; schedule segment lengths and teacher phases via DATM’s difficulty alignment (allocating longer/later segments as synthetic set size grows). Combine with MTT’s constant-memory unrolled gradient computation and FRePo-style pooled short runs for robustness and cross-architecture transfer. This yields stable, unbiased trajectory-matching updates that can scale to large-class settings and close the gap between biased truncated meta-gradients and lossless distillation at single-GPU throughput.

result.text: The paper addresses how to design policies for Markov decision processes when both the objective and constraints are expressed as dynamic coherent risk measures, which complicates standard constrained MDP solution techniques. The key insight is that if the risk objectives and constraints admit a Markov risk transition mapping, the constrained risk-averse control problem can be cast in a Lagrangian form whose policy-synthesis subproblems admit a difference-of-convex structure. The authors propose an optimization-based method that constructs Markovian policies by solving these DCPs using the disciplined convex-concave programming (DCCP) framework, thereby generalizing the linear-program approach for expected-cost constrained MDPs. They validate the approach numerically on a rover navigation task using CVaR and EVaR measures, demonstrating tractable policy synthesis and effective risk control.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of achieving transferable targeted adversarial attacks—widely believed to be very difficult and typically addressed by costly methods that train models or use extra data per target. The authors systematically evaluate this simple approach across standard and three new realistic settings (low model similarity ensembles, low-ranked target classes, and attacks on Google Cloud Vision), show it rivals state-of-the-art costly methods, and demonstrate its effectiveness for generating targeted universal perturbations in a data-free, training-free way. Their results argue for more meaningful, diverse evaluation protocols to avoid misleading comparisons between attacks.

result.text: The paper tackles efficient computation of the Projection Robust Wasserstein (PRW) distance, a max–min formulation over the Stiefel manifold designed to mitigate the curse of dimensionality in high-dimensional optimal transport. Its key insight is a novel reformulation of the entropy-regularized max–min PRW problem that enables a Riemannian block coordinate descent (RBCD) strategy with much lower per-iteration cost than prior Riemannian gradient-ascent-plus-Sinkhorn schemes. The proposed RBCD alternately updates blocks on the Stiefel manifold using closed-form or cheaply computed steps while solving simpler transport subproblems, and the authors prove an arithmetic complexity of O(ε−3) to reach an ε-stationary point—vastly improving on the O(ε−12) bound for RGAS. Empirical results on synthetic and real datasets confirm the method’s scalability and superior efficiency, particularly when the sample size is very large.

We pretrain this architecture on massive synthetic appliance- and circuit-level traces (in the spirit of BuildingsBench) using masked event/duration prediction and cross-home contrastive objectives to learn cross-appliance transferable features as in PowerPM while capturing regime-dependent dynamics as in RED-SDS. args.text: Hessian-Adaptive Off-Policy TD is an online critic-learning scheme that removes target networks and large replay by explicitly controlling curvature during bootstrap updates. We estimate a lightweight proxy of the critic’s Hessian operator norm via per-batch stochastic traces or gradient-covariance, and adapt normalization strength (e.g., LayerNorm scale, weight decay) and n-step bootstrapping to keep training in a low-curvature, near-linear regime suggested by width–Hessian scaling analyses. result.text: The paper addresses why stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in deep learning often exhibits heavy-tailed behavior and how that relates to generalization measures like flatness, step-size-to-batch-size ratio, and tail-index of weight spectra. The key insight is that, depending on the curvature (Hessian) at a minimum and the algorithmic parameters (stepsize η and batch size b), SGD does not necessarily converge to a Gaussian-like stationary distribution but can instead converge to a heavy-tailed stationary law with potentially infinite variance, linking flatness, noise magnitude, and spectral tail behavior. Methodologically, the authors rigorously prove this phenomenon in the analytically tractable setting of linear regression with Gaussian data by characterizing the stationary distribution and tail-index of SGD iterates as functions of η, b, dimension, and curvature, and then corroborate and extend these theoretical predictions with experiments on synthetic problems and neural networks.
