result.text: The paper addresses the lack of efficient algorithms for learning synaptic transmission delays in discrete-time feedforward spiking neural networks (SNNs), which are important because spike-timing and coincidence strongly affect SNN expressivity and performance on temporal tasks like speech recognition. The key insight is to represent inter-layer delays as sparse 1D temporal convolution kernels with a single nonzero weight per synapse whose position encodes delay, and to learn these positions jointly with synaptic weights using Dilated Convolutions with Learnable Spacings (DCLS). args.text: We propose Budgeted Revival Dynamic Pruning (BRDP), a single-pass, hardware-aware sparse training algorithm that maintains and updates a structured mask on-the-fly to meet a target latency/FLOPs budget. Periodically, BRDP solves a Lagrangian-relaxed knapsack using per-channel/group latency lookup tables and a multi-layer sensitivity score that blends lookahead Frobenius distortion with curvature inferred from a gradually increasing L2 penalty; units with the highest expected accuracy gain per latency cost are (re)activated while low-ratio ones are removed. We then apply lightweight re-fill/re-group operations to consolidate nonzeros into hardware-friendly channel/group patterns, and continue training with a feedback signal that can revive mistakenly pruned units. This yields a budget-feasible, structured sparse model in one run, combining dynamic-sparsity accuracy with platform-specific speedups and obviating post-hoc fine-tuning.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of designing practical, high-performing active learning algorithms that work with deep neural networks by revisiting Fisher-information–based selection objectives. Its key insight is that bounds on maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) error expressed via the Fisher information can guide selection of informative batches, and that this classic criterion can be made tractable and efficient for neural models by exploiting linear-algebraic structure. The authors propose BAIT, an algorithm that selects batches by optimizing a Fisher-information–based bound on MLE error and implements this optimization with scalable matrix computations suited to modern hardware. Empirically, BAIT consistently outperforms prior active learning methods on both classification and regression tasks and is adaptable to different model architectures.

args.text: We propose Fractional Sparse Convolution (FracSparseConv): a layer that jointly learns a small set of fractional Fourier orders per channel to project features into task-adaptive intermediate space–frequency domains, and a sparse set of convolution taps in each domain with continuous, learnable positions. Building on multi-order FRFT operators, we learn the orders and, inspired by learnable-spacing dilated kernels, interpolate weights at continuous tap locations within each transformed plane; a spectral envelope regularizer (from continuous kernel parameterizations) encourages smooth, alias-resilient scaling as receptive fields grow. For efficiency, we fuse FRFTs and sparse mixing using FFT-as-block-matmul kernels and frequency-sparsity to approach depthwise-conv throughput while retaining long-range modeling capacity. We anticipate gains on non-stationary signals (e.g., remote sensing, ultrasound) and long-range image modeling, and evaluate resolution generalization, robustness to resizing, and compute–accuracy tradeoffs.

args.text: We propose FedSubspace-EF, a bidirectional, acceleration-ready FL scheme that maintains a global low-rank gradient subspace at the server and communicates only subspace coefficients plus an induced-unbiased, error-compensated compression of the orthogonal residual. Each round, the server updates an orthonormal basis via streaming PCA; clients project local updates onto this basis, transmit a few coefficients and an induced-unbiased Top-k residual with EF-style memory, while the server broadcasts model deltas in the same subspace-plus-unbiased-residual format to support one-shot clients. Plugging this compressor into accelerated variance-reduced solvers yields convergence where the compression penalty scales with the unexplained variance (1−ρ) of gradients rather than ambient dimension or generic ω, giving ADIANA-like rates with ω effectively replaced by (1−ρ)ω and extending cleanly to partial participation. By unifying subspace reuse, induced unbiasedness, EF-style stabilization, and downlink compression, the method targets cross-device FL and predicts large gains when gradient energy concentrates in a low-rank subspace.

result.text: The paper studies why fast single-step adversarial training with FGSM can suddenly fail—“catastrophic overfitting”—losing robustness during training, and questions whether the commonly used random initialization fixes the issue. The key insight is that randomness only helps by shrinking effective perturbation size and that catastrophic overfitting arises from local nonlinearity (even in tiny networks or a single filter) which makes the FGSM linear approximation invalid. To address this, the authors introduce GradAlign, a regularizer that maximizes alignment of input gradients within the perturbation set so the FGSM perturbation better matches multi-step solutions, thereby preventing overfitting and enabling effective fast adversarial training for larger ℓ∞ radii. Experiments show GradAlign narrows the robustness gap to multi-step methods while keeping training efficient.

result.text: The paper addresses how to make large language models (LLMs), especially closed‑source black‑box APIs, reliably express uncertainty to support trustworthy decisions; prior approaches needing internal access or fine‑tuning are often infeasible for these models. args.text: We propose Certified Refusal via Randomized Prompt Smoothing (CRPS), which treats an LLM’s safety decision as a binary classifier and applies discrete randomized smoothing over guard-prefix paraphrases and token-level perturbations to obtain formal certificates against bounded jailbreak suffix edits (e.g., Hamming/Levenshtein distance). Concretely, at inference we sample from optimized non-Gaussian discrete noise distributions (token dropout, synonym flips, template shuffles) over the system/prefix and user suffix, majority-vote the refusal decision, and compute per-input certificates with exact binomial bounds; we restrict input-dependence of the noise to satisfy recent validity conditions. We then adversarially train prompt suffixes (as in robust prompt optimization) to directly maximize certified refusal radii rather than empirical attack success, yielding attack-agnostic guarantees. Evaluation on standardized jailbreak suites would report both certified and empirical robustness, establishing the first nontrivial certificates for LLM safety decisions under bounded discrete prompt perturbations.

The outer objective enforces that the perturbation functions as an augmentation-invariant shortcut for contrastive pairs while driving supervised learners toward near-zero loss on perturbed views that fails to transfer to clean data; to resist simple orthogonal-projection recovery, we constrain updates to a high-rank, data-dependent subspace sampled across images and augmentations rather than a fixed, low-dimensional direction. args.text: We propose Instruction-Grounded Token-Region Alignment (IGTRA) for open-vocabulary and few-shot object detection: given a concept and a handful of multimodal exemplars, an instruction-tuned VLM produces fine-grained, region-referential descriptors (parts, attributes, context) and counterfactual negatives that condition the detector. Training builds soft region–text correspondences by combining caption-only region cues from mosaicked pseudo-regions and co-occurrence discovery, then aligning multi-mode textual tokens to region features via hierarchical optimal transport—yielding token-level supervision that replaces coarse category names. Practically, we realize this by (i) mining descriptor/rationale prompts with an instruction-tuned VLM, (ii) generating proposal-level soft labels from mosaic/co-occurrence cues and token-level OT, and (iii) fusing image-level scene priors and exemplar-conditioned prompts to reweight detections at inference. IGTRA aims to boost small/occluded object recovery and fine-grained disambiguation without box-level text annotations, while enabling rapid K-shot adaptation by simply swapping exemplars and instructions.

result.text: The paper addresses instability and inefficiency in multi-agent reinforcement learning caused by simultaneous policy updates—non-stationarity—and the challenges of sample inefficiency and lack of per-agent monotonic improvement in sequential (agent-by-agent) update schemes. Its key insight is that updating agents sequentially with a carefully designed trust-region-style objective can both tighten monotonic improvement bounds for each agent and improve sample efficiency, while the order in which agents are updated matters and can be analyzed within a extended non-stationarity theory. The proposed Agent-by-agent Policy Optimization (A2PO) method derives a per-agent trust-region update that guarantees monotonic improvement tighter than prior algorithms, incorporates mechanisms to share samples efficiently across sequential updates, and explicitly models and studies the effect of agent update order. Empirically, A2PO consistently outperforms strong baselines across diverse benchmarks including StarCraft II, Multi-agent MuJoCo, Multi-agent Particle Environment, and Google Research Football.

args.text: I propose a safety-certified inverse-design framework for PDE-governed systems that backpropagates through a boundary-enforcing neural-operator surrogate to optimize designs while guaranteeing both boundary conditions and probabilistic safety. We train an FNO/LNO surrogate of the dynamics and apply BOON-style kernel refinement so the operator satisfies Dirichlet/Neumann/periodic BCs exactly, then treat the surrogate as a neural network dynamic model and synthesize stochastic barrier functions that certify a lower bound on safety probability along long-horizon rollouts. Design parameters are updated by unrolling the surrogate and differentiating through trajectories as in task-agnostic learned-simulator inverse design, while an active-learning loop focuses data acquisition on states and parameters with small barrier margins to tighten worst-case guarantees. This combination aims to deliver fast, task-agnostic inverse design with certifiable guarantees under distribution shift.

args.text: We propose Source-free Universal Category Discovery: adapt a source model to an unlabeled target that mixes shared and novel classes by jointly discovering unknown categories and calibrating known ones without any source data. We build a reciprocal-neighbor graph and optimize an attract-and-disperse objective to form compact, separated target clusters, while a HiLo-style factorization disentangles semantic from domain features and a ProtoNCE-style EM maintains two prototype sets—known prototypes aligned to the source classifier via bipartite matching and emerging unknown prototypes grown from high-confidence neighborhoods. A bimodality test on maximum probabilities combined with teacher–student disagreement flags likely-unknown samples, and a mean-teacher consistency head maximizes mutual information between pseudo-labels and inputs to stabilize cluster assignments and follow the source taxonomy where appropriate. An uncertainty-adaptive margin curriculum gradually incorporates low-confidence samples, yielding reliable open-set rejection and fine-grained novel-category discovery in one training loop, improving over prior UniDA, SFDA, and GCD baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses detection of backdoor attacks in convolutional neural networks, where a model is trained to respond to a specific trigger without degrading normal performance by poisoning a small fraction of training data. The key insight is that neurons that mediate the backdoor exhibit distinct pre-activation distributional differences between benign and poisoned inputs—differences in moments that are invariant across attack types—so these “backdoor neurons” can be exposed by statistical measures. Building on mild assumptions about activation distributions, the authors propose two practical detection methods: ranking neurons by their differential entropy and by the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the empirical benign pre-activation distribution and a poisoned-statistics-based hypothetical distribution; experiments show these strategies efficiently and effectively locate backdoor neurons across various attacks.

result.text: We propose Active Perception Tokens (APT), an LLM-in-the-loop visual tokenization scheme for unified autoregressive multimodal models. Decoding begins from a compact set of semantically grouped, coarse visual tokens; at each step the language model monitors its predictive uncertainty and cross-modal attention to request localized, hierarchical refinements from the tokenizer, yielding variable-length, targeted token updates over time. Training jointly optimizes next-token likelihood with a token-cost regularizer and uses differentiable soft routing or straight-through estimators so the refinement policy learns to spend tokens where they most reduce entropy. This closes the loop between perception and generation for efficiency and alignment, and naturally extends to video by budgeting refinements across keyframes and motion tokens.

result.text: We propose a density- and discrepancy-aware curriculum for GAN training that reconciles the gains of instance pruning with rare-mode coverage. result.text: The paper addresses the mismatch between standard trajectory-prediction benchmarks and real-world autonomous driving performance, arguing that current evaluations ignore how predictors influence agent interactions and the runtime costs of deployment. Its key insight is that prediction models not only estimate future motions but also shape the closed-loop dynamics of a driven system—so dataset-based, open-loop accuracy metrics and neglect of computational efficiency produce a substantial "dynamics gap" that misrepresents downstream driving utility. To remedy this, the authors propose an interactive, task-driven evaluation that measures predictors within a simulated or real closed-loop driving stack—capturing predictor-induced behavioral changes of other agents—and incorporates computational constraints (latency and throughput) alongside accuracy to better reflect real-time autonomous driving requirements.

We propose Performative Optimal Experimental Design (POED), where the data-generating process depends on the deployed design policy, so the goal is to select experiments that both learn about the system and steer it toward desirable performatively stable outcomes. We formalize sequential design with performativity as an MDP whose transition dynamics encode endogenous distribution shifts induced by deployments, and target equilibria by augmenting the reward with stability/consistency terms. Practically, we train amortized design policies that blend information-gain objectives with equilibrium-regularization via deep RL and contrastive bounds, and use two-timescale updates that interleave policy improvement with fixed-point evaluations to manage the greedy-vs-lazy deploy trade-off. This yields real-time, exploration-aware strategies for adaptive experiments with human or strategic participants, unifying BOED and performative prediction.

result.text: We propose SmoothSplit-Auth, a keyed protection scheme that couples selective critical-weight obfuscation with a smoothed, certifiable challenge–response for ownership and integrity. During training, we learn multiple disjoint sparse masks of critical weights whose removal collapses accuracy; at deployment the obfuscated model runs with a TEE-restored secret mask (which can be rotated), while a randomized-smoothing watermark is bound to the restored parameters to certify that removing or evading the key would require a large ℓ2 parameter change. To frustrate data-free model extraction, we jointly learn a lightweight randomized input transform that is adaptively activated on suspected extraction/challenge queries, and embed key samples that elicit distinctive logits only when the secret weights are present. This unifies functionality denial to unauthorized users, certifiable ownership/tamper evidence, and black-box extraction degradation without harming normal utility for authorized executions.

result.text: This paper tackles the problem of crafting transferable adversarial perturbations for complex natural scenes containing multiple semantically related objects, where prior attacks have largely focused on single-object images and single-object classifiers. The method, called GAMA, trains a generative perturbation network adversarially using CLIP’s joint image-text features as the objective (rather than only visual logits), so the generator learns to produce perturbations that disrupt semantic alignment across objects and transfer to unknown victim classifiers and data distributions. args.text: We propose a manifold-guided targeted transfer attack that edits images in latent diffusion space while aligning perturbations with cross-model-stable attributions and disrupting layer-wise class separability. Concretely, we aggregate integrated gradients along randomized paths across a Bayesian surrogate ensemble to obtain stable, architecture-agnostic guidance, and combine it with a distribution-entanglement loss at mid-level features to steer the perturbation toward the target class in a way that generalizes across models. The guidance is injected into a latent diffusion sampler with cone-style regularization to constrain edits to realistic, minimal semantic changes, yielding photorealistic adversarial examples with strong targeted transfer without training the victim or requiring extra data. Using mildly robust surrogates further tightens cross-model feature alignment, boosting success on both CNNs and transformers under standard black-box protocols.

The method trains an encoder to map multiple camera images into a latent code while a NeRF decoder reconstructs images from that code, using the NeRF reconstruction loss as supervision, and then uses the learned latent as the RL agent’s state input (NeRF-RL), showing improved performance on tasks like hanging mugs, pushing, and opening doors.

args.text: We propose an anatomy-verified prompt–mask cycle for 3D foundation segmentation that converts a single generic, image-level medical prompt into precise instance-specific volumetric prompts by coupling a medical VLM with a SegVol-like 3D segmentor. Inspired by ProMaC, we deliberately elicit rich (potentially hallucinated) anatomical candidates from the VLM and iteratively verify/prune them with a 3D anatomy-aware masker that enforces cross-slice consistency and organ topology constraints; verification failures trigger targeted slice suggestions for minimal user clicks. The verifier leverages self-supervised 3D features to score anatomical plausibility and slice-wise coherence, enabling accurate volume segmentation with far fewer interactions than standard interactive workflows. This hallucination-verified, anatomy-constrained prompting loop improves robustness on out-of-distribution scans while reducing expert prompting effort.

We propose spectral hidden-state amplification for decentralized DP-SGD: in gossip-based optimization where only neighbor-averaged messages are observable, the cumulative privacy loss contracts rather than composes linearly, at a rate governed by the mixing matrix’s spectral gap and graph distance. Leveraging a pairwise network-DP viewpoint with a hidden-state RDP analysis, we derive per-node, per-pair RDP bounds that decay geometrically with the number of mixing rounds, yielding topology-aware privacy–utility trade-offs that can approach trusted-curator performance on well-mixed graphs. We instantiate this with a practical protocol that alternates clipped local gradient steps with randomized gossip and lightweight masking/secure averaging to preserve state hiding, and validate the predicted decay on synthetic and real federated topologies.

args.text: We propose Change-Aware Joint Subset Selection (CAJSS): a budgeted frame selector trained from differential video captions to cover atomic temporal change events with minimal redundancy. CAJSS converts differential captions into event spans and learns a transformer mask predictor (e.g., Gumbel-top-k or mask-diffusion) to pick complementary frames that maximize change coverage, optionally conditioned on user/query text for task-specific focus. We couple selection with downstream heads: for recognition/summarization the task is trained only on the selected frames; for long-horizon video diffusion with arbitrary masks the same selector supplies conditioning frames and is trained end-to-end to maximize reconstruction and temporal coherence of withheld segments. This unifies language-grounded supervision and joint subset selection, promising higher efficiency and better temporal fidelity on long-video understanding and generation.

args.text: We propose an inference-demand–aware repetition-scheduling policy for data-limited LLM pretraining that jointly selects model size, total tokens, and per-example repetition to maximize marginal utility per training FLOP under a fixed combined training+inference budget. Marginal utility is estimated online via a cheap, label-free pruning score to rank examples by importance and a repetition discount that downweights additional passes, with a broken-scaling fit used to detect breakpoints and stop over-repetition. To make runs reusable across candidate budgets, we train with a constant learning rate plus cooldown and apply SWA so the same trajectory can be truncated or extended while recomputing the allocation. result.text: The paper addresses tabular scenario-based question answering (TSQA), where systems must answer questions grounded in mixed-format scenarios that include both text and structured tables—a common and challenging setting for tasks like high-school exam questions that require synthesizing multiple table cells and integrating domain knowledge. The key insight is that converting useful parts of tables into natural-language sentences and selectively feeding those sentences into strong machine reading comprehension (MRC) models can make TSQA more tractable. To this end the authors introduce GeoTSQA, a 1k-question geography dataset with tabular scenarios, and propose TTGen, a table-to-text generator that synthesizes candidate sentences from tables and uses a ranking model conditioned on the scenario, question, and domain knowledge to select the most informative sentences for a downstream MRC solver. Their TTGen-augmented MRC approach significantly outperforms several strong baselines on GeoTSQA.

args.text: We propose Hash-Primed Expert-Choice (HPEC), a routing scheme that combines hash-based shortlisting with expert-choice selection under fixed expert capacities. Each token is first mapped via a balanced, consistent hash on local token features to a small candidate set of experts; experts then compute lightweight scores and select up to capacity from their candidate pools, allowing tokens to be served by a variable number of experts. This yields BASE-like balanced utilization without a global solver, keeps routing overhead and parameters close to hash-MoE, and adds content-aware specialization beyond pure hashing. Training can use straight-through estimators on the selection or a score-free variant, and we evaluate load balance, convergence speed, and downstream quality against expert-choice and hash-only baselines.

The key insight is that differential extrinsic plasticity (DEP), a self-organization mechanism, naturally generates rapid, state-covering exploratory behaviors in overactuated systems and thus can bootstrap effective experience for RL. The method integrates DEP as an embodied exploration module that drives the agent’s actions early on, producing diverse trajectories within seconds, and then hands control to (or augments) standard policy optimization to learn tasks; this DEP-RL hybrid yields substantially faster, more robust learning of reaching and locomotion on musculoskeletal models than existing exploration strategies.

args.text: Unify retrieval-grounded API knowledge with tokenizer-aligned constrained decoding to guarantee well-formed, safe tool calls throughout multi-step agent planning. Concretely, at decode time the agent retrieves up-to-date OpenAPI/SDK specs and compiles them into a subword-aligned constraint automaton (DOMINO-style) that enforces endpoint/argument names, types, and auth while propagating schema contracts across steps; planning and error recovery operate at the toolkit level to enable rapid fallback among functionally equivalent tools. We propose Spectrally-Guided Hyperbolic Diffusion (SG-HD) for graph generation, which trains a latent hyperbolic diffusion model while explicitly matching target Laplacian spectral profiles to preserve hierarchy and topology. The diffusion dynamics are factorized into radial/global updates that construct a coarse hierarchical backbone and angular/local refinements regularized by a Bernstein-polynomial spectral prior, penalizing deviations in empirical spectral density and motif spectra; denoising is further conditioned on per-node degree targets using discrete edge-removal guidance. Practically, we initialize generation via localized expansion from seed nodes and mix endpoint-conditioned trajectories toward predicted final topologies for faster, topology-aware convergence. This hybrid yields scalable generation with closer adherence to degree distributions, clustering spectra, and community structure than prior approaches, while maintaining interpretability of hierarchical organization.

result.text: We propose a manipulation-resistant recourse fairness audit that certifies subgroup disparities under small input perturbations and plausible model updates, closing the loophole where nominal counterfactuals can be exploited to appear fair while delivering cheaper recourse to targeted subgroups. A hierarchical semi-supervised estimator produces posterior intervals for these certified disparities, and the audit reports a "manipulation gap" (nominal vs. certified disparity) as an explicit risk indicator. For linear and differentiable models we provide convex/bi-level relaxations building on robust-recourse and local-smoothness tools to keep computation practical, and we scope actions to causal pathways to align with recourse fairness notions.

args.text: We propose augmentation-graph distillation: for each image, sample a diverse set of augmentations and use a strong teacher to induce an invariance graph whose nodes are augmented views and whose edge weights are teacher similarities; train a small student to match this graph structure (e.g., via pairwise similarity or a Laplacian loss) instead of single-view targets. To respect student capacity and view choice, learn a curriculum over augmentations that gradually lowers inter-view mutual information, guided by student error on edges, so the student first masters easier invariances and then harder ones. We propose the Atlas Neural Tangent Kernel (A-NTK) for union-of-manifolds data: a gating network defines soft chart assignments and induces a mixture kernel K(x,x') = Σ_i g_i(x)g_i(x')K_i(x,x'), where each chart-specific NTK K_i is computed in learned (pseudo-)Riemannian tangent coordinates. args.text: Deep SNN residual architectures implicitly assume synchronous feature timing, but spatio-temporal dispersion and pooling introduce path-dependent lags that break exact identity mapping and exacerbate time-based gradient pathologies. We propose Delay-Aligned SEW-ResNets: extend each residual block with a learnable, bounded per-channel temporal shift on the main and/or skip branch, implemented as a one-hot 1D temporal convolution (discrete delay) so the spike-element-wise residual merge occurs at zero lag. Training adds an alignment regularizer that maximizes zero-lag cross-correlation between pre-merge spike trains (while penalizing large delays) and uses invariant-preserving backward kernels, yielding stable gradient flow even with average pooling. This delay-aware residual alignment is hardware-friendly (small FIFO buffers), reduces reverse-gradient effects, and should improve accuracy and reduce required timesteps on ImageNet and neuromorphic benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses improving transfer-based adversarial attacks—crafting examples on a surrogate model that reliably fool other unseen models—by targeting regions of the loss landscape that yield examples with better cross-model generalization. args.text: We propose Source-Free Universal Category Discovery (SF-UCD): adapt a source-trained classifier to an unlabeled target domain with unknown class overlap while discovering and learning novel classes, using only the frozen source weights. args.text: We propose Joint Optimum–Hyperparameter Entropy Search (JOHES), an information-theoretic acquisition that maximizes the expected reduction in entropy of the joint posterior over the optimizer’s input–output pair (x*, y*) and the GP hyperparameters θ, unifying JES-style optimality targeting with active hyperparameter learning. Concretely, we estimate ΔH[p(x*, y*, θ | D)] via fantasized observations and scalable posterior draws over many θ by leveraging decoupled GP sampling, avoiding the cubic blowup of naive hyperparameter marginalization. The objective naturally decomposes into terms that first prioritize θ-informative evaluations and then focus on x*, reproducing SCoreBO’s self-correcting behavior but with a single principled criterion. result.text: We propose Hierarchical Tree-PPO with Sibling-Advantage (HTPPO-SA) for training tool-augmented LLM agents: using a single Tree-Planner pass to sample diverse complete plans, we build an action tree and assign at each decision node an n-way utility over sibling branches that blends task success, latency, and tool-cost, then convert this into a centered "sibling advantage" reward attributed to the node’s action-prefix tokens. We optimize with PPO using per-token forward-KL control and a dynamically tuned KL coefficient calibrated from batch informativeness, while reusing off-policy failed branches via importance weighting to improve sample efficiency. To improve robustness and recovery, we plan and learn over function-clustered toolkits rather than individual tools, and inject adversarial toolkit dropout so the policy learns fast intra-toolkit re-selection. Compared to stepwise DPO/PRO on trees, HTPPO-SA provides better credit assignment and exploration while preserving stability and cost-efficiency through single-pass plan sampling and active execution of only the most uncertain nodes.

result.text: The paper addresses how to combine pretrained models with the same architecture and initialization to merge their capabilities without expensive gradient-based fine-tuning. args.text: We propose certified latency robustness for input-adaptive multi-exit networks by producing per-input certificates that upper-bound exit depth under bounded perturbations, yielding provable worst-case inference time guarantees. The proposed Selection-Inference (SI) framework implements this by iteratively selecting supporting facts and then applying an LLM to infer the next conclusion, repeating until the final answer is reached; in a 5-shot, zero-finetuning setting the method more than doubles performance of a vanilla baseline for a 7B model and even outperforms a 280B baseline on a suite of logical tasks. By generating causal, human-readable reasoning traces alongside answers, SI also improves interpretability and supports safer, more trustworthy deployment.

args.text: I propose a Bayesian Integrated-Gradient Ensemble Attack that unifies path-integrated attribution, parameter-uncertainty averaging, and backward linearization to boost targeted transferability. Concretely, we sample multiple surrogate parameter instantiations from a Bayesian posterior, compute random-path integrated gradients with a linearized backward pass, and optimize a layer-wise objective that explicitly reduces class-wise feature separability at deeper, model-specific layers identified by distributional analysis. To further align cross-model representations, the surrogate is trained with mild adversarial robustness and optional gradient-smoothness regularization, and in no-box settings it can be fit from a tiny exemplar set before posterior approximation. This single framework is designed to produce perturbations whose attributions are stable, features are broadly aligned across models, and decision boundaries are traversed smoothly, yielding strong targeted black-box transfer without extra data from the victim.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning non-discriminatory predictors when sensitive attributes (e.g., race) cannot be freely collected because of privacy or legal constraints, which prevents standard fairness procedures that require those attributes. Its key insight is that individuals can release privatized versions of their sensitive attributes via a suitable local differential privacy mechanism, and that existing fairness-aware learning algorithms can be adapted to operate on these privatized attributes with provable guarantees that the resulting predictors remain non-discriminatory while still achieving good utility. result.text: The paper tackles the computational intractability of the Projection Robust Wasserstein (PRW) distance—a robust variant of the Wasserstein distance designed to compare high-dimensional probability measures but hindered by a non-convex, non-smooth optimization formulation. Its key insight is that, despite theoretical minimax hardness results, the original PRW/WPP formulation can be practically and efficiently optimized by exploiting the low-dimensional search structure through Riemannian optimization on the Grassmann manifold, often outperforming convex relaxations. The authors propose three simple Riemannian algorithms (with provable complexity bounds for each) that directly optimize the projection subspace and transport plan, and validate their approach with extensive synthetic and real-data experiments showing improved robustness and computational efficiency. result.text: The paper addresses regret minimization in the stochastic shortest path (SSP) setting, where an agent must learn unknown transition dynamics to reach a goal with minimum total expected cost and episode lengths are variable and action-dependent. The key insight is that regret can be controlled without dependence on the minimum instantaneous cost by relating learning difficulty to the expected cost of the optimal policy B★ and carefully accounting for variable episode lengths, yielding near-optimal dependence on problem parameters. Methodologically, the authors design a new exploration-exploitation algorithm for SSP that leverages confidence sets and cost-aware optimistic planning to achieve a regret upper bound of Õ(B★ |S| √(|A| K)), and complement this with a matching lower bound Ω(B★ √(|S||A| K)) to show the bound is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors.

result.text: The paper addresses improving stochastic local search (SLS) for the (Weighted) Partial MaxSAT problem, where current clause-weighting strategies inadequately handle the interplay of hard and soft clauses and are sensitive to initial weight settings. The key insight is that (a) the initial soft-clause weights substantially affect SLS performance and (b) hard and soft clauses should be treated with different update conditions, rather than using a single uniform weighting rule. The authors introduce NuWLS, which combines a principled weight-initialization method for soft clauses with a novel clause-weighting scheme that applies distinct update criteria to hard versus soft clauses, and integrate these into an SLS framework. Empirical evaluation on six benchmarks from MaxSAT Evaluations 2019–2021 shows NuWLS substantially improves over existing SLS and even SAT-based incomplete solvers, and a hybrid combining NuWLS with a SAT-based solver won all incomplete-track categories at MSE 2022.

The paper addresses how to design and initialize diagonal state space models (SSMs) as efficient, easy-to-implement alternatives to the S4 layer for sequence modeling, focusing on why a diagonal restriction can match S4’s strong long-range performance. The key insight is that although almost every SSM has an equivalent diagonal form in theory, initialization is critical: a particular diagonal approximation of S4’s HiPPO-derived matrix recovers S4’s convolutional kernel in the infinite-state limit, explaining why the DSS-style initialization preserves performance. Building on this, the authors systematically analyze parameterization and computation choices for diagonal SSMs, derive simple, stable initialization schemes, and present S4D—a minimal two-line kernel computation implementation—that empirically matches or exceeds S4 across image, audio, medical time-series tasks and the Long Range Arena.

result.text: Bayesian Router for Zero-Shot Adapter Composition: instead of learning a controller to fuse many task adapters, compute per-input (optionally per-token/per-channel) adapter weights from a Laplace-approximated predictive marginal likelihood, using each adapter’s local curvature (Fisher/precision) around a shared base to score how well it explains the input. These evidence scores drive a training-free mixture over adapter deltas or selection among masked supports, yielding dynamic composition akin to a MoE router without additional data. To reduce interference and cost, restrict routing to task supports discovered by mask-based merging or lightweight modulators and fall back to the base when no adapter has sufficient evidence. We hypothesize this Bayesian gating closes much of the gap to learned multi-adapter routers while preserving the simplicity and robustness of Fisher/Laplace-based merging.

args.text: Existing hybrid table-and-text QA either fuses evidence statically or reranks text dynamically, but they do not condition retrieval on the evolving tabular state or unify table execution with step-wise evidence selection. We propose a state-conditioned fusion RAG for tabular reasoning that, at each program step, executes the partial plan to materialize an intermediate table and then reranks both textual passages and candidate table slices; the top items are packed into a fused block for the reader. Concretely, we combine a Chain-of-Table or SQL executor to maintain state, a DyRRen-style step-wise reranker conditioned on the current program and intermediate table, an OTT-QA–style fused reader with BigBird attention, and a CABINET-like relevance weighting to suppress distractors, trained end-to-end with execution and retrieval supervision. This should improve multi-hop numerical reasoning in FinQA and open-domain settings like OTT-QA and OpenTab, and we will also test on Text2Analysis-style ambiguous analytical tasks to show robustness.

result.text: The paper addresses the tradeoff between expressivity and scalability in permutation-equivariant graph learning: standard message-passing GNNs are insufficiently expressive to represent all permutation-equivariant functions, while higher-order architectures that are universal require tensorial or subgraph enumerations that scale exponentially and ignore graph sparsity. The key insight is that by using sparsity-aware heuristics inspired by graph isomorphism techniques, one can design permutation-equivariant networks whose computational cost adapts to the number of edges and local structure, yielding a continuum of models that interpolate between efficient message-passing and fully expressive higher-order schemes. Concretely, the authors introduce SpeqNets, a class of architectures that build higher-order representations only over selected node tuples determined by sparsity-sensitive selection rules and then apply permutation-equivariant aggregation and transformation, achieving universality while drastically reducing memory and time compared to full k-order methods. args.text: Projected Spectral Gradient Flow (PSGF) is a post-generation refinement that follows the DGflow view of entropy-regularized f-divergence gradient flows but computes critic gradients in a joint spatial–spectral, pretrained-feature space. Concretely, we feed real and generated images through a frozen multi-scale feature extractor as in Projected GAN and attach a lightweight frequency-domain head inspired by SSD-GAN; the resulting vector-valued critic defines a stable McKean–Vlasov flow whose updates explicitly penalize spectrum gaps while preserving semantic structure. For GANs, we execute the flow in latent space by differentiating through the generator, reusing DDLS-style latent Langevin updates to keep compute low; for diffusion/flow/VAEs we refine in image space. This targets the documented excess or attenuation of high-frequency content in modern generators and should improve detail without overfitting or rejection, leveraging robust gradients the standard discriminators miss.

We propose Tail-Adaptive PAIRED (TAP), a UED framework that trains an adversarial environment generator to maximize the agent’s Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) regret over a minibatch of tasks, explicitly targeting hard-but-learnable tail cases rather than mean regret. TAP schedules the CVaR quantile τ from moderate to extreme tails as learning progresses and aligns the student with a CVaR-optimized objective, mitigating oversampling of already-solved tasks and concentrating signal where learning remains possible. We adapt risk-sensitive optimism and confidence-set construction to provide tail-regret guarantees across curriculum phases, and treat exogenous perturbation parameters (e.g., observation-noise magnitudes) as part of the environment context so the curriculum jointly spans dynamics and sensing shifts. result.text: This paper tackles trajectory similarity computation for trajectories constrained by road networks, noting that prior methods designed for Euclidean trajectories ignore network topology and multi-relation semantics of points. result.text: PowerPM addresses the challenge of learning a general, transferable representation for electricity time series (ETS) data, which are hierarchically structured, influenced by exogenous variables, and exhibit complex temporal dependencies and diverse instance behaviors. The key insight is that jointly modeling fine-grained temporal dynamics with cross-level hierarchical relations and training with complementary self-supervised objectives yields robust, generalizable features for many downstream power-system tasks. Concretely, PowerPM combines a temporal encoder that integrates exogenous variables with a hierarchical encoder that captures correlations across hierarchy levels, and it is pretrained using masked ETS modeling plus dual-view contrastive learning to capture within-window temporal structure and across-window discrepancies. Empirical results on five real-world datasets show that large-scale pretraining of PowerPM achieves state-of-the-art performance, strong transfer to public datasets, and improved few-shot and ablation study outcomes.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of automatically discovering the symmetry (equivariance) present in a dataset when the correct symmetry group is not known a priori, since using the wrong symmetry can degrade model performance. The key insight is to cast symmetry discovery as a generative-adversarial game where a generator learns a set of transformations that leave the data distribution invariant and thus fool a discriminator, while representing the learned symmetry as an interpretable Lie algebra basis. result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of offline reinforcement learning with learned dynamics models, where existing model-based approaches require explicit uncertainty estimates—difficult to obtain with complex function approximators—to safely plan under model bias. The key insight is that pessimism can be achieved by directly regularizing the value function on out-of-support state-action pairs produced by model rollouts, yielding conservative value estimates without any explicit uncertainty quantification. COMBO implements this by learning a dynamics model from logged data, generating synthetic rollouts, and applying a conservative penalty that lowers value estimates for out-of-distribution tuples so the policy optimization maximizes a provable lower bound on true policy value; the authors prove this bound is tighter than prior bounds and empirically demonstrate strong performance on standard and image-based offline RL benchmarks.

result.text: Confidence-Adaptive Expert Expansion (CAEE) is an inference-time policy for MoE models that starts with a minimal expert set and incrementally activates additional experts for a token only when predicted uncertainty or cross-expert disagreement is high. A small marginal-utility head on the router is trained to estimate the expected gain in log-likelihood from adding the next expert, using targets formed by contrasting outputs under weak versus strong activation during training, with a monotonicity regularizer to encourage diminishing returns as k grows. This yields per-token, compute-aware routing that adapts activation size at inference without retraining and complements expert-choice load balancing. We expect improved calibration and accuracy at a fixed average FLOP budget compared to static top-k or globally tuned k, validated on language and vision MoEs.

args.text: We propose a source-free universal domain adaptation framework that discovers and aligns classes by combining disentangled semantics with a Bayesian nonparametric prototype prior. A HiLo-style encoder separates semantic and domain factors to suppress domain cues, while a reciprocal-kNN consistency loss and an MI-based self-labeling objective on semantic features yield compact, predictive clusters. We initialize target adaptation with known-class prototypes and place a Dirichlet/Pitman–Yor mixture prior over prototypes so low-likelihood samples relative to known classes can spawn new prototypes, modeling heavy-tailed novel class sizes; detection of target-private samples follows a statistics-based confidence test, and training interleaves attract–disperse neighborhood regularization with entropy-based alignment/rejection. This yields an online, label-free method that jointly aligns shared classes, rejects private ones, and splits unknowns into multiple coherent novel categories instead of collapsing them to a single unknown.

result.text: The paper addresses detecting backdoor (Trojan) attacks in classifiers for the general X2X setting where multiple arbitrary source classes may each map to arbitrary target classes—a setting unsolved by prior (mostly single-target) detectors. The key insight is that backdoor class pairs exhibit measurable transferability patterns and share reverse-engineered trigger characteristics, so jointly inferring and assessing candidate (source, target) pairs yields stronger unsupervised detection than treating classes independently. The proposed UMD method first computes a novel transferability statistic and clusters class-pair behaviors to select putative backdoor pairs, then reverse-engineers trigger sizes for those pairs and aggregates them through a robust unsupervised anomaly detector to decide if the model is compromised; experiments on CIFAR-10, GTSRB, and Imagenette show substantial detection improvements and resilience to adaptive attacks.

args.text: We propose Cert-Exit, a verification-and-training framework that provides provable upper bounds on inference depth (and thus latency) for multi-exit perception models under bounded input perturbations. By expressing exit triggers (e.g., patience-thresholded logit margins) as verifiable predicates and propagating bounds layer-wise, Cert-Exit certifies that at least one early exit will fire for all inputs within an l_p ball, yielding a certified maximum exit index that meets real-time deadlines. We pair this with margin-maximizing, slowdown-adversarial training and integrate the certified budgets into a closed-loop driving stack to schedule control updates, evaluating under SlowTrack-style availability attacks with interactive, latency-aware metrics. This shifts defenses from heuristic hardening to provable latency guarantees, directly addressing slowdown threats while preserving adaptive efficiency.

Its key insight is that an API can actively steer an attacker’s training updates by redirecting gradients computed from the attacker’s queries, enabling targeted, efficient manipulation of the stolen model’s learning trajectory rather than bluntly withholding outputs or adding noise. The authors introduce gradient redirection, a provably optimal algorithm that crafts adversarial responses to push the attacker’s surrogate model toward a chosen target behavior, and integrate this with surrogate-network improvements and a coordinated defense strategy (GRAD^2) that reprograms attackers with minimal utility loss and low overhead. They empirically show GRAD^2 outperforms prior defenses by achieving strong protection with small utility trade-offs and demonstrate the approach can enforce arbitrary attacker behavior, opening new directions for model-stealing defenses.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of backdoor attacks in federated learning (FL) — stealthy, malicious modifications during decentralized training that cause models to fail on specific sub-tasks — and whether FL can be made robust to such attacks. Its key insight is that strong defenses against backdoors are fundamentally hard: achieving backdoor robustness would imply solving adversarial-example robustness (a major open problem), and detecting backdoors is computationally unlikely under reasonable oracle/time assumptions. The authors introduce "edge-case backdoors," which target rare, tail-region inputs that are unlikely to appear in training or evaluation yet cause targeted misclassification, and they demonstrate how an adversary can reliably insert these across tasks by carefully crafting and tuning poisoned client updates. They validate the concept empirically on diverse tasks (image classification, OCR, text prediction, sentiment analysis) and argue these backdoors pose real risks to fairness and safety in FL.

args.text: We propose dual-head, system-aware routing for MoE: a content router selects a small logical set of experts per token, while a placement router maps those experts to physical replicas using live network telemetry (queue length, bandwidth, topology) to minimize step time. We train the placement head with a latency-regularized objective (task loss plus a differentiable surrogate of measured all-to-all time), use expert-choice buckets to cap per-expert queues, and let tokens adapt k via a global communication budget; if congestion spikes, a gating-dropout fallback keeps tokens local. Coupled with granularity adaptation, this co-design turns topology-aware dispatch from a static heuristic into a learnable controller that stays in compute-bound regimes and improves convergence speed and stability on large clusters. We further replicate hot experts across racks under a fixed memory budget and learn replica selection that trades extra memory for reduced cross-rack traffic.

result.text: The paper addresses optimization for performative prediction, where deploying a model changes the future data distribution through agents' responses, distinguishing deployment from mere parameter updates. The key insight is that performativity creates a trade-off between updating frequently (which causes repeated distribution shifts) and updating lazily (which accumulates optimization error under a fixed distribution), and that this trade-off depends on the strength of performative effects. Under smoothness and strong convexity assumptions, the authors analyze two strategies—greedy deploy (deploy after every stochastic update) and lazy deploy (perform multiple updates per deployment)—and derive non-asymptotic convergence rates that interpolate to the standard O(1/k) rate as performativity vanishes, identifying regimes where each strategy is preferable; they validate these theoretical findings with synthetic and strategic-classification experiments.

args.text: We propose Anti-aliased Frequency-aware Merge-and-Refine (AFMR) for fine-grained visual classification: a ViT that dynamically merges tokens when a learned low-pass prefilter certifies low risk of aliasing, and spawns subpatch refinements only where high-frequency residuals and class-attention indicate discriminative parts. Concretely, each block maintains a Laplacian/low-pass decomposition of patch features; tokens with low residual energy are ToMe-style merged after anti-aliasing, while a quadtree-style expander splits patches whose residuals and class–patch attention jointly exceed a margin. A gradient- and edge-consistency loss, inspired by CAP, enforces that post-merge logits and saliency match their anti-aliased pre-merge counterparts, while a confusion-aware contrastive loss focuses refinement on patches implicated by TransFG-style attention in confusing class pairs. result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of learning actionable policies and dynamics models from the abundant but action-free videos available on the web, a gap that has prevented large-scale pretraining in reinforcement learning. Its key insight is that the true action structure can be recovered purely from observed state transitions by learning a latent action space that explains dynamics and permits inverse dynamics and policy learning without any ground-truth actions. The method, Latent Action Policies (LAPO), jointly learns a latent-action representation, an inverse dynamics model, and world-model components from video-only data, then uses a small labeled action dataset or online reward signals to rapidly fine-tune the latent-action policy into expert-level controllers. By demonstrating recovery of true action structure even in procedurally generated environments, LAPO shows a path toward pretraining generalist policies and world models on large-scale, action-free video corpora.

args.text: We propose a hidden-state, pairwise-Rényi DP analysis for decentralized SGD with gossip, showing that when only mixed neighbor messages are revealed (and node states remain hidden), the cumulative pairwise privacy loss between any two nodes saturates to a topology-dependent constant and decays exponentially with iterations at a rate governed by the graph’s spectral gap. Our analysis combines pairwise network DP with the hidden-state view of iterative learning and tracks privacy via privacy-loss random variables under Rényi DP to yield tight, composition-friendly bounds across many rounds. Practically, this suggests private decentralized algorithms can train for far more iterations than composition would allow, with privacy leakage depending on graph distance and mixing quality rather than linearly on time. We outline an algorithm that pairs local noise with randomized gossip schedules to maximize mixing, and provide utility guarantees by coupling the privacy analysis with unified convergence bounds for decentralized SGD.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of high quantization error in post-training quantization (PTQ) for large language models by expanding the class of allowed transformations beyond simple per-weight scalings. Its key insight is that optimizing an equivalent affine transformation between pre- and post-quantized weights (and applying the inverse to preserve outputs) enlarges the optimization space and can substantially reduce quantization-induced error while retaining PTQ’s efficiency. The method, AffineQuant, directly optimizes an affine matrix for each layer subject to invertibility constraints enforced via a gradual mask optimization that starts with diagonal entries and progressively frees off-diagonal elements—leveraging the Levy–Desplanques theorem to maintain invertibility—and applies the corresponding inverse to keep pre- and post-quantization outputs equivalent. Empirically, this approach yields consistent improvements across LLMs and settings (e.g., better perplexity and zero-shot accuracy in 4/4-bit quantization) without runtime overhead.

args.text: We propose SCM-Local Kernel Shapley: a causal-and-local baseline for Shapley attributions that (i) defines feature absence via do-interventions on a given structural causal model and (ii) restricts the reference to a kernel-weighted neighborhood on the manifold of exogenous variables, yielding on-manifold, causally consistent, instance-specific value functions. We implement this efficiently via RKHS mean embeddings of interventional and conditional distributions, enabling closed-form or low-variance estimates and seamless interpolation between purely interventional, observational, and local regimes by tuning kernel bandwidths and graph constraints. Further, we add a training-time Shapley regularizer that bounds total attribution along prohibited causal paths or non-ancestor features, integrating directly into Shapley-as-latent architectures to steer models away from spurious, non-causal signals. args.text: We propose Distributional Projection-Robust Wasserstein (DPRW), which replaces the single worst-case k-dimensional projection in PRW with an optimized distribution over k-dimensional subspaces on the Stiefel/Grassmann manifold, yielding a smoother yet robust discrepancy. The subspace distribution is defined in an energy-based way with density proportional to an entropy-regularized projected transport gap, upweighting informative subspaces as in energy-based sliced distances, and is estimated via importance sampling over a hierarchical subspace basis to cut projection cost. We solve the resulting stochastic min–max on product manifolds with a Riemannian corrected extragradient method, interleaving block-coordinate transport updates as in efficient PRW solvers, to attain Euclidean-like last-iterate rates up to curvature factors while maintaining low per-iteration cost. DPRW is expected to stabilize optimization and improve sample efficiency over max-PRW while retaining robustness to high-dimensional nuisance variation.

We propose DP-JL-Skellam: each client clips its gradient, applies a shared sparse Johnson–Lindenstrauss sketch (e.g., CountSketch/sign-JL), randomly drops a subset of buckets to reduce bits, quantizes with unbiased rounding to a few bits, and adds discrete Skellam (or discrete Gaussian) noise in the sketch domain before secure modular aggregation; the server de-sketches via least-squares or heavy-hitter recovery. By combining privacy-from-compression with sparse random projections and closure of discrete noise under summation, the scheme targets near-optimal per-client communication (matching central-DP accuracy within Õ(min(n^2 ε^2, d)) bits) while preserving utility. Finally, we plug in SoteriaFL-style shifted/variance-reduced compressed estimators to counter sketch bias and sparsity, aiming for practical 1–2 bits/parameter regimes with central-DP-level accuracy.

args.text: Physically-Grounded Cage-NeRF couples category-agnostic cage-based NeRF deformation with an SDF surface representation and a differentiable elasticity prior so interactive edits plausibly obey material behavior. result.text: I propose Uncertainty- and Diversity-Aware Channel Pruning (UDCP) to directly address the Similarity and Applicability issues in channel-pruning criteria. result.text: The paper addresses inconsistent and sometimes poor-quality samples produced by deep generative models by proposing a post-generation refinement procedure that improves individual outputs rather than discarding them. The key insight is to view refinement as following the gradient flow of an entropy-regularized f-divergence between the generated and real data distributions, which yields a non-linear Fokker–Planck PDE whose particle dynamics are given by a McKean–Vlasov process driven by the discriminator (critic) gradients. The method, called Discriminator Gradient flow (DGflow), simulates this process via discretized stochastic updates on generated samples using gradients from vector-valued critics (and applicable to VAEs and flows as well as GANs), thereby nudging poor samples toward higher-density regions of the data distribution without rejection sampling. Empirically, DGflow consistently improves sample quality across synthetic, image, and text benchmarks and outperforms prior refinement approaches like DOT and DDLS.

result.text: We propose Token-Adaptive Mixed-Precision for LLM inference: a budgeted per-token bitwidth scheduler that allocates precision across layers and attention heads based on lightweight features such as pre-LN norms, attention entropy, and KV-similarity drift, directly targeting the memory-bandwidth bottleneck in single-batch generation. The scheduler is learned with differentiable bitwidth parameters and a bit-sparsity regularizer to yield discrete per-layer/head bit windows, and we co-train a representation-aware fine-tuning objective so quantized weights are robust to the distribution of token-conditioned precisions; at inference, a tiny LUT enforces a global per-step bit budget for predictable latency. Unlike static mixed precision or per-activation bit skipping, this approach adapts precision where it matters most for each token while keeping KV-cache formats stable to avoid thrashing, promising substantial bandwidth reduction at near-4-bit accuracy. We hypothesize 1.3–1.7× bandwidth savings on LLaMA-style models with <0.5 perplexity degradation by combining token-aware scheduling with end-to-end learnable quantization choices.

result.text: The paper addresses how to define and achieve proportional outcomes in approval-based participatory budgeting when voters’ satisfaction can be measured either by number of approved projects or by total cost, noting ambiguity over which measure reflects true utility. args.text: We propose confounding-robust off-policy evaluation in partially observable control by marrying short-memory decodability with bridge-based identification and stationary density ratios. When latent state is decodable from a length-m history, we define the history–Markov chain and learn a proxy-bridge density ratio that maps observable futures and histories to the Radon–Nikodym derivative between target and behavior stationary occupancies, optimizing a GenDICE-style convex–concave objective with IV-style orthogonal moments for robustness to latent confounding. This yields consistent, near-horizon-free value estimators and a doubly robust plug-in; we adaptively select m via a forward–backward sufficiency diagnostic to guard against misspecification. result.text: The paper tackles no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) by addressing the gap between large multimodal models' (LMMs') strong relative/comparative judgments and the need for continuous perceptual quality scores usable in practice. The key insight is to teach an LMM to act as a human-like visual comparator using large-scale, scaled-up comparative instructions across diverse IQA datasets, then convert the model’s discrete comparative outputs into a continuous score via soft comparisons against multiple anchor images and a maximum a posteriori (MAP) optimization on the resulting probability matrix. The proposed method, Compare2Score, trains the LMM on pairwise and multi-level comparisons to learn robust preference likelihoods and at inference computes the probability that a test image is preferred to predefined anchors, then infers a final quality score by MAP-based conversion; experiments on nine IQA datasets show superior accuracy and that the probability-matrix conversion also boosts zero-shot performance of general-purpose LMMs.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of "over-squashing" in graph neural networks, where information from distant nodes gets compressed and distorted during message passing, limiting GNN performance on tasks needing long-range interactions; this is commonly attributed to graph bottlenecks but lacked a precise formulation. The key insight is that over-squashing corresponds to negatively curved edges in the graph: such edges act as combinatorial bottlenecks that concentrate and distort many incoming messages, and can be detected via a novel edge-based discrete curvature measure. The authors define this new curvature, prove a formal relationship between negative curvature and the deterioration of information flow in message passing, and propose a curvature-driven graph rewiring algorithm that adds or reweights edges to reduce negative curvature; experiments show that this rewiring alleviates over-squashing and improves GNN performance on long-range tasks.

A graph–language co-reasoning core tightly couples LM states with GNN states, letting situational nuances from text prune or revise edges while the graph injects structured constraints back into the LM before answering or generation. To stay fast and cover long-tail concepts, rare entities are represented by lightweight pseudo tokens distilled from their relation triples, and the model is primed with concept-centric generative/contrastive pretraining to bias toward relational consistency. The key insight is that learned invariances can be extracted explicitly as generators of Lie groups by identifying vector fields on input space whose induced infinitesimal transformations leave the network’s output approximately unchanged. The method fits parametric vector fields (Lie generators) to minimize changes in the network output under infinitesimal and finite flows, evaluates invariance quality across architectures, and analyzes how depth and parameter count affect the fidelity of the recovered symmetries. result.text: The paper tackles online multiple object tracking and segmentation by improving how temporal information is used to both associate objects across frames and produce their segmentation masks. Its key insight is that a compact set of learned space-time prototypes can distill rich spatio-temporal memory and, when combined with prototypical foreground/background appearance representations, enable effective retrieval and propagation of object-specific information via cross-attention. A lightweight router conditions on acoustic features and online uncertainty (e.g., CTC/CE entropy) to send only ambiguous tokens through sparse attention while most tokens follow the SSM path, enabling dynamic test-time compute. The authors propose Guided Non-Autoregressive Knowledge Distillation (GNARKD), which distills trained AR models into NAR architectures by aligning intermediate representations and outputs while adapting the network to parallel generation. Instead of master-driven ADMM, we periodically perform exact aggregation of only boundary Gaussians via spanning-tree RelaySum, yielding heterogeneity-agnostic convergence with bounded latency while avoiding slow-mixing gossip. To keep communication practical, we adopt Grendel-style pixel-shard visibility culling so relays carry only Gaussians that intersect neighbor shards, and apply EF-BV-style compressors with independent randomness plus error feedback to quantize updates without sacrificing linear-rate convergence. We propose a unified certification framework for offline RL that jointly handles test-time observation perturbations and limited training-time poisoning by combining randomized trajectory smoothing with conservative neighborhood regularization and robust aggregation. Concretely, we train a policy and Q-function with pessimistic Bellman updates over smoothed state neighborhoods, then compute offline certificates that (i) lower-bound finite-horizon return under any adaptive observation adversary within an L2 radius and (ii) remain valid provided up to k trajectories are poisoned via trajectory-level aggregation (e.g., partitioned median-of-means). Our analysis marries smoothed return bounds for Q-derived policies with offline conservative neighborhood guarantees and COPA-style aggregation to yield data-dependent certified radii and k-tolerance; the certified gap scales with smoothing radius and corruption budget but tightens with improved coverage. This provides the first offline RL certificates that simultaneously address adaptive test-time perturbations and bounded training-time poisoning while remaining a plug-in atop simple conservative offline algorithms.

args.text: We propose View-Adversarial Unlearnable Perturbations (VAUP) that specifically target contrastive learners by breaking positive-pair consistency while remaining imperceptible to humans. VAUP optimizes per-image perturbations to minimize augmented-view similarity across a bank of self-supervised checkpoints and augmentation pipelines (a self-ensemble over SimCLR/MoCo-style snapshots), making the perturbations transfer across training recipes and time. To resist simple orthogonal-projection recovery, VAUP explicitly spreads energy across multiple augmentation-variant subspaces (e.g., color, local phase/texture, and mid-frequency bands) with diversity regularization, so no single linear projection can recover clean features. Unlike prior unlearnable examples designed for supervised training, VAUP is tailored to InfoNCE-style objectives and degrades downstream linear-probe accuracy by inducing systematic view misalignment during pretraining.

result.text: We propose Frequency-Balanced Gradient Regularization (FBGR) for limited-data GANs: decompose each input into multiple frequency bands and explicitly match the discriminator’s input-gradient energy on real vs. fake within each band, closing the gradient gap not only in aggregate but per-frequency. A lightweight spectral head supplies band-specific real/fake feedback and stabilizes gradients in high-frequency regions, complementing the main spatial pathway. To avoid consistency-induced artifacts, we apply band-conditioned consistency regularization only across perturbations that preserve band structure (e.g., mild magnitude jitter or phase-preserving transforms), aligning predictions within bands rather than between augmented and unaugmented outputs. By equalizing gradient flow across frequencies, FBGR addresses the discriminator’s insensitivity to low-magnitude high-frequency signals and reduces spectrum mismatch, improving fine detail without destabilizing training.

The key insight is to introduce mixed finite-element “extra fields” to rewrite the PDEs so those boundary conditions become linear constraints, then derive analytic general solutions of those linear BCs and embed them into a neural-network ansatz that satisfies the BCs by construction. The resulting hard-constraint framework trains networks using only the PDE residuals (no boundary-loss terms), which stabilizes training and mitigates loss-term competition, and experiments on complex geometries show improved accuracy and robustness over state-of-the-art baselines.

result.text: Confidence-Adaptive Expert Expansion (CAEE) is an inference-time policy for MoE models that starts with a minimal expert set and incrementally activates additional experts for a token only when predicted uncertainty or cross-expert disagreement is high. A small marginal-utility head on the router is trained to estimate the expected gain in log-likelihood from adding the next expert, using targets formed by contrasting outputs under weak versus strong activation during training, with a monotonicity regularizer to encourage diminishing returns as k grows. This yields per-token, compute-aware routing that adapts activation size at inference without retraining and complements expert-choice load balancing. We expect improved calibration and accuracy at a fixed average FLOP budget compared to static top-k or globally tuned k, validated on language and vision MoEs.

result.text: The paper tackles scalable detection of backdoor attacks in deep neural networks, where existing optimization-based defenses become prohibitively slow as the number of classes grows because they try to find minimal triggers for every possible target label. The key insight is to frame label selection as a K‑arm optimization problem akin to multi‑armed bandits: by stochastically and iteratively focusing optimization effort on a small set of promising target labels guided by an objective, the method both cuts complexity and reduces uncertainty about which labels are likely poisoned. The proposed K‑Arm scanning algorithm alternates between selecting candidate labels according to estimated rewards and running trigger‑finding optimizations on those labels, refining selections over iterations; this yields much faster scanning and higher detection accuracy, outperforming prior techniques on thousands of IARPA TrojAI models.

result.text: BEVFusion addresses the problem that current LiDAR-camera fusion methods for 3D object detection break catastrophically when LiDAR malfunctions, because they treat point clouds as mandatory queries for image features. The key insight is to decouple the camera stream from LiDAR input so the image-derived bird’s-eye-view (BEV) representation can be produced independently, enabling robust fusion even if LiDAR fails. The method constructs separate BEV feature streams from images and LiDAR and then fuses them in BEV space, allowing the camera-only branch to produce predictions when LiDAR is absent or degraded; this simple design not only outperforms prior fusion approaches in standard settings but also yields large mAP gains (15.7%–28.9%) under simulated LiDAR malfunction.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that standard GAN architectures, which push a unimodal latent distribution through a continuous generator, necessarily produce target distributions with connected support and thus struggle to accurately model disconnected manifolds. The key insight is a formal “no free lunch” result showing there is an unavoidable upper bound on precision because continuity forces the generator to produce low-quality samples in transitional regions between disconnected modes. To mitigate this, the authors propose a rejection sampling scheme that identifies and removes those low-quality samples by using the norm of the generator’s Jacobian as a proxy for sampling from unwanted transitional regions. They demonstrate that this Jacobian-norm-based rejection method improves sample quality across several generators, including experiments with BigGAN.

result.text: The paper addresses scalable learning on large text-attributed graphs (TAGs), where each node has associated text and jointly leveraging powerful language models and graph neural networks (GNNs) is computationally prohibitive at scale. Its key insight is that alternating, variational EM-style updates can decouple training of the language and graph modules while still allowing them to interact and reinforce one another, avoiding the cost of end-to-end joint optimization. The proposed method, GLEM, formulates a variational EM framework in which the E-step updates the language model (or its text representations) conditioned on current graph beliefs and the M-step updates the GNN parameters given the updated text embeddings, iterating these steps to convergence; this enables separate, efficient training of each module yet yields mutually improved representations. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets show GLEM achieves strong performance and efficiency gains compared to jointly trained baselines.

result.text: This paper tackles image-goal navigation without relying on simulators, reinforcement learning, or ground-truth maps, motivated by the expense and sim-to-real gap of existing methods. The key insight is that passive video of an agent roaming through environments contains sufficient self-supervised signals to learn navigation policies without active interaction or explicit rewards. The method, called No RL, No Simulator (NRNS), trains a policy purely from offline roaming videos using self-supervised objectives that learn correspondences between images and actions (e.g., predicting visual goal-directed progress or relocalization) to guide navigation at test time. NRNS is simple, scalable, and empirically outperforms prior RL-based approaches on image-goal navigation, offering a strong baseline for future work.

result.text: This paper tackles the problem of generating realistic piano audio from silent videos of a performer, testing whether visual cues alone suffice to recover music. The key insight is to intermediate via a symbolic, time-aligned representation (a piano-roll) inferred from hand and keyboard appearance and then enrich that roll with learned temporal correlations to make it suitable for synthesis. Their Audeo pipeline first predicts per-frame piano-rolls from video, refines them to capture temporal dependencies critical for natural-sounding notes, and finally renders audio with MIDI synthesizers. Evaluated on in-the-wild performances, Audeo produces smooth, recognizable music that music-identification tools can match with high precision.

result.text: The paper tackles detecting training-set backdoor attacks, where poisoned examples cause a learned model to respond to a trigger, and questions whether such examples can be distinguished from benign data. Its key insight is that without prior structural knowledge of the data distribution, backdoor patterns can be indistinguishable from legitimate predictive features—making general-purpose detection impossible—and thus defenses implicitly rely on latent assumptions. Leveraging an alternative, explicit assumption that the backdoor corresponds to the single strongest feature in the training data, the authors formalize this setting and derive a detection primitive and algorithm with theoretical guarantees. result.text: We propose dual-head, system-aware routing for MoE: a content router selects a small logical set of experts per token, while a placement router maps those experts to physical replicas using live network telemetry (queue length, bandwidth, topology) to minimize step time. Coupled with granularity adaptation, this co-design turns topology-aware dispatch from a static heuristic into a learnable controller that stays in compute-bound regimes and improves convergence speed and stability on large clusters. We further replicate hot experts across racks under a fixed memory budget and learn replica selection that trades extra memory for reduced cross-rack traffic.

A gradient- and edge-consistency loss, inspired by CAP, enforces that post-merge logits and saliency match their anti-aliased pre-merge counterparts, while a confusion-aware contrastive loss focuses refinement on patches implicated by TransFG-style attention in confusing class pairs.
