result.text: The paper tackles the gap between standard composition-based differential privacy (DP) analyses for iterative learning algorithms—which assume an adversary sees the algorithm’s internal state and therefore yield privacy loss growing linearly with epochs—and the more realistic setting where the internal state is hidden. The key insight is that hiding state enables strong privacy amplification by subsampling and randomized post-processing, so the cumulative privacy loss for noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD) need not diverge but can instead converge rapidly. Concretely, for strongly convex smooth losses and commonly used mini-batch schemes (“shuffle and partition” and “sample without replacement”), the authors derive R\'enyi-DP bounds that decay exponentially with iterations and are much tighter than composition bounds after a few epochs. args.text: We propose Capacity-Calibrated Relational Distillation (CaReD), which aligns a student to the teacher’s relational structure while explicitly respecting the student’s capacity. Rather than matching the full teacher similarity graph, CaReD learns a meta-adapter that (i) low-rank projects the teacher’s batch similarity matrix to a rank the student can reliably track and (ii) predicts per-relation temperatures/weights from teacher–student features and online approximation error, suppressing edges/classes deemed undistillable. This induces a curriculum: begin with coarse, high-temperature, low-rank relations (bags/clusters) and progressively increase rank and sharpen weights as the student improves. By combining relational/self-supervised distillation with teach-less principles, CaReD preserves informative structure while avoiding over-regularization from overly strong teachers.

result.text: The paper addresses the "multiple manifold problem," a binary classification task in which a deep fully-connected network must separate two low-dimensional submanifolds on the unit sphere, and asks when randomly-initialized gradient descent can rapidly and perfectly learn this separation. The key insight is that depth and width play complementary roles—depth provides a fitting resource making networks smoother and more capable of separating class manifolds, while width supplies a statistical resource that concentrates the random network and its gradients—so that in an overparameterized NTK regime training succeeds with high probability when width and sample size scale polynomially with depth. result.text: The paper tackles the domain generalization problem in person re-identification, where models trained with batch normalization (BN) on source domains degrade when applied to unseen target domains due to BN's training-domain bias. The key insight is that updating BN statistics and parameters at test time using self-supervised tasks can quickly reveal domain-specific cues from unlabeled target images and thereby recalibrate feature normalizations for better generalization. The proposed method, Batch Norm Test-time Adaption (BNTA), uses two self-supervised auxiliary tasks—part positioning to capture structural/body-part layout and part nearest-neighbor matching to capture part-level identity consistency—to adapt BN parameters on the target data before inference, improving feature alignment without target labels. Extensive experiments on three re-id benchmarks show BNTA yields superior performance compared to prior state-of-the-art approaches.

args.text: Self-Contrast Pessimistic MoE for Offline RL: replace the Q/value function with a soft Mixture-of-Experts trained on fixed datasets, but use expert-choice routing so experts select and balance the states they serve by TD error and behavior-mode affinity. At evaluation and policy improvement, run two forward passes with weak vs strong expert activation (e.g., top-1 vs soft top-k) and treat their divergence as an epistemic signal, subtracting a calibrated margin from Q to obtain a conservative target; additionally penalize gating mass assigned to experts with low data support for the queried state-action. This yields a pessimistic, support-aware value lower bound that scales with model size while avoiding OOD overestimation in offline RL. We hypothesize improved performance on D4RL and image-based offline tasks over COMBO and standard ensembles, with ablations isolating the roles of expert-choice routing and self-contrast margin.

result.text: We propose Hardness-Adaptive Multi-Teacher AR-to-Diffusion Distillation for VRP: a non-autoregressive diffusion student that samples routes in parallel is distilled from a panel of autoregressive teachers specialized on diverse instance distributions. The student aligns intermediate representations and action distributions along its diffusion trajectory with GNARKD-style guidance, while a learned hardness estimator and a reinforced per-instance teacher selector weight teacher signals and schedule a curriculum over automatically generated hardness levels. To reduce reliance on labels and tightly couple diffusion with KD, we optimize a reverse-KL upper-bound on the VRP objective augmented with teacher-guided score matching, yielding a fast NAR solver with AR-level quality and strong out-of-distribution generalization.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of LLMs being vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks that manipulate prompts to elicit unsafe or undesired outputs, noting that prior defenses struggle against new or adaptive attacks. Its key insight is to model the adversary explicitly within the defensive objective and optimize a compact, transferable suffix that hardens the model against worst-case adaptive jailbreaks. The method, Robust Prompt Optimization (RPO), formulates an optimization-based defense that searches for system-level prompt suffixes by iteratively simulating adversarial attacks during training and minimizing attack success rates. Empirically and theoretically, RPO substantially improves robustness—dropping ASR on JailbreakBench to 6% for GPT-4 and 0% for Llama-2—while remaining lightweight and transferable.

result.text: We propose Topology-Aware Broken Scaling Laws for MoE: a unifying model that augments granularity-based MoE scaling with an explicit communication model to predict wall-clock loss vs. budget across routing/topology regimes. The key insight is that aggregating predictions across many carefully constructed submodels trained on randomized subsets of the data (and then “flipping” or otherwise combining their outputs) can bound the influence any bounded-size poisoning set has on the final decision, yielding a certificate of robustness against a specified number of poisoned examples. The method, BagFlip, builds ensembles by repeatedly sampling bags of training examples, training base models, and aggregating their outputs with a flipping-based rule that produces a certified label when a margin condition holds; empirical evaluation on image classification and malware detection shows BagFlip matches or exceeds state-of-the-art defenses for trigger-less attacks and outperforms them for backdoor attacks.

The key insight is that one can obtain joint, dependent predictive distributions at test time by autoregressively factorizing the CNP’s conditional into a product of conditionals (inspired by NADE), thereby inducing complex, non-Gaussian dependencies without changing the model or its training. The method simply orders target points and sequentially queries the trained (factorised Gaussian) CNP to sample or compute each conditional given past sampled targets, forming an autoregressive CNP (AR CNP). Empirically, AR CNPs capture rich joint structure and substantially outperform independent CNPs, matching more complex dependency-aware models while retaining the original model’s training simplicity.

result.text: We propose Rational Spectral Neural Operators (RaSNO), which replace unconstrained learned weights on truncated spectral modes with learnable, stable rational multipliers expressed as Padé-like functions of frequency or Laplacian eigenvalues. This rational parameterization yields smooth, low-complexity approximations to PDE solution operators with built-in stability (via positivity/H∞ constraints) and improved cross-resolution generalization; on irregular domains we apply the same multipliers through rational–Krylov evaluations on graph/mesh Laplacians, removing the need for FFTs or equispaced grids. By explicitly matching spectral responses across discretizations, RaSNO mitigates operator aliasing and preserves the intended continuous-operator behavior, while pointwise stages can use rational nonlinearities to compactly capture stiff local physics. args.text: Preference-Grounded Video Plan Search (PG-VPS): Inspired by RLHF-style preference modeling in summarization, we train a video-plan reward model from pairwise human comparisons over short imagined rollout videos and plug it into video-language tree search to score and select candidate plans, directly aligning planning with user desiderata like safety, legibility, and efficiency. Building on video planning that searches in text-to-video space and on pipelines that translate imagined frames into executable actions, the critic operates on full plan videos and exposes attribute heads for zero-shot preference switching as in preference-conditioned diffusion. result.text: The paper tackles the problem of training reinforcement learning agents that remain robust when the environment can vary according to multiple different uncertainty sets, a setting where pure system identification can be too slow and standard robust RL assumes a single predefined uncertainty set. The key insight is to combine the strengths of system identification and robust control by actively reducing uncertainty when interactions allow while preserving robustness to the remaining ambiguity, effectively treating uncertainty as drawn from one of multiple sets and adapting behavior accordingly. The authors formalize this multi-set robustness objective and propose an algorithm that performs online inference to shrink the set of plausible perturbations when possible and otherwise optimizes a worst-case robust policy over the remaining uncertainty, and they empirically show improved worst-case performance on diverse control tasks relative to methods that use only system identification or only single-set robust RL.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that existing dataset distillation methods, particularly trajectory-matching approaches, fail to scale with increasing images-per-class (IPC) because they cannot capture complex, rare features of harder samples, leaving a coverage gap between easy and hard test examples. The key insight is that starting synthetic sets with purposefully selected real samples and restricting updates to only part of the synthetic pool during trajectory matching lets the distilled set achieve an appropriate difficulty distribution as IPC grows. SelMatch implements this by combining selection-based initialization (choosing representative and hard samples to seed synthesis) with partial trajectory-matching updates that focus optimization on subsets of synthetic images to preserve diversity and hard-feature coverage. Empirically, this hybrid approach yields consistent gains over selection-only and distillation-only baselines on CIFAR-10/100 and TinyImageNet across subset ratios from 5% to 30%.

result.text: The paper tackles learning risk-sensitive policies in reinforcement learning specifically optimized for the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), observing that naive use of distributional RL with the standard action-selection strategy can converge to policies that are neither the dynamic (Markovian) nor the static (non‑Markovian) CVaR objective. The key insight is that the distributional Bellman optimality operator and typical greedy action selection must be modified to correctly represent and propagate the CVaR criterion across states and trajectories. The authors propose a new distributional Bellman operator and corresponding algorithmic adjustments—simple extensions of standard distributional RL methods—that ensure correct CVaR optimization while remaining compatible with deep RL architectures. Empirical results on synthetic and real tasks show the modified approach more reliably learns CVaR-optimized policies and expands the applicability of distributional RL for risk-sensitive decision making.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of improving transferability of black-box adversarial attacks, where perturbations crafted on a surrogate model often overfit to that model or specific data patterns and fail to fool different victim models. The key insight is that forcing perturbations to succeed across a distribution of slight data and model variants—treating each combination as a separate task—encourages more generalizable attacks. Concretely, the authors apply simple data augmentations (random resizing and padding) and a novel model augmentation that randomly alters backpropagation while keeping forward predictions unchanged, and then embed these augmentations into a meta-learning loop that learns perturbations robust across tasks; this Learning to Learn Transferable Attack (LLTA) yields substantially higher transfer success rates, including strong results against Google Cloud Vision API.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently approximating the Pareto set for NP-hard multiobjective combinatorial optimization (MOCO) problems without expensive per-instance search. Its key insight is that a single, preference-conditioned neural model can directly generate high-quality approximate Pareto solutions for any trade-off preference, thereby learning a continuous mapping from preferences to solutions instead of producing a finite set of discrete solutions. args.text: We propose DP-UCAC: an unsupervised, cluster-aware adaptive clipping scheme that mitigates DPSGD’s group-wise gradient misalignment without requiring sensitive-attribute labels. DP-UCAC maintains differentially private online summaries of per-example gradient norms and directions to discover a few latent gradient archetypes (proxy subpopulations), and assigns each archetype a non-monotonic per-sample clipping/weighting rule chosen to minimize the clipping-bias disparity measure driving misalignment. Practically, we implement this by combining DP-safe online clustering of gradient features with automatic clipping and non-monotonic weighting, and show that per-archetype calibration reduces inter-cluster bias while retaining the convergence guarantees of DP adaptive clipping methods. We hypothesize improved fairness (reduced error gaps across latent groups) and accuracy under DP on vision and language benchmarks, with no access to protected attributes and minimal extra tuning.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of learning useful feature representations from unlabeled 3D medical images to reduce reliance on costly expert annotations for downstream tasks. Its key insight is that popular self-supervised proxy tasks can be extended from 2D to fully volumetric 3D formulations to better capture spatial structure in medical scans, yielding richer semantic features than 2D slice-based pretraining or training from scratch. The authors implement 3D versions of five methods—Contrastive Predictive Coding, Rotation prediction, Jigsaw puzzles, Relative patch location, and Exemplar networks—and show via experiments on brain MRI and pancreas CT segmentation (and transfer to 2D fundus images) that 3D pretraining improves data efficiency, accuracy, and convergence speed, and transfers well from large unlabeled 3D corpora to small task-specific datasets. They also release an open-source library containing their 3D and 2D implementations to facilitate adoption.

result.text: The paper addresses how to jointly satisfy communication and (ε,δ)-differential privacy constraints while minimizing estimation error in distributed mean and frequency estimation problems common in federated learning and analytics. The key insight is that communication-efficient compression can itself amplify privacy: by having each client send only a randomly selected partial sketch of its data, the effective privacy loss per client is reduced, allowing optimal privacy-accuracy trade-offs with far fewer bits than uncompressed protocols. Concretely, the authors prove that optimal error under (ε,δ)-DP can be achieved when each client transmits Θ(n·min(ε,ε^2)) bits for mean estimation and Θ(log(n·min(ε,ε^2))) bits for frequency estimation, yielding substantial savings whenever n·min(ε,ε^2)=o(d). Their method constructs randomized compression schemes and sampling-based communication protocols that integrate with noise addition to meet (ε,δ)-DP while exploiting privacy amplification from partial, randomly selected transmissions.

result.text: We propose Fisher-Transposable Sparse Updates (FTSU): select and update only a subset of parameters under a hardware-friendly, transposable N:M sparsity pattern while capturing most task-relevant curvature. Concretely, we initialize a transposable N:M mask by maximizing accumulated Fisher information mass under the transposability constraint (via a min-cost flow solver), then train only those weights to obtain end-to-end sparse forward/backward speedups. To mitigate suboptimality of a fixed mask, we periodically refine the structure using a bounded-variance policy-gradient estimator that proposes local N:M-preserving swaps using only forward passes, maintaining full sparsity throughout. FTSU aims to match or surpass unstructured fixed-Fisher sparse-update accuracy while delivering practical training and inference acceleration and reduced memory/communication costs for PEFT and distributed settings.

result.text: The paper addresses min-max optimization problems posed on Riemannian manifolds—common in applications like optimal transport and robust dimensionality reduction—where translating Euclidean convergence guarantees to the geodesic setting has been challenging. The key insight is that geodesically strongly-convex-concave structure admits the same favorable last-iterate linear convergence as in Euclidean space once algorithms are corrected for manifold geometry and curvature. Concretely, the authors analyze a Riemannian corrected extragradient (RCEG) method and show it attains linear last-iterate convergence in the geodesically strongly-convex-concave case, and they extend the analysis to stochastic and nonsmooth settings to obtain near-optimal rates (matching Euclidean bounds up to curvature-dependent factors), demonstrating that no fundamental performance gap is necessary between Riemannian and Euclidean min-max optimization.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of evaluating dynamic link prediction: current benchmarks and sampling practices make methods look better than they are by favoring easy negatives and ignoring recurring edge patterns in time-evolving graphs. The key insight is that many edges simply reoccur over time, so a strong memorization baseline can perform well under existing evaluations, revealing that negative sampling strategy critically shapes apparent performance. The authors introduce EdgeBank, a pure memorization baseline that records past edges and predicts their reappearance, propose two harder negative sampling strategies that produce more realistic and challenging evaluation splits, and release six new, diverse dynamic graph datasets to better reflect real-world scenarios and stress-test future models.

args.text: Cipher-Invariant Safety Moderator (CISM): a lightweight sidecar that detects policy-violating semantics even when content is obfuscated via ciphers, homoglyphs, or non-standard codepoints. We train CISM via self-play against a shadow obfuscator that adaptively generates diverse encodings to maximize moderator misses, while CISM learns contrastive, obfuscation-invariant safety labels and enforces a semantic–surface consistency gate on both inputs and outputs. Deployed alongside base LMs, CISM functions as pre-/post- moderation and a cross-check on model responses, and composes with prompt-level defenses. We evaluate on cipher-focused attacks and guardrail evasion as well as standardized jailbreak suites and forbidden-information metrics, comparing standalone and composed (CISM+RPO) settings for attack success, false positives, and helpfulness retention.

result.text: The paper addresses real-time, high-fidelity novel view rendering for dynamic scenes, where prior NeRF-based approaches rely on slow per-scene MLP deformation models and yield limited quality. The key insight is to replace implicit deformation networks with an explicit, clustered Gaussian representation: grouping 3D Gaussians that share similar properties (rotation, translation, location) into compact "superpoints" so motion can be modeled and rendered efficiently. The method reconstructs the scene with explicit 3D Gaussians, forms superpoints by clustering based on Gaussian attributes, and uses superpoint-driven Gaussian splatting to render dynamic frames with minimal extra computation. This yields state-of-the-art visual quality, real-time high-resolution rendering, and improved scene manipulation on synthetic and real-world datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles offline stochastic matching where edges exist independently with known probabilities and probes are costly and limited by vertex patience, aiming to maximize the expected size or weight of the matching. The key insight is a new family of ordered contention resolution schemes that carefully schedule edge probes in random or structured orders to balance exploration and exploitation, yielding stronger survival probabilities for desirable edges than prior schemes. Methodologically, the authors design and analyze these ordered schemes to derive probing policies for several settings—general graphs with patience constraints (achieving a 0.382 approximation), graphs without patience constraints via random-order probing (0.432 approximation and implications for prophet secretary under edge arrivals), and bipartite graphs with unit patience on one side (0.632 approximation)—thereby substantially improving previous guarantees.

result.text: The paper tackles few-shot tabular learning by addressing the challenge of leveraging large language models (LLMs) for feature engineering without incurring heavy per-sample inference costs or prompt-size constraints. Its key insight is that LLMs can be used once, in-context, to automatically synthesize high-quality predictive features or rules from a small labeled dataset, and those features can then power a simple downstream model at inference time. The method, FeatLLM, prompts an LLM to generate candidate features and transforms for the entire dataset, selects and encodes the most informative ones, and trains a lightweight predictor (e.g., linear regression) on those engineered features; this eliminates the need to call the LLM per test sample, requires only API-level access, and scales across domains. Empirically, FeatLLM produces robust rule-like features that improve few-shot performance on diverse tabular benchmarks, outperforming prior LLM-based approaches by roughly 10% on average.

args.text: Adversarial-through-Reconstruction (ATR): optimize adversarial 3D objects end-to-end through a differentiable implicit-surface reconstruction pipeline so that, after real-world sensing, UDF/SDF meshing, and resampling, the reconstructed point clouds still induce misclassification. We compose a differentiable proxy of a UDF reconstructor and polygonization with the victim model and backpropagate the attack loss through this stage, while regularizing a surface-parameter deformation field to remain low-distortion and preserve multi-scale local topology. This couples manifold-aware perturbations with spectral topology constraints, yielding C1-consistent, imperceptible changes that survive denoising and reconstruction and thus improve physical robustness and transferability. The approach unifies object-level optimization, manifold parameterizations, and UDF-based reconstruction priors to target realistic post-processing pipelines.

result.text: We propose Online Householder KV-Preconditioning for PTQ: during autoregressive decoding, each attention head maintains a lightweight online estimate of its dominant outlier direction in key space via Oja’s rule and constructs a single Householder reflection that redistributes that energy across channels. The same reflection is applied to both queries and keys (per head), preserving attention logits exactly while making the rotated tensors far more 4-bit-friendly; the reflection is updated infrequently (e.g., on drift thresholds) and costs O(d) per token. This dynamic, content-adaptive orthogonal preconditioning complements fixed, model-wide rotations and blockwise transforms, specifically targeting the evolving KV cache where outliers accumulate over long contexts. Empirically, we expect improved end-to-end 4-bit stability on long sequences with negligible overhead and full compatibility with standard round-to-nearest quantizers.

result.text: We propose an inference-demand–aware repetition-scheduling policy for data-limited LLM pretraining that jointly selects model size, total tokens, and per-example repetition to maximize marginal utility per training FLOP under a fixed combined training+inference budget. Marginal utility is estimated online via a cheap, label-free pruning score to rank examples by importance and a repetition discount that downweights additional passes, with a broken-scaling fit used to detect breakpoints and stop over-repetition. To make runs reusable across candidate budgets, we train with a constant learning rate plus cooldown and apply SWA so the same trajectory can be truncated or extended while recomputing the allocation. We hypothesize this yields better deployed quality than fixed-epoch or uniform-repetition policies in the data-limited regime, especially at high request volumes.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of current table question-answering research, which largely targets SQL-like or simple retrieval tasks and fails to evaluate models on more advanced data-analysis scenarios and real-world, unclear queries. Its key insight is that expanding benchmarks to include complex analytical tasks (e.g., forecasting, chart generation) and ambiguous user questions better reflects practical needs and more rigorously tests model understanding and reasoning. To realize this, the authors construct Text2Analysis: a dataset of 2,249 query–result pairs over 347 tables that incorporates advanced analysis tasks and unclear queries, created via five novel annotation methods that leverage large language models to boost annotation quality and scale, and they evaluate five state-of-the-art models across three metrics to demonstrate the benchmark’s increased difficulty and potential to drive future research.

result.text: This paper addresses the practical challenge of reducing memory and inference cost for fine-tuned sparsely gated mixture-of-experts (MoE) models by pruning entire experts without degrading downstream accuracy. The key insight is that experts whose associated router weight vectors change least (in L2 norm) from the pretrained model contribute least to performance after fine-tuning, so prioritizing their removal can preserve test accuracy. The authors prove—in a simplified MoE setting for binary classification—that pruning experts with small router L2 changes is provably safe, and they operationalize this by ranking and removing experts based on router L2 drift. They validate the method empirically on large vision MoE models (VMoE, E3MoE) fine-tuned on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet, showing substantial reductions in model size and compute while maintaining accuracy.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of long-horizon decision-making from pixels, where current agents struggle to decompose tasks into subgoals and plan across thousands of steps without manually specified goal spaces. result.text: Drift-Responsive Equal Shares (DRES): We propose a streaming participatory budgeting rule for nonstationary or even adversarial arrivals that maintains per-voter pacing but updates them via mirror-descent on a convex surrogate of worst-case group proportional deficit over sliding windows, with buyback-style slack tracked by stable price certificates. By leveraging strengthened, satisfaction-agnostic priceability, the same updates simultaneously protect proportionality under both cardinal-by-cost and cardinal-by-count utilities while remaining polynomial per arrival. This extends Equal Shares and pacing-based online equilibrium ideas beyond stationarity, providing robust proportionality with graceful degradation under drift.

result.text: We propose confounding-robust off-policy evaluation in partially observable control by marrying short-memory decodability with bridge-based identification and stationary density ratios. When latent state is decodable from a length-m history, we define the history–Markov chain and learn a proxy-bridge density ratio that maps observable futures and histories to the Radon–Nikodym derivative between target and behavior stationary occupancies, optimizing a GenDICE-style convex–concave objective with IV-style orthogonal moments for robustness to latent confounding. This yields consistent, near-horizon-free value estimators and a doubly robust plug-in; we adaptively select m via a forward–backward sufficiency diagnostic to guard against misspecification. args.text: Limited-Memory Quasi-Newton ICL (LM-QN-ICL): build a looped, weight-shared transformer that implements an L-BFGS-style in-context learner by storing and updating a compact set of curvature pairs (s, y) in fast weights and replaying the two-loop recursion across recurrent passes. Linearized attention viewed as a fast weight programmer provides the outer-product slots and delta-rule updates to write s := Δw and y := Δg with learned damping and noise-aware rescaling, while the looped recurrence executes successive quasi-Newton steps that approach Newton-like convergence using far fewer parameters. To operate on long prompts, a block-recurrent state carries the limited-memory curvature buffers across token blocks, and a learned pruning gate selects which token-level constraints to retain so the working set remains stable and informative. We predict superlinear in-context convergence on ill-conditioned, heteroscedastic regression and improved data-efficiency over GD-like or pure-Newton ICL, with ablations isolating the benefits of two-loop recursion, damping, and example pruning.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of reliably detecting and attributing content from powerful generative models as their outputs become indistinguishable from real data, proposing a mechanism for “responsible disclosure” that lets model owners mark outputs so they can be later identified. The key insight is that instead of trying to detect artifacts in generated content after the fact, one can deliberately embed distinct, robust fingerprints by training many lightweight variants of a base generator so each model produces outputs with a unique signature that survives typical transformations. Methodologically, the authors propose an efficient, scalable procedure to synthesize large populations of models parameterized by 128-bit fingerprints (yielding >10^36 identifiable variants in principle), and demonstrate via experiments that these fingerprinted models produce detectable, attributable outputs while satisfying practical robustness and distinguishability requirements for deep-fake detection and source attribution.

The paper addresses the problem of generating counterfactual explanations for neural networks that remain valid under realistic (potentially large-parameter) model updates by defining robustness to “naturally-occurring” model change, i.e., changes that may be large in parameter space but induce limited prediction change on the data manifold. The key insight is that robustness can be quantified by a Stability measure based on the local Lipschitz behavior of the model around a point, and that high Stability implies probabilistic guarantees of counterfactual persistence under such model changes via concentration bounds for Lipschitz functions of Gaussians. Methodologically, the authors formalize naturally-occurring model change, define Stability for differentiable models, derive theoretical probabilistic guarantees linking Stability to counterfactual validity, and propose practical relaxations and algorithms to compute or approximate Stability for finding realistic, close, and robust counterfactuals for neural networks.

result.text: The paper tackles scalable and generalizable learning of symbolic logical rules for knowledge graph (KG) reasoning, addressing limitations of prior rule learners that either cannot search large KG spaces efficiently or fail to generalize beyond training distributions. The key insight is to represent rule bodies as compositional structures that can be broken into small, reusable sub-compositions and merged recurrently with attention, allowing the model to discover and assemble effective multi-step inference patterns without exhaustive search. The proposed method, Neural Compositional Rule Learning (NCRL), uses a recurrent attention-based unit to iteratively combine relation compositions in a rule body into progressively larger compositions and ultimately predict a rule head, enabling end-to-end learning of interpretable rules; experiments demonstrate NCRL is scalable, yields state-of-the-art KG completion results on large graphs, and generalizes systematically from small observed graphs to larger unseen ones.

result.text: The paper tackles feature-based knowledge distillation, where conventional approaches match a single teacher layer to a single student layer and can fail to transfer the teacher’s intact representation. The key insight is that forcing multiple student sub-representations to jointly approximate the teacher’s representation (an N-to-one matching) preserves more teacher information and yields stronger supervision while adding no inference cost. Methodologically, they insert a lightweight two-layer linear Feature Transform (FT) after the student’s last convolution: the first linear layer expands the student feature channels by a factor N, the expanded vector is split into N non-overlapping segments that are each matched to the teacher’s feature, and the second linear layer contracts back to the original dimensionality so the whole module can be merged into the following fully connected layer at inference; this simple training-time trick improves accuracy across several vision models and ImageNet.

result.text: RelaySparseGS: an exact-consensus boundary synchronization scheme for distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting over unreliable, heterogeneous networks. Instead of master-driven ADMM, we periodically perform exact aggregation of only boundary Gaussians via spanning-tree RelaySum, yielding heterogeneity-agnostic convergence with bounded latency while avoiding slow-mixing gossip. To keep communication practical, we adopt Grendel-style pixel-shard visibility culling so relays carry only Gaussians that intersect neighbor shards, and apply EF-BV-style compressors with independent randomness plus error feedback to quantize updates without sacrificing linear-rate convergence. Trees are rescheduled and rebuilt to handle churn; when partitions disconnect, local training proceeds and merges exactly on reconnection, preserving quality and wall-clock throughput at city scale.

result.text: The paper tackles detecting training-set backdoor attacks, where poisoned examples cause a learned model to respond to a trigger, and questions whether such examples can be distinguished from benign data. Its key insight is that without prior structural knowledge of the data distribution, backdoor patterns can be indistinguishable from legitimate predictive features—making general-purpose detection impossible—and thus defenses implicitly rely on latent assumptions. Leveraging an alternative, explicit assumption that the backdoor corresponds to the single strongest feature in the training data, the authors formalize this setting and derive a detection primitive and algorithm with theoretical guarantees. Empirically, this method proves effective, and the analysis clarifies which assumptions underpin prior defenses and when they succeed or fail.

result.text: Learned invariance probing for backdoor detection: Learn a semantic-preserving augmentation group by training a contrastive model on auxiliary clean data, then probe each untrusted training sample’s representation for invariance across these learned transforms using multiple backbones trained with differing inductive biases. The method splits spectrograms into patches, feeds only unmasked tokens through a Transformer encoder, then reorders and decodes the encoded context padded with mask tokens to reconstruct the full spectrogram, and finally fine-tunes the encoder with lower masking on target datasets; this simple extension achieves state-of-the-art results on six classification benchmarks.

args.text: Bayesian Path-Integrated Feature Entanglement Attack (B-PIEA): To improve targeted black-box transfer, we compute integrated gradients along a distribution of stochastic paths while sampling a Bayesian substitute ensemble and aggregate these attributions into a single perturbation that is robust to model uncertainty. We generalize prior TAIG by sampling both baselines and random piecewise paths, but use smoothed surrogate derivatives during backprop to avoid truncation effects and stabilize the IG signal across architectures. The perturbation is optimized to reduce class-wise separability and increase entanglement at selected mid/high layers across the ensemble, while also minimizing the variance of path-integrated attributions across samples to promote invariance that transfers. This objective can be combined with simple logit-based losses and standard transfer tricks, and should yield strong targeted transfer without extra data or training.

Its key insight is that fine-tuning separate copies of a pretrained model on different reward functions yields weight solutions that remain linearly connected, so linearly interpolating these specialized weights can produce models that trade off objectives and approach Pareto-optimal behavior across preferences. args.text: We propose DP-Subgroup-Consistent Adaptive Clipping (DP-SCAC), a per-sample reweighting scheme that enforces alignment fairness by learning cluster-specific clipping weights to equalize each subgroup’s contribution to the batch gradient while preserving end-to-end differential privacy. At each iteration we form a DP sketch of per-example gradient directions via randomized projections and perform DP online clustering to discover proxy subgroups, then apply a non-monotonic weight function per cluster (extending DP-PSAC) whose dual variables are updated to control inter-subgroup cosine-misalignment and clipping rates. Theoretically, building on bias analyses of clipped SGD, we show the steady-state update deviation includes a subgroup-bias term that our controller contracts, yielding the same asymptotic rate as DP-SGD/PSAC but strictly tighter bias and a bound on disparity in group-wise gradient alignment. Empirically, on vision and tabular benchmarks with both known and locally-DP privatized sensitive attributes, DP-SCAC improves accuracy–fairness tradeoffs over DP-SGD with fixed or automatic clipping.

We propose PromptFlow3D: a pipeline that converts a few annotated slices into volume-consistent text-and-mask prompts for a 3D foundation segmenter to enable few-shot volumetric medical segmentation. First, we select representative slices per volume and, on each, use a ProMaC-style hallucination-mining prompt generator to distill precise, structure-specific text prompts that, together with the user-provided slice masks, seed a promptable 3D model (e.g., SegVol/SEEM-style) for initial predictions. A bidirectional inter-slice prompt propagation module—built on a GRU that passes prompt embeddings and mask features across adjacent slices—synthesizes per-slice prompts for unlabeled slices and enforces anatomical consistency, enabling iterative self-training over the full volume. We hypothesize this reduces manual prompts/annotations by 5–10× while achieving near full-supervision performance and robust cross-scan generalization.

result.text: The paper addresses stable and accurate reconstruction in snapshot compressive imaging (SCI), where high-dimensional video frames must be recovered from a single compressed, noisy measurement. Its key insight is to cast SCI reconstruction as a deep equilibrium (DEQ) problem: by learning an implicit nonexpansive operator whose fixed point is computed analytically, one can attain unlimited effective network depth and guaranteed stable convergence while keeping constant memory use. Methodologically, the authors embed DEQ formulations into two popular SCI reconstruction paradigms—recurrent neural networks and Plug-and-Play algorithms—training the implicit operator and computing its fixed point during inference to produce high-quality, stable reconstructions, and validate the approach on simulated and real datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of combining client-level differential privacy with communication-efficient federated learning, noting that existing compression techniques and privacy mechanisms have not been jointly optimized. Its key insight is that by unifying compression operators with a flexible family of local gradient estimators (including variance-reduced methods and shifted compression schemes), one can design algorithms that preserve local differential privacy while improving communication complexity without degrading utility. The proposed method, SoteriaFL, first analyzes the pitfalls of naively compressing differentially private SGD and then introduces a general framework that integrates noise-adding for local differential privacy with tailored compressed gradient estimators and variance-reduction/shift strategies. The authors provide theoretical characterizations of the trade-offs among privacy, utility, and communication, showing SoteriaFL attains strictly better communication complexity than prior private federated learning methods that do not use compression while maintaining comparable privacy and utility.

result.text: The paper tackles the claim that large, sudden drops in performance from post-training quantization—so-called “quantization cliffs”—are an inevitable emergent consequence of model scale. Its key insight is that large-magnitude activation outliers, which drive quantization sensitivity, are not intrinsic to model size but are instead induced by pretraining optimization conditions and thus can be suppressed by a quantization-friendly training recipe. The authors develop and apply optimization and training adjustments that reduce activation outliers and demonstrate that models from 410M to 52B parameters can be post-trained-quantized with minimal performance loss, showing that quantization robustness can be conditioned by training design rather than being solely determined by scale. This finding suggests both practical paths to more efficient quantization and a broader perspective that some emergent behaviors may be modifiable via optimization and architecture choices.

result.text: The paper addresses the high computational cost of estimating Shapley values for explaining black-box models, which typically require many model evaluations per input. The key insight is that the Shapley value can be approximated by a learned explainer that amortizes computation across inputs by framing Shapley estimation as a weighted least-squares problem and training a neural explainer to predict contributions in one forward pass. The method trains this explainer with standard stochastic gradient optimization to minimize a loss derived from the Shapley characterization, yielding a model that produces near-Shapley attributions dramatically faster than sampling-based estimators. Empirically, FastSHAP delivers high-quality explanations with orders-of-magnitude speedups, making real-time Shapley-style explanations practical.

result.text: The paper addresses the poor transferability of white-box adversarial perturbations on 3D point cloud classifiers, which limits their effectiveness in realistic black-box attack scenarios. The key insight is that a full adversarial perturbation can be randomly factorized into sub-perturbations that themselves often remain adversarial, so jointly considering a perturbation and its random factorization encourages perturbations that generalize across models. The proposed method augments the standard attack objective by optimizing both the full perturbation and sampled random factorized components (i.e., applying the loss to the original perturbation and to its randomly split parts) during generation, producing adversarial point clouds that retain attack strength while significantly improving transferability. Experiments on benchmark datasets show this simple augmentation yields more transferable attacks with little extra computation.

result.text: The paper tackles the claim that large, sudden drops in performance from post-training quantization—so-called “quantization cliffs”—are an inevitable emergent consequence of model scale. Its key insight is that large-magnitude activation outliers, which drive quantization sensitivity, are not intrinsic to model size but are instead induced by pretraining optimization conditions and thus can be suppressed by a quantization-friendly training recipe. The authors develop and apply optimization and training adjustments that reduce activation outliers and demonstrate that models from 410M to 52B parameters can be post-trained-quantized with minimal performance loss, showing that quantization robustness can be conditioned by training design rather than being solely determined by scale. result.text: The paper tackles the problem of efficiently and reliably certifying solver outputs when solvers use advanced reasoning like parity (XOR) handling, where existing DRAT proof formats become impractically large or inexpressive. Its key insight is that pseudo-Boolean (PB) inequalities augmented with extension variables can naturally and compactly capture XOR deductions and other richer constraints, forming a strict generalization of DRAT that supports concise proof traces. The method implements XOR reasoning within a SAT solver by emitting PB-inequality-based proof steps (with extensions) to justify derived clauses, and experimentally demonstrates orders-of-magnitude reductions in proof logging and verification time compared to DRAT encodings. This approach not only enables practical certification of parity reasoning but also extends to 0-1 and constraint programming encodings, pointing toward a unified, machine-verifiable proof framework for richer combinatorial paradigms.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that standard graph neural networks suffer from a fundamental bottleneck—over-squashing—where exponentially many bits of information from distant nodes are compressed into fixed-size node representations during neighbor aggregation, preventing effective long-range message propagation and hurting tasks that require distant dependencies. The key insight is that the common aggregation mechanism, which treats incoming edges equally and compresses many incoming messages into a single vector, inherently limits representational capacity and makes models like GCN and GIN particularly vulnerable, whereas architectures that manage or diversify edge absorption can mitigate this effect. The authors analyze how this bottleneck prevents even fitting training data, empirically demonstrate over-squashing in extensively tuned GNNs, and propose breaking the bottleneck—by altering message-passing or graph connectivity—to improve performance, achieving state-of-the-art results without extra weights or hyperparameter tuning.

result.text: We propose Spectrally-Guided Hyperbolic Diffusion (SG-HD) for graph generation, which trains a latent hyperbolic diffusion model while explicitly matching target Laplacian spectral profiles to preserve hierarchy and topology. The diffusion dynamics are factorized into radial/global updates that construct a coarse hierarchical backbone and angular/local refinements regularized by a Bernstein-polynomial spectral prior, penalizing deviations in empirical spectral density and motif spectra; denoising is further conditioned on per-node degree targets using discrete edge-removal guidance. Practically, we initialize generation via localized expansion from seed nodes and mix endpoint-conditioned trajectories toward predicted final topologies for faster, topology-aware convergence. This hybrid yields scalable generation with closer adherence to degree distributions, clustering spectra, and community structure than prior approaches, while maintaining interpretability of hierarchical organization.

result.text: We propose Algebraic-Diffusion IP-IRM, which augments iterative partition-based invariance with unsupervised discovery of continuous symmetries. We learn a small set of Lie-algebra generators in feature space from local view pairs, build a diffusion operator to estimate invariant subspaces and orbits, and alternate between (i) partitioning by orbit components to enforce subset-invariance and (ii) sparsifying cross-subspace interactions while applying a factorized-support regularizer to decouple correlated factors. This yields modular, approximately group-equivariant latents without prespecified groups, and ties downstream predictors to sparse subsets of generators/subspaces to enhance identifiability and OOD transfer. We hypothesize that the learned generators converge to true data symmetries when present and to approximate stabilizers otherwise, improving disentanglement and transfer on correlated-factor benchmarks while enabling plug-and-play equivariant layers.

result.text: We propose Fractional Fourier Neural Operators (FrFNO), which replace the fixed Fourier basis in FNO layers with a learned mixture of fractional Fourier transforms (FRFTs) at multiple, potentially spatially varying, orders. To make this practical at scale, we implement FRFTs via a block matmul decomposition and fuse them with spectral multiplications, adapting FlashFFTConv-style partial and frequency-sparse block skipping for speed and memory. We hypothesize FrFNO better captures non-stationary, chirp-like dynamics and heterogeneous coefficients in PDEs, improving accuracy and resolution-agnostic generalization over FNO and recent localized operator augmentations.

args.text: We propose a unified certification framework for offline RL under dual threats: training-time trajectory poisoning and test-time adaptive observation attacks. result.text: We propose dual-head, system-aware routing for MoE: a content router selects a small logical set of experts per token, while a placement router maps those experts to physical replicas using live network telemetry (queue length, bandwidth, topology) to minimize step time. We train the placement head with a latency-regularized objective (task loss plus a differentiable surrogate of measured all-to-all time), use expert-choice buckets to cap per-expert queues, and let tokens adapt k via a global communication budget; if congestion spikes, a gating-dropout fallback keeps tokens local. Coupled with granularity adaptation, this co-design turns topology-aware dispatch from a static heuristic into a learnable controller that stays in compute-bound regimes and improves convergence speed and stability on large clusters. We further replicate hot experts across racks under a fixed memory budget and learn replica selection that trades extra memory for reduced cross-rack traffic.

result.text: We propose Video Landmark Memory (VLM), a random-access attention architecture for long-video LMMs that adapts landmark-based infinite context to the spatio-temporal domain. Videos are partitioned into blocks, each distilled into a few query-conditioned spatio-temporal landmark tokens that summarize objects, motions, and subtitles; at inference, language queries first attend to landmarks to pick relevant blocks, then perform fine-grained attention within selected blocks, while a lightweight streaming update maintains landmarks online for hour-long inputs. We train landmarks with segment-level supervision and referring-reasoning signals so they become keys to the correct temporal neighborhoods, yielding large accuracy and latency gains on long-video QA versus dense tokenization. This design preserves native attention compatibility, enables constant-memory retrieval over very long videos, and aligns with referring-context evaluation protocols.

args.text: We propose VLM-anchored Attribute Transport (VAT-GCD) for generalized category discovery under domain shift. The method extracts language-grounded attribute directions from known-class prompts using a vision–language model and projects unlabeled target embeddings into this attribute space to decouple high-level semantics from low-level domain cues, aligns known-class prototypes via bipartite matching, and discovers novel categories by clustering in an attribute simplex with a compositional prior and neighborhood-consistency regularization. result.text: Learned invariance probing for backdoor detection: Learn a semantic-preserving augmentation group by training a contrastive model on auxiliary clean data, then probe each untrusted training sample’s representation for invariance across these learned transforms using multiple backbones trained with differing inductive biases. Clean samples should maintain near-invariant, full-rank feature statistics, whereas poisoned/triggered samples—including feature-space backdoors—exhibit anisotropic, low-rank deviations that are unstable across backbones; a multi-backbone invariance-variance score can flag and downweight or remove such samples and guide alternating unlearning/relearning. This approach operationalizes the explicit structure required by impossibility results via learned semantic invariances, uses memorization-capacity insights to set detection thresholds, and advances fixed-transform FCT by replacing hand-crafted transforms with learned ones and adding representation-space checks. We expect improved robustness in pretrain–finetune regimes and black-box transfer to new tasks via portability of the learned invariance group.

result.text: We propose Symmetry-Adaptive Neural Diffusion Processes that model function-valued posteriors with a mixture of equivariant diffusion score networks, enabling the degree and type of symmetry to vary across tasks and input regions. Each expert score enforces a (sub)group or partial equivariance via steerable/partial-equivariant architectures, while a permutation-invariant gating network over the context set predicts input-dependent mixture weights that are used to combine scores during the reverse diffusion to sample finite marginals. This unifies Neural Diffusion Processes with equivariant Neural Processes and Mixture-of-Experts, yielding exchangeable, non-stationary function priors that recover fixed-symmetry and stationary models as special cases and improve calibration and sample fidelity on data with approximate or locally varying symmetries. We train end-to-end with the diffusion loss plus a diversity regularizer on experts and evaluate on spatio-temporal and image-like tasks where symmetries drift or hold only approximately.

result.text: The paper addresses understanding and unifying policy gradient methods by formalizing them as the repeated application of two operators: a policy improvement operator I that outputs an improved (possibly unrepresentable) policy and a projection operator P that maps that improved policy back into the class of realizable parameterized policies. The key insight is that many policy-gradient algorithms can be interpreted as alternating I and P, which clarifies how approximation and optimization interact and links policy-based updates to value-based operators (e.g., showing REINFORCE and the Bellman optimality operator are conceptually related). Methodologically, the authors derive operator-based variants of standard algorithms (REINFORCE, PPO) within this I–P framework, analyze properties such as performance bounds, and introduce a new global lower bound on expected return that follows from the operator decomposition, thereby providing both theoretical insights and practical algorithmic reformulations.

args.text: We propose Risk-Calibrated BB-NPG, a bilevel natural policy gradient that jointly learns a state-value baseline and per-state trust radii to enforce high-probability lower bounds on optimal-action probabilities even when reusing off-policy data. Concretely, the learned baseline shapes the NPG preconditioner while off-policy reuse is guarded by adaptive importance-weight clipping whose thresholds are set by DEON-measured off-policyness and off-policy policy-improvement bounds; inner-loop gradients use SRVR-NPG with TSIVR-style truncation to control variance without bias blow-up. The bilevel objective minimizes a confidence-adjusted upper bound on probability-collapse risk that incorporates density-ratio uncertainty estimated via a GradientDICE-style critic, with decoupled sampling to ensure coverage. We hypothesize global O(1/t) convergence with improved constants from baseline-induced aggressiveness control and markedly better sample efficiency than PPO-like off-policy clipping under sparse rewards and distribution shift.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of multimodal fake news detection, where prior approaches that inject external knowledge often introduce noisy, irrelevant entities and fail to model complex interactions between text, images, and knowledge. Its key insight is that selecting a compact, content-relevant subgraph of knowledge for each news item and then learning cross-modal relations over that refined graph yields more reliable, discriminative signals than using all candidate entities statically. The method, AKA-Fake, uses reinforcement learning to adaptively extract a subset of entities and their contextual neighbors from a knowledge graph per news instance, then applies a heterogeneous graph learning module with topology refinement and modality-attentive pooling to capture trustworthy cross-modality correlations for final detection. Experimental evaluation on three benchmark datasets shows the approach outperforms existing knowledge-enhanced and multimodal baselines.

result.text: We propose LAMP: a layout-to-action multimodal program inducer that, given a UI/web screenshot and a natural-language instruction, jointly predicts HTML/CSS code and an executable interaction program whose actions (e.g., click, type, scroll) are grounded to the predicted DOM via selectors, enabling end-to-end automation and accessibility. LAMP builds on screenshot-to-HTML pretraining and instruction-tuned web-to-code for faithful code synthesis, augments with an instruction-aware visual querying module and a focus-conditioned pathway to localize task-relevant regions, and trains with render-and-compare consistency plus script-execution feedback. Structurally, it first predicts a coarse region-level layout skeleton before completing HTML-like DSL code, then compiles action primitives against the induced DOM. We hypothesize this yields stronger generalization and robustness on multi-step UI tasks than vision-only or code-only baselines.

result.text: The paper tackles grounding high-level natural-language goals (e.g., “make breakfast”) into concrete, admissible actions for embodied agents without task-specific training. The key insight is that sufficiently large pre-trained language models already encode useful procedural knowledge and—when prompted correctly—can decompose goals into mid-level plans zero-shot, but their outputs often do not align exactly with an environment’s action space. result.text: The paper tackles poor cross-domain generalization of CLIP fine-tuning methods on fine-grained tasks, attributing failures to prior prompt-learning approaches that only inject global image features into prompts and thus miss transferable visual concepts like color, shape, and size. Its key insight is that explicitly modeling and transferring multi-level visual concepts into the textual prompt space yields stronger alignment between vision and language and improves generalization across domains. The proposed Concept-Guided Prompt Learning (CPL) builds a visual concept cache from pretrained CLIP features and uses a learned projector to transform multi-level visual features into text-feature-like embeddings that guide prompt generation, producing concept-aware prompts that enhance visual–linguistic consistency. Experiments show CPL substantially outperforms state-of-the-art prompt tuning methods on generalization benchmarks, especially for fine-grained datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of translating wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) into clinically useful electrocardiography (ECG) for continuous, low-cost cardiac monitoring, where standard diffusion models struggle to capture fine-grained ECG temporal features. The key insight is that indiscriminate noise injection across an entire signal hinders modeling of critical ECG regions (e.g., QRS complexes), so selectively treating regions of interest (ROI) during the forward and reverse diffusion processes can disentangle and preserve diagnostically important structure. They propose the Region-Disentangled Diffusion Model (RDDM), which applies targeted noise addition to ROIs in the forward process and performs separated denoising for ROI and non-ROI regions in the reverse steps, enabling high-fidelity PPG-to-ECG translation in as few as 10 diffusion steps. To validate clinical utility, they introduce CardioBench, a comprehensive benchmark of cardiac tasks, and show RDDM achieves state-of-the-art performance across heart rate and blood pressure estimation, stress classification, and detection of atrial fibrillation and diabetes.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of performing Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) adaptively in real time for implicit simulation models that lack tractable likelihoods, where traditional BOED is too computationally expensive to run during experiments. The key insight is to amortize experiment-time cost by training a design policy network offline that learns to map current data and context to near-optimal next-design decisions, enabling millisecond-scale deployment without requiring closed-form likelihoods or conditional independence. The method, called implicit Deep Adaptive Design (iDAD), trains the policy on simulated differentiable samples from the model using objectives that capture expected information gain (or related utilities) and then applies the learned policy online to select experimental settings rapidly. Empirical results demonstrate that iDAD yields fast, effective adaptive designs across multiple tasks, extending policy-based BOED to a much broader class of implicit models.

Its key insight is that existing studies—limited to short-term, single-population data—cannot reliably assess how models generalize across different users and years, so a large, diverse, multi-year dataset is essential to benchmark and drive progress. The authors introduce GLOBEM, the first multi-year passive sensing collection spanning over 700 user-years from 497 individuals with mobile and wearable sensor streams and rich well-being labels, and they demonstrate its use by benchmarking 18 depression detection and domain-generalization algorithms. result.text: The paper addresses the vulnerability of deep neural networks to backdoor attacks, where a small number of poisoned training samples cause malicious behavior only when a trigger is present. The key insight is that end-to-end supervised training causes poisoned samples to cluster in feature space, so decoupling representation learning from label-driven fitting can reduce this clustering and mitigate backdoors. The proposed method trains the backbone with self-supervised learning (ignoring labels) to obtain robust feature representations, then freezes the backbone and trains the classifier head on labeled data, and finally identifies low-credibility samples (likely poisoned), removes their labels, and performs semi-supervised fine-tuning of the whole model. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show this three-stage decoupling substantially reduces backdoor effectiveness while maintaining high benign accuracy.

result.text: CoDet tackles the challenge of obtaining reliable region-word alignments from image-caption pairs for open-vocabulary object detection, avoiding reliance on pre-aligned vision-language models that can mislocalize or fail to generalize. The key insight is to reframe alignment as a co-occurring object discovery task: images whose captions mention the same concept will contain objects of that concept that repeatedly co-occur across the image group, so discovering visually similar regions across such groups yields robust region-word correspondences. Methodologically, CoDet groups images by shared caption concepts, mines visually similar regions across each group to identify co-occurring objects, and aligns these discovered regions with the concept to train an object detector; this approach scales effectively with larger backbones and achieves state-of-the-art open-vocabulary detection performance on benchmarks like OV-LVIS.

result.text: The paper addresses single-image illumination estimation for realistic 3D rendering, noting that prior methods either regress low-level light parameters or generate full illumination maps that are hard to optimize and often inaccurate. Its key insight is to decompose illumination into a spherical light distribution, light intensity, and an ambient term, and to supervise distribution regression with a novel spherical mover’s loss—inspired by Earth Mover’s Distance—that better captures the geometry and subtleties of distributions on the sphere. Methodologically, EMLight trains a regression network to predict the three illumination components and uses a neural projector guided by the predicted spherical distribution, intensity, and ambient term to synthesize panoramic illumination maps with realistic frequency content, yielding more accurate estimates and higher-fidelity relighting than prior approaches.

The paper addresses how to design decision policies and counterfactual explanations when individuals can strategically change features in response to explanations to improve their chances of favorable decisions. The key insight is that while optimizing explanations for a given policy is NP-hard, the utility objective is nondecreasing and submodular (and the joint policy-plus-explanations objective is a non-monotone submodular maximization), which enables efficient approximation via greedy and recent randomized algorithms with provable guarantees. The authors therefore cast explanation selection as a submodular optimization problem, apply a greedy algorithm for the constrained (monotone) case and a randomized algorithm for the joint (non-monotone) case, and introduce matroid constraints to promote diversity of explanations across the population. Experiments on synthetic and real lending and credit-card datasets confirm that their algorithms produce explanation sets and policies that yield higher utility than several baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of multi-source-free domain adaptation (MSFDA), namely how to estimate the importance (contribution) of multiple pretrained source models when adapting to an unlabeled target domain without access to source data. The key insight is a Bayesian framing that links the posterior probability of a source model’s importance to two interpretable factors—discriminability (how well a source’s decision boundary fits the local target data habitat) and transferability (how similar a source’s data distribution is to the target)—and that jointly reasoning about both yields better importance estimates. The proposed method, Discriminability And Transferability Estimation (DATE), implements this by (1) a proxy discriminability perception module that measures per-sample habitat uncertainty and density to assess local discriminative fit, (2) a source-similarity transferability perception module that quantifies distributional similarity across domains and enforces reasonable importance allocation via a domain diversity loss, and (3) integration of these cues into a Bayesian importance estimate that can plug into popular SFDA backbones; experiments show DATE yields more accurate, objective source importance estimates and substantial adaptation gains.

args.text: We propose Parameter-Path Integrated Gradients (PPIG), a transfer attack that optimizes perturbations using an attribution signal integrated jointly over an input path (baseline→image) and a parameter path that traverses diverse surrogate instantiations. The parameter path is realized by sampling and interpolating models from a Bayesian posterior over weights or between mildly adversarially trained and standard sources, producing gradients that stay salient under plausible weight variations and hence generalize across architectures. We further reweight the joint attributions using layer-wise class-separability estimates to emphasize later, model-specific features for targeted transfer, and embed the procedure in a lightweight meta-augmentation loop to avoid overfitting to any single surrogate. This unifies path-based attributions with model diversity and task-aware layer weighting, predicting state-of-the-art targeted transferability with only a small constant-factor increase in backward passes over single-model IG-based methods.

result.text: The paper addresses improving Pareto Front Learning (PFL) for multi-objective optimization, noting that existing PFL methods treat each preference independently and thus fail to capture relationships among solutions, degrading Pareto front quality. The key insight is that generating and optimizing multiple diverse solutions jointly via a hypernetwork allows exploiting inter-solution relationships and directly maximizes a population-level quality measure (the Hypervolume indicator) rather than optimizing solutions in isolation. The proposed method, PHN-HVI, uses a hypernetwork conditioned on trade-off vectors to produce multiple candidate solutions per optimization step and trains it to maximize the Hypervolume of that solution set (HVI), thereby encouraging diversity and Pareto-optimality; experiments on several MOO tasks show substantial improvements over baselines.

The key insight is that learning a small number of latent “anchor” points for the source and target distributions and constraining transport to flow through those anchors both regularizes the rank of the transport map and exposes interpretable local structure. The authors develop an end-to-end system that quantizes device-held values, samples and adds discrete Gaussian noise on-device, and uses secure aggregation to reveal only the noisy sum, accompanied by a novel privacy analysis for sums of discrete Gaussians and a study of quantization and modulus choices. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning N:M structured sparsity masks from scratch for fast inference on modern hardware while preserving accuracy when using adaptive optimizers like Adam, which currently suffer notable accuracy drops compared to non-adaptive optimizers. The key insight is that Adam’s poor performance in this setting stems from unreliable second-moment (variance) estimates caused by masked weights, so stable mask learning requires explicitly accounting for variance estimation. The method, called STEP, splits training into two phases: a precondition phase that computes a reliable, fixed variance estimate by dynamically sampling variance changes and testing concentration, followed by a mask-learning phase that uses that fixed variance as a preconditioner to guide N:M mask updates; empirically STEP reduces accuracy degradation and is robust across CIFAR, translation, and LLM fine-tuning tasks.

We propose a check-in–amplified sketched matrix-mechanism for user-level private federated learning under secure aggregation that jointly designs compression, participation, and noise across rounds. Each participating client transmits a few integer-valued random projections of its clipped update (via sparse CountSketch/JL) plus calibrated Skellam noise, and the server only observes modular sums; across rounds, the projection matrices are co-designed as a banded lower-triangular factorization (matrix mechanism) so their aggregate approaches an information-optimal measurement of the updates under a fixed bit budget. Independent client check-ins and subsampled coordinates yield privacy amplification, enabling smaller per-round noise, while the total sketch dimension and quantization are chosen to meet near-tight distributed-DP communication lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We provide analysis and algorithms that make the measurement design robust to random participation, giving end-to-end RDP/DP guarantees and showing improved error-vs-bits compared to per-round fixed sketches or DP-SGD without coordinated measurement design.

result.text: The paper tackles the storage and transmission burden of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) for large language models, where methods like LoRA still require substantial per-task parameter checkpoints. result.text: Existing hybrid table-and-text QA either fuses evidence statically or reranks text dynamically, but they do not condition retrieval on the evolving tabular state or unify table execution with step-wise evidence selection. We propose a state-conditioned fusion RAG for tabular reasoning that, at each program step, executes the partial plan to materialize an intermediate table and then reranks both textual passages and candidate table slices; the top items are packed into a fused block for the reader. Concretely, we combine a Chain-of-Table or SQL executor to maintain state, a DyRRen-style step-wise reranker conditioned on the current program and intermediate table, an OTT-QA–style fused reader with BigBird attention, and a CABINET-like relevance weighting to suppress distractors, trained end-to-end with execution and retrieval supervision. This should improve multi-hop numerical reasoning in FinQA and open-domain settings like OTT-QA and OpenTab, and we will also test on Text2Analysis-style ambiguous analytical tasks to show robustness.

result.text: The paper addresses the underutilization of unchosen experts in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, noting that simply activating more experts can degrade output and that different routing strategies produce substantially different, non-synergistic outputs. result.text: The paper tackles scalable Bayesian inverse reinforcement learning, aiming to infer a posterior over latent reward functions without relying on costly inner-loop MDP solvers or environment interaction, which limits prior Bayesian IRL to small tabular problems and makes non-Bayesian scalable methods unsafe for high-stakes offline settings. Its key insight is to cast reward inference as a variational latent-variable problem that jointly learns an approximate posterior over rewards and a corresponding policy, enabling Bayesian reasoning about rewards while avoiding repeated planning or online rollouts. The method, Approximate Variational Reward Imitation Learning (AVRIL), optimizes a variational objective offline by parameterizing a posterior over rewards and a policy and training them together to maximize a surrogate ELBO that balances reward likelihood under demonstrations with regularization, allowing application to large or continuous state spaces. Empirically, AVRIL demonstrates Bayesian reward inference and competitive imitation performance on control tasks and real medical data where prior Bayesian IRL methods do not scale.

args.text: We propose Motion-Token Planning for cross-embodiment policy-as-video agents: factor video into a high-quality content frame and a compact, robot-agnostic motion latent, then perform language-conditioned planning directly in the motion-token space rather than pixels. A content–motion video autoencoder is pretrained on web-scale human/robot videos; a planner generates and scores motion-token trajectories (via value models over reconstructed rollouts), while lightweight, per-robot decoders map motion tokens to executable controls using small labeled datasets augmented with dense correspondence supervision to align human and robot motions. This decoupling reduces compute and improves long-horizon coherence, and the embodiment-invariant motion tokens enable efficient transfer from human demonstrations to diverse robot morphologies. The approach can drop into existing video-planning pipelines, replacing pixel-level tree search with motion-latent search for faster and more reliable manipulation planning.

We propose Budgeted Policy-Guided Order-Dynamic Multimodal Mamba (BP-ODMM), an RGBT tracker that learns a per-frame scheduling policy to allocate compute by controlling Mamba scan order, depth, and modality gating at token/region granularity. The policy conditions on per-modality uncertainty estimates and predicted challenge attributes to decide which tokens to process first, which to skip or downsample, which attribute-specialized fusion branch to route through, and when to trigger online template refresh versus relying on a long-term template. Built atop Order-dynamic Fusion Mamba, we expose discrete actions (scan segmenting, cross-modal gate scaling, template update triggers) and train the scheduler with budgeted reinforcement learning to maximize IoU under a FLOP cap. We hypothesize this policy-guided scheduling yields stronger robustness to occlusion/illumination changes and a superior accuracy–efficiency Pareto front compared to fixed or heuristic ordering.

result.text: Drift-Responsive Equal Shares (DRES): We propose a streaming participatory budgeting rule for nonstationary or even adversarial arrivals that maintains per-voter pacing but updates them via mirror-descent on a convex surrogate of worst-case group proportional deficit over sliding windows, with buyback-style slack tracked by stable price certificates. DRES funds a project when paced contributions clear cost and sets personalized Lindahl-like prices consistent with balanced stable priceability; it guarantees windowed PJR and EJR-up-to-one for every length-W prefix and sliding window under bounded variation of the arrival process, and attains O(sqrt(T)) group-deficit regret against the best static Equal Shares benchmark in hindsight. By leveraging strengthened, satisfaction-agnostic priceability, the same updates simultaneously protect proportionality under both cardinal-by-cost and cardinal-by-count utilities while remaining polynomial per arrival. This extends Equal Shares and pacing-based online equilibrium ideas beyond stationarity, providing robust proportionality with graceful degradation under drift.
