result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of sample-efficient reinforcement learning in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), where standard hardness results imply learning can be statistically intractable because the agent never directly observes latent states. Its key insight is that many practical problems admit "hindsight observability," meaning the latent state can be revealed or computed after the fact during training, and this additional retrospective information can be leveraged to bypass the usual hardness. Building on that, the authors define the Hindsight Observable MDP (HOMDP) formalism and develop new algorithms for both tabular and function-approximation settings that use hindsight state labels during training to achieve polynomial sample complexity even for POMDPs that are otherwise hard; they also prove a matching lower bound showing the tabular algorithm’s dependence on latent-state and observation cardinalities is optimal.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem that standard fairness-aware machine learning methods lose their guarantees when the deployment population differs from the training data (demographic shift), so models that appear fair during training can behave unfairly in practice. The key insight is that one can design algorithms that provide high-confidence, distribution-robust behavioral guarantees by explicitly accounting for possible changes in subgroup prevalences even when no labeled deployment data are available. The authors introduce “Shifty” algorithms that construct fairness constraints and confidence bounds over a class of plausible demographic shifts and optimize models subject to those robust constraints, and they validate this approach on the UCI Adult dataset and a university-exam dataset, showing Shifty maintains fairness under shift while prior methods fail.

result.text: Barycenter-Guided Multiscale Graph Diffusion (BMGD): a conditional graph generator that steers denoising toward class- or attribute-specific FGW barycentric templates computed hierarchically. We first derive HOT-based hierarchical FGW barycenters that summarize recurring substructures; during denoising (via endpoint-conditioned mixtures or discrete edge-removal), we add a control signal from the differentiable FGW coupling between the current sample and the selected (sub-)barycenter to bias edge additions/removals and feature updates toward the target topology. For scalability to large graphs, we use localized diffusion-based expansion that, for each growing region, selects a matching sub-barycenter and aligns only locally, yielding subquadratic costs and better size extrapolation. Optionally, a hyperbolic latent parameterization encodes hierarchical depth in the radial coordinate while barycenters provide lateral motif guidance, improving preservation of degree distributions, hierarchy, and clustering.

result.text: The paper addresses how to connect multicalibration—ensuring predictions are well-calibrated across many subgroups—with boosting for squared-error regression, aiming to achieve Bayes-optimal predictions without strong realizability assumptions. The key insight is a characterization of multicalibration as a "swap-regret"-type condition on squared error, which lets one turn any standard squared-error regression oracle for a class H into a simple iterative procedure that both boosts weak regressors and enforces multicalibration. Their method runs an exceedingly simple algorithm that repeatedly fits residuals (using the regression oracle) and updates predictions; under a weak learning condition on H (necessary and sufficient) this procedure converges agnostically to the Bayes-optimal predictor and yields multicalibration for H (and, under a relative weak-learning relation, for other classes C), with empirical results and open-source code provided.

result.text: The paper addresses how to control language model generation to optimize desired rewards by casting alignment as a tokenwise KL-regularized reinforcement learning objective. Its key insight is that control can be modularized: a separately trained prefix scorer that estimates a value function can guide a frozen base model at inference to provably sample from the RL solution, enabling post-hoc control without retraining the generator. The method trains this prefix scorer on rewards and uses it during decoding to bias token selection (including blockwise decoding), supports combining multiple prefix scorers for multi-objective control, and transfers to unseen base models without additional tuning. Empirically, this controlled decoding approach matches RL-style control on benchmarks while offering flexibility, composability, and efficiency compared to retraining-based methods.

result.text: The paper addresses Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) under realistic, dynamic domain shifts where target domains recur with varying frequencies and short, unpredictable durations—conditions in which existing methods that adapt the same model parameters struggle with slow convergence, forgetting, or wrong reuse of past adaptations. The key insight is that maintaining a compact, editable set of domain-specific visual prompts (a "prompt coreset") and selectively updating or reusing them based on similarity lets the model quickly align to brief revisits while preserving past knowledge without retraining full parameters. DPCore implements this by combining visual prompt adaptation for lightweight alignment, a prompt coreset that stores representative prompts for past domains to prevent forgetting, and a dynamic update mechanism that edits close prompts or adds new ones when incoming domains differ substantially; this yields state-of-the-art CTTA performance across benchmarks while cutting trainable parameters by 99% and compute by 64%.

args.text: We propose quantile-adaptive delayed SSP, addressing stochastic shortest path with unknown transitions and adversarially varying per-episode costs when trajectory and cost feedback arrive after random, heavy-tailed delays. The algorithm couples optimistic transition estimation with a delayed credit-queue, but schedules occupancy-measure mirror-descent updates using per-(state,action) delay quantiles and a principled skipping rule for super-quantile feedback, borrowing quantile bookkeeping from delayed bandits to keep variance controlled without paying for the full delay mass. Analytically, this yields regret that matches delay-free SSP rates up to additive terms scaling with chosen delay quantiles rather than total delay (giving strict gains under heavy tails), with full-information and bandit-feedback variants and a best-of-both-worlds switch to exploit i.i.d. costs. This framework unifies optimistic SSP learning with quantile-aware delay handling and skipping, advancing beyond bounds that depend on aggregate delay.

result.text: Krylov-ICL: implement conjugate-gradient-style in-context learning in a looped, weight-shared transformer that incrementally builds a small orthogonal basis of task-specific directions across recurrent passes. Each pass computes residuals for the current predictor on the prompt, uses attention plus fast-weight delta-rule updates to store and orthogonalize a new direction, and updates predictions by projecting queries into the learned Krylov subspace, yielding condition-number-robust convergence with few iterations. Compared to depth-based Newton-like ICL, looping decouples compute from parameters and enables budget-adaptive halting; compared to preconditioned-GD linear attention, the explicit basis memory targets ill-conditioned and noisy regimes with stronger sample efficiency. Evaluate on linear and kernel regression and long-context streaming settings, measuring error vs iterations and examining learned bases.

result.text: The paper tackles the limitation of unsupervised Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) in capturing global structural and semantic relationships among nodes that are not locally proximate, which harms the quality of learned node representations. The key insight is that explicit structural and semantic contrastive objectives can inject global graph knowledge into representations even when using a much simpler encoder than a graph neural network. To realize this, the authors propose S^3-CL, a framework that pairs a lightweight neural network encoder with two contrastive schemes—structural contrast to align nodes with similar global topological roles and semantic contrast to group nodes with similar attributes or semantics—so that the learned embeddings preserve both structural and semantic global patterns; experiments show S^3-CL outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised GCL methods on various downstream tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses Graph Domain Adaptation (GDA), where graph-structured training and testing data differ, causing shifts in node features, labels, and especially graph connectivity that break usual graph-based label inference. Its key insight is that adapting pairwise relationships—by reweighting edges to correct conditional structure shift (how neighbor labels relate given node features) and reweighting label losses to correct label shift—directly mitigates the core causes of poor generalization across graphs. The proposed method, Pairwise Alignment (Pair-Align), computes edge weights to recalibrate neighbor influence and label weights to adjust classification loss, yielding a theoretically principled scheme to align conditional structure and label distributions across domains. Empirically, Pair-Align outperforms baselines on synthetic and real benchmarks, including a new large GDA dataset for region-shifted social networks and a particle collision pileup mitigation task.

result.text: Megaverse tackles the bottleneck of slow, resource-limited 3D embodied simulation for reinforcement learning by providing an extremely high-throughput engine that can run physics-based, egocentric, fully-shaded scenes at over one million actions per second on a single 8‑GPU node. The key insight is that batching many simulator instances and executing physics, rendering, and interaction logic on GPUs unlocks massive parallelism and amortizes overheads, yielding up to 70× speedups over prior platforms like DeepMind Lab while still supporting complex interactive objects and multi-agent scenarios. Methodologically, the authors build a GPU-centric simulator that performs batched physics and rendering pipelines, design a diverse benchmark of single- and multi-agent cognitive tasks, and validate the platform by running model-free RL baselines to demonstrate feasibility and provide open-source tools and data for future research.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of answering complex first-order logic queries over incomplete knowledge graphs, where existing neural embedding methods struggle to leverage broad world knowledge for robust logical reasoning. Its key insight is to harness large language models’ reasoning capabilities by decomposing arbitrary logical queries into binary-tree structures and using a curriculum that orders training from simpler to harder logical constructs so the model can progressively learn reasoning patterns. The proposed method, LACT, applies binary tree decomposition to generate instruction-style training data for LLMs and employs a logic-aware curriculum tuning strategy that schedules examples by difficulty, enabling the model to better generalize across diverse complex query types. Experiments on standard benchmarks show LACT yields substantial gains (about +5.5% MRR) over prior state-of-the-art approaches.

result.text: The paper tackles the scalability bottleneck of Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) methods, whose exact kernel computations are too expensive for large datasets and high-resolution images despite NTK’s strong predictive performance. The key insight is that NTK (and its convolutional CNTK) can be approximated accurately and efficiently by sketching the polynomial/arc‑cosine feature expansions and combining random features with leverage‑score sampling to preserve the kernel’s spectral properties. Concretely, the authors develop a near input‑sparsity–time sketch for the CNTK that maps an image in time linear in the number of pixels, and they prove spectral approximation bounds for the NTK matrix by applying randomized feature maps plus sketching; empirically, a linear regressor on these CNTK features matches exact CNTK accuracy on CIFAR‑10 while running roughly 150× faster.

result.text: ODTrack tackles the limitation of current visual trackers that rely on sparse, offline pairwise frame associations by enabling dense, online temporal reasoning across arbitrary-length video sequences. The key insight is to compress target discrimination and localization cues into compact token sequences that are iteratively propagated forward as contextual prompts, so past frame information directly guides inference on future frames without complex online update rules. Methodologically, ODTrack ingests consecutive frames, extracts and purifies localization tokens, propagates and associates those tokens across time in an online manner to build spatio-temporal trajectories, and uses the propagated tokens to condition per-frame inference, yielding efficient computation and improved representation. The approach achieves state-of-the-art results on seven benchmarks while running in real time.

result.text: KD-Zero addresses the problem that hand-designed knowledge distillation (KD) methods are often suboptimal across diverse teacher-student architecture pairs by automatically discovering tailored distillers. The key insight is that a generalized distiller can be decomposed into knowledge transformations, distance functions, and loss weights, and that evolutionary search guided by objectives measuring sharpness and representation gap can find better combinations than human-crafted designs. The method constructs a search space of advanced operations for those three components, evolves distiller populations via crossover and mutation while using efficiency strategies (loss-rejection, search-space shrinkage, and proxy settings) to speed search, and then applies the discovered distillers in final distillation to close capacity and cross-architecture gaps. Extensive experiments across classification, detection, and segmentation show KD-Zero consistently surpasses state-of-the-art KD methods and yields practical design insights.

result.text: The paper addresses the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) caused by fixed numbers of temporal timesteps, which can waste computation on easy inputs or underperform on hard ones. Its key insight is to treat the number of timesteps as an input-dependent variable and dynamically stop inference early for confident samples, thereby reducing redundant temporal processing without sacrificing accuracy. The method, called SEENN, implements this via two mechanisms: SEENN-I, which applies confidence-threshold early exits to terminate after few timesteps when predictions are reliable, and SEENN-II, which uses reinforcement learning to choose the timestep budget per sample; both approaches work with directly trained SNNs and ANN-to-SNN converted networks. Empirically, SEENN substantially lowers average timesteps at inference (e.g., ResNet-19 on CIFAR-10 achieves 96.1% accuracy with just ~1.08 timesteps) while preserving accuracy.
